[SPOILER FREE]
Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishment is a beautiful and impressive  adventure puzzle game starring a very popular detective  who players will enjoy playing as to solve crime and choosing  thier own choices in a case's outcome through deduction.
First off, the graphics of the game use the unreal engine 3 and a step up for the series.The facial features of the characters such as pores, scars, and even the detail on the clothing.  Not only is the character  detailed but so are the aesthetics and details put into each of the maps that the players will traverse to solve crimes, which gives it a it more immersion.
The music is appropriate for the game and kicks in at the right moment though the rest of the time the game is pretty quiet to letting concentrate and could use more to bring immersion. The voice acting is also decently done for most of the characters in the game and brings them to life in the game world.
Players can  play the game with either a keyboard and mouse or with a game pad. Both are configured well and didn't include key binding, which isn't too bad since there aren't many keys to press for this type  of game genre. Players be able to play this game in first or 3rd person whichever choice you decide.  The controls may feel a bit stiff but overall it is not too bad at all.
Each of the maps in this game is really focused on the area where the crime appears. You won't find yourself in unnecessary places or free roaming since it isn't that sort of game though it is something to suggest for a future sequel. The game uses a fast travel system to travel around the map with a push of a button. With a button click, players can  bring up a map and click on locations to travel where they need to go whenever you want. With each loading screen, Sherlock in the cab where the interface can also be brought up for the  menu to look over the clues, evidence, and deduction while they wait. The menu itself is very sleek and organized.
The game play to Sherlock is to solve puzzles, gather evidence and to come up with deduction and solve crimes. The puzzles range from ordinary lock puzzles where you match locks to complicated puzzles where you rebuild molds, combine chemicals or find clues to fix certain situation, compare notes, Extreme arm wrestling and lots more variety to keep the game intriguing. There is a skip function for those that get frustrated or stuck at a puzzle but keep in mind that it is a puzzle game, and that self-satisfaction comes from solving by oneself.
Sherlock is armed with an arsenal of tools to help him combine clues and solve puzzles. Focus will help him see things that he will miss at times such as small marks and such. Imagination is  when he gathers enough clues to solve a puzzle, he will be able to recreate the scenario in his mind to gather more clues and evidence and finally when he does get all this, he will be capable to go into deduction.
In deduction mode, Sherlock can look over his facts and evidence, draw a line between them and form bubbles and by doing so created deductions. Sometimes there is only one deduction in a bubble but other times. There will be two totals. As players look through all these bubbles, they'll be able to draw and combine a conclusion to the case. If the case is a contradiction, it will tell you between the bubbles. If it combines there will be a larger bubble and there will be a choice to the entire  scenario. Either the person is guilty/innocent or an alternative choice route opened will be up to players to decide by finding enough clues and evidence.
The game introduces five case scenario total and may take a player 12-15 hours total to complete depending on how good they are at gathering clues and puzzles.
My opinion is that this is possibly the best puzzle/adventure game I have yet played. I enjoyed it though some of my cons are that the disguise function wasn't used as greatly as I thought and that the game hopefully will be even frequently more expansive with the deduction system in the future because that felt like the real meat of the game to me personally.
+ The graphic details are beautiful. You can see the details of the faces of characters, clothes, and the aesthetic to the background looks great with the Unreal 3 engine.
+ The puzzles are brilliant
+ The case themselves are very realistic  in a sense
+ Brilliant story and cases. Especially the third case Blood Bath.
+ The voice acting is decently done. Most of the characters sounded great.
+ Deduction offers the players choices and replayability. Multiple choices on how to punish a crime or finish it off with another outcome.
+ Game lasts 12-15 hours
- Though beautiful the maps were decently sized and it felt too closed in especially with parts blocked off. Hopefully we'll see even larger areas in the future.
- Disguises weren't used as much in the game
- There is a skip button that pops up everytime that just seems to invite players to push it. Should be something you can turn off
- The online feature should take in more stats instead of just who chooses the choice or discovering it.

The Nightmare Cooperative is an interesting turn based strategy Rogue-like / lite. It features a whimsical cartoony visual style, with cerebral gameplay mechanics. The game also has an enjoyable class based system, where you can gain allies who have their own special trait that you can exploit in order to progress through the game.
The Nightmare Cooperative has some pretty strong mechanics, but it is a little light on features. You're getting the game's campaign mode and that's about it. there's no multiplayer, hardcore mode, or any other game modes to try. It's all about the base game, and collecting things to fill your collection.
Overall, the Nightmare Cooperative is an interesting game that should serve well as a fun distraction from the main games you're currently playing.

I'm almost done with the second chapter of Cognition and I wanted to write a quick positive review before I forget.
I don't know why it took me so long to "get into" this game after I bought it, but finally I forced myself to give it a whirl (after one abbreviated initial attempt).  It's been totally worth it.  One of the most engaging story-themed games I've played in a long time.
Yes, there are some flaws.  Some dialogue is a bit silly.  And while some of the obstacles in Agent Reed's way are typical of an adventure game, those same obstacles seem convoluted for a story that's supposed to be more realistic.  (In just one example, Agent Reed has to pick the exact type of snacks an interviewee craves before he can be interrogated. This is a guy who is homeless, by the way, presumably hungry, and who supposedly wants to help avenge his dead wife by providing info.)
But if you're willing to go with some of the silliness of the story, and buy into a lot of storytelling tropes (Agent Reed's superiors barely stop short of ordering her to turn in her badge at certain points, Reed never calls for backup, etc) then you'll get pulled in.  It definitely has that Jane Jensen feel--that lady who is most famous for creating Gabriel Knight, and who is here credited as a story consultant.
Most of the voice acting is very good, including, thankfully, the lead actress playing Erica Reed.  Others have noted some sketchy graphics quality.  Well let me tell you, while the in-game animations are a little awkward/robotic (they're "good enough"), the stylish, comic-book-panel like cut-scenes more than make up for them.  VERY polished and effective, the art style in those instances.
I'm scratching my head a bit as to why Adventure Gamers' reviews of Cognition seemed so critical at times.  (Again, I'm only finishing the second chapter now, but I thought it was just as fun as the first.  AG gave it a pretty negative review, by contrast.)  I can only assume that their harshness was partially due to the fact that they were waiting around for the chapters to be individually released.  (I bought the "game of the year" edition, and can play it all at once).  They probably were more critical of any flaws as they saw each chapter as a singular experience instead of just part of the whole experience one gets when they buy all chapters together.
Even though I'm only now getting around to playing Cognition, the game is already a couple years old.  If Phoenix Online Studios ever wants to make a sequel season (or even crowdfund one), I'm definitely on board.
***
Update:  I finished the second chapter, and frankly, it's stronger than the first one.  I'm not sure what Adventure Gamers was thinking with their rating for it.  I feel like they got hung up on some nitpicky things (like maybe how cartoony the new field director character was) so that they overlooked how much tighter this chapter was compared to the first one.
Also, the final puzzle in Chapter 2 (The Wise Monkey) was downright brilliant.  Hilariously over-the-top-twisted, yes, but brilliant.  If you enjoyed the involved nature of the Regression/Interrogation puzzle in the first chapter, then you'll really appreciate Chapter 2's final puzzle when Reed has to use her new "Synergy" power on, well, a bunch of body parts.  It's like a crazy twist on the old Adventure Game Inventory puzzle, with a dash of Jeffrey Dahmer.
Update #2:  I'm well into Chapter three now, and I can honestly say, this is one of the most clever games I've ever played.  The best I can describe the game at this point is "META."
The game is getting crazy with the way the plot is referencing itself like some kind of mobius strip.  Here in chapter three we have a case of TWO people with psionic powers--one who can see the future, the other the past.  And with them both being psions, they can mentally interact with each other across two different time periods, both viewing the same environment with different eyes, and both inadvertently planting ideas in the other's head with their observations.
If it sounds crazy and convoluted, it is.  It's starting to resemble a hall of carnival mirrors at this point, and I love it.
Additionally, the game lets you reflect on the events of the first two chapters from a whole new angle.  In the first two chapters Erica Reed found scrapbook notes and dossiers (of potential victims) meticulously made by the serial killers she was after.
What's funny about Chapter three is, Erica discovers a dossier made by the mystery person hinted at in the first two chapters.  This mystery person is a sort of serial killer of other serial killers.  And here we get descriptions of THIS person's encounters and plans on how to target the original killers.
As I say, meta.
***
Update #3:  I'm writing this update for the second time, having just finished Chapter four, and thus the whole game.  I originally complained that Cognition's final chapter didn't quite "stick the landing" perfectly.  (There are definitely pacing issues; it feels like the story hits a wall immediately after the breathless cliffhanger of Chapter 3.)  Having considered things further, my thinking on it now is, "But it was close enough."
Seriously.  This chapter turns the tawdriness and melodroma of the previous chapters up to 11.  And that's either a good or bad thing depending on your point of view.  Whatever it is, it's certainly "Cognition."  And as I said in my original conclusion:  "At least I can appreciate that when a train does go off the tracks, it's only because the people running it aren't afraid to go full steam ahead."
Does the origin of the Cain killer (and his dynamic with Cordelia) feel 100% organic?  No.  But as I continued playing, I eventually accepted it--until finally after the story's balls-out conclusion, I was able to appreciate what they were going for.  ("You'll be an angel among those who are like us."  Damn.)
Heck, I even liked the final "fight sequence" between Erica and the bad guy.  "Action" sequences are usually something adventure gamers avoid like the plague, but I thought this was creative as hell, showing the fight through comic book panels.
Concluding thoughts:  That's it.  It was a heck of a ride.  44 hours on record.  (Give me a break, I never used a hint guide.)  I give Cognition 4 out of 5 stars.  The Adventure Gamers reviewer must've been on crack.  And I'm ready to help back season two of Erica Reed, just say the word.

Krosmaga is a different kind of cardgame than others I have played.
The lively board and animation for the charecters is definately this game's strongest draw. And if you are familiar with Ankama's charecters you will enjoy recognising and playing with the charecters that you know and love.
Most of the charecter designs are really good,
I enjoy how you earn experience points for your Infinite rarity cards, so even if you lose a match it doesnt feel completely wasted if you got some exp for your cards.
There are tons of fun comboes to pull of in this game with the variety of cards, some obvious like a certain creature type that works well with others of its kind, some more subtle.
The premise is good, and the different mechanics to the different gods makes sure that you can find a playstyle that suits you.
Now the gripes.
Like any free game Krosmaga is pretty much pay to win, most Gods have certain cards that are so objectively good that your decks will be very inferior if you don't have them.
Many other cards can only be unlocked through leveling up your Infinite cards to a very highest levels, and those cards will are incredibly powerful and can usually turn the tide of a game to your favor or end it right then and there. And this is the ONLY way to get these cards.
Its a fun idea with lore and alternative versions of the card being unlocked as they level up, but keeping those cards that ensure your victory out of anyone who doesn't either pay or spend thousands upon thousands of hours is simply unfair game design.
Balancing is still an issue, there are tons of cards that are both overpowered or underpowered, and some Gods get the lions share of good cards. They are still updating and working on balance issues though, so I hope they will make the Gods equally matched.
Sometimes its not clear what order even't will take place in. Unlike in for example Magic The Gathering if a card deals 2 damage to all creatures, all creatures wont take damage and/or die as a cause simultaniusly, and it seems impossible to predict if an event caused by the death of a creature will happen before or after others take damage and/or die. This needs to be made clear for the players n a way.
The biggest gripe though, is how stingy Krosmaga is when it comes to giving gold. You get no gold for losing a match, which isnt too bad BUT you only get 5 gold for winning. And when the packs you want cost 100 or 300 gold each, and only yield 5 cards each, the progress can feel painfully slow.
TLDR: Its an interresting game to play, and very pretty, with fun designs, and cute animations for the Gods. The mechanics are interresting and the combo's are plentiful. But the progress is very slow unless you pay and there are problems with balancing between gods, and sometimes clearity about the chain of events.
I recommend everyone to try it though, because the game has charm.

As someone who has grown up playing JRPGs my entire life (specifically the Lunar series on Sega CD and the Shining Force series on Sega Genesis, as well as several others, all of which rank in my top favorite games), I was excited to see the numerous JRPGs on Steam.  Then I stumbled across The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky.  After checking it out a bit, I decided to get it and see what it was like.  What I found amazed me.  I found a game that had just about everything that I could have asked for in a game of this genre.  I felt invested in the story from the start, something that many games try to accomplish, but fail.  I discovered a cast of eight like able and relatable main characters, along with a good many well-done supporting characters, expansive towns that were filled with NPCs that had unique and diverse dialogues, and a game that takes well over 50 hours to beat.  The soundtrack is amazing:  I did not hear a single track during the game that I did not like or that I did not think was appropriate for the circumstances.  The humor is well done, and dispersed widely enough that I did not feel that it was coming too quickly, but I was still left with a smile on my face for most of the game.  The graphics are a little dated, but since I prefer a compelling story over good graphics, I was able to overlook that, and despite the fact that they are dated, they still look really good.  The combat runs smoothly, without dragging on like it is liable to do in some games.  All in all, I would highly recommend this game to any fan of the JRPGS genre, and I know that I will definitely return to this game for many years.

The whole game is about music, commerce, everyone wanting to join the circus, and cow skulls that have magical properties.
To no surprise the game ends with me demanding my brain to come up with the answer as to what the hell I just played and its meaning. In response my brain said to me 'let’s try something easier like the meaning of life and then let’s look at this game'.
On my second play through I just gave up entirely looking for a meaning. Instead i got high on some marijuana cookies, went down to the train station and got my groove on in a dance battle with a train attendant and stared for 20 minutes at a cow wandering what life would be like as a computer generated cow.
The overall objective of this game is to find parts of a train ticket scattered around a train station which has been dedicated to art and music commerce. From there you will learn stories about the attendants which revolve around making money and those who make money off of those who make money. What the developers actual statement to us all here was completely lost on me. The fact that the game ended in nothing more than a vague question mark isn't a bad thing thanks to an incredibly rich detail of art work and a groovy repertoire of funky music.
In a nutshell a single developer which sends us on a 45 minute art acid trip to contemplate 'stuff'. What stuff are we supposed to contemplate is a 'question mark'? The relaunch of The Secret World as Secret World Legends fixed up my biggest complaint with the old game, while introducing several new problems that were absent from the original game.
The combat in TSW was dull, but it existed in a world rich with lore and presented in such an interesting manner I played anyway. For awhile, until the boring grindy combat was too much. Thankfully, the combat in SWL has been revamped and streamlined. No longer are you just hitting 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 4 in combat, it takes a bit of inspiration from third person action games. Your mouse now aims the camera, and you need to have a target when you use an ability. There is no autolock on or cycling through targets with the tab key, you point at the enemy you want to hit and fire off your attack. I prefer this, as it adds movement to the combat.
You can only equip a six abilities between your two weapons, similar Guild Wars. These map to Q, 1, 2, E, and both mouse buttons by default. You will have different builds even while using the same weapons depending on fights. Changing the abilities from just being on the number bar to being on the mouse and keyboard helps to spice the combat up from just hitting 1, 2, 3, or 4.
The world is still presented in much the same manner, but quests have been streamlined to prevent you from needing access to multiple zones. When you pick up a quest, about 90% of them will have all the objectives in that same zone. No more needing to globe trot to finish one quest. This makes the hub cities less important, as you will mostly only need to report back once after you finish a zone, rather than multiple times in each zone to increase your faction rank.
Many of the DLC issues have been folded into the main game already. Issues we had to pay for in TSW are unlocked for everyone in SWL. This aids in he flow of the storyline, as you will not have to go back to Egypt at max level to complete Last Train to Cairo, you just run through it as you are leveling normally in Egypt and it seems like a natural progression.
Some new problems creep up in SWL that were not present in TSW, so its not 100% better than its sister game (yes, TSW is still running, you just need to download it through Funcom's site, not through Steam). Crafting was a mess in TSW, and despite watching youtube videos I never understood it. It has been streamlined extremely here in SWL, you take two pieces of gear and fuse one into the other to raise its level. It functions like gacha does in mobile games. Much easier, however it does lend itself to some real grind. A side effect is that story dungeons no longer drop blue gear as they did in the past, they drop slightly better green gear that you upgrade yourself. It lessens the impact of getting cool drops in favor of grinding out trash loot to enhance your main gear.
They server caps have been lowered by an awful lot in this game. Outside of the Agartha travel hub, you will be hard pressed to run into other players in the same instance as yourself. This was done to help reduce lag when many people are gathered in the same place, and to preserve the atmosphere of you being a unique, powerful individual rather than just player #654,132 in zone #3. It does make the game feel a bit lonely, however, and people more used to traditional mmos might even assume the game is empty and dead when they run across only one other player in their zone.
The monetization is also awkward. There is an optional subscription fee to gain patron status, but then there are also lots of things that can only be unlocked via aurum (real money points) or keys bought with aurum. When I pay a subscription fee for a game, I don't want to continue to be nickel and dimed after already handing over 15$.
+ Great writing
+ Interesting storylines
+ Unique modern horror setting similar to World of Darkness
+ Fast combat that encourages movement
+ Streamlined questing
+ Creepy soundtrack
+ Boss mechanics vary, few tank and spank encounters
- Gacha gear grind
- Unimpressive loot drops
- Fewer players per zone might discourage some players
- Unclear monetization

He also likes fruit! Incredipede is straddled between the think a lot strategies of Briad and the sheer virutosity of Mario, it requires reflexes and brains and a little patience. I wish some of the levels had a little more explanation or gave you ideas on how to move your incredipede, because the solution is not always obvious and you might find yourself mashing buttons to get the right movement, but if you take a little time to figure it out, and a little luck comes your way it'll be alright. Cognition is a decent effort, but it has definite problems.
On the positive side, it has a fairly interesting story and a strong atmosphere.  Like many point-and-click adventure games, the graphics might be considered "primitive" by some, but they are well done and have a definite artistic style that is attractive.  Erica Reed's "cognition powers" are fairly fun and the puzzles generally strike a nice balance in difficulty.
On the negative side, the game is buggy.  I didn't come across any game-crashing bugs, but several things give this game a "less than polished" feel.  Animations, interactions with characters or objects, even trying to walk can be problematic and sloppy.  The inventory system is poor. The writing and dialogue have a flowery "fan fiction" style, which combined with the bugginess gives the game an amateur feel.
As a whole, I give a cautious recommendation to those who like adventure games, mysteries, or who dig the music or graphical style.  Those who are used to more polished games from established studios should look elsewhere.

The core of this game is excellent - deep and diverse digital CCG gameplay with lots of variety in strategies and classes. However, it has one enormous flaw that everyone going in should know about: many of the rare cards are objectively better than non-rare ones and top-tier decks are often built around these rare cards for that reason. This means that a new player without many of these rare cards is at a direct disadvantage against someone who does. Now the counterpoint to this is that every rare card can be made using a recycling currency and you can buy packs that will guarantee you at least one of a rare type (though it still gives duplicates). So obviously if you want to spend money you can catch up quickly. You can still catch up without paying anything, as the game is quite generous with in game currency through in game daily quests, and can probably earn enough to buy a gold card pack (the highest tier) in about a week's time.
Overall I still recommend the game because the core is solid but I wouldn't blame anyone for not wanting to put up with the frustration of losing against players with better cards. In my opinion new players should get some rare packs for free, like most mobile games do.

Ill keep it brief. I've been playing point and click adventures for as long as I've been gaming and I LOVE Cognition. I'm a big fan of the Gabriel Knight series and it sorta feels like getting some more of that (especially considering Jane Jensen's involvement). I casually played the first episode, but somewhere in episode two I got HOOKED and played non-stop until completion. I love that the puzzles pretty much always follow a logical progression. I'm not completely opposed to nonsene puzzles of some other games, but I liked that with proper use of my noodle, I could always deduce the solution.

SUMMARY:
Thrilling murder mystery point&click game with novel post-cognition mechanic. A great episodic adventure where each consecutive episode builds up on the mystery of preceeding chapters to the grand climax of the final episode. Game's presentation is pleasant, but lacks certain degree polish you'd expect from title having jane jensen's name attached to it.  Needlessly amateurish character models and animation. Enjoyable 20 hour trip despite minor flaws and glitches.
GOOD:
fairly well told mystery murder story with several twists along the way
interesting congnition mechanics, where puzzles are, at times, solved by observing past history or items/people
well acted voiceover.
nicely painted backgrounds
20-ish hours of gameplay for very acceptable price.
BAD:
Opening sequence can be off putting since it presumes you caring about the protagonists without prior familiarity.
Some puzzles lack a clear build-up, leaving player without any clues to pursue.
Occasionally buggy pathfining causes Erica to take her sweet time to walk where you point her to with you cursor.
Occasionally flaky animation where torso walks facing one direction, and legs face opposite direction (sand crab walk)
Bad mesh topology on character models. When erica turns her head, her neck twists into a knot resembling a wet gym towel being squeezed out. Facial animation occasionally causes stray polygons to pop out of characters' faces, making them look like creepy man-bots.

Personal Rating: Solid game, not recommended for casual players (like myself)
Classic Rating: ★★★☆☆
Strong Points:
✓ Exceptional Graphic Art, you can feel many hours spent in game developing: characters, backgrounds and cut scenes are very detailed and good-looking.
✓ Soundtrack: It's composed by two Volumes (as DLCs) and I only got the first one but it's been a pleasure listening to it even when I wasn't playing the game - absolutely no complaints.
Mixed Points:
✘ Inventory and Psion features: They are not easy to use and sometimes understand, on the contrary they get pretty messed-up. The complexity of game's puzzle probably demanded that but developers should have tried and found out a better compromise.
✘ Story and puzzles: The story is one of the strongest and weakest point of this game. Very, very deep, probably too deep. Aided by the fact that English isn't my primary language, it was very difficult to follow the story progress over each chapter.. it got each time more and more complicated and so did puzzles. Very often you are left without sufficient enough clues to solve them, that your only hope is trial and error. I got so frustrated playing the last chapter that I quit in the middle of it without completing the game.
So, it's basically what I said on top: this game has a lot of qualities and maybe you're going to fully enjoy it; however if you're not a "point and click" hard-core gamer but you still like this genre, I can't recommend to play "Cognition" - there are many more accessible and funner games than this one.

This game is fantastic!  The characters are memorable, late game strategy is fairly complex and there's no lack of challenge at higher levels.  I love the story, and I can't wait for the next installments.  If you enjoyed Xenosaga/Xenogears or some of the earlier final fantasy installments you're going to love this game.
Best features:
- Characters all play very differently.  The story gives you plenty of time to learn each character's strengths and weaknesses, and while you cannot control your party until the end of the game (for truly legitimate storyline reasons), once you have that control you can put together some really interesting dynamics for the end game.  Teamwork is important, and many characters have skills that allow them to function in multiple roles without breaking away from their overall archetype.
- Deep and engaging storyline.  For a first chapter I'm really excited to see what happens next.  The initial story is fairly self contained, but the characters are developed just enough to give them true depth without revealing everything about them.  It seems clear that the next installments will expand on each character, and I honestly can't wait to see it.  The bad guys are developed in a similar manner as well, and there are already indications that some of them will be returning in the sequels.  Character motivations are unambiguous (except for when they need to be), and personal conflicts are well defined.
- Unique skills are awesome!  Individual character skills are highly accessible, very powerful when used properly, and thematic to each character.  A full party can shift gears from offense to defense at just about any time with these skills, and the enemies are vicious enough to reward both aggressive and conservative playstyles when necessary.
- Very Limited level grinding.  XP received is based on your character level.  If you're below level for an area you will gain levels very quickly.  If you're overpowered for an area you will gain levels extremely slowly.  As such, you will quickly rise to the appropriate level for a given area until it's time to move on.
Areas that need improvement:
- Itemization is dull.  There are only a few game changing pieces of equipment.  Most are just currency sinks that keep you in line with the enemies' power curve.  In most cases characters will upgrade automatically (aside from the two main characters).  It would've been nice to see more variety in the gear.
- You can miss out on sidequests.  If you're not careful you'll bypass a lot of hidden quests, or if you advance the story line too quickly you'll lose access to some quests forever.  There's no real reason for this other than "time constraints."  The only benefit of this system is that you can't really overpower the sidequests, but for completionists it's a pain.
- Magic feels underpowered.  For the most part you won't really need to use magic aside from healing.  At low levels you don't really have enough MP to build a dedicated mage, and at higher levels it's difficult to stack quartz in a way that really maximizes the power of magic since the quartz that boosts magic damage is blue, and blue is primarily for healing magics that heal for a fixed amount and are not based on your magic stat.  Since you need to stack the same color to gain access to the most powerful spells, the system seems to work against itself as a result.  Magic is used in a few very specific circumstances, but any character can do the job for the most part.
Overall: 9.5/10.  The games flaws are minor and nitpicky.  It's strengths are glorious.  This game is worth every cent.

When I launched this game, I had problems with characters turning into large black boxes. To fix this issue, go to your library, click on games, then right click on "The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky". Click "Run Configuration". In Display, uncheck hardware vertex shading, and that issue is resolved.
I also ran into a problem where my gamepad was not working. To fix this issue, "Run Configuration", click on Input, and click on Reset Default (or whatever it says). The issue should then be fixed.
Onto the review:
Awesome, AWESOME game! Do I recommend this game? Yes. Is it worth the current price? Yes. Is it THAT good? YES.
This game reminds me of Grandia II, and Skies of Arcadia. It's a JRPG, and a good one at that.
All of the NPCs have something to say, and after the plot changes, they say something different. The game is challenging, and there are lots to do. You have to be careful, or you might miss something.
After my first walkthrough, I did not finish my recipe book, I did not collect all of the news, or complete all of the quests. Nonetheless, Estelle was Lvl 38 when I finished the game. The detail is amazing, the personalities are real, and the gameplay is engrossing.
Turn-based combat works great for this game, especially since you are controlling a party of characters.
Now, my challenge to you is: can you beat this game without using a guide or walkthrough? If you can do that through your first time through the game, I applaud you.
Seeing that XSEED is going to release chapter 2 in December 2014, or in 2015, I recommend that you buy this game NOW. There is even a New Game+ available after you play the game, so what are you waiting for?
P.S. After beating the game, if you cannot wait for Chapter 2 to come out, or want to play something else apart from New Game+, I recommend Ys Chronicles I+II. Falcom also made these two, as well as Ys: The Oath of Felghana. Check them out on Steam.

Warning: DPI overscan problems prevent this game from working on modern PCs.
This is a derivative puzzle game which functions like a 3D version of Bust-A-Move/Puzzle Bobble.   You rotate a shape made of coloured cubes around three axes, and drop additional cubes onto the structure.  When you match 4 cubes of the same size, they disappear.  If you add too many cubes, it explodes (critical mass).  If you wait too long, you lose.
Not terribly original, but a fair enough attempt at a puzzle game.
The problem is that they did zero testing on modern PCs.  Almost every modern PC requires DPI scaling be set to enable text to be readable on retina level displays, like UHD.   The people behind Critical Mass never tested this, so they don't know that you can't use the interface because your mouse only hits 1/4 of the screen.
However, they do still want your money, and because of this technical issue which prevents the game from working, I must warn people away.  Don't waste your money on unplayable games like this.

Green Game: TimeSwapper is the most roller-coasterish game I've ever played. Starts out excellently, goes horrible in the middle, then rewards the patient player with a rather good finish.
In the game, you control the Bird - or moreso, you don't control the Bird, but manipulate the environment to control the Bird. Set up wind directions to change the course of the Bird's flight, and change obstacles to make sure the Bird doesn't collide with them (and doesn't die, as a result) - all this by controlling a single dial, based on the setting of which the environment changes its behaviour. Your mileage may vary, but I immediately fell in love with this control scheme - adding in the jazzy music and the barebones visual style, which I also love, I was ready for a really superb action-platformer(-ish game).
However, after 15-20 levels the game's two major faults are obvious - the very uneven level design and the collision detection. Yes, dear player, this game made in 2016 doesn't do proper per-pixel collision detection, but lazily detects the collision of containing rectangles, leading to deaths where the hazard is half a bird away. Since it's the second game I come across in a few weeks with this fault, I wonder if there could be some underlying engine issue, but in any case, dear Creators, shame on you, because it's ridiculous. I very nearly gave up the game on level 23 due to this, but then soldiered on, learning to keep a much bigger distance than apparently necessary.
Level design goes from fine-introductory through OK-ramping-up to horrible-when-trying-to-be-difficult. Besides the collision issues, the other low point of the game are the levels from 20-30 (or thereabouts). This could easily be explained by lack of level design prowess, however, the last 15-20 levels again range from good to excellent, and they have some clever tricks to be deciphered.
All in all, I enjoyed TimeSwapper very much in 70% of the gametime, and hated it in 30%. Recommended - very cautiously.

It's a “sequel” to the “Red Game without a great name”. Unlike the predecessor I can't recommend this one. It ain't bad, but if in the Red Game controls were just clunky here they are horrendous even thought they are actually much simpler! In this game you have no direct control over the mechanical bird at all. The only thing you control is “time” of objects on the level. With that you can control which valves are open which walls are broken and position of other obstacles like pistons and spinning blades. The bird is in her own time bubble and isn't affected by the flow of time on the level. So, it just flies straight and change direction in steam streams.
Basically, the only thing you control in this game is that green beam of light pointing from the top of the screen. You can move it into 3 main positions to point at the bottom-left or bottom-right corners of the screen or in the middle. For that you have to press left mouse button and move mouse to the left or right. In fact, you don't have to grab the beam. It works anywhere on the screen.
Simple, right? Here are two problems with that: the game will occasionally forget you still holding a mouse button and stop dragging a beam somewhere in the middle and in 90% of cases that is a death sentence (unless you have a very good reaction); also, default mouse speed in your system could be a bit too fast and even a small movement will cause your doom at spinning blades. They are quite sensitive. Good for you if you have a DPI switch on your mouse and can switch into a “precise” mode at any moment.
The music in this game is nice and there are more sound tracks than in a Red Game. However, there is no song in the menu. It was a nice touch and lack of it is a bit disappointing.
So, it's a nice action puzzle with unique controls, but more than 2/3 of deaths on each level won't be from your own mistakes and bad decisions, but due to terrible controls. I've finished the game anyway since I actually like it and I really want to recommend it, but due to controls I seriously can't. Unless you have a touch screen or a Steam Controller, I guess. Touchpad or a graphics tablet may also do the trick for you. Otherwise, it will be a frustrating experience.
As for achievement hunters be aware of “die 1000 times” achievement. Even with terrible controls you most likely won't reach this number and will have to grind it. I recommend running level 38 with auto clicker.
BTW, the whole “don't die” mechanic is not for a hard challenge, but only to screw your “flawless” achievement in case you won't figure out how it works. Well, with such controls it's actually a good thing. Only death counter on the level counts towards “flawless” playthrough and it's easy to reset it. Unlike the Red Game “Reset” button in the pause menu won't work, though. In order to reset local death counter exit to the level selection menu and enter a level again.

Green game: TimeSwapper is a sequel to the Red Game which I have not played, but would like to try out in the future.
In the Green Game you control a mechanic world and time itself where you guide a bird from one cage to another.
As you control time itself the layout of the level changes. You can rot things to create ways for you to go through, turn on or off steam valves that blow you into the way you want to go through and go through portals.
The art style is outstanding, every time you shift time stuff in the background changes and it's just awesome to look at.
The gameplay is pretty simple, you guide the bird through the stages by turning on steam valves to blow him in the right direction, this can be achieved by using either the mouse controls or the keyboard, but I highly suggest using the keyboard as the mouse controls are kind of unresponsive.
The soundtrack at first is quite decent, but the it gets tiresome to listen to, so I suggest muting the game and adding your own music.
The game also has one major flaw and that's that a lot of the later levels are more trial and error than anything, being that most levels are massive it makes things tough to navigate and more or less a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to reach the ending of the level.
The game consists of 50 levels and for the most part everything is pretty easy, there are a few really hard levels, but the challenge comes from collecting three blobs hidden in each level and sometimes it's hard to collect them.
The game lasted me 2 hours to finish, but if you will try to find all three blobs in each level might take some time and might get frustrating.
Overall, I suggest getting the game on a sale cause it's a pretty great puzzle game, not too challenging, but never too easy. If you like these types of games Green Game: Timeswapper is definitely for you.
Pros:
+ Amazing Art
+ Interesting Gameplay mechanics
+ Level Design
Cons:
- Too many Trial and Error levels
- Forgettable soundtrack
- Broken mouse controls
Final Rating:
7/10

Green Game: TimeSwapper is iFun4All’s second game on Steam following the December, 2015 release of Red Game Without a Great Name. This title has also been released onto PS Vita, Android, iOS and is one of those rare games that is suitable for all of the platforms that it is on. The game is pretty simplistic to learn the basics of but features some very complex and well designed puzzles that will be certain to be the bane of your existence if you allow yourself to be suckered in by its charm.
The charm is in the presentation. The music is fantastic and is among my favorite soundtracks in an indie game this year. The soul jazz soundtrack really does the job of establishing the mood and the atmosphere for the game but at the same time reminds me of television shows from when I was a child (1980’s) and prior. It’s sweet sound is melodic and a natural fit for a game that I think attempts to be the ideal chill out indie game that you can relax to and complete a few levels after work. The green graphics are suitable for the game as well and again add atmosphere to the game.
The gameplay mechanics are simple. I used my controller to play the game – I believe that is the best way to play the game – and you dial the use the time switches in order to set the smoke which pushes your mechanical bird in the direction it is blowing – if you decide to allow it to steam – otherwise the bird will keep flying in the direction that it is currently flying which may end with the bird flying into one of the deadly traps on each level. It sounds easy and the game begins easily enough but the challenges become increasingly difficult as the game goes on. As well as the smoke switches there are also teleportation markers on the field that will transport you from one area of the map to another. Although the game can be completed in one sitting I tend to be of the opinion that the mechanics would get a little boring.
There are fifty levels within the game with each level of varying lengths. One mistake takes you back to the start. There are also power ups within the game which all have their own special ability such as immortality. All of them have been thoughtfully considered and amount to relatively decent changes in the game play when you unlock them. The value proposition has been considered with the game hitting its mark nicely at the current US$4.99 mark.
There are  fifteen total Steam achievements within the game and the game has a 5-card set of trading cards. Neither are listed on the Steam page which is something that I hope the developers rectify as it is undoubtedly a way that they can garner more purchases without it costing them a cent and they’ve already done the work.
I enjoyed my time with the game and I can certainly recommend it for arcade indie fans who are seeking a relaxing challenge.

I invested a lot of time into the original The Secret World, and all in all I find this current iteration to be almost a complete step back from the original experience. I find the combat droll, but that's also because they completely gutted the original ability wheel - none of the abilities in the new tree are fun and exciting to use (cept maybe the elite abilities) - and the feeling of synergy and choice has been thrown out the window.
The ultimate downfall of SWL vs TSW is the complete disconnect of what the original game offered in terms of story. In this version it feels like you are just pushed through all the starting zones to reach Translyvania/Kaidan, and are expected never to return to Kingsmouth/Egypt. There was a lot of fun content that was worth farming, and watching all the cutscenes back in TSW in all of the zones - that offered rewards for doing so. Which is next;
The current rewards/gear progression is about as♥♥♥♥♥as I can explain. There's only like 2 things that drop off mobs - lootboxes that require keys to open & museum parts that require an absurd amount of anima to do anything with. The rest of your progression is trying to find 3 pip dungeon/lootbox drops and then you have to pump infusion into them in order to advance your power level.
So gone are the days of spending a new CD worth of time in a Nightmare Lair farming for signets, AP/SP, and consumables. Now they want you to quickly dash through the story and focus on a shallow character progression.
The TSW servers are still online, and if you can scrounge up a solid 5+ man squad for Nightmare Dungeons - then I think you'll have a better time there than here if you're a MMO ethusiast.
If you're a fan of the horror genre, and don't want an MMO style environment to invest in and are just looking for a pretty solid chunk of time to spend either by yourself or with a friend or two - then this is a viable option. Just pay close attention to the story as you go - cause what's there is solid and enjoyable - just quickly brushed under the rug, and never really worth returning to in it's current state.

CCGs are always going to have a certain amount of randomness in them due to the mechanic of drawing cards from a deck. This game compunds that by also adding an element of randomness to the victory condition, concealing te Dofus you are meant to capture and adding two 'fake' ones. This would still be an acceptable level of randomness because there is a degree of strategy in bluffing and representing real or fake Dofus in the way you choose to defend them.

It's actually really thrilling and good. As proof that I mean it, the same company did another game WITH Jane Jensen, my personal game development hero, and I think this one is stronger. Hurts to say, but I'm being honest. I crave a sequel.

I voted for this origonally on Greenlight and I'm certainly not dissappointed in the outcome!

I'd highly recommend this for any fan of adventure games!
Edit: Forgot to add, There is a problem when playing this game on 64bit systems so I suggest doing the same work around as mentioned on their forums here:
It's due to hyperthreading issue with the engine and the solution makes the game focus on just one core instead of getting confused with multiples. After I applied this fix the game ran nice and smooth with 0 crashes in it.

Having recently completed Grim Fandango (probably the most famous point and click ever), I was looking for something that would top the experience and this did! I absolutely loved this game. The characters are all extremely interesting and Erica Reed is a really likeable, relatable girl, who even has the power to see into the past. To me, the graphics and the animations are brilliant (even when you get the odd glitch, it's just funny!) and the soundtrack is second to none. I have never played a game that has been so addictive and the storyline is so immersive,that I was lost in this for a week, like a book I couldn't put down. At times, the gameplay was so intense I felt like I was going to have a heart attack, but in a fun way! I genuinely cared for the characters, which makes the game all the more shocking when you do make a wrong move. I'ts gory, intelligent and daring. The puzzles are logical and made sense to me (although I doubt I could have completed them without the hints - thanks Dad!). If you are considering buying this game, do it. It's so so so so good. Every decision you make will affect the future of the game and also the lives of the characters you will grow to love, ever so fondly. It's genius.

Overall, Cognition is a good game. The story is very compelling and the game play is pretty good. Episode 1 is very rough around the edges, and I almost gave up on the game, but things really start kicking in episode 2 and the game finds its groove. I definitely enjoyed it overall.
Pros:
+ Good story with lots of twists and turns
+ Story has a ton of suspense and moves along at a good clip
+ Most of the point and click puzzles are pretty good. And when they're not, there's a built-in hint system to keep the game moving.
+ The character's psychic abilities give the game a unique feel.
+ Pretty good music.
Cons:
- Graphics are really rough and buggy, especially in episode 1. I am not a person who ever complains about graphics, but the weird, creepy facial expressions and body language are downright distracting. Sometimes Erica gets weird lines on her face like the Joker, or sometimes a character might contort their body in ridiculous ways.
- The voice acting is pretty hit and miss. People's accents come and go, and a couple characters are really bad--like the actor is reading their lines off of a piece of paper. Again, this is not something I normally complain about, but it can be pretty distracting.
- A few game mechanics were swings and misses, like episode 4's half-hearted attempt to make dialog choices and relationships matter. Apparently there are two ending, so your choices matter a little, but not really.

This game took a while for me to get into, it is quite slow, most of the characters are unlikable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and the character animations are jerky, unnatural and prone to hilarious glitches. However by the time I got into the second episode I had been sucked into the story and couldn't wait to carry on. The use of the characters' paranormal abilities adds a nice twist to the usual point and click puzzles. In contrast to the terrible character models the background art work is excellent and rather reminiscent of Grey Matter, which is kind of a shame because this game really doesn't measure up to that game. So this is not the greatest point and click game but I'm giving it a thumbs up predominantly for the story.

To be perfectly clear, I'm bad review purely because of technical problems. By the end it was like trying desperately to watch a DVD with a scratch, or watch a streaming video when your internet keeps dropping out. The game would freeze up on me so I'd have to kill it in task manager. It never happened in the 1st episode, happened twice in the 2nd, happened regularly in the 3rd, and the 4th was nearly unplayable. There's a scene in the 4th where two characters talk in the car, with no opportunity to save partway through in case of a crash. It took me more than a dozen tries to get through that scene, because it kept freezing up in the middle. Honestly, if I wasn't so into the story, I would have given up on it, so take that as you will.
I've glanced at the discussion boards, and it looks like the developers were fighting alot of these issues. It looks like they were very responsive too. But the game is 2.5 years after release, and it still feels like early beta.
Ok, technical issues aside, I loved the game. If you play the demo, I just need to say: the game is better. Each episode was better than the previous. Now the 4th episode was an exception... I thought the ending was pretty weak, but I may have just been distracted by the crashes. There were a few little things... Erica's voice actor was obviously working on her accent as the games progressed, so her dialect drifted from midwestern to boston as the games progressed. Still though, the game really was one of the most intense point n clicks I've ever played.
So I loved the game, except that the freezes ruin it. If there's a 2nd season, I would definately be interested, although I might watch the forums to see if they got their tech stuff in order before buying it.

Well for starters it’s pretty presumptive to call this “An Erica Reed Thriller” when it’s also the only Erica Reed mystery.  I also highly doubt they are going to make anymore, considering it’s 2016 and this game came out in 2013.  It also really doesn’t deserve anymore, it’s a pretty bad adventure game.  Certainly by no means the worst, but it fails on the #1 requirement of good adventure games.  A great story!  My God this plot is painfully bad, I am baffled at what the writers were thinking.
I’ll get into the plot later.  It has a bunch of other problems besides that.  For starters it feels like a beta.  Characters move weirdly…both just you clicking to move around the screen and worst of all in animations.  I don’t know what horrendous demons from the seven hells have possessed these characters bodies, but it is frightening how awful they move in animated scenes.  Nothing is naturally about how they move, it’s actually hard to describe other than to say “possessed.”  I also don’t know why they did this.  If they didn’t have the skills to expertly animate these scenes they could have taken the easy way out like most adventure games do and just have a portrait pop up with the chars face.  They didn’t need to go full out 3d models and they clearly couldn’t afford to.  The end result is just a mess.  It also distracts from the story.  At one point my chars head fell off her body and she started juggling it between her hands…I don’t know what sassy animation she was trying to pull when doing this.  Seriously, unless you are pouring millions into this project just go with the Gabriel Knight Style portrait facial animations.
So the bulk of this review I saved to bash the story, because it is so horrendously bad that I can’t recommend this game, so spoilersssssss!

Dear potential "The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky" buyer,
as you are probably looking throught the reviews to read about the pros and cons about a game which you want to spend your hard earned money on, you came to the right place ! (or review ... ^^)
Now that I already was on the same spot as you are now, I now want to cover some point of what you have to expect.
First off, I have now finshed the game, which took me about 40 hours so I can confidently say I know the game a bit ;)
These are the points I want to cover:
-) Story
-) Gameplay
-) Controls
-) Graphics
-) Sound
-) Conclusion
You know that feeling when reading a good book and don't want to stop because you wanna know what happens next ? Well, welcome to The Legend of Heroes !
It is really a very well written story with a lot of emotion. You can expect a rollercoaster ride with your heart once you are fallen with the characters. There is everything you want from a good story: love, hate, friendship, betrayal and tons of unexcpected events which makes it hard to stop playing.
Even the NPCs (they don't deserve the name in this game as each and every of them as a personal story) are inflicted in the story and make it more complex.
The only drawback is that this game only covers the first part of the trilogy (the other two part may arrive on steam too)
I do not want to tell any of the story here as you should experience it for yourself ;)
A little warning tough: If you don't like a lot of reading and and a deep an long story you are maybe wrong at this game.
TL;DR: If you are fed up from shooter games with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story, feel free to jump in a game which will blow your mind.
I would call the gameplay genre standard. It is a typical jrpg with turn based combat system. There is everything from basic attacks over special attacks (which are specific for every playable character) and magic (which is available through so called orbments). If you are familiar with the grandia series then you know how it works in this game. The game is not too hard nor too easy and has tons of quests and sidequests which you should complete to get more money to invest in better equiment and items to improve the stats of the characters. Important: You can beat the game without having to farm monsters. Speaking of monsters: The game is splitted in different areas called maps. Maps can be towns, passways, caves, buildings etc. and may contain enemys. You have to defeat enemys to make progress in the game and level up your character, which also increases stats.
I am using the Xbox 360 Controller and the only thing that I have done is reassigning the X,Y,A and B buttons as it was not 100% comfortable at default.
Other that that the controls work flawlessly.
I cannot say how this game plays with keyboard and mouse as I didn't use them at all.
The graphics are beautiful and look good, similar to the grandia series.
XSEED recently started patching the games with HD textures (as stated on their facebook page), so it should get even better over time.
It supports high resolution screens and I can safely say I had no issues and/or crashing the whole 40 hours.
I really enjoyed the orchestral soundtrack, which underlines and supports the story and makes it even more intense and dramatic. Be ready to get epic battle music when the big bosses show up.
Other than that, the music is a little bit repetitive but it was not that big of a deal.
P.s: the whole soundtrack is located in game directory (folder "BGM") and features high quality .ogg files.
If you like JRPGs or you want to take a break from the plain old shooter games, than I can safely say that this game has very well earned your money and time. You get an awesome game with even better story, graphics and sound which will set you back 40 hours of great gameplay.

This game is a short little indie game about transportation, specifically transportation in New York's Grand Central Station. You arrive at the station where you are tasked with finding the missing pieces that make up a train ticket. By exploring the station, which contains an abundance of art and merchants, the game provides a commentary on transportation hubs and the intersection of art and commerce. It's a neat little game with a lot to say. The creator of the game put a lot of his personal life and experiences into the game via conversations you have with some of the characters you meet in the game. There are aspects of the game that sometimes go over my head (it's abstract in nature) but I still thought it was super smart and complex.
Perhaps the best part of the game is it's presentation. The art style in this game is fantastic. Pieces of art adorn the walls and every corner of this train station that you are exploring contains new and interesting ideas. The music in the game is also pretty great. It sets the mood perfectly and keeps the game moving.
This probably isn't a game for everyone, but I'd still say it's worth a try. It's pretty short and it's free on Steam so there's really no excuse.

The game stands out by its very well made fantasy setting and an excellent soundtrack. Personally i found the graphics and the music to be outstanding back in the day.
The graphics aged of course but they aged quite well, for the most part they look good even by today standards. They might be technically dated but artistically they are still great.
The combat is solid and quite varied for a hack and slash game. The choice of character is vital because the game is pretty difficult and some characters will do a lot better than others in certain levels. Every level can be completed with any character but the difference in difficulty can be unforgiving.
The levels are not very big but most of them are intricated enough to allow some exploration in search for hidden stuff.
It was one of my fave PC action games back in 2003 but i still enjoy playing it today.

If there is ever a game that lives as an example of "Metacritic reviews don't mean♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, it's this one. First off, a 70 from Metacritic, yet a 92% positive rating on Steam. Really makes you think what these critics actually know, or don't know.
Game is actually really easy to control, which came as a surprise to me. I honestly thought you were some floppy ragdoll and you just threw yourself around like a lifeless bean bag. It's actually really easy to control and interact with the environment.
The levels are awesome and bring all sorts of challenges. I never felt like I was repeating something when I went to the next level. One level had a construction site where you got to use construction equipment to complete the level. Another had boats you had to use to get to the finish line. Another had canes, lamps, and catapults you had to use to get to the exit. It's amazing how much variety there is level to level, and it's really refreshing to not feel like you're just grinding out the same level over and over again like in most other puzzle games.
Despite the online being in alpha, it's actually pretty well done. My friends and I were able to easily connect across distance and have very low latency. There was the occasional time where one friend tried to join and he was constantly falling through the sky on his screen, but on the ground on our screen. It was fixed by restarting the game, and it only happened with one person so it may have been his Internet.
Character cretion is what you want it to be. They have custom clothes you can put on your character, or you can even paint your player freehand. It's actually quite fun to use, and it even lets you isolate body parts so you don't accidentally paint your arm when you're trying to perfect your torso.
The soundtrack for this game is one of the best I've ever heard. It may not have the nicest sounds seeing as it was rendered with virtual instruments in some DAW software, but hearing it fills me with a confidence I don't have.
As someone who is really picky about games, I highly recommend this game to anyone.
If you have friends to play with you, what are you waiting for? Buy this now!

I reviewed this game for Game-News.co.uk with a copy of Green Game: Timeswapper being given for the purpose of the review.
Time control seems to be a big theme in gaming at the moment, where players are given the control of time and are allowed to use it for the benefit of good. Or to play a series of twisted experiments with a cute critter that can fly. Green Game: Time Swapper takes players into a world where they can indirectly control the environment through the fragment of time that allows certain elements to change. This, in turn, allows a flying bird to escape a number of traps and it’s up to you to make sure it flies safely to the exit.
The flying bird cannot be controlled and moves in a single direction, unless made to do otherwise. You can change his trajectory by using various placements in the level and often these are controlled by the aspect of time. The player can control time by moving a dial from the left to the right of the screen; this changes certain aspects of the game world, from bringing machines to life that can push the bird in another direction, to huge obstacles that can, and probably will, kill that poor bird.
It’s a solid and rather dynamic concept for a puzzle game, where the environment reacts to your positioning of the dial. You must attune the dial to different positions at the right time, planning ahead of the bird’s movements and all within an extremely short amount of time. It’s clever as it tests your lateral thinking and reflexes.
Green Game: Time Swapper offers a good challenge with a simple design and mechanics that are easy to learn and remember. The game presents some nifty visuals with a mixture of silhouettes and surrealist colouring.
The overall challenge in the later parts of the game become a drag as the game fails to introduce enough new elements and even misuses some, such as power-ups that slow the bird down which are often placed in the right places while others just seem needless. They’re either too close together or are strangely absent when they could be needed most. The game never really delivers new challenges or ups the ante to make a bold spectacle.
The complexities of some levels become an annoyance when having to replay them over and over again due to its trial and error format of design. This isn’t helped when certain elements that alter the game feel a little buggy or too sensitive to the constant shifting of time. The trajectory of objects that push the bird in a different direction are difficult to judge and if you move them the slightest when the bird is close enough his flight pattern will reset and ruin your planned route.
The soundtrack is also rather irritating with little variation and just plain generic sounding. Not great to hear looping over when you have to repeat a level several times.
Green Game: Time Swapper is a stimulating and solid puzzle game with nice visuals and a dynamic mechanic. Yet it lacks any variation in structure for its puzzles/levels and becomes a short-lived affair when you start to see that the game becomes too repetitive without introducing other interesting elements. It can be fun and rather challenging, but sadly not fulfilling enough to ensure a healthy playtime.
+Simple yet enjoyable puzzle elements
+ Neat time control mechanic works well with the game's design
+ Nice visuals
- Becomes very repetitive around the half way point
- Certain puzzles drag on too long
- The soundtrack is rather annoying

For context, I am long time adventure gamer.
In brief, loved this game. It had a great story and mixture of puzzles. Loved the subject matter although may be gory for some (i.e. serial killers and graphically violent scences). It has been a long time since I played a game, maybe even watched a film that captivated me as much as Cognition did. If like myself you're a fan of detective games then this is a must. I can't even compare any other games that match it in terms of how well thought out the story is. The twists, murders, story/skills development and style flow seamlessly from episode to episode. This is how episodic games should be done, full stop. The suspense and cliff hangers at the end of each episode have subtly been built up from the beginning of each ep, they're not just thrown at you in the last 5 minutes in hopes to keep you invested long enough to buy the next one.
The use of the cognition skill works really well in the game. You do equal amounts of normal detective work with a nice topping of physic abilities. You don't feel as Erica is over powered in anyway, even without the powers she makes a kick♥♥♥♥♥detective. With some top quality voice acting going on I might add.
The puzzles are original and unique the majority of times. So you don't run the chance of becoming immune to them, you can't just jump head first into them because there's a good chance you could get yourself killed. They're not gonna hold your hand either, there's a level of effort you got to put in.
So negative point, I found the animations to be a bit jerky, and it would take Erica nearly 10 seconds to register how to  turn around and walk across the room. I don't know whether this was because I played most of the game on the "Fastest" setting (cause's some hilarious glitches in the character model) but for the last ep I did change the settings to beautiful and most of what I just mentioned above disappeared. So do yourself a favour and don't play on the fastest settings; your computer can handle it at peak quality! I was just an idiot.
End mark, I give it a 9.5 out of 10. It's orginal, well made and worth every penny.

Great game, honestly better than hearthstone coming from an Ex-Legend player in HS.
Now, why is it better? Well, quite simply: It adds onto the genre. It has the same classic TCG mechanics that Magic, Yu-gi-oh and Hearthstone all have, with the same archetypes, decks, etc, we've all come and love, i.e: Zoo with the tofus/piwis, Midrange/Control with Xelor and Eniprisa, etc.
The thing that differenciates Krosmaga is, obviously its field. It makes for a much slower game, more exciting game, where agro decks (imo the cancer of TCG's) aren't that prevalent, seeing as they can't attack your "face" (dofus) so quickly. The fact that 2 out of 5 possible dofus are fake also make the game more fun, as in the end, Krosmaga turns out not to be only a classic skill card-game, it can also be a mind game where you and your opponent try to find out which of the enemy's dofus' are real and which are fake, while also trying to cover your own.
All in all, pretty good game, although it has a very small english-speaking community, due to the fact that Ankama (the company) is french.

I’ve played Hearthstone, Shadowverse, Duelyst, Faeria, Magic the Gathering, Gwent, Elder Scrolls Online, blah blah blah. Point is I’ve played a bunch of online card games. I’ve been playing the game for a week and right now I am really liking Krosmaga, so I thought I’d write a review to encourage new players to play, and to address some of the criticisms the game has gotten. For ease of understanding, I am going to compare this game to Hearthstone since it’s the most popular online card game. If you want me to compare it to some other card game, message me or something.
1.	Mechanics
2.	Free to Play – Getting Packs
3.	Free to Play – Building a Competitive Deck
4.	RNG (Cowpie) (Can't say ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t)
5.	Cowpie cards
6.	Conclusion
Mechanics
Krosmaga has units travelling along rows in order to deal damage to the enemy’s eggs. There are 5 eggs, 3 real, 2 fake. Smash 2 eggs and you win the game. While on paper that sounds like fairly simple concepts, they change a lot when you compare it to other games.
In Hearthstone, you have 1 turn to react to a minion. With haste, you have 0 turns. That’s it, 0-1 turns to react to your opponent. This is why you often get those “Answer this or I win” moments.
In Krosmaga, you normally get 3 turns to react to a minion. With haste, you get 2 turns. Why? Because the minions have to travel down the rows. This is great as it means that SMORC decks can’t zerg you down as easily. This allows the game to go into the late stages rather than ending at turns 4-6 (*cough* Pirate Shaman/Warrior/Hearthstone in general). I personally really like that.
Another interesting thing are the “fake” eggs. This screws over SMORC decks the most. They have cards that can shrink the reaction time from 3 turns to 1 turn. HOWEVER, they need to spend like 3 cards in order to do this. And if they smash a “fake” egg, then they get put really far behind. By contrast, mid-range or control decks don’t really care that there are fake eggs. I play a mid-range deck, and I’ve rarely been screwed over because of “fake” eggs (let’s say 1/20 matches).
Please note, just because the mechanics discourage SMORC type play, effective SMORC decks still exist. For those who want “short” games, try a bow meow deck, iop rush deck, etc…
Free to Play – Getting Packs
Krosmaga is better than Hearthstone in every aspect regarding free to play. Don’t believe me? I am going to prove it using…….. MATH (AWWWWWWWWWWWWW YEAAAAAAAA). To begin with, Krosmaga is twice as better as Hearthstone regarding getting cards. Why? In Hearthstone, on average you get 50 gold per day (40 from quest + 10 for 3 wins). It takes 100 gold to buy a pack so 2 days. In Krosmga, you get 60 gold per day (40 from quest + 20 for 4 wins). A pack costs 60 gold. Therefore, in Krosmaga you can buy 1 pack in 1 day whereas in Hearthstone you can only buy 1 pack in 2 days. Simple math.
In regards to INFINITE (legendaries), we’ll need more complicated math so bear with me. Infinites have 3 versions of themselves, and these cards “level up” as you play them. Every 3 levels, (4 and 7) you get another version of the card, and a bonus card at level 9. On the one hand, this is great. By getting 1 infinite card, you potentially get 4 cards in total. On the other hand, levelling them takes FOREVER. FORGET about levelling through playing. Plan on spending gold. In order to level an infinite from 1 to 9, you need to spend 1500 gold. That’s 25 packs. To be fair, I should include the cost of getting the infinite in the first place. You can get them in “gold packs” which cost 300 gold. So in total it costs 1800 gold or 30 packs. But remember, getting packs is twice as easier in Krosmaga than in Hearthstone, so in “Hearthstone-effective packs”, it really requires 15 packs. In Hearthstone, you need to buy on average 20 packs in order to get a legendary
. So in Krosmaga, it requires less packs, and you get 4 cards. So in regards to getting legendaries, Krosmaga is roughly 4 times better (15 packs = 4 legandaries vs 20 packs = 1 legendary).
Sooooooooooo yeaaaaaaaaa…. Don’t know why people keep complaining that the game is “pay 2 win” or that the developers are “greedy”. Like Jesus Christ. Check yourself before you wreck yourself :P
Free to Play – Building a Competitive Deck
I can use math for this too…… I don’t want to. It’s a lot more complicated. I don’t have the attention span to do it and you don’t have to attention span to read about it. I am just going to use myself as an example. I am rank 20 (effectively rank 5 in Hearthstone roughly speaking). I’ve only been playing for a week. I DID spend $7.50 (CAN$) to get the starter pack. Otherwise I didn’t spend anything. I am not even playing an aggro deck but a mid-range one. So yea in regards to building a “competitive” deck you can do it reasonably within 1 week (feel free to ask for my decklist). Building the deck without the pack, purely from dust with NO luck (i.e. crafting EVERY SINGLE CARD), it would take 1 month excluding legandaries. With the starter pack, it's shortened to 10 days. I got a bit lucky so I was able to build it faster.
However, my deck is not “complete”. I can already imagine improving my deck with multiple legandaries. Doing so will take me roughly 150 days (1,800 gold / 60 gold per day * 5 legandaries = 150). So in order to build a COMPLETE deck, yea it’ll take a while. But the legandaries don’t make or break the deck. They only marginally improve it. I am still having fun with my deck that only cost me $7.50, a week of playing, and a bit of luck.
RNG (Cowpie)
None. Nil. Naughta. Zippo. Zilch. Ain't no thang but a chicken wang. There’s no knife jugglers, babbling books, primordial glyphs, stonehill defenders, crystalline oracles, etc etc etc
There’s still DRAW Rng. Yea no shiat. It’s a card game. It’s going to have that. All card games do. Having said that, I’ve never had “topdeck” moments. I.e. if only he/she didn’t have THAT card I would’ve won or if only I drew THIS card and I would’ve won. Like, draw RNG plays a FACTOR, but I’ve never had it decide games. Deckbuilding and skill are far more important based on my 1 week of knowledge.
Cowpie cards
Have to be fair. They exist in this game, just like in most card games. I hope they nerf some of them T_T . No point in listing what, cause then I’ll have to explain why and blah blah blah. Just know that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t cards are restricted to legandaries (in my opinion) and a deck is made of 45 cards with only 5 legendaries allowed. So chances are you won’t see those legandaries….. hopefully.
Conclusion
Soooooo yea that’s what I think about the game. I love the mechanics, the free to play is actually very generous (relatively speaking), there’s no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments, some cowpie moments but ah well hopefully the developers will fix that. I hope you found this review helpful and that it will encourage you to give the game a shot.
