The Wonderful End of the World is an interesting experiment, seeing if the collect-and-grow mechanic from Katamari Damacy holds up in isolation. And for an indie game studio, the result is admirable.
On the whole, the dynamic of collecting object to grow larger to collect bigger objects is still compelling and Dejobaan Games has come up with some fun levels to race through, such as the arcade, sky mall and the so-called 'Word Forge'.
On the other hand, while some levels are inspired, others feel lackluster and could have used some more revision to smooth out the progression. There are also minor technical issues regarding the collision, camera controls and frame rate crop up enough to be noticable. But the biggest issues are regarding the design. Wonderful End of the World removes the  fun, yet frustrating ball rolling movement of Katamari, but doesn't have anything to replace it with, making the game less engaging than its inspirition. But even without that absence, both games have the same core flaw, that the collect-and-grow mechanic just doesn't have legs. There isn't anywhere to really go as a challenge for the player and that is what caused the Katamari franchise to burn itself out.
I don't mean to sound overly critical. For a small indie, Dejobaan Games and Wonderful End of the World was able to faithfully recreate the mechanical spark that inspired it, even if it couldn't go beyond that.

The basic conceit is that you are a goddess gathering as much of earth as possible before the Apocolypse. You send your marionette down to earth to hoover up as much stuff as possible before the unnamed disaster destroys it all.  The story telling is as threadbare as any indie FPS.
The music is in a similar vein to KD, upbeat and bouncy, though not quite so as big an ear worm.
The controls are responsive; your toon can turn on a dime.  He does take some time to get up to speed when you are nearing the mass cap for the level.  There are no fancy special moves or tricks to master, just one speed forward, WASD, and hope you haven't grown so large as to absorb the ramp!
Getting stuck between objects is a constant problem, and unfortunately only moving objects repel you.  For other objects you either get stuck for precious seconds before clipping through or worse simply phase through like a ghost.  This is especially apparent with the tables in the cafe level.
The levels are MUCH, MUCH smaller that KD's and the time limits are an order of magnetude lower.  Instead of tens of minutes, you will have a hundred or two seconds.  Thus you grow faster and the levels are more tightly compact and hectic.  A wrong turn or hesitation is much more costly, and the levels are much more easily memorized.
The game is short.  There are only 14 levels with no level editor or DLC available. I had already played it completely before buying it on steam and I "A" ranked every level in just over an hour, many on my first try.  If you are good at KD, you will have little trouble with tWEotW's difficulty.  There are
very few collectables to hunt down.  I think the total number is under 5.  There are only 10, maybe 15, fairly easy achievements.  Any replay value will mostly come from challenging a friend to beat your high score.
There's no multiplayer.  It's a single player only experience.
The game is showing its age.  It wasn't graphically impressive or particularly polished when released in the PS2 era, nor are the "animations"... very animated.  It hasn't aged terribly, but it hasn't gotten any more impressive either.  Expect a low polish "indie" experience.
However, despite all that, the game is still fun, especially the first time through.  Yes, it's a low-rent Katamari Damacy, but that formula works marvelously even without the polish.  The music is good, the level design is servicable, and the controls hold up.  If you can get it for just a couple of bucks on sale, it's a very enjoyable hour or two.  It's just a shame the devs never released mod tools custom levels could be fan created.  We could have had so much more.

First of all, I have been a JRPG since I could remember.
I started playing Secret of Mana ever since I was a kid on the SNES and it's been a wild ride since then.
Fast forward to today, where I will be writing my first review EVER.
I was certainly persuaded to write a review for this game for you people on the fence, as well as to support this game's company for their localization efforts.
The Legends of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is what you'd term a "classic" JRPG.
I don't really want to delve into the story too much because that would be spoiling it, but it is an amazing ride.
The game is designed to be completed as a "Trilogy" so knowing that, you can see the huge emphasis on character development.
It definitely shows.
Each character has their unique backstory, as well as traits and "things" going on in their own life that makes the game very engaging.
The battle system is interesting, though not truly unique. For you FF fans, it's like modified ATB where you can jump positions based on your actions.
The story itself is a great ride. It starts off slowly, and builds up, just like any game really does, but the main selling point of this game in my opinion is the development of the 2 main characters.
If you haven't really decided yet, please go ahead and buy it.
Support this effort and you will not go unrewarded.
I am already anxiously awaiting Chapter 2 of this game, and rest assured that when it is finally announced on Steam, I will be pre purchasing it.
It has been out on PSP for a while now, but since I don't own a PSP, I did not know of this.
It has been one of the best JRPG's I have played in a long long long time.
I would definitely put this up there among the list for consideration of games that I truly enjoy.

Firstly, for those of you who don't know what a "JRPG" is:  A world map, towns and caves and other places to visit, combat that involves you and the monsters taking turns - it's a formula that has been around for ages. Critical Mass asks a simple question: What happens when you turn a Match-3 game into a 3D model? And that is what you get: A mass of cubes that requires you to match 4 cubes of the same colour to clear the level, and the idea alone is rather fascinating...
...Except that the main mode is basically a time trial mode, where the mass of cubes expands all the time and explodes at "critical mass" level. Once it does that, the whole level restarts and you lose all your previous power-ups.
I find this implementation frustrating, as it never gives you the right breathing room to think about your cube placements. I understand that there is a Zen Mode where you are free to clear cubes at your own pace, but the fact that I can't play through the vanilla ranked mode properly leaves a bad taste to me. If only they have a time limit for each level instead of making the mass of cubes a timed bomb, I would have enjoyed this game much more.

Well, this was a beautiful and mesmerizing journey. A musical adventure where you follow a pair of mayflies (or butterflies...something like that) as they try to keep each other alive and express the joy of their love for one another. Along the way, they find allies in beetles and bees, and fight off a gigantic boombox (yes, the stereo type) carrying spider.
Visually, this game is stunning. The nature of the gameplay means there will be a ton of actual fireworks and such, with a lot of cool imagery that comes with that, along with flowers, and a ton of other great stuff to look at. I suppose you also go through the seasons as well although this is a bit more ambiguous.
There is no dialogue. The music conveys all the meaning in this one. Speaking of the music, as a game based around a musical journey, you would expect the tunes to be stellar, and they in fact are that and more. This is the type of soundtrack you could easily jam often. Really great sounding music. The way this game is presented musically reminds me a lot of Karmaflow, so I wonder if it is the same people, although at first glance, it doesnt appear to be.
So, what is the game itself? Baically, it is a speedrun click fest. The music and the clicking start out slow and manageable, but as the music picks up tempo, so to does the clicking. Where it isnt clicking, it is click and drag. I'm not very good at this personally, so I didnt manage anything even resembling a perfect sequence, lol. It isnt required for the story progression, but some of the achievements seem to be tied to this. Also, there is apparently a secret level, but I havent found it yet. So, after your first playthrough, it definitely becomes a game of skill and speed.
So, anyway, all told, I think this game warrants 9 bad♥♥♥♥♥riffs as a pair of butterfly dragons swirl and fly through the air while fireworks explode around them, out of 10.
Additionally, I would definitely assign this must own status for pretty much everybody. I cant imagine somebody playing this and not enjoying it.

This is a simple extension into the third dimension of a typical match-x game. You start with a vaguely cube shaped pile of blocks and then fire predetermined color blocks onto the mass attempting to connect at least four of a color, causing them to be removed. In it's base mode each fired block causes the mass to grow while matching blocks causes it to shrink. Take too long or fire too many blocks without clearing any and you'll reach critical mass and lose.
The interesting thing about this game is that at it's heart it seems to want to be a competitive game. In the base mode there are only 10 levels and they have to be completed in one sitting to get a final score and attempt to get on the leaderboard and this leaderboard seems to be what the developers hoped would keep you coming back. Personally I'm not really a fan of this type puzzle game and the competitive aspects are not a draw to me. If you enjoy doing something multiple times in an attempt to hone your skill then this will be well worth the price of entry. If, like me, you're looking for a more encapsulated experience then its probably best to move on.

I got my 0 dollars out of it and felt the need to pay based on the writing alone. The limitations that the negative reviews are fuming over were not apparent to me anywhere near the severity described.

Firstly, let me say that this game has an awesome concept = secret societies investigating magical phenomena, while not completely original, is still and intriguing idea! The idea that we would also get puzzles to solve and woulf have to translate old texts and so on also drew me to the game; an MMO with puzzles and secrets and mysteries, oh my!
Sadly, the game is like nearly every other MMO out there. Pick your faction (IE you team jersey and the accent of the pompous character who will give you your quests), then go to a point and kill monsters. Not great, but not bad. An interesting story, but at least I don't have to grind, right?
Wrong.
You grind, boy howdy do you GRIND, just to try to keep the story going. I was getting stopsigns from level 12 onwards. Sure, it makes the game last longer but this is the equivalent of filled your sandwich with actual sand. Yeah, it'll take a few more hours to eat but your sure as hell don't enjoy the experience.
After several hours and levels of "Going to higlighted area and killing the thing." I actually was worried that there weren't any real puzzles beyong "Go to point and find key to open the door to kill the thing."
But I was pleasantly surprised when I got a radio tower puzzle the required me to translate morse code... until I realised that the player was broken. I couldn't pause the player, it was skipping or ending before the message was finished and to try to replay the morse code message you had to exit, walk around a bit, and then interact to play it again....making it a frustrating task of futility. In the end the in game browser became helpful because I entered "Morse code tower puzzle" and was rewarded instantly with the translated code. Hooray.
Shortly after that the game glitched out and froze my other quests, making them incompletable. However, the player base was helpful and friendly, if a bit impatient with people learning the ropes, and they did hold my hand for a bit yet had no answers or suggestions for fixing the broken quests - they shrugged it off and said to start again. Which made me realise that they were used to the game breaking horribly - some spoke of getting stuck in geometry, falling through the map or even getting stuck where they respawned and having an eternal loop keeping them there...
So all in all, good idea, broken game. Don't waste your money or time on it.

The ultimate downfall of this game is the bad economic model. I felt that I was forced into giving money right from the start. There are no welcome boosters or starter packs for new players - you actually have to pay 5-6 bucks to get the starter pack which only has half a dozen boosters or so. You get starter decks for each god however getting any boosters or money from quests is at such a slow pace that you often feel like this game is pay2win. On top of that there are tire boosters which is a terrible idea that should have died years ago. A simple comparison of this game to Shadowverse (which gives you a tone of boosters at start and over time) or even some of the less popular card games shines a negative light on Krosmaga.
I cannot recommend this game considering how much it wants to milk your wallet for money every opportunity it gets.

I love point-and-click adventure games, but when it comes to a point-and-click thriller, this one really takes the cake.  Where do I start?  Let me break this down for you.
Storyline - 10/10 - Absolutely fan-♥♥♥♥ing-tastic!  And I do not put that lightly.  It's very deep with multiple twists and turns and on top of it all: it is INTENSE.  The term "thriller" for this plot is an understatement.  You will encounter situations and plot twists that will rack your brain, wrench your heart out, and even disturb you greatly.  Simultaneously, you will also find yourself getting rather attached to the characters you encounter and the relationships you develop with them is on point.
Gameplay - 8/10 - Controls are simple enough since this is a point-and-click game so you only need the mouse.  The downside is that sometimes things can get a little slow.  For one, there are a few glitches here and there that affect if you can interact with something.  Granted, I only encountered this with a figurine in the very last episode.  So, yes, there are glitches, but they are rare.  On top of that, it can get tedious getting around to different locations and picking up items from certain places, then taking them to other places, etc.  Other than that, the gameplay is very engaging and the puzzles are challenging but not impossible.  Overall, it's very excellent.
Artwork - 10/10 - This is a bloody beautiful game in more ways than one.  The artwork ranges from beautiful, to disturbing, to frightening, to aesthetic, to calm, to intense, etc etc etc.  It's never boring visually with this game.
Soundtrack - 10/10 - Very original soundtrack and it is very fitting for each situation you encounter.  Personally, I love it.
Now, here's my regret.  I did not pay full price for this game.  In fact, I bought it on sale.  But even if I paid the full price, I definitely would have gotten my money's worth and Phoenix Online Studios would deserve every penny.  Trust me when I say, this game is definitely worth the price and I'm praying for a Season Two which I will definitely pay full price for if it is ever released!

I got this game gifted to me by a generous friend and was excited to play it because I enjoy match 3 games, especially any that try to do the genre in a novel way. I was very satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like the match 3 genre, score attacks, and playing on a 3D-plane, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are simple but nice - you are playing with different-colored blocks in a space theme. The music is nice and calming (drum & bass-like), however, there is only one track, so I quickly muted it and used my own. You can listen to the track on the store page video to know what you'll be listening to.
The controls are very simple - everything is done with the mouse. There is a brief tutorial popup when you start playing, however, I feel that a bit more information could have been provided. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with match 3 games and speed at searching/scanning.
Gameplay consists of you rotating a jumble of blocks around while adding a single block with every mouse click. Feedback will always be given on what color the block will be. Although it is a match 3 genre, you need to actually connect 4 blocks of the same color before they are eliminated. Chaining longer combos will give you a higher score multiplier. More importantly, larger combo chains will give you more time - the blocks move closer and closer to the screen (your time limit). Every time you clear blocks, the jumble will move back a distance depending on how big your combo was. As the jumble comes closer, the edges will turn red to signal that you are about to lose; the music will also stop and the blocks will start shaking.
An interesting element is how ONLY same colored blocks will be eliminated when you match a minimum of 4 blocks. I initially thought that any pieces that were separated from the main body would also be destroyed - they actually stay floating in space. This is a cool concept because it allows you to try creative ways to achieve larger combos. When you eliminate a color, you will not spawn it until the next level.
There are a variety of game modes to play: classic, survival, meditation, and rush. Classic mode is your typical match 4 setup - powerups charge depending on the length of your combo. The three powerups include a score multiplier, slowing down time (jumble moves toward screen slower), and a mass reducer (I believe this allows the pieces to exceed past the screen, which would normally cause you to lose). Survival mode periodically adds more blocks to your jumble. Meditation mode is a more relaxed experience and a good way to just play around. Rush mode constantly subtracts from your total score, forcing you to act quickly.
Overall, the game is a great title in the match 3 genre, and anyone interested in score attacking and being challenged should give this a try.
Recommend!

This game is an example of difficulty done poorly. It is hard, but in an incredibly boring manner.
It consists of wandering through a ship with 5 levels, each consisting of bland grey corridors that all basically look the same. You're supposed to fix things that break and keep yourself alive by looting in the process. To make this a challenge however, the maps displayed around the ship give next to zero informatron about where the key facilities are (such as oxygen production, temperature regulation, etc.).
For example, if you stand in a cold room for all of 30 seconds, you may receive 5 new diseases. To fix this, you should go to an infirmary. If only you knew where it is. Have fun trudging around each floor looking for one, only to forget where it is later should you need it because every part of the ship looks exactly the same. Perhaps you could hand draw a map or list of what each floor has, but I personally never felt motivation to put through such effort for this game.
There are no animations for anything. Not for the food and drink you have to spam throughout each day, not for the mysterious diseases you receive, not for the containers you look through to find more stupid crap. Nothing ever moves except for the particles of poison fuel gas (I forget the name), fire, doors, and your camera.
There is nothing rewarding at all about staying alive. Parts of the ship will break that you didn't even know were there and fixing them consists of raising your tech-glove while suffering whatever malady is affecting the room until its gone. Oh, and you might get injured just for fixing them, because ♥♥♥♥ you. The only motivation to continue living/playing that I can think of is just to be stubborn.
At the end of the day, as irritating it is to keep up my character's Morale stat by finding random items, the biggest challenge is keeping up my own morale to keep playing. I write this review after having played a round until I died and by the end I just wanted to die so I could play something else.
Now, the one positive note that I can leave is that the AI voice does have a few good lines that I appreciate. Hopefully they will help you bear through the silence broken only by your footsteps. I really do like the concept of what this game should be, but the execution is just terrible at this point. Perhaps this game will get better, but I'm going to spend my time with other games for now.

I wasn't sure what to expect with this game as the trailer doesn't really say much about the game. The UI could use some improvements, and a brief tutorial would probably help, but overall it's pretty fun. I hope the developers continue to make improvements.
The core gameplay is essentially fixing problems on the ship, researching new abilities/technologies, crafting upgrades, and maintaining your hunger, thirst, morale, and health. The upgrades and technologies do things like make your thirst or hunger decrease more slowly, making the med bays more effective, and even give you an option to land your spacecraft before the whole thing explodes. You load resources into the storage unit attached to the console (of which there are an abundance within the storage rooms throughout the ship) and kick off the research cycle.
The ship is broken up into 5 levels (T-2, T-1, T0, T1, and T2. This could be vastly simplified by levels 1-5 as the first three games I played I thought there were only 3 levels and got lost a ton), each level having one or several functional bays: comms, medical, lab, water recycling, etc. Every time a day passes, one of these might break, new breaches might be ripped in the ship, fires might break out, etc. You risk injury by putting out fires, fixing leaks, and breathing poisonous gas which you must manage through medical items or the medbay. Each of these injuries, if left untreated, worsen every day.
The weakest part of this game for me has been the way they handle the ending of each day. It feels like you're on the clock every day (maybe this was a design choice), but it completely pulls you out of the game at the end of every day to (ostensibly) save and then generate a daily report. The problem is that daily report is unclear and is lost in what looks like a chat log -- there's no clear way to scroll through it and there's rarely enough information for it to be useful (it will tell you there's a fire onboard, for instance, but it won't tell you where). The only thing you end up seeing are these icons sliding down on the left side of the screen, which you can't hover over or click on because there's no intuitive way to free the cursor. Some of these may be design choices, but most of them just feel sloppy.
Overall, it's got some interesting intricacies, but it lacks polish.

Combat also pretty cleverly side-steps the turn-based problem of it turning into a chore, by adding a bunch of little variables that keep you engaged to optimize your results.
This is a fantastic game and I STRONGLY recommend it.

The problem is that the way they implemented it, it's more like you're the athletic but kind of dumb girl, and he's the smart, handsome guy that all the ladies desire and who constantly reminds you of how much you suck in comparison.  Gameplay wise, he's just better than you at everything, including hand to hand combat, to the point where your character almost feels unnecessary.  And for the first two hours, he just won't stop reminding you of how dumb your character is.  Any individual line about it would probably just look like normal banter between siblings, but it's pretty much unending in the early portion of the game, and your character rarely does more than pout about it and get annoyed.  The shear volume of it makes it come off as straight up bullying.  And it's not just in response to your character doing dumb things.  That light bulb thing and calling you a ditz just for commenting on how a room looks were me paraphrasing real things he says to you.
And it gets worse with him.  A few missions in, you have a little cut scene between your character and a friend of hers.  The friend goes on and on about how handsome your brother is, how all the girls desire him, and how incredibly nice he is.  You know, the guy whose only interaction with you outside of business has been abuse.  I guess that's not fair.  In the first dungeon, he does tell your character that she was pretty good at what she did.  Of course, he finished it off by calling you stupid again, undercutting his whole point, but hey, it seemed like he actually gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you for a minute.  Oh, and this friend also points out how it would be totally OK for your character to hook up with him, since he was adopted.  Yeah.
Anyway, at the end of that mission, he insists that he wants to kill these now defenseless creatures, and it takes a while to talk him out of it.  You head back inside, and he reveals to you that he doesn't feel compassion and still wants to kill those things.  So how does your character react to her abusive brother admitting he's a sociopath?  By reassuring him that he's totally not like that, and she would know since they bonded so well in the five years that happened off camera between him joining the family and the start of the game.  Then she says she's glad he finally opened up to her, since he usually hides his feelings.  It's not clear how she thinks she knows him if he never opened up over that period.
So why am I going on about this one guy so much?  HE'S YOUR ♥♥♥♥ING LOVE INTEREST!  Yes, in order to appreciate this game's story, you have to be OK with a woman getting nasty with her abusive, sociopatic brother.  Even aside from that, the guy is an obvious Mary Sue, completely with a dark and mysterious past.  It's like what would happen if you found a 13 year old who was really into Final Fantasy games and had him come up with the protagonist for an RPG.  He's totally awesome and badass and gets to tell other people how much better he is without retaliation.  Oh, and he's totally the protagonist.  You play his love interest.
But that's not the entire game, and I've heard that they cut down on the insults as the game goes on.  I've gotten to that point, and honestly, without many insults to get mad about and being unable to care about the protagonist of the game, it's mostly just kind of boring.  The writing tends to try way too hard to be witty and is needlessly wordy and repetitive.  I mean like there's one part where you find an elevator that doesn't work, so you find a guy 20 feet away who gives you a key and says you can use that and that the elevator goes down to your objective.  So you run 20 feet back and try to use it, and your brother then explains that you can use this key on the elevator, that it goes down, and that you should probably do so.  Why they didn't just have the elevator work when you have the key rather than give you 4 text boxes, I have no idea.
Gameplay wise, I have mixed feelings.  The idea of initiative manipulation in combat is interesting, but I'm not sure if it always works.  There isn't much you can do to manipulate it aside from one special attack that you get once every few fights.  And the fact that spells don't always take effect right after your caster does them can be frustrating, mostly because you can't tell when they'll take effect until the caster's turn.  There've been a few occasions where I decided to attack with one character, then heal with another only to find that the enemy got a turn before I could heal.  Once this even happened when the enemy didn't get that turn for the same damn spell earlier in the battle.  This game doesn't have random encounters, but it might as well have had them.  You can only see enemies as you get close to them, and some enemies blend in on some backgrounds, anyway, so you'll still get surprise fights.  And this is one of those games where your whole party trails behind you as you move, and you get attacked if any of them are touched by the enemy.  And in a given area, it's often the same one or two groups of enemies that you fight over and over.  Once you figure out the best way to deal with them, all the battles there just become tedious.  At least Dragon Quest games let you mash A to get past the more repetitive battles.  The complexity of the combat system seems to make random encounters last longer and take more effort than it does to make anything fun.
If there's anything positive to say about this game, it's the presentation.  This looks and sounds fantastic.  I highly recommend getting a copy of the soundtrack.  If someone made a mod of this game that removed all but the necessary, mission relevent dialogue, this game might have gotten a recommendation for these things alone.  But sadly, the mediocre gameplay and bad writing just make the whole thing an aesthetically pleasing slog.  There are far better JRPGs out there than this for almost any platform.

A paranormal serial murder thriller packed into a point ‘n’ click adventure? It’s easy to sell this concept, harder to actually pull it off. Cognition luckily manages to do that, although not without problems.
Psychic cops and serial killers are always a good mix in the hand of capable writers, and Cognition: An Erica Reed Thriller is a nice example of that. It follows the struggles of the titular FBI agent, who needs to tackle not one, but four different murderers preying on the streets of Boston.
Her story is structured like a television miniseries with four self-contained episodes. Arguably, the first two ones are the best as they remain close to the concept of being about the investigations, while the third episode is just a huge plot dump constrained into a single location, and the fourth hastily ties everything together using a set of rather tired clichés (including the classic ‘you are suspended!’ one).
Still, the plotting is spectacular; each episode has endings that would make you grip the edge of your chair if they wouldn’t also feature the best, most complex puzzles, with perfect music to boot. The developers really knew how to reward patience.
As for the rest of the game, Cognition is a fairly standard point ‘n’ click (with an uncomfortable interface) that adds cognitive powers on top of the usual item manipulation. The use of these powers is not really consistent; there’s one that you invoke maybe three times in the entire story, even though you spend half an hour acquiring it.
Graphics aren’t too spectacular: the backgrounds look good, but the characters are weird and glitchy. The audio is a lot better with a memorable soundtrack, and all main actors do an astounding job playing their (fairly stereotypical) role. It really helps getting immersed in the game, which is always great for thrillers like this.

I had never heard of this game before, however I saw it on sale and since I’m really into rhythm and music games I decided to give this one a try. Then I missed a note and I noticed the music didn’t stop, nor did the game, nor did anything; then I just let the game run by itself without touching the mouse and while it kept going  without any input I said to myself “This is going to be one of those days isn’t it?”.
Ok, fine, whatever I decided to play along and honestly I found it to be extremely disappointing in almost every aspect
you say,
I answer,  and that’s just the tip of the iceberg with this game.
Ok first let’s talk about the positives, the visuals are pretty and the story is told without a single word of dialog and even though it’s a pretty simple story line about two dragonflies falling in love but it’s still told in a well-done matter. The tempo is also spot-on and the notes are very easy to tell apart from the background, even though they take different shapes and forms with each stage.
And now for the negatives: Everything else. As I said in the beginning you can’t really die or lose, ever, and as such the game has limited replay value. You can only get an extra stage if you get every single note without missing a beat, that’s all the replay value this game has and I can’t be bothered.
Why?
Because the game is quite obviously a poorly done Ipad/Tablet port, there’s only one resolution and the mouse controllers are incredibly wonky, in other words,
. This makes it very hard for me to replay the game as I don’t have a touchscreen monitor, nor am I planning on buying one sometime in the future and I really despise the mouse implementation in this game, I REALLY do.
The music isn’t something that I would write home about either, to me it felt like an amateur composer made the entire score much like I did scores when I started playing piano “Check it out mom I can play from C# to B and back!”. There was only one song that I liked from the soundtrack, ONE, which is not something I usually say about rhythm games.
Finally there’s the stages, I can sum them up like this: one stage is recycled three times and one of them is… Do you remember that mind-numbingly boring lawn mowing game where you do nothing but mow the lawn? That mini-game is in this game as a stage, yes, really.
Actually, yes, I can. The whole time I was playing I was thinking that I would’ve enjoyed this game a lot if I was about 15 or 17 years younger,  so if you’re a parent looking for a game without any violence for his kid I can fully recommend this one.
I get the feeling with the overall positive reception of this game I’m going to end up receiving some very… interesting mail in the near future but I don’t care, this game is clearly not for me and I don't think it was worth the three dollars I paid for it.

TL;DR: Amazing zombie game with lots of player freedom
THE ENEMIES
The enemies in 7dtd consist of zombies, zombie dogs and bears.
Generic zombies are the biggest threat to your survival in 7dtd. There will be a huge amount of zombies spawning at all times, depending on how "noticable" the actions you do are. For example, using a campfire will attract more zombies then doing something small like opening your backpack. The zombies run at night, and can break any block in the game. They have a large amount of health and can kill you quickly if you are not careful.
Zombie dogs, although rare, can be a serious threat to you if you are not careful. They have a small hitbox, do a huge ammount of damage, and run regardless of the time of day. They spawn most often in the wasteland biome and often appear with hordes of zombies.
Bears are a small threat to you, as they have a low spawn rate and you need to get close to them for them to attack you. When you kill them though, you can get some good resources that can boost your progress.
PLAYER FREEDOM
7dtd has 99% player freedom, with every bit of terrain and buildings can be destroyed. You can also use a variety of blocks to build and defend a shelter, and craft a huge assortment of makeshift items. The only real things that block player freedom are that the huge hub city in the center of the map, and other settlements of varying size, are unclearable. 7dtd also has skills you can level up to make you more proficient with certain types of tools, but there are bugs with the system in numerous areas.
ISSUES
7dtd, as good as it is, has some huge issues in it. There are lots of bugs with the random gen world, and the game isn't very optimized. Enemies constantly have bugged hitboxes, mostly zombie dogs. The gunplay in 7dtd needs improvement. Some parts of the gameplay can be tedious, like leveling up skills to get better quality weapons and armor. Using some things like a forge take to much time to use, and don't give enough resources.
CONCLUSION
7dtd is a fun, although tedious, zombie survival game. If you want pvp zombie survival you should probably look for something more like dayZ, but for coop and singleplayer this game shines. Just don't buy this game expecting a finished, polished game.

I am a simple salaryman who has to commute to and fro work every day by train. My work place is rather far from where I live, and travelling takes around an hour for each trip. The trains here, in this very city I live in, is the same as any other: packed with people like pickles in a jar. These rides are essential, though never at all entertaining. As such, after each of these mundane hours, I appreciate the few tranquil hours after work which I can finally sit down, relax, and enjoy a few moments or two in front of my computer. It so happens that, today, I have decided to dedicate some time to this title I come across randomly on steam: Off-Peak. Guess what?
It’s a game about getting on a train…
… and you need to find your own ticket…
… which is hidden in pieces all over the station …
I know, for a game of its price, which is literally nothing, it is a great title, as you have nothing to lose but all to gain. The controls, dialogues and graphics are all reasonably sound, though Still, having to go through all that again in a virtual world that is half-finished, surreal and yet equally banal, especially after a long day at work, it won’t get much of my attention. They got me, seriously. I wasn’t expecting someone to appear but, yeah, I got a little more awake after that.
Great title if you are looking for a little extraordinary out of the ordinary and have 10 or so minutes to kill.

I hate bashing on Ozzie companies. ;p And this isn't an evil, unplayable game. My first impression was good, I played it for a bit, expected to play more, had it installed forever, yet every time I fire it up, I close it after 5 minutes.
It's a match 3 game with some 3D tetris elements. The concept is good. The graphics are polished. The music isn't bad. The controls feel annoying at first, but they're actually mostly okay. The problem is, the gameplay doesn't feel satisfying. It expects (and rewards, scorewise) big combos and long term strategy. It also expects you to be fast and responsive. This should theoretically work, in that zen-like way games like this work, but it doesn't. The rythym and pacing feels all off, it feels like the speed jumps from 1,2,3,4,5 to 50 to 150. Once you get into the zone and start planning ahead for later big score combos, it feels like you blink and the game jumps speed, asking you to go for quick, "just don't make a mistake" placement. That may be totally subjective of course, or it could be that the feeling gets exacerbated by the clunky cube placement process. It simply isn't visually always obvious or easy to correctly target the location you want on a constantly rotating cube, which really hurts the game when it picks up speed. People misplace blocks on tetris too, but usually feel it's their fault, here it feels like the cube jumps place three times before you can be sure it's where it should be. By which time the game has jumped two speed gears and you're basically done with.
Again, not a bad game, in theory. I just never feel like playing it long, because it doesn't feel very enjoyable. The thumbs down is just trying to balance a "very positively" reviewed game, with an 80 something metacritic score that few people seem to actually play much (notice the curiously short play times of the majority of the positive reviewers?). So I'd suggest to approach with caution, and at least play the demo first.

Remember those days in middle school when you would go your local afterschool program, hopped on a computer, and booted up the first flash game site you could find? Whether it was
, Addicting Games, or Newgrounds, Battleblock Theater serves as the manifestation of the classic platformer you'd find on those sites. Collect x and get to the exit.
The plot is simple: You and a group of friends get stranded on an island, kidnapped, and are forced to go through a series of platform-based levels to amuse the island's feline inhabitants, all the while trying to rescue others from your boat who were captured.
With quick wit and style does Battleblock Theater serve to both amuse and delight the player, the game blends black comedy through the outspoken narrator with excellent and generally basic gameplay into a single entity that can provide hours of entertainment.
Levels play out in unique ways to the classic platformer, yet pay homage to those of the genre that have come before it. Unlike most platformers, in a typical level, you can die as many times as you want, and the goal is simply to get three gems in a level to exit. However, due to the construct of the game, you'll likely, based on constructed OCD, end up collecting all possible and the yarn too. Gems can be spent on unlocking new characters which can be in turn used in future levels, while yarn unlocks weaponry.
New concepts, such as specific baddies, blocks, and other functions of the game, are slowly introduced to the player in individual levels to provide for your ability to cope with them in the future. The game makes sure of your understanding of them by forcing them into the completion of levels so you're ready for them in the future.
Battleblock Theater is one of the most addictive games on Steam, and arguably the best platformer the service has to offer. In case it needs to be said, I strongly recommend you add it to your library as soon as possible.

I already owned the game before I added it to Steam. For the time it was made the graphics were amazing and still hold their weight  today. Textures are crisp and I can play this game at 1080p with no issue, the only downside is FoV is locked, though at 95 it isn't that bad.
Story progression is ok. Light vs Dark and a rift that divides both. Unfortunately the rift is shrinking and both sides are now butting heads. I only wish the characters you meet in playing through the game had at least some back story or names, rather than just Warrior, Druid, Halfling, etc..
Combat is fine. Melee combat offers 3 weapon classes, Sword, Axe and Hammer.  Melee weapons also have some form of a combo in where if you swing successively 3 times it produces an end effect. Bows offer a wide range of ammunition from sniper bolts which lets you zoom in at far away targets, standard bolts that allow you to stack them up for a burst shot, fire bolts for damage over time, and explosive bolts for aoe damage. Crossbows are your medium ranged weapon and can be used by both ranged and melee classes. Staffs used by your mages offer a standard attack, close ranged aoe attack, and a shield to block melee and ranged hits.
Character customization goes as far as how much gold you've collected in your play through. Gold acts a point system and it's scattered throughout the game world, some in pots and others in the form of gems.  The more gold you've collected the better things you can equip. This can range from better armor, weapons, shields, staffs, more ammo for bows, etc... I would say your bow users as well as your engineers/bombardiers are more demanding in gold requirements due to how much stuff they can equip while other classes like warriors don't require much at all. Gold you've collected stays with you for your entire progression. Also collecting it all awards something special in the end.
The only sad part about this game is there's no multiplayer, which at the time would have been great as it looks like it could have supported at least 4 players (Just judging by the wave levels in the campaign). All in all it's a good game.
I also still hope for an Enclave 2.

EARLY ACCESS review, 6/1/16
A lonely, barren, poorly rendered spaceship crumbles around you as you futilely try to patch up your broken little world just enough to survive the inevitable decay, prolonging your lonely, barren, poorly rendered existence for one more day.  First-Person-Survival that could work as an art piece for the meta 'feels'... but not so much as a full fledged game.
Drift into Eternity is a survival game that puts you in the shoes of the only wo/man alive on a wrecked spaceship that is falling apart a little more every day.  You must scavenge supplies from all around the ship to fix up the hull breaches, fires, and broken life support systems that crop up in greater numbers every day as you try to survive in hope of a rescue that may never come.
The game's hook is interesting, and it certainly has potential to become a game worthy of playing, but in its current early access state it unfortunately lacks the content a $15+ game is usually expected to deliver.
The graphics aren't great, and even the current visuals caused numerous hitches on my machine. The audio is equally mediocre at this point, consisting of a lone voice telling you about objects when you press the tutorial button, the constant rumbling of your spaceship, and the ubiquitous wailing of sirens as things break down around you.
The gameplay itself just doesn't have enough substance at the moment to retain interest for very long.  You open endless containers (which usually don't resemble containers or have any highlights or animations to mark them as such), 'take all' of the endless parts, then hunt down an endless number of broken/smoking/flaming things and right click to fix.  Meanwhile you must eat/drink/self-medicate just enough to stay alive....endlessly.  This repetition definitely adds to the atmosphere of desperate futility the game seems to be going for, but doesn't provide much in the way of entertainment value (which ironically, is one of the things you have to do to survive in the game - keep your character entertained).
All in all, Drift Into Eternity has an interesting concept that could be neat to try, but probably not at the current point in development for the current price.  However, the developers do seem to be very active, patching the game frequently along with providing a clearly labeled timeline of what they hope to achieve in the next six months  - and visibly active development is a definite positive for an Early Access title.  So, if the concept of the game intrigues you, you could consider supporting the development of the game and hoping for the best... but if you're searching for a survival game to fully enjoy, you may want hold off until release is a bit closer before picking this one up.

It's not an easy game. It doesn't hold your hand.

Drift Into Eternity:
~~~~~~~~~~~~
What a ride, you might say! You are the sole survivor of a crash-landing on an unknown planet. The good news – well, you are alive! The question is, for how long? Your spaceship has sustained a lot of damage and as days goes by, more breakages occur!
Drift Into Eternity is a First Person survival game set in a fallen spaceship. At the start, you will wake up in your personal cabin and learn the basic functions of the game. Then you will be advised on how many breaks the vessel suffered on a daily basis via the logbook. You might have some specific equipment to fix or even to extinguish fires in several rooms. You will be able to identify where the breaks are located by the flashing red lights and the sound of the alarm in front of the room where the repairs are needed. Green smoke is also a sign of damage, so make sure you go through the area with a fine comb.
A small point I forgot to mention is that you start with absolutely nothing on you, and not only do you have to repair the ship but you have to make sure you find enough food and water to survive another day in this grim environment! Be aware of the rotten food which can cause you illness and make sure that your state of mind is at its optimum by reading comic books, magazines or listening to music. Try to stock as many useful items as possible in your inventory, so when you come across equipment to repair you hopefully have the right component to fix it.
The vessel has two decks that you can explore and you will have to find a teleporter to move from one deck to the other. Remember to read your log book carefully as damage can occur on both decks on a same day. One thing that I miss in this game is a mini-map; sure you have maps of the ship on the walls here and there, but I find it to be not so helpful.
The graphics are average but the game runs very well. I like the Keyboard rendition before starting the game but there is nothing else in regards to the sounds apart from the sound effects, which are footsteps and alarms.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Great music intro
-	Well-designed decks
-	Plenty of items to find and use
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No mini-map
-	Graphics need to be polished (Early access)
-	No trading cards
This game is currently in early access and shows good potential. I look forward to see more updates.
7/10

Hull BreacH is a sci-fi first person survival game. You found yourself on a ship all alone and have to survive basically. Reminded me a lot of the movie The Martian to be honest. The game is still in Early Access so they’re improving it all the time.
The graphics are average, nothing fancy the FPS is good and game runs smooth.
There isn’t any music or voice acting in the game other than the one line at the start of the game. Only your footsteps and the breaches’ alarms going off is all you’ll hear. I guess it adds to the lonely atmosphere.
The gameplay involves you running around the ship fixing breaches and in the process keeping up your basic needs such as hunger, thirst, morale, oxygen etc. It’s a good concept and the atmosphere of the game really gives that all alone in space scary feeling.
You have to survive the days, as a day goes past you get new breaches such as fires, and atmosphere leaks, you have to fix those, you can find them by looking for alarm cues and sort of like a waypoint which tell you where the breach/broken thing is. After fixing you then have to concentrate on keeping yourself healthy by going to the medical rooms and getting in the med pod to heal your diseases, they can also be healed with medicine . Once you’re done with fixing breaches and eating food water, there’s basically nothing much to do after other than wait for the 24 hours to be over and to do all that all over again. Surviving isn’t hard at all because there’s plenty of supplies all over the ship.
One annoying thing in the game is the lack of a minimap, I know there are plenty of maps all over the ship which tell you where you are currently but a minimap is always helpful especially if the rooms and the ship looks the same everywhere you go.
Though there is many bugs but that’s expected as the game is still in Early Access and many bugs should be fixed by the developers. The most annoying bug I ran across was when I adjusted FOV to be a bit wider FOV kept increasing automatically and the viewmodel and the onscreen menus became so small that they were unreadable. So I had to keep adjusting the FOV to be able to read the menu not to mention the wider FOV makes everything look weird even at 80 FOV. Yea, imagine doing that everytime you want to look in your inventory and/or check your health status.
The game is not bad but it can be improved a lot and more interesting mechanics can be added. Bug fixes should be fixed and some sort of story should also be added. If you like survival games you should give it a try otherwise I’d say wait for the game to come out of Early Access and/or sale on the game.

Use them. There is a log that tells you the everyday maintenance ship status, also your hunger and thirst status. You will be able to check the oxygen level and other important things like fires and breaches. At options you'll be able to see all commands, that's helpful.
Again, beware the poison food, some of the food and drinks are poisoned and you will have to look for the cure. You don't want to get poisoned if you have to survive for 15 days on that ship.
Sometimes I felt a kind of "lack of action". I'm not saying I have to run all the time but days can be a little longer without something to do.
I liked the "Star Trek" touch. In the cabins, you'll see the Enterprise in a poster. Also, if you look like the ship looks a little like the old constitution class.
+ Great environment for a ship
+ Lovely intro music
+ Difficult to pass, like that
+ The Star Trek touch
- The graphics effects should be polished
- The voice at the beginning should be a recording or nothing, sounds very off topic
- There are not so many things to do
- A lot of items you don't know what are used for
This game has potential. If you look for a survival adventure escaping from crazy aliens this is not your game. But, if you look for a good environmental and realistic immersion and maintain a ship in conditions, this is definitely your game.

Having played the original The Secret World years ago (I disliked the pay once play forever system they used which resulted in slow rollout of updates), the f2p model is a really welcome change in Secret World Legends - especially in a day and age where people are not willing to hand over money before trying and starting a game. This was one of the best stories told in any RPG, with animated cutscenes for every major mission (quests).  However it is not without its flaws.
After playing through the game to the end of the current story, I've decided to write this review.
Pros:
- Excellent story in a standalone RPG game
- Great RPG that has MMO implemented features. Story can be completed solo without having to bother about the MMO parts of the game. MMO features such as an Auction House, Cabals (Guilds) add to the game rather than take away from it.
- Very different modern day setting.
- Has at least 200 hours worth of story game play with more promised (fingers crossed)
- F2P model works especially with very casual players.
- Patron (subscription) model works well with more dedicated players.
- Loot boxes are available for pay to win players to speed up progression.
Cons:
- Dated - essentially a repackage of a 2012 game and it shows.
- Clunky controls - as someone who has played games since the 80s, I can overlook this, but this will be a turn-off for some people.
- Bugs! Bugs! Bugs! - A lot of jarring visual bugs, geometry bugs, etc.
- MMO endgame loot needs to be better spread out, content is a little lacking, PVP is entirely lacking.
Overall I'd rate it as a very good game that is a bit dated.
DLC and additional content
For folks who have tried, and liked, and want to spend real cash to support the game, I would recommend purchasing patron status, then aurum. I do not recommend the steam exclusive DLC unless you must really have the vanity items.

While the game released not long ago and a lot of the features you'd expect in a card game are still in development, it is a charming game with gods that each have a unique mechanic they can use to gain an upper hand.
While the game isn't very well balanced yet and some content really needs some polishing, the development team is actively working on fixing most of the problems.
I agree that some infinite cards are stronger than others, but I don't remember a single time an oponent playing a certain infinite that would straight up win him the game or vice versa, if you play hearthstone you know legendary cards and how in most cases you can't rely on them, well here you have 45 cards in a deck and can only have 5 different infinites, so relying on them won't get you anywhere (though one infinite exists that does draw you another infinite, so if you have just 2 in your deck you double your chances of drawing it).
Also while crafting cards is harder than in hearthstone due to te dust ratio, the number of packs you get from the gold from daily quests and daily log-in tokens is quite higher, making your colection grow quickly and once you are happy with a deck, you can just spend the gold on leveling up your infinites to unlock the other versions of them.
The only problem I have with this game is that starting out is hard.
If you play this game for a month, you will get most of the cards you need to build a fun deck to play and be able to craft the rest with the dust, but getting there is kinda annoying as you will have to use sub-par decks (same as in most card games I guess). Also it is really annoying that while you get all the basic cards for a god just by completing a tutorial, you can get those same cards randomy in deck and their dust value is quite low, so getting them in packs is a disappointment, so i hope they change it soon (though packs are cheaper relative to most CCGs).
Overall the game is not "pay to win" but i'm sure spending some money on packs will bridge the gap between "just started" and "kinda competitive deck" which is helpfull, I personally spent nothing and have a quite good xelor deck now in my opinion, but I just suggest you find a cheap deck to build early on and try doing that, as some of the cards you don't start out withwith are really good in certain decks, also I recomend buying golden packs untill you get at least 2 infinites that fit your deck, than just buy bronze ones to fill your colection, it's what I did.
All in all it's nothing that you wouldn't expect starting out a CCG, but the powercurve of cards could be improve a bit.

Krosmaga is a lane-based card game with an interesting concept, but terrible balance and strange design choices when it comes to cards.
What is the first thing most people do when starting a card game? They go look up what is popular or being played by competitive players. I quickly discovered that the majority of the most desirable cards fall under a card type called "Infinite" cards. My first assumption was it was basically the games lingo for "legendary" in games like hearthstone.
Not quite. Infinite cards are cards that start off weak, and take a ton of grinding (aka using them in a match) to get to their "actual" form that is featured by all the high end decks and prominent players. For someone who doesn't want to grind, they have to spend ludicrous amounts of money to expedite the process. Because of this, any "Infinite" cards you may open up will be completely underpowered compared to someone who either spent a fortune or did so much grinding it isn't even feasable for someone with a normal life. It's an utterly abysmal design choice, and punishes casual/free to play players.
On top of this, there are horribly blatent balance issues between the classes, with some of them so clearly better than the others it's almost mind blowing that it even exists in its current state.
The gameplay itself is interesting, but very slow. Most matches end up being a slog to see who runs out of stuff first, and then it turns into a top-deck war.  When things come together it is pretty cool though, and overall the game is not one I would call bad.
But the insane card issues make it almost unplayable. I can't in good conscious recommend it even to someone with money to spend because of the "Infinite" system. I am typically a person who has no issue spending a few dollars to make a deck or two, and once I figured out this system existed i dropped this game flat.

I really liked Watch Dogs. Like everyone else I was disappointed that it didn't live up to the graphical splendor of the early footage, but I thought the game itself delivered. The sandbox was fun, the story was interesting, the stealth and combat game play was excellent. I've been anxiously awaiting Watch Dogs 2 since it was announced, and it's certainly different from the first game in many ways.
Ubisoft has publicly said that they've learned form their past mistakes of showing off upcoming games too early and vowed to turn over a new leaf in that regard. WD2 falls under their new and improved policy. It was unveiled for the first time only about five months ago, so virtually all of the downgrading and compromising they had to do happened behind closed doors, where it belongs. What they showed us is what we got. Overall I think it looks better than WD1. The world of the Bay Area definitely has more character than WD1's version of Chicago, which I thought was good but did have a bit of boxy design going on, like it was modeled with Legos. WD2's world has more character and is a lot more colorful. Ubisoft was pretty open and transparent that GTA was a major influence on Watch Dogs. I'm pretty sure they used GTA4 as a big chunk of inspriation for WD1, and that GTA5 was a big inspiration for WD2. I certainly see some similarities in the overall visual design and presentation. Much of the San Francisco bears more of a resemblance to GTA's Los Santos than it does to WD's Chicago, and I'm not just talking about architecture and climate.
Anyone who's familar with WD1 and has seen WD2 previews should know that the tone of the game is completely different. WD1's story and atmosphere was very grim and stone faced, with only a few occasional bits of comic relief. It was about Aiden Pearce, a criminal out to avenge the death of his niece, a death which was his fault. Hard to blame him for not being a fountain of one-liners and going around with a permanent frown. Again it seems like Ubisoft used GTA4 as the model for WD1 and GTA5 for WD2. WD2 is goes completely in the other direction, virtually always upbeat and wacky. Everything is parody and satire. It walks a fine line between lionizing hipster hacker SJWs and mocking them. Very tongue in cheek and self aware. Story wise, it's very different from WD1 in that that game had a very linear sequence of events where every mission provided a new clue that lead to the next mission, until Aiden achieved the revenge he set out for in the beginning. WD2 does lay out the clear goal of taking down Blume at the beginning of the game, but from then on it's basically a hodge podge collection of disconnected missions that only share the commonality of hurting Blume in one way or another. They're often similar to GTA5 heists; When you receive a new mission it's actually a sequence of a few separate missions to complete a project. e.g. A) Steal a particular car. B) Steal an experimental computer chip. C) Install the chip in the car and then use the car to ________. These all fall under one mission heading in your DedSec phone app, but you're able to free roam between each step if you want to. The story isn't exactly what you'd call a direct sequel to WD1's story, but it does reference and connect to it. They often refer to "what happened in Chicago in 2013" and there are some cameos. WD1's had lots and lots of miscellaneous side missions that had nothing to do with his revenge mission, and it often felt wrong to stop and deliver stolen cars or take down some random criminal convoy when you knew you were supposed to be in a race against time to save your nephew or sister or whatever. Ironically, WD2's flow would be much more suited to doing random sub-missions whenever you feel like it, but compared to WD1 liberally peppering them all over the map, they're few and far between.
The stealth component feels very much like WD1. I tend to lean towards stealth in these game whenever possible, but WD1 seemed to deliberately throw you into situations where combat was the way to go. WD2 seems to emphasize stealth more. The stun gun is probably a big part of why. The character you play as, Marcus, was wrongfully deemed a criminal threat by ctOS, and that's his primary motivation for wanting to bring down Blume at the beginning of the story. So it feels odd to have him then proceed to become a violent criminal to achieve his goal. However I think it's important that Ubisoft put the choice in the players' hands rather than force everyone to play as a harmless white hat. Letting the player choose make the non-lethal choice more powerful. Going non-lethal definitely adds a layer of challenge, because the stun gun only knocks out enemies temporarily. Pretty sure Ubisoft was playing some MGS while they designed WD2. However, melee take downs seem to knock them out permanently. Sometimes they look so brutal I wonder if they're actually lethal. The game doesn't seem to keep track. One of the few disappointments I have is that they got rid of WD1's Focus ability. Since the game is designed to be online at all times and not just during adversarial invasions, I guess it just wasn't an option. Too bad, I relied on it often in WD1. I miss it, but I'll cope.
Oddly enough, you can still pop into restaurants and bars for a coffee or a beer. Marcus has the exact same drinking animation that Aiden and T-Bone did. But without a Focus gauge to extend, it doesn't seem to serve any purpose. I like that they left it in anyway. I remember being pretty disappointed the first time I played GTA5 and realized you couldn't enter fast food joints anymore.
The driving is definitely an improvement over WD1. I remember really hating WD1's driving when it came out, and it took me a while to get comfortable with it. I've been replaying WD1 and its Bad Blood DLC over and over for the last few weeks because I was so excited about WD2, so these days WD1's driving has felt very natural and second nature to me. The other day I popped in GTA5 for a bit, and was surprised that its driving suddenly felt really weird to me, and I'd have to readjust my brain to get used to it again. Clearly WD1 has re-wired my brain. Recent WD2 previews were saying the driving in WD2 was different from WD1, so I was kinda nervous about that. When I first started playing, I did think it felt kinda twitchy. But I got used to it very quickly. I think it's similar to WD1, but definitely improved.
There was a rumor that the online MP was so broken that the day 1 patch required to fix it was going to be so huge that depending on your internet connection you might not be able to play WD2 until the day after you got it. The good news is that the day 1 patch is relatively small, less than 220 MB I think. I was able to play within about 15 minutes of inserting the disc. The bad news is that online MP is indeed broken, and has been disabled until they release a big patch. Luckily for me, I don't care about the online MP stuff.
Bottom line, WD2 is in many ways an improvement over the original. Heartily recommended to those who liked WD1, those who didn't like WD1, and those who never played WD1.

This is a wonderful game with a well-crafted and deeply engrossing story. It is basically a point & click adventure with some innovative twists to it. I highly recommend reading the prequel-comics before playing, as it sets out the background very well.
Since this game is so good, I'll get the bad out of the way first:
- Most animations are unskippable, as are some dialogues. If you accidentally click on an object at the other side of the room, you are forced to wait until Erica walks all the way over there and interacts with it before you can continue playing
- Unlike the classic take of point&click games where you could just pick up everything you might ever need, Erica often won't pick something up unless she knows she's gonna use it. This results in having to backtrack and having to go through places you've already searched just to get something you couldn't before.
- It isn't always clear what to do. It feels at times like the game is forcing you to use the hint system.
- Episode 4 drifts away from the standard point & click style and into choice-based dialogues where you die if you say the wrong thing. It isn't as fun as the previous chapters (gameplay wise).
Ok, now the good:
- Great detective story with many twists and turns, interesting characters and a well designed investigation at its center
- Erica's powers provide a very cool and unique take on the genre
- The game remains refreshing, providing new powers and other gameplay mechanics in each chapter
- Fun, challenging puzzles that will make you think outside the box
- Comicbook like graphics that fit the game perfectly
- Wonderful soundtrack that keeps you in the mood
If you're into the genre, this game is definitely worth your money.

I've just played through the first chapter and only the first chapter, so take this as more of a first impression than a complete review - though, spoilers, i intend very much to continue through the other chapters when I have the time.
In short, because I get carried away easily;
PRO:
- beatiful hand-drawn artstyle
- compelling and well-told story
- some very good voice-acting
- intuitive controls
- creative puzzle-solving mechanics
- satisfying level of interaction
CON:
- animation duration
- glitches [mostly minor]
- some forced choices and obscure solutions
Recommended for adventure-game fans and those in to interactive novels, since it fulfills most of those expectations either well or excellently. Most gripes arise from gameplay, which, if sufficiently engaged [and that's definitely possible], will be tolerable.
One of the first things you need to be aware of is the length the game takes to play. Clocking in at 5.6 hours for one of four chapters seems to be on the fairly slow side when looking at the other reviews, and is in itself not a bad thing either. But it's not JUST the lenght of the story that caused this time. It is also the overall slowness of animations that are, as far as I could tell, unskippable [some dialogue is skippable and some isn't, and depending on your memory and/or trial and error you may find yourself listening to a minute+ long unskippable piece of dialogue in order to verify a single statement]. You can run with double-click, which is nice, and in some cases you can directly exit a location, but overall the movement of the protagonist is slow. As someone who generally likes slow pacing, I'm not as bothered by this as others may be, I do however have a problem with the animations when sitting in front of a computer [a nice animation, though] or when opening a door. For the amount of times you have to do these actions, the animations become too slow too quickly. Finally, I tend to visit every location whenever I get new information, so that I can see all dialogue options and find potential hidden stuff. If you are anything like me, you can spare yourself the trouble [though if your anything like me, I know you won't]. There are cases where you are clearly meant to backtrack, but it's always clear where to if you paid attention ["get food" for example], and there are cases where you are convinced you don't have to backtrack, yet no option you have available works [when asked to "get food", you already have food in your inventory that isn't usable], in which case the duration it takes to go somewhere and back again will make you readily inclined to use the very direct but sufficiently helpful hint system. So overall, very sluggish gameplay-wise. Since it also lags occasionally, be prepared for slow progression and/or long playing sessions.
The plus-side is that the game's story is quite engaging. You have enough options and freedom to make you feel like you're actually doing some work on your own, and there are different ways to solve certain problems - though this is the exception - as well as a few different choices you can directly make [like accepting or declinging an invitation]. I can't comment too much on the story; so far it hasn't been the most original, but it was well-told and fairly well-paced, with appealing characters and adequate to very good voice-acting. The other strong suit of the game is the artstyle. I really like the comic style of the characters, but am particularly impressed by the backgrounds, so much so that I spent quite a while just looking at the pictures before even seeing what I can interact with. The cutscenes, aside from direct dialogue, are mostly minimally animanted [very minimally, like blinking], which I've seen done a lot worse and I think works nicely. The gameplay animation is 3D and might be quite glaring at first. It seems to go for a comic-like 3D effect akin to many Telltale games, but it comes across jagged and quite glitchy, with many animations clipping through each other [most glaringly the fact you can walk straight through most character models]. I got used to it quite quickly, but considering it is a major part of the game and does NOT look like the handdrawn backgrounds and cutscenes, you should be at least okay with them in order to gain any enjoyment from the game.
Though I generally liked the artstyle, the presentation, the possibilities provided by the gameplay, the characters and the story, there were a few more undesirable aspects aside from the speed that I feel need a mention. Firstly, the game never crashed for me, but there is a chance that it might; save regularly [no or very rare autosave]. Instead, the game nearly froze three times in the span of five hours. All three times it was when I tried to move somewhere, and it wouldn't respond. Every other option was still available and I could highlight them, but none responded to clicking. After a while, the protagonist simply warped to the position I initially clicked for her to go. The last time had me waiting for her to "warp" for well over a minute, after which I noticed that I could just hit the dialogue option with nearby characters to make her warp instantly, allowing me to edge my way towards the elevator and to the next floor, where all worked fine again. A very minor glitch that may be entirely due to my graphics card is that the shadows cast by moving objects came out pixelated.
Secondly, there are FAR too few dialogue options when clicking around stuff in the background. Perhaps I'm spoiled, but in a point-and-click game I expect more variety than the exact same dialogue for ~five crypts or –six graves [as well as their seperately selectable but identical gravestones], especially when you are expected to click on all of them in order to find something specific. Also, don't bother clicking on things more than once - so far, the dialogue has never changed [but if you're like me, you'll check anyways].
And thirdly, while the puzzles are generally good, well-integrated and of various difficulty, some are highly obscure, especially when there's a perfectly reasonable way to solve them that the game simply doesn't recognise [I already mentioned the food]. Some of these problems have to do with the interface - you can choose to look at or interact with an object, sometimes with whatever item from your inventory you selected. But not all items allow for experimentation, and sometimes you get the option only after having checked something else first [which I could never stand adventure games doing]. A frustrating point specifically was when I needed to borrow an item from someone that was clearly very important to them. As soon as I was done, I wanted to return it, but there was no option to do so up to the end of the chapter despite me repeatedly trying [the text once even said "these two just don't match" or something, which is clearly false regarding the object that you supposedly only temporarily borrowed off the guy]. Probably the game will have me use the item once more [hopefully without also losing it in the process], or the guy I got it from will "remind" me to return it, as if I as the player have forgotten also. Speaking of which, there are a few instances where you have no choice but perform a ludicrous action that you yourself don't want to do. SPOILER: When reminded by my father to bring flowers to someone's grave, I was presented with the option to take them from another grave. I didn't want to do that, but I found NO other way to get one, even after revisiting every single open location. Finally I had to succumb with the justification that I had "forgotten" to bring flowers, even though I had done anything but that. Minor things like this can be very irksome when the game otherwise allows you reasonable liberty.
Despite its flaws, I was engaged enough through visuals, narrative and interaction, allowing the game to more often than not get away with it.

In my short time of playing a selection of World at War custom maps, I was pleasantly suprised at how far the modding community would take it - custom textures, huds, weapons, music - you name it.  When I heard that Black Ops III was going to feature modding tools, I was worried that they'd be dumb down and limited so that people couldn't create content nearly as spectacular as those found in World at War. There's been a certain push for that kind of "gentrified" toolset for user content as of late, so seeing Activision, a company infamous for perfecting the season pass and splitting their games up into dlc, embrace mods after all this time was a little concerning.
Thankfully, my worries were quashed. Speaking from a purely Zombies point of view, Black Ops III is modding heaven. The amount of user made content is overwhelming - from goofy to rivaling-Treyarch-in-terms-of-quality, there's an incredibly diverse selection. I don't know the first thing about modding tools, but whatever insane intern asked the higher ups to let the community have access to such powerful tools, I thank you for risking being laughed out of the meeting. I have none of the Zombie DLC maps, and, quite frankly, don't feel that there's a glut of content I'm missing out on because of these mods - there's DLC guns in some of theme, for pete's sake!
The only reason I'm leaving multiplayer mods out of my praise is that there simply not enough populated dedicated servers to   join at the moment. I'd love to try CoDware and the like but there's simply no one to enjoy it with. Obviously, Zombies doesn't have that problem because of how easy it is to fill up four slots with freinds.
If you at all enjoyed World at War's Zombie modding scene, Black Ops III is a darn fine upgrade.

Biggest issue I have with this game is that in big cities, commercial buildings are the dominant, tallest, biggiest buildings and "office" buildings (which replace all your industrial areas), are short, 2 or 3 story structures.
Visually, this throws off the whole game for me. I live in the U.S. where big cities are made up almost entirely of the tall OFFICE buildings, then smaller or perhaps similar sized (still tall) commerical buildings (but what is that really in a big city?), and somewhere mixed in all that are residential in those same buildings or different but still usually tall.
In Midtown Manhattan, the tall buildings are offices. Uptown are short residential, On the BOTTOM of the office buildings are commerical spaces. Same building. Downton the buildings are shorter. Commercial space on bottom, residential on top. Or maybe and office or art stuido or whatever on top. But it's the same way in other cities around the country as well. Office buildings are BIG. Residentials are usually not as big or if they are, they are mixed office/res/commerical.
Maybe we need mixed zones? A hybrid zone type?
I guess I just don't like this concept that the offices, one of the 3 main zones in the game, are so short by default. This is just a different world from where I come from.
I've played this game many many hours.
But this nagging issue turns me off more and more over time as my cities get bigger.
They look like cities, sure, but not ones I've ever seen. A bazzillion small office buildings all over the place with huge tall residential and commerical buildings in he middle.
I don't know what I'm looking at and I lose interest.
