This game is something else, truly. For starters it has beautiful graphics for it's time, it look wonderful and you can tell the developers worked really hard on them. The same goes for the weapon and shields, they are very nice to look at, and you feel a sense of accomplishment when you can buy that sword, axe, staff, that completely obliterates your enemies in 2-3 hits.
Now, gameplay, the controls are very solid and quite easy to control. At times it feels the mouse is a tad slow when it comes moving around and viewing everything, but it's easy to adjust in the menu. Also, there is no delay in the buttons so it is very nice.
The fighting is very unispired and makes combat feel more like a chore. After completing the main objective in the quest, towards the end of the game I just bolted out of there. No experience is gained whatsoever, so what's my incentive? Oh, that's right, gold!
Gold, you must collect gold througout the campaign. Some which is hidden VERY well and is extremely UNFAIR to get. When I say unfair, I mean that in this game, there are VERY FEW checkpoints. And if you aim to 100% this, you are going to pull out  your hair. Thing about checkpoints is, if you happen to reach one, but die..you lose gold. And that means you have to start over on the level completely in order to get all gold. Note, you need gold if you want to 100% the guy, buy more items and also  unlock all the characters. Again, it wouldn't be so bad if they weren't in such ridiculous spots. Earlier I said the controls are spot on, which they are, but the way these pots of gold and jewels are placed, it's beyond ridiculous.
Storyline, it was very meh. You don't connect the chracters at all and the cutscenes and whatnot are very short and semi-informative. I didn't really play it for the storyline, mainly nostalgic reasons. I played it previously on Xbox and just had to relive this games graphical beauties one more time.
Overall, I do recommend this game. And give it a 6/10. The graphics are what really makes this game, but also the nice weapons you purchase as well. The combat is very so so and the story is..well it's a story. Fun game if you want to hack and slash, but that's all you're really getting out of it.

[tl;dr] If you're new, SWL (the F2P version) is far more accessible than TSW (the old version). If you're a veteran starting over, beware: SWL is a much more conventional MMO than TSW. I think that's a good thing, but YMMV.
I started playing TSW in late 2015. I fell in love with it, so much that I bought a lifetime membership shortly before that option was retired from the Funcom store.
80 hours in, the game got more complicated and real life intruded. I suddenly didn't have time or focus for MMOs, and stopped playing for over a year. When I recently went to reinstall, Steam told me I was now playing SWL, a F2P relaunch of TSW. I verified my account, fired it up and found one character slot, no characters and no bonuses.
No character transfer? OK, I get that. The games are different, and it'd been a long time. I'd missed the first transfer period by six weeks. But losing the Grandmaster perks offended me. Happily, a single email to Funcom customer support was all it took to get lifetime patron status reinstated. I've since put almost 100 hours into SWL. F2P limitations haven't been an issue.
Playing as a lifetime patron with full-time job and family, SWL is more accessible and gratifying for short-session play than TSW. The differences are striking: character skills and levels, equipment upgrades and combat tactics have all been reworked. The result is a more mechanically conventional MMO that's still unlike everything else out there. If you've never played SW, this is the easiest version to dive into. If you've played TSW, how much you like SWL will depend on your tolerance for change, and your willingness to grind simpler MMO mechanics.
Bottom line: I like SWL. I'm not sure I'd have the time, energy or motivation to restart TSW, which was a much more demanding game. SWL provides the millieu, atmosphere and excellent writing, without requiring memorization of crafting patterns or assessing quest difficulty without levels. I'm sure the changes and overall simplification will offend many TSW long-timers, and I understand their objections. But ultimately I think SWL is the best way to keep this still-excellent game alive.

Now they left cosmetics as is, reduced number of bundles because well bundles gave you discounts. Removed discounts for subscription members / patrons (-20%-->0), made it so that your inventory space runs out really fast and that you HAVE TO spend real life money (1£€$ per slot) and not in-game currency on it as stacks are shamefully small (10 for items you have around 30 in general) as well as stuff that doesn't stack for well no valid reason. Not to mention that event fun items like fireworks or pumpkins will clutter your inventory (10 slots out of 35 you have). Maxing sprint speed costs 25$€£ (more then the base game back when it was still the secret world) and overpriced gatcha random loot boxes that cost a fortune to open give you pretty much nothing useful with ungodly low chances of dropping any cosmetics (I for one opened around 40 of them and got 0 cosmetics ZERO).
I'm also one of those people that both lifetime subscription back in the day for around 180£$€ as well as the base game 20€$£ and some micro-transaction points like 20$€£.

Three years later, the investigation into Scott’s murder has gone cold -- but Erica’s work has only just begun.
Jump into Cognition: An Erica Reed Thriller, the exciting four-part series that brings Erica face to face with the deranged demons of her past. A serial killer is loose in Boston -- one who seems to be leaving deliberate clues that only Erica, with her unique post-cognitive abilities, can uncover. Is she finally on her way to solving Scott’s murder? Or, blinded by vengeance, is she falling into a trap that could cost Erica her life? And how does this new killer know her secret?
Developed by Phoenix Online Studios (makers of the King’s Quest spin-off The Silver Lining), with contributions from veteran game designer Jane Jensen (Gabriel Knight, Gray Matter) and comic book artist Romano Molenaar (Batman, X-Men, The Darkness), Cognition is a thrilling adventure that grips you and won’t let go.

Overall, loved the game. I admit knowing nothing about the Iranian Revolution of 1979 before playing the game and I can't pretend I know a lot more, but it is a good introduction to the subject. It is very ''Telltale like'' and I do love this kind of games. For people complaining about the graphics and that it ruins the immersion, I say to hell with this. It is not like Mass Effect : Andromeda where we know they could've done better. This is not about the graphics. Yes, it is a little weird and cringy sometimes, but I was able to play the game regardless. I can also see why this game has such controversy and I can't really comment on the historical accuracies since I have no knowledge of the subject.
The only Cons I would talk about are that you can't skip some dialogue (when you have to start over a scene) wich can be annoying at some point.
And the ending...the ending is a major flaw for me. When you build up so much tension and end it in such an abrupt way, it leaves you a bit confused. I would've understood if there had been a part 2 to this but it does not look tha way. It is not really a cliffhanger for me it is just a...''that's it ?'' kind of thought.
Besides that, I really enjoyed playing and will probably play again. I got the game on sale so it was only about 5$ and was worth it.

Decent narrative driven game providing an unique historical insight. I understand the genre means it's more about the events than the action, but it would have been nice to feel more involved. That said, the central purpose to provide an account of what to me was rather alien and previously unknown was achieved. Nice to have history made interactive. Bit confused why the game has caused controversy because I felt it maintained an equilibrium and wasn't promoting a particular political view. Well worth a look and listen with eyes and ears open.

This is a very educational and interesting game which has a quite weak and uninteresting plot and very short length.
Gameplaywise, it's not so great. It has few quick time events, dialogue trees and shooting with camera, and that's it. The choices you make doesn't affect the story much.
However, what this game succeeds in is the portrayal of what the Iran looked and felt like before the revolution of 1979. This is a very interesting era of history when compared to what it looks like nowadays in the country. Iran was very liberal country before the theocracy, which is something that many of us westerners often forget. This same kind of regression could happen in west too.
So, as a person interested in Iranian history and politics in general, I found a lot of things here that I enjoyed and I think it is very educational game to play for those who are not familiar with the subject. However, I have to admit that otherwise as a game this is very mediocre. And honestly I think I may actually rather watch a documentary about the same subject.
Still, I'm very glad that this game exists and I would therefore recommend it if you got it cheap enough.
6/10
P.S: I would have preferred it to have the option to have voice acting in farsi while having the english subtitles. It would have given a lot more authentic vibe for the whole game and I think I would have enjoyed it more. I hate it when they mix up the languages in voice acting.

Quite frankly the most competitive and most well coordinated first person shooter I have ever played. Normally the people who review these kind of games seem to judge the game by it's graphics or the price. What makes this game so great is the dependence on other players, social interaction prevails over skill in this game. You most work as a squad of five players (against another team of five too), as a team to work to complete the objective and score victory for fellow team mates. As I lack in skill and am rather inept at aiming, I must point out that the genuine aiming and combat mechanics are very smooth. Weaponry is dependent on classes such as the S.A.S, Spetznaz and other special forces groups as well as different characters enables you to have a vast selection of different gameplay styles as different weapons and items vastly alter the playing experience. Items such as a Barricade and also tactical grenades such as smoke and stun grenades give you key advantages over your enemies. Thankfully unlike many other first person shooter games the community seems to be rather welcome to new players such as myself, I was not criticised for my lack of skill but rather I was given advise and help. Social interaction and proper team work is what many games seem to lack and in this game it works efficiently

From what I have salvaged so far, great game. I recommend it and please by the complete version, the starter version has various restrictions.

+ Overall game flow. It's just... perfect. Pacing is perfect, events structured logicly, everything is interesting. I'm gonna probably stop fan boying here about this game and will say one last thing.

If you've ever wanted to play a Katamari game, I highly recommend that you do so. They're full of charm, great visual design & music, and a unique, intuitive control scheme.
If, on the other hand, you would like to play a game which has none of those things, this may be right up your alley.

A wonderful little game that although tiny, provides an excellent homage to the Katamari series, through both visuals and mechanics.
Visuals:
Nothing amazing, nothing bad though. Bright colours, simple models, a nice cheerful atmosphere. A nice effort has been put into giving each world a theme. After playing though, I can't help feel more direction could have been given to the art. Perhaps even a stylised Borderlands-like approach could have differed it a little more from Katamari.
Gameplay:
Smooth with some minor hiccups. Sometimes the character can get a little stuck-ish between objects (because of the way it grows). The actual mechanics of the game work smoothly, being almost a clone of katamari. One thing I notice is its time restraints aren't nearly as strict as Katamari, so the experience is more relaxing. I did however, find it annoying that I had to pass 11 levels in order to unlock a new game mode.
Additional:
Music is top notch.
Overall:
A nice, small, relaxing game that's been carefully crafted. I don't think of this as a duplicate of Katamari, it's more of a game that just provides more Katamari-like gameplay that we all know and love. Not the most amazing game out there, but a solid experience none the less and well worth the purchase if you have a bit of time to waste.

I briefly played the original TSW and loved the story, but bounced off it due to the clunky combat and monthly subscription. SWL fixes quite a bit of that, taking it from an awkward MMORPG to a smoother action RPG experience that you can perfectly solo if you feel like it. The simpler combat still has enough depth to it to be engaging, even if it's definitely a more chill experience compared to most MMORPGs.
Above all... the story is intact, and just as good as the original. If you haven't experienced it yet and are tired of space marines and elves, see what a modern day mystery-horror story can really deliver. It's worth the price of admission which, hey, is conveniently free!

Critical Mass is an action puzzle game where you match colored blocks to remove them.  The more of a color you remove, the bigger the combo. This review is from a disabled gamer (I only play with a mouse).
Loading the game, you can easily access options and change the game to Windowed Mode.  Windowed Mode is borderless so you can change windows without exiting the game.  There's multiple resolutions you can set the window too.  It also has Colorblind Mode which adds a symbol in addiction to the blocks color.  Another option I was impressed with was the Mouse Button option that let's you swap each buttons role.  There's also a single option for the mouse but it seemed to be picky on exactly where I cllicked which slowed me down.  I opt'd to keep using  the reversed option.
Actual game modes include Classic, Survival, Meditation and Rush.  While most modes do require you to work within various time tables, Meditation is a completely untimed relaxing strategic gameplay.  To play the game, rotate the mass with your left mouse button and place blocks with your right mouse button. Many games actually didn't require much rotation so I completed many levels using only 1 mouse button.
If you're a mouse user who can left & right click gameplay should be a breeze!  Colorblind gamers should also be fine with colorblind option enabled.  It's actually my favorite way to play.

A game that follows the Telltale formula, but because it's played more as a documentary, it makes sense that you don't get to have a massive effect on the way the story unfolds. If you're a fan of history, like me, then it's a pretty safe buy. You'll get to experience an interesting journey through one of the events that shaped the 20th century.

This game's design is significant for those interested in how stories are told, and more specifically, how histories are told. It sets out a few interesting ideas for how to resolve the conflict between history - which is typically a pre-determined sequence of events - and the medium of games, where the player ought to have an influence on the sequence of events within the work.
Note that although this is as much as a retrospective essay as a review, there are no spoilers from the game's story, albeit the game's key mechanics are detailed.
solves the conflict between ideally linear history and ideally non-linear games in two ways: first of all, by putting the player in an inconsequential position in the greater scheme of things, so that they can make effective decisions without changing the arc of history; and secondly, by making the player's decisions inconsequential.
Now, there's not anything inherently wrong with inconsequential decisions. The act of deciding can be just as important as the impact of the decision, as demonstrated in Telltale's
, for example. The issue here is that these decisions - chiefly dialogue options - feel like they're meant to be significant, but the player goes into them consistently under-informed. "Should I back Ali or Bibi?" Wait a minute, which one's which again? And why should I pick one over the other? Arguably, this could contribute to the atmosphere of chaos and moral confusion that accompanied the revolution for many, but these uninformed and inconsequential decisions are placed at the heart of the player's interaction with the world, leaving you feel purposeless and unengaged.
This is most disappointing since, as I'm sure you instantly noticed, it isn't necessary for the decisions to be inconsequential. You could tell a different story with your little group of characters without affecting the truth of the overall history. I don't doubt this was ruled out by iNK Stories as it would demand more content than they had the time and resources to develop, but a more non-linear narrative would certainly be a way for the genre to advance in future, to give a sense of player purpose even as history remains inevitable.
The key and obvious reason why a game should be used to tell history is to engage its audience, and, while they're hooked, sneak in a bit of education. Engaging in facts and figures is a chore, but engaging in a story, with a character and with an interactive system should be "fun". So, it is puzzling why
so heavily depends on blocks of text to teach history.
Whenever you photograph something with your handheld camera, you gain access to a historical photograph and a big block of text explaining the context of that photo in more detail. While it may sound like a sensible idea for a game trying to teach history, it actually defeats the purpose of the whole endeavour. Blocks of texts are the No. 1 Public Enemy for all those trying to make an engaging game. They take the player out of the game world and push the idea that in order to complete the game, they should read lots of factoids.
In order to truly exploit the potential of games as tools for teaching history, all the history should be conveyed within the game's systems, ideally with images and sounds rather than text. Unless the idea is to be a kind of documentary-game, the player should be
the history rather than having to
it themselves, and they should be engaged in the history through all the usual tools of game design.
(Disclaimer: while design is my first and foremost interest, I don't actually think everything else is "superficial".)
The music is very well suited to the atmosphere of the game, effectively conveying the sense that revolution is in the air - words like "fear", "terror", "anticipation", "tension", "despair" and "gravity" come to mind. Unfortunately it does occasionally clash with the dialogue, but in general it is nonetheless a suitable soundtrack.
The visuals are unfortunately a little bit less than could be expected for a game released in 2016, doubtless partly because it was released simultaneously on PC and mobile platforms. While this explains the limited texture resolution and lack of moving parts - whether the crowds that use several copy-and-pasted animations or the hair made out of play-doh - it doesn't explain the underuse of colour, lighting and composition even where it would have no effect on performance.
The writing and voice acting, on the other hand, do attain a laudably high standard. Characters are conveyed convincingly. This is reinforced by the animation, which for such a small project, could afford to be hand-crafted for every scene, and the benefits are clear to be seen. At no point did I have to forgive the developers for half-baked writing, acting and animation, as one so often does in this industry.

1979 Revolution: Black Friday, as the title suggests, is a game about the revolution in Iran in the late 1970s. Its basically a Tell-Tale-style game about this time in history. You can read the summary of the game on the Steam page if you want more info.
The choices here seem pretty varied. You can choose to act violent, peaceful, neutral. The story doesn't change much. Choices really just affect who likes you and who doesn't like you.The story itself is very interesting. Black Friday I think is a piece of history that most people in the US won't have too much knowledge about unless you have family or friends that were affected by it. This game definitely follows in the roots of similar games like The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us. It's a great story with morally difficult choices and options that will have you regretting your decision for a long time after the game ends.
The game falters in the graphical fidelity and model animations department however. As engrossing as the story is, the lackluster animations really take you out of the game. This is incredibly evident in the earlier scenes with the large crowds gathered in the streets, you see models and animations repeated. It is definitely to be expected because of the indie nature of this game, but it really does take the edge off of the dire nature of the plot. The third person walking segements are by far the worst part of this game. They are just used to deliver the real world examples of Iran in 1979 via picture taking and NPC interaction (a la Dead Spaces tapes), but with the previously mentioned animations and the slow-moving character makes the sequences just dreadful to get through.
I like the precedent that this game sets of using real-world history that a lot of people aren't really privy to to tell a unique story from a perspective that a lot of the audience just doesn't have. It was enlightening to learn about this important part of Iran's cultural identity through the medium of a video game. However, the glaring faults of this game really show the cracks and difficulties of be taken seriously as an art form in the entertainment industry.
I can't recommended this game unless you are interested in the subject matter. $6 is not a lot to spend, but maybe you're better off spending it on something else.

Certainly one of the more unique and surprising games I've played. The concept had peaked my interest, as I'm a film-maker and interested in politics myself, and also interested in world history. I believe you cannot truly make an informed choice, until you understand the context behind what you believe, and the bigger picture. I'm well aware of Iran's history in the 20th century, from the CIA/British coup against Mossadeq, to the current day Islamic republic. When I'm told by the media that 'Iran is evil', my first thought is 'why?'. It seems in today's world, we're expected to hate on command, rather than to think critically and dig deeper. With that in mind, I was keen to see how the events were depicted in this game.
Black Friday is a character-driven story set during and after Iran's Islamic Revolution about photographer Reza Shirazi, from a wealthy loyalist family. Whilst taking photographs of the turbulent times of the 1979 Revolution, he quickly becomes roped into revolutionary circles, against his will, because of the pictures he's taken. The story is choice-driven, and you can disagree with being exploited by revolutionaries, or you can embrace it. Either way, this is not a story about heroes and villains. Everyone has their flaws, and most of the revolutionaries are more driven by their own paranoia and distrust for one another. The game doesn't glorify or specifically demonise anyone, but simply lets you see them as they are. From that, you can form your own decisions. Speaking of decisions, your decisions will carry real weight in this game, and Reza will face the consequences of his choices. There are even choices such as engaging in prayer, which can lead to different interactions within the story with other characters, some of which will happen in surprising ways. The two endings I've seen so far were totally different, and the second especially surprised me. The game is fairly short, so a second playthrough is no trouble at all, and it's great to see how differently things can happen as a result of your choices.
It plays largely like a Telltale Games adventure title, with a photography minigame built into some sections, where you capture the images of the revolution. Each time you do this, it'll unlock the actual photo it is based on, and the story behind it. In that sense, it's very informative and feels almost like an interactive museum of the 1979 Iran Revolution.
The characters are memorable, realistic, well-written, and well-acted. The production crew did a great job of telling the story of people caught up in dangerous events. Nobody comes out of it clean, nobody wins. In the end it is a sad story about the downfall of a nation, and the bloodshed involved. As I stated: there are no heroes here. Even if you play moralistically, you'll still be roped into dangerous circles.
In terms of story, writing, and events. This game reminds me heavily of Spec Ops: The Line. In the sense that it does not shy away from difficult subjects, such as depicting variations of Islamic faith, or the western interventions that have taken place in Iran's history.
My only issues with this game are:
-It sometimes stutters right before you make a choice.
-I had a bug where I was stuck in photography mode during a cut-scene.
-Some characters sounded way too American.
-Reza's father's head is way too big.
I'd recommend this to anyone who has an interest in history, and I'd recommend really taking the time to find all the stories and information. As someone who already knew a fair bit about Iran's history, I still learned some new things here. And unlike most Telltale games, I actually felt compelled to play it through a second time, which yielded a very different experience.
I've seen some downright silly reviews and claims, such as 'Muslim propaganda', 'biased towards communism', 'I wanted something anti-muslim and this isn't it!'. These are shallow, simplistic, misguided claims. The game objectively shows no bias, yet you can bias your protagonist's choices however you please. You can be pacifistic, you can be violent, you can be religious, you can be secular. All have different outcomes and they are interesting to see. In the end, this is not a story about Islam, it's the story of a dangerous time, in a turbulent place, and the story of characters caught up in it. Every character has a human side, every character has flaws, whether moralism, idealism, spirituality, brutality...
Overall, an educational experience. Ignorant folks could actually learn a lot from it, if they'd stop making presumptions and stopped to think for a moment before opening their mouths.

The game tells the events of the Iranian revolution by putting you in the role of a person that has ties to both sides and while your role is pretty fixed, you have to make some important decisions along the way. Historical info is presented in an interesting way mainly by taking pictures or interacting with the environment.
The story gets under your skin and even if the game is packed with information, it's the events that are the most important. The few quick time events are very well integrated into the story and make the game even more immersive.
I really enjoyed the experience and I highly recommend playing the game if you are interested in recent history or just a well told story.

The Wonderful End of the World by Dejobaan Games
Playtime: .7 hrs
Final ranking: At least A in all levels, mostly A+
EDIT: I had contacted Dejobaan about the issues with TWEotW and they advised me that they would look into the driver issues. If this fixes it I don't know but afterwards they also offered me a CD key to any of their other games to make up for the problems. Good customer service practices but still be aware before you buy.
TWEofW is a Katamari Damacy rip-off without the charm, crazy storyline and with a fraction of the fun.
The game offers M+K controls as well as gamepad but it doesn't have the dual stick setup like KD, so you're left either trying to us WASD and an overly sensitive mouse or getting used to using only the left stick because the right stick apparently moves the camera (but not really though.)
The graphics are appropriate for the setting, although a few levels break of the style and use random different art styles for better and for worse. I enjoyed the originality of collecting the word blocks during one level but another level broke the "3D cartoon" look in favor 2D flat sprites which threw me for a loop.
The music and sound is rather grating overall. I won't comment much more than that because I played for most of the game with the volume set around 10 to avoid listening to it.
TWEofW is far too short though and there's really no cohesive storyline. In one level you see a billboard reading "Do you know this woman?" with a picture of the redhead who appears on the game art. Really? I wasn't aware I was playing as anything other than Vectorman over here. Then after scoring at least an A in all levels (Not a very challenging task) you go to the final level, where fire and destruction are matched with billboards as "THE END IS HERE" and so on.
Also, On first run the game wouldn't start. It crashed right after the loading splash. Couldn't get it to work. Then one day when my internet was out I tried it again. AND IT WORKED! Hooray! It's got Kane & Lynch 2 disease, right? Well, then I had to  RMA my graphics card and I figured I'd give it another shot. Well, It worked again. So I have no idea what is wrong with this game.
Bottom line: Someone needs to give us a solid PC contender for Katamari Damacy and TWEofW isn't it.
HOWEVER, I was almost tempted to still recommend this game. The big break for me was the non-running game issue. If the game runs for you, you'll get a solid few minutes of "meh" experience.

As many others have mentioned, this game is basically Katamari Damacy on PC... except it is not as good as the real thing. Not that it's a bad game either, actually I had a lot of fun playing it, it's just that it's very short and has a few gameplay issues. To those not familiar with the Katamari games, the gameplay basically consist of moving around picking up any object/animal/person smaller than you. As you pick up stuff you grow in size and thus are able to absorb bigger stuff. Levels are timed and the goal is to absorb as many objects as possible within the time limit. The main difference is that in the Katamari games you roll a ball around while in The Wonderful End of the World you control a walking humanoid made out of spheres. Now lets get on with the review:
- It's Katamari Damacy on PC! The gameplay is the same and, to the best of my knowledge, it's the only Katamari clone in existence, so lets be grateful for having it on PC.
- The music is good for the most part, with some tracks bearing a style very reminiscent of Katamari Damacy (although I found the track from the Word Forge level very annoying).
- Levels are varied in design, there's indoor and outdoor locations and a few themed levels (e.g. Arcadia, Word Forge).
- As you beat levels you can unlock two other gameplay modes: time attack and free exploration. The latter is a blessing for OCD completionists like me ;-)
- Controls are responsive and you can configure the mouse sensitivity. BTW mouse-look provides you with more spatial awareness in comparison with the dual stick controls of Katamari Damacy.
- Levels are too short and there's too few of them. You have 12 levels clocking around 3-5 minutes each. This means you easily go through the whole game in 2-3 hours if you don't aim for all the achievements, and half of that time will be spent in replaying the levels to get the A grade required to unlock the final level. As reference, I got 100% achievement after 5 hours of gameplay.
- Level design could have been better. All levels are square areas (no around-the-world levels) and there's only a couple of them that deserve to be called big. There's nothing compared to the massive Katamari levels where you can end up engulfing cities, continents, planets and stars.
- Graphics are very simple and rough but get the job done. However, most of the objects are pretty plain, e.g. furniture, dogs, fruits, tools, average people, etc. Half the fun in Katamari was the charm and personality transmitted by the quirky characters and scenes you could find around the levels, they felt truly alive. TBEOTW levels feel more static.
- There's not enough challenge, most levels can be beaten with an A grade in one or two tries. However there's one notable exception: the Internet Cafe is a PITA, I ragequit several times when aiming for the A and A+ grades.
- The sound effects are just meh, I found the standard sound for when you pick up something lame, overused and, eventually, a little bit annoying. There's only a few objects with specific sound effects, (e.g. dogs bark, phones ring).
- There's little replay value. The alternate gameplay modes get old real fast since the levels are very short to begin with, there's not a lot to see. The main use for the free exploration mode will be to tackle a couple of achievements but beyond that there's no secrets or collectibles.
- Playing as a walking humanoid is not as intuitive as rolling a Katamari ball: it's difficult to judge your size and contact points with objects. Considering It's a time based game, it's VERY annoying and frustrating when your character gets stuck in a pass that at first glance seems wide enough to get through. Also, as you grow in size it becomes more and more difficult to pick up small objects even though you walk right on top of them, because the walking animation doesn't provide a consistent contact area with the ground.
- Unlike Katamari, in this game it's not size that matters, it's the number of objects you have absorbed what determines which objects you can pick up (eg. the object counter must reach X number for you to be able to pick up Y object). This means that sometimes you can't pick up objects that look small enough and, conversely, sometimes you can pick up objects a tad bigger than you'd expect. So you can't always trust your eyes to plan your pickup routes, you'll be forced to rely in trial and error.
- When you walk against an obstacle you just stop, but sometimes when you walk against a narrow pass you get repelled back a considerable distance. This is annoying as sometimes you get thrown against other obstacles or outside the boundaries of the level, losing many precious seconds as you scramble to get back on track.
The Wonderful End of the World feels like a poor man's Katamari Damacy that conforms with providing the same basic gameplay experience. It plays exactly the same but lacks its charm and challenge. That said, it's a decently fun game, albeit very short and rough around the edges. I wouldn't pay full price for it, but if you're like me and need to scratch your Katamari itch, I think it's worth getting during a sale.

Zombies, another virus, and wrestling.
Resident Evil 6 contains all of the above, and seemingly upset quite a few people in the process, but is it a bad game? Definitely not. While the survival horror series' sixth main installment is lacking quite a bit in the survival horror department, angering fans of older titles, it stands on its own as a fast paced action game, and a good one at that.
The base game comes with four campaigns, one from Leon S Kennedy and series newcomer Helena Harper's point of view, one from Chris Redfield and series newcomer Piers Nivans' point of view, one from Jake Muller (another newcomer) and Sherry Birkins' point of view, and a final campaign from Ada Wong's.
Each campaign is good, but Leon's stands above the rest, being the closest to the survival horror action of 4, and containing great setpieces that deliver action thrills while maintaining a little (only a little) atmosphere. Leon traverses an American town, it's large, imposing church, and eventually the backstreets of China, getting the most variety in locales. This seems like the obvious campaign to play first, and one fans wishing for survival horror may find enjoyment in too.
After Leon's campaign, Chris' and Sherry's are the two to play, and unfortunately for some, they focus much more on action and shooting than Leon's, with the new J'avo enemies replacing zombies as primary fodder. These J'avo function as soldiers, able to use guns and other weapons, and while some of the shootouts are great, the game too often makes the mistake of setting a vague objective and spawning endless J'avo until that objective is reached, making some sections a little monotonous, the worst of which being in Jake and Sherry's campaign. That being said, the C-Virus changes these campaigns a little as J'avo will react to damage in certain places with inspired mutations, and the odd full mutation can add more variety and excitement to the game. Ammo is scarce, but if the early chapters from these campaigns are played like survival horror games, players can easily amass a surplus for use in later levels.
The final campaign players should play is Ada's. It functions as an extra, and clears up many loose plot threads left dangling in the other three. If treated as a bonus for beating the game, it's easily enjoyed, and features some classic Resi puzzles.
The combat in the game is great. Unlike previous Resident Evil titles, you can now aim and move at the same time, making combat more fluid, and every character has access to a variety of melee moves. Leon, for example, can roundhouse kick, judo throw, and bulldog, though Jake seems to have stolen his head-popping suplex from 4. As in 4 and 5, shooting enemies in different parts of the body will elicit different reactions- the head will daze, the arm will turn them around, and the leg will often make them fall to the ground. Tougher enemies will play with this, especially in Leon's campaign, as heads may not always be the weak spot.
Bosses are of a high standard in all the campaigns, serving as many of the highlights of the game. The design is often inspired, as with that of the enemies, and while I won't spoil any of them here, they're often tense and exciting.
For fans of crazy action games, Resident Evil 6 is well worth your time, which makes sense as it comes from a company whose pedigree in combat is indisputed with games like Devil May Cry 3, Devil May Cry 4, Street Fighter 2, Street Fighter 4, and Asura's Wrath under their belt. For fans of survival horror, perhaps look elsewhere for scares, but try it for action anyway.

Rest in peace The Secret World.
I clocked about 50 hours in TSW, and though that's not much, I can admit that the game was pretty darn fun from what I played. I'm no great horror lover, but the way this was done was absolutely brilliant, and both the larger and smaller stories were extremely interesting, and from what I can tell, some of the story is still there, which is good.
However, what is utterly dead and buried is the old UI and character mechanics. Gone are the days of pick two weapons and play the way you want to, gone is the massive wheel o' skills, gone is the nice big ability bar with few restrictions as to what could be there. I put what, maybe 2 hours into Secret World Legends, and I doubt I'll invest much more. The new ability bar is awful, you can only have one basic ability, you used to be able to have as many as you liked, and that really bothers me, because suddenly though you have two weapons, you have to blatantly prioritise, and each weapon does different things, it used to be so rounded, so flexible, now it's rigid, like most MMOs these days.
The UI got gutted, one of the most unique things about the game has been outright removed, and I'm sat here wishing I could have my £20 back, because Funcom has let me down, and let me down hard.
I mean, if you want to give it a try then sure, the story is probably still intact for the most part, but it wasn't exactly easy when I first played it and I doubt that Funcom would dilute the difficulty, or they'd be pushing it to call the game Secret World Legends, it'd be better named The Secret Ripoff (Pansy Edition).

I don't write reviews very often, but I feel like this game has gotten a bad rep for all the wrong reasons, especially when I am perusing the steam comments. There is a common thread in most that, at its core, this is the same game released five years ago by Funcom. The same game that many said there was a great deal of potential in, with stiff combat and subpar end game content that really held the game back from being great. Full disclosure, I was one of those people that purchased the game back when it was The Secret World, and enjoyed it for about a month before setting it back down and thinking, “Nice, that was a good game for 7 bucks”. Now the game has a price tag of zero which, in my opinion, elevates it to a must play experience. You are really doing yourself a disservice if you don't decide to sink your teeth into the delicious beginning of this game full of gods, cults, secrets, and devils, who, incidentally, are always wearing kevlar.
Don't get me wrong though, there are issues that prevent this game from being the definitive free to play MMO experience, and I think they are much more harmful than what most people are complaining about; aka the core of the game being unchanged, and those parts that have changed being changed for the worse. This is all true, but not to the deal breaking level that many of the “old guard” claim, at least in my opinion. Item upgrading is different, combat is different, progression is different; not good, not bad, just different. It feels like Funcom went through the game and thought, “Alright, new game launch, time to shake it up” but didn't really pay attention to what a lot of the vets wanted in what is essentially a fresh coat of proverbially paint on an almost classic car. My point is, to the new player these changes don't matter and, frankly, there are much more troubling things that should be brought to their attention.
This brings me to my major gripe about the game; there is a soft cap for Marks of Favor that can be made each day. This is the main currency used by players to purchase items on the AH and buy cosmetic gear, and as it stands today there is no way to actively farm the currency. It does not drop randomly off of mobs, you don't receive it as a quest reward, and instead the only way to earn it is selling items on the AH, or through dailies. Selling items on the AH is mostly a no-go; they are deleted as part of the gear upgrade system, in most instances sell for a pittance, and can't randomly drop from mobs. Dailies are usually very simple “quests” that amount to kill 50 mobs, or complete three side quests, but the point is that there is a maximum amount of ~20k that can be made each day through them. To put this into perspective, that is ~1 leather trench coat and the unlockable garments are on a per character basis. Want to re-roll to become a wizard hobo dressed in rags and only answers to Bubble Gum Joe? Too bad: you will have to play for a month looking like Average Joe which completely breaks the role play experience that is so crucial to this game. There is only one way around this, and it is the reason why I can't recommend this game to anyone who actually wants to sink into the world long term; you can convert the real money currency into Marks of Favor to the tune of 1 Aurum → 163 Marks of Favor. That means, for $50 you can fast track your cosmetics on a per character basis by printing ~630,000 MoF, provided you can actually sell the Aurum to other players. And you better hope the demand for Aurum continues long into the game's life, otherwise even this won't be a good way to make money.
Now, on the face of things this doesn't seem like a big deal. “Who cares, they are only cosmetics after all. Why don't you complain about being able to buy end game equipment from the AH for real money instead?”, I hear you say. The answer is that cosmetics are everything in this game, it is the entire point to creating your character and going on your journey. The cosmetics are what allow you to create your gruff no-nonsense retired cop with a heart of gold, your skater chick who simply refuses to remove her ear buds in even the most desperate times, and your gosh darn Bubble Gum Joe. RP fantasy and interacting with the world is the best part of this game, and the fact that non-paying players are effectively deprived of that experience, even on alts, is a baffling move by Funcom which is, in my opinion, the nail in the coffin for this game. It is heartbreaking to have to play the first fifteen hours of this game as “Random Schmoe with his Kicks, Boot Cut Jeans, and Camo Jacket” on every single character.
That all being said, the price for entry is perfect at zero dollars, and the initial story really is a fun romp through a series of bizarre characters that are a joy to talk to and interact with. Just don't stick around for the end game, or long enough for Funcom to convince you to throw money at the screen for virtual raincoats.

This is one of the very best point and click adventure/detective games I've played ever.  In most point and click adventure games, you just click some items on the screen in order to progress the story.  But in this game, you actually feel like you're a real detective, doing the gumshoe thing and piecing evidence together in order to track down the murderer.  You use your psionic abilities to see into the past, you pick up photographs and items and try to figure out what they are and their significance to the case.  I highly recommend that when playing the game, you have a real pen and little notebook with you so you can quickly jot down notes and be more immersed in the game.

The game's low point would definitely be the graphics: the characters' skin has a weird shine on it, while movement is unnatural and glitchy. Overall, I hesitantly recommend it, if you don't think the glitchy graphics would ruin your experience. It is a shame however, that it was not built around its strongest point which is its art style.

It's a Telltale like adventure set in Iran in 1979 during the revolution.

While the game is rather short with like 3 hours, it's still very thrilling because the pacing is ace and the character are, even if not the deepest, fairly believable in their actions.
It's funded by some islamic film fond if that's somethign you care about. It's not the most polished experience, but compared to Telltale it definitely holds up. It's certainly not worse, save for the voice acting. That isn't very good. I think they should've gone with persian voice actors and english subs instead imho. "How much do I know about Iran in 1979?"
It's the question I asked myself when seeing this game pop up in my queue some time ago. I was able to start some "Wasn't that when..." sentences and remind myself that I watched a Ben Affleck movie in the past, but in general I had to admit that the most honest answer was: probably not that much.
It's for that reason I bought the game (the gameplay as well) and probably ended up spending more time in the 'Stories' section than playing the actual game. I wanted to learn more and I did. However, that also means this isn't a game to pick up for light amusement or just to bide time.
The story told in this game (to me) felt very specific, personal and thus also from a singular perspective with some other voices appearing only momentarily (in scenes and stories). In my case it caused a bit of confusion; realizing my character and those surrounding him were 'fighting' for something I myself wasn't actually too sure about. In return it made me want to learn more. And, if that were the objective of this game then kuddos.
There were only a few letdowns for me:
*Babak always blocking my path.
*Short time to make choices.
*Abrupt ending that didn't seem on par with the tempo of the rest of the game.
*The transition to learn more about 'stories' entries did not feel natural and broke immersion.
And some things I very much enjoyed:
*Taking pictures, genius move there, although I would've loved it if I'd been able to switch angles.
*The information (Stories) on events in the game both large and small.
*The story in general (til the ending).
*Voice acting.

Its a short game, you can finish it in about 3 hours but its engaging and also historical. Credit to the devs for trying to tell an important story and educate people on history and politics. The subject matter is great. Unfortunately the game isn't.

It's really short, but very well done. The game is well written and the characters feel real and the voice acting is excellent. The gameplay consists of walking around using WASD and taking pictures with your camera and interacting with objects and people. Because of the length, sometimes the story might feel a little rushed and it seems like the characters could have used a little more development.
As pointed out by other reviewers, the choices presented to you do not really matter THAT much. Some things might play out differently, albeit leading to the same conclusion.
Overall, it's a decent game, however it's really short. Can be finished within 2 hours. Considering this, it truly deserves a sequel, or at least another episode.

This is one of those few games that people who bang on the drum about video games are art will point to as an example. I am usually one of those people, and although I can confirm the game does reach in that direction, it falls a bit short.
However, this game has attempted to do something no other game has. Give a history lesson.
This game walks you through about 48 hours of the events of Iranian revolution. It shows you, in one way or another, all sides in the conlfict as well as their motivations and end goals. The game kind of railroads you through a handful of action sequences to keep the pace up, but it almost doesn't really need them. The details are rich and a lot of  questions Americans have about Anti-American sentiment are well explained.
Its a fascinating story, but it is a bit short. I completed the whole game in a bit over three hours. And although a part of me wanted more, they pack so many emotional moments and so much backstory and explainations into the game that it feels very heavy and exhusting to get through.
I would recommend to anyone with the spare cash, as I genuinely hope this becomes a new format of video games in the future.

Man, when I started this game I was like, a point&click game.. it's full of glitches, the cell shading characters are not what I like the most but I played this game for almost 15 hours !
The story tells about an FBI Agent Erica Reed investigating in the Cain Killer case. She has the power to see in the past and find out the memories that people forget.
It is a 4 Episodes story, each one follows the story amazingly and I got into it.
Some parts of the story are really morbid and disturbing (cutting body parts, killing her own brother, hangmens.) and to enjoy the game at max it requires a full walkthrough.
So if you like thriller stories with some horrible things, this game is for you.

A detective Adventure Game with an interesting "psy" mechanic/puzzle: what is more to say? oh. ok. Cognition is pitched for Adventure gamers and it delivers a great detective story even if a little flawed. It shows that this is not a big budget title, but this is still a very good indie title.
Visuals are reasonably good but are jarring at times (just plain ugly and an occassional graphic glitch). Voice Acting and Sound is good. The occassional Graphic Novel styling is good and not used enough. Puzzles are usually tricky and/or complicated. Interface is ok: it is likely that it may cause you trouble at times. The real star is the interesting story & overall good dialogue which keeps everything rolling on. Erica Reed is good main character,  but the entire supporting cast is just forgettable.
A rare treat for Adventure Gamers: this is a must. It might be a a little intimidating to people new to Adventure Games: get it if there is a really good sale.

If you are a fan of the point and click genre, get this without second thought. You play as the guttsy Erica Reed, an fbi agent trying to find her brother's murderer. The gameplay has a nice new twist from the usual point and clicks as she uses her psionic abilities to solve puzzles, like touching an object and seeing its past, memory manipulation to recover lost memories and more. The story gets more and more intriguing as it unfolds, all the puzzle pieces comes together to form a  clear and crazy picture at the end.
This game has it all, from amazing plot twists to ball busting puzzles. If point and clicks are your thing, or even if they're not, this game will keep you coming back for more.

All episodes have unique gameplay features, different extraordinary powers and duration of each of them is about 5-8 hrs.
An intriguing plot with logical and interesting puzzles, accompanied by beautiful soundtrack.

Fantastic game. One of the best stories in a video game I've played. Intriguing yet disturbing, and full of tense moments. The closest analog I can think of are the Ace Attorney/Phoenix Wright games. Now imagine those games without the court cases. Now add in much deeper investigation scenes accompanied by extremely cool "cognition"  techniques, and you basically have Cognition.
I can not emphasize enough how good the story is. Big budget $60 games struggle to achieve anything close to this. The characters have real emotions and real backstories, and the player will feel for them. Some characters make me want to punch them in the face, others make me tear up inside. Its these bonds that really make the player attached to Erica and her situation.
The story really takes off due to the tense moments. Although all games have tense moments, Cognition handles these so much better. The intensity never lets up. Just when the tense scene seems to be ending, something even crazier springs up. Best of all, Cognition is not afraid to have harmful consequences. In other games, I am relatively calm even in tense moments because I know everything will be fine once I complete the scene. Not so in this game. Even if everything is executed correctly, key characters will die, gruesome imagery will haunt the player and the sanity of the player will be repeatedly questioned. All in all, a must play and a must buy.
+ Incredible story
+ Engaging characters with personable backstories
+ Mood appropriate music
+ Innovative "cognition" mechanics
+ Vivid imagery
+ Intelligent puzzles that are never too vague
- Minor graphical glitches

Critical Mass is a puzzle game where you clear the field of blocks by matching sets of four same-colored blocks, as fast as possible. In this game, speed is much more important than smart block placement, so the game tends to be hectic and fast-paced (though, I usually prefer games that are the other way around). The game works pretty well, for the most part, and the puzzle action is fun. The graphics are clear and functional, though not terribly pretty, and the sound works, but you don't lose much by muting the sound.
The achievements for this game are unfair. Many require you to reach the top of the leaderboards.
If you're a fan of puzzle games and like challenges that require you to think quickly, or if you enjoy the competition of online leaderboards, then this is the game for you. Other puzzle fans should consider Critical Mass, especially since the price is good.

I've seen comments that this is a biased view of what happened, and yeah, it probably is. I don't think that matters, however, and people who complain about that seem to be wildly near-sighted. The strategy counterpart to Ultimate Chicken Horse.
Many of you have probably player UCH, which is a frantic game with no time limits on rounds, but utilizes platforming mechanics, traps, and coins as each person vies for the top score. Trapper's is similar in some of these regards, but differs on multiple key aspects:
First, the graphics of Trappers is a 3d-Poly design versus the drawn 2d graphics of UCH
Trappers has a time limit on rounds, but also the pace of movements is 'calmer' and more strategic
You can misdirect trap placement with Trappers by holding A and then moving the cursor, which is especially useful for one time use traps. These mechanics and traps like these are generally not present in UCH.
Coins and trap deaths increase you score in UCH, in Trappers, you instead build up a separate meter that helps you get more powerful/unique Supertraps.
Both games have a sort of balancing feature where offered items per round seem to vary if everyone performs poorly. However, Trappers still lets you build up to Supertraps if you get kills with your traps or collect coins. With UCH, the coin is only valid if you reach the goal with the coin.
Both games have built in level editors, but Trappers you download any number from the Steam Workshop, whereas with UCH you choose four for quick access with a Code system.
Trappers has a steeper learning curve with it's mechanics. I have found that UCH holds a better reception for a wider audience, but my matches in Trappers with people who enjoy it are more intense and exciting.
Stalling/camping is a viable strategy in Trappers: you can get ahead and then make the map impossible. This is theoretically possible in UCH but not really, especially without knowledge of a defined round count.
There is no autobalancing in Trappers, also, it is possible to individually customize your character but it is hard to really see what customizations you have done, and your sprite/avatar is relatively small to begin with.
UCH operates on a single level map for the entirety of the match, Trappers cycles through multiple maps in your playlist after a set number of failed tries on a map. This keeps gameplay somewhat fresh, especially if maps are made impossible.
UCH has multiple modes, but you cannot individually enable/disable traps. Trappers allows you to precisely select each trap you like or dislike, and has lots of fine tuned customizations available for the mechanics.
UCH maps tend to be more sparse, and rely upon platforms and moving objects to build a path to the finish. Trapper's maps tend to be finished maps with built in traps by default, but bridges and secret bridges are available.
UCH traps are always visible, Trappers has some traps that are invisible and others that blend well with surroundings.
UCH has fun dancing animals, although Trappers has a fun win screen.
Trappers has theoretical support for 8 players where everyone speed runs a map and no extra traps are placed. This mode is OK, but only really works well with certain maps. UCH does not have this feature nor would it benefit from it.
UCH has a higher sticker price but does occasionally go on sale, I got it from Humble Bundle so that was great. Trappers has a lower sticker price and may go on sale for a cheaper price.
Overall, while these comparisons may seem biased in favour of Trappers, especially with my longer experience owning and playing it, the real purpose of the comparison is to show the various differences between this game and another well known game with a similar concept but very different execution. Both are great games and I would personally recommend buying both games, keeping in mind which audiences are best suited for each, and that both don't have single player gameplay.

Quirky and dystopian, this excellent-value homage to 8-bit loses a few points for relying heavily on action mini-games 8/10
If you haven’t read the store description, this definitely isn’t a children’s game. Rather it is a lampoon of the cutesy pony games, and it goes into dark places. Demons and trapped souls make up the main story. The excellent writing makes the thought of souls trapped in an 8-bit video game seem perfectly believable. There isn’t a lot of realistic blood and gore that can be done with a limited graphic set, so the story line brings the creepiness to the game. The game juxtaposes cute and terrible to great effect.
There are 3 kinds of mini-games:
1.	Action sequences like a pony arcade game
2.	Programming puzzles
3.	Miscellaneous others
The programming puzzles are clever and the miscellaneous ones require out-of-the-box thinking. I found the pony action sequences to be repetitive and difficult after a bit, and require really fine timing and reflexes. If you're into classic arcade-style games, then this is actually a selling point. If you're not an expert, then the other good points of this game more than make up for it. There were a few times in the game where I had to look up help to get around a puzzle, and one point where I didn’t even know if I was in some sort of fool’s errand Purgatory with no solution. (make sure your screen brightness is cranked up)
The story is where the game excels. It’s creepy in ways you couldn’t guess... Several times it leans heavily on the fourth wall. For the price, the value is excellent. It took me 10 hours to beat the game, and I want to go back and get all the achievements. Definitely value for the money, I wish that more of the first-person adventure games that cost far more would have writing that’s equally good. The artwork is excellent too and imitates the 8-bit world right on the money.

The level size in Mad Bullets may be small, but thanks to its randomiser, this rail shooter offers incredible replay value and game time for a low price.
Mad Bullets is an arcade rail shooter that only has three (main) stages, but it uses a simple yet ingenious trick to offer more than other games with three times as many level: a randomiser.
This randomiser is truly global, as not only it affects enemy spawn, type, and aggression, but it also mixes up bonus item locations and even the levels themselves (all stages are built on the fly from a number of pre-set segments).
Mad Bullets is also not an easy game. Like in most endless shooters, the longer you manage to stay alive in a session, the more difficult it becomes with a larger amount of more aggressive enemies (even their projectiles seem to be faster). These are not the only things that can hurt the player, as accidentally shooting civilians, hostages, or one of the randomly spawning bombs can also quickly end a session when the events get frantic enough.
To further boost replay value, the game has an upgrade system, where players can collect gold during gameplay, and then spent it on either permanent or session-specific bonuses. These are the usual stuff: more health, ammo, better score multipliers, more item spawns, and so on.
There is only one major issues with Mad Bullets: due to a glitch, reaching level 20 essentially prevents you from competing for high scores anymore, so make sure to unlock only it when you are ready to move on.

In Off-Peak, you are penniless and play as just a city boy or small town girl (your preference), who is interrupted on their journey by train to find out that some megalomaniacal, giant-enslaving, rejected Dr. Evil minion named Marcus has cut back on transit funding (HE WILL REGRET THIS!). You first encounter Luke, a rejected ZZ Top member who worked with the Pawn Stars of the History Channel fame. Now, unemployed and still without a beard satisfactory for ZZ Top, he offers you a ticket out of the train station ahead, albeit the ticket has been torn into highly conspicuous fragments scattered about the station. This is where the adventure begins.
Step into a world where all people do is play complex board games, eat pizza and ramen, and collect classical sheet music. You can steal all the sheet music, grab the all the vinyl records, sample all the stale acid cookies, and consume all the pizza. For some reason, you can’t touch the ramen. The merchants don’t seem to mind the pillaging too much; they just raise a mild objection and then pretend that nothing happened.
Also, acid-tripping Mark Wahlberg break dancing at a desolate train platform.
You will also encounter identical triplet women who are probably of the children of Agent Smith from the Matrix and the twin girls from the Shining. These women have even harnessed the power of a longhorn skull to act as a 2-in-1 teleporter and Men in Black neuralizer. This is great news for the University of Texas and Longhorn Steakhouse.
Combining all this with grotesque modern paintings and pizza makes for an interesting affair, to put it mildly.
For the price of free, it will be worth your while to download this game and have a pseudo-psychedelic experience.

I'm giving this game an honest try  and I'm still only in the first Chapter, but as is, I cannot recommend it unless you are severely in lack of JRPG. Believe me, I like me some JRPGs and tacky stories about elements and whatever. I can put up with those, that's fine, and the story here is more or less pretty original, but there's a few different issues: as of yet, this is an handheld import with unimplanted features (such as the Monster book).
The protagonist is a girl which's main trait is being a ditz, which we are reminded of CONSTANTLY. The dialogue, which the game is nearly overloaded with, consists of doubtful jokes and a 'will they won't they' relationship between the protagonist and her adopted brother.
The grid battle system, while functional, is a bit clunky, as you cannot decide from which facing some characters will hit the target. This results in the occasional issue where a character with reach and mobility will knock an enemy beyond the reach of a shorter ranged character, artificially lenghtening combat, which already is trivial. There's no real penalty to dying, either, as you can just press the 'retry' button and redo your battle from scratch. There is a lot of back-and-forth travelling in this game, which sincerely becomes redundant. You also HAVE to set the camera on free rotation, as the awkward 45 degree angle will otherwise block important features on the field.
Only get this game if you're a hardcore fan of JRPGs, as it is average at best, and get it while it's on sale. For anyone else, you're free to pass this and play better games.

Pony Island is a psychological horror game. It's difficult to say what the gameplay is like, since it changes it's mode of gameplay often. But, the gameplay can be roughly divided up into three parts.
The first is a simple 2-D side scrolling game similar Canabalt or Robot Unicorn Attack. A pony runs to the right of the screen while jumping over gates and other terrain in the way. If the pony hits an obstacle, then they are taken back to the start of the level. Eventually, enemies appear. After acquiring a power up, the pony can defeat these enemies by shooting lasers out of its mouth.
Next is a hack-the-game puzzle game. In this puzzle game, three "columns" of code are presented. A pointer (representing code execution) starts on the top left corner and moves down. The goal is to get the pointer to a command at the bottom of the screen. The player does this by dragging arrows into boxes. When the pointer reaches that box, the pointer will move in the direction that the arrow points in. The game gets a little more complex once variables and jump statements are introduced into the game.
The third part occurs outside the game itself. As the player plays through the game, they will eventually “break out” of  “Pony Island.” Once this is done, the player gets to interact directly with the system running the game. This segment “plays” a lot like clicking icons on a windows desktop. Most of the story unfolds here.
As the narrative unfolds, It becomes apparent that Pony Island is no ordinary game. At some point, the player is asked to “insert their soul” to continue. Does this mean the game has come to devour the player's soul? By playing past that point, am I in an eternal struggle to win back my soul?
Well, not really. Or, at least the game doesn't make me feel that way. While the tone and ambiance of the game is dark and foreboding, the game does a poor job convincing me that it is evil. This is because the “evil developer” feels more like a nervous, insecure individual rather than anyone I should fear. The over world feels more like “hack your way through this area” rather than anything scary. Things get ridiculous when the game that is supposed to trap the player asks you to take a break because the rest of the game hasn't been coded yet.
Even so, I still like the premise of the game. I really love it when something innocent hides something monstrous deep down. Even if the game feels like it's pretending to be more evil than it is, it still carries the ambiance of a horror game. The sound and graphics of this game feel the slightest bit off. The “arcade cabinet” the game displays on feels old and decrepit. There is this eerie droning sound as you play much of the game. The music that does play feels spooky and demonic. And, there's even a few jump scares thrown in to boot.
The narrative slows to a crawl in some areas. This is the result of two problems. First, Many of the ghosts and/or AIs you interact with S-L-O-W-L-Y spell out their messages one letter at a time on screen. Second, there are parts with many too many hacking mini games clumped together. This is especially pronounced towards the end of the game.
Still, I like the game because I love cerebral horror. I was interested in seeing a horror game that would break the fourth wall and scare me. The game gets the ambiance right, but needs work in other areas. I still enjoyed it though. As a person with five dollars to spare, I enjoyed the game.

Alright, let’s get the obvious stuff out of the way. Yes this is a katamari rip off, yes the game is short, and yes the gameplay leaves much to be desired. But let me explain my reasoning.
I enjoy the original katamari games, even to this day (Katamari Damacy is one of my favorite PS2 games). They had a feel and a style not many games had at the time of release. I am not sure how many "katamari" rip offs there are on the PC, but if you are interested in the original idea of katamari, you’re better off getting the original games.
Right from the start of this game, you get a feel for the experience you have ahead of you. I don't want to judge a game from its cover, but all the menu buttons are small spinning circles, and the options menu is just a wall of comic sans-ish text for crying out loud. Once you start a level you will find it is very much like its source material. You roll around, pick up objects smaller then you, work up to larger ones. That is one of the very first of many issues with the game though. In katamari you have a ball to judge what you can and can’t pick up, and it works well. Here, when you pick objects up, you absorb them and they sort of morph into a human like shape. This makes it very hard to see what you can and cannot pick up. There are some objects that you are clearly much bigger then, however you cannot pick it up, or vice versa. You also have very limited camera control, and are only allowed basic left and right camera movement. This is not usually a problem, but in some cases it makes it hard to find objects.
Now, on to the music. The Katamari soundtracks were more than memorable, the music in this game, well, not all of it was terrible, but it was nothing great, just general stock music, some that I even recognized. Now I know this game had a much smaller development team then katamari, but it's hard to fill in such large shoes, and since they decided to try, it's only fair that I critique them on it.
Overall I do not recommend this game. I got very little playtime out of it, even though I unlocked every level. Almost every level made me feel like I was trapped in a small box, and there was little to nothing that I could take away from the game, experience wise. And for the current whopping price of $10, it’s a novelty to own at best, a low grade rip off at worst.

The Wonderful End of the World is, in short, a PC clone of Katamari Damacy, so it is easy to just say if you like that style of game you will like this one, but there are some quirks you should know going in.
The idea of the game is simple, you play this walking man made of magnetic balls that when you get near objects of your size or smaller you pull them into you, letting them become a part of your body and making you grow, you keep growing bigger and bigger and your objective is to reach a set score before the timer runs out, this is the main game mode, once you beat all twelve levels you unlock endless modes and whatnot, letting you goof around.
This concept is fine and the game itself is fun but there are some mixed feelings I have for it, to start the sound design leaves much to be desired, basically every item you pick up makes the same sound save for a telephone or something of that nature, all the sounds in game were obviously done on the cheap with what sounds like people making noises with their mouths, but that is not entirely a bad thing and has some charm to it as well.
The music is very well done and as with most Dejobaan games the overall design of the game is well put together, comical and tight, though there are issues that can be nitpicked, the controls are at times quite loose, it is not a very hard game or long either, you can beat the whole game in one sitting (In fact there is an achevement for doing that) and though the levels are very well made with unique art designs, there is very little replay value.
It is impossible to not compare this game to Katamari, but if you do so you will find that Wonderful falls a bit short from reaching that charming and very Japanese series of games, however despite that I still recommend this game, it's a fun time waster, doesn't cost a lot, and has just enough charm in it to get by, not to mention that if you are a fan of Katamari you have very few options on the PC for games like it.
You walk around, stuff sticks to you, you get bigger and finally, you consume the whole world. Katamari Damacy on PC. And it's fun. And funny. Buy it. It's Dejobaan Games.

Drew me in very deeply into a part of history I've thought about but had never considered with the texture on display here. An enlightening experience, well-acted, well-written with a lot of detail and production that is exemplary of the adventure genre. The only downside is, at two hours long, your choices definitely influence the story but the climax feels almost unresolved even if all of the relationships are.

To be honest, I'm quite surprised by this game and the almost unbiased picture it tries to paint; a picture of a part of history that seems to be almost lost within the fog of time - one that is not only crucial to fathom parts of the modern past of the middle-east, but of the whole world back then... and now.
You'll see the events of the Iranian revolution unfold through the eyes of aspiring photographer Reza Shirazi, who just returned to Iran, amidst the growing chaos and confusion in which he'll have to find his place and finally put his convictions into action. You do so mainly by interacting with the environment, NPC's and in particular by taking pictures with a camera Reza always carries with him and by which you'll be provided with additional information regarding the people of Iran and key players/events of that time.
Despite its short playtime and thus limited information on some subjects, 1979 Revolution: Black Friday largely succeeds at storytelling and neither needs to hide itself from or even avoid its competitors - on the contrary, the weight of the subject matter and how they handled it is elevating videogames in general to a level where their relevance in today's society and how they have matured truly has to be recognized - but before I lose myself puffing it up too much, it unfortunately doesn't do that well in the gameplay department. Minor bugs and things like a sometimes too small and narrow window, in which you have to react and decide in which manner you want to handle situations presented to you, tend to pull you out of the otherwise great immersion this game creates and hinders one at reflecting over the moral ambiguity such conflicts often inherit.
Nonetheless, 1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a game I can wholeheartedly recommend, not only to those particularly interested in the subject at hand, but to anyone that likes to question why the world spins like it does... and what better way is there to start while playing a videogame?
If this game in the end fully accomplishes what it wants though, or fails due to the complexity of the topic, is nothing I wanna judge over and since there's never an easy answer, no simple black or white, I wanna end on a quote that buzzed through my head while playing this truly unique presentation of these somehow almost seemingly forgotten historical events:
"Power is not a means, it is an end. One does not establish a dictatorship in order to safeguard a revolution; one makes the revolution in order to establish the dictatorship." - George Orwell

This is a game that brings memories of my teen years at the arcades. An on-rails shooter like a few of the games that were very popular late 80s/early 90s.
Gameplay:
You're a gunner in the wild west. Shoot everything that moves and is flashing red. Shoot anything in the environment. Shoot, shoot shoot. That's the basic concept behind the game. It sounds simple yet the game is not easy.
As an on-rails shooter, you have no control on your movement, you keep moving forward on a set path and you have to shoot things that pop up on your way plus projectiles that may also come your way. There are also things that you must not shoot so it's not just go-trigger-happy.
Graphics:
The game's graphics are simple with cartoony style. There are no graphics quality control options to speak of but, despite this, the game looks good.
Music/Sound Design:
Music is energetic which works to keep you on your toes (or should I say on the trigger? heh) and the sound effects are also fitting and what one would expect.
Pros:
-Not a genre you meet very often, specially on the PC.
