Lots of Jrpgs puts you quickly into a situation where you have to save the world, slay gods, stop religion and whatever...
They never take the time to build the world up first. Fleshing out the characters, and giving them a proper reason for what they are doing.
Trails in the Sky is different. This game is very slow paced... But that's the appeal of it. It never rushes to do anything. It takes it's time to build a coherent world, give everything a meaning and introduce many various characters. Who develops nicely throughout the game.
The main characters are Estelle Bright and her adopted brother, Joshua Bright. They are raised by their father, Cassius Bright, to become full fledged Bracers.
Bracers are guild members who are tasked to protect the well being of their fellow citizens and country. In this case, Liberl. A small and peaceful kingdom, that got invaded by the Erebonian Empire 10 years ago. In what was essentially called ''The Hundred Days War.''
Liberl suffered heavy losses, but still managed to drive the Empire back and survive the invasion. With the help of the military and strong support from the Bracer guild.
But at the cost of many lives, like Estelle's mother. This is what pushed Estelle into becoming a Bracer, if not only for her father. To become strong and experienced, so she can protect her friends, country and most importantly, her family. From another invasion attempt.
Lots of Jrpgs tend to focus way too much on the main characters and not enough on non-playable ones, but not in this game.
For instance, you are introduced to two news reporters within the first 2 hours of the game, Nial and Dorothy. They both have their own unique personality, character portrait and goal in their mind, with a lot of dialogue there to explain said goal in detail. From all this, we can assume they are somewhat important and MIGHT play a bigger role later in the game.
A lot of the characters you meet in the game are portrayed like this, and this is one of the many strengths of the game. To make every character look even a tiny bit important, whether they are friendly or not.
And in most cases, even when our heroes are faced with enemies that are human, they don't kill them. They stop them or knock them out. This helps present our heroes... As actual HEROES.
This is a great way to empathize with the characters we are in control of. It would be a bit hard to empathize with murderers.
This is what the game is good at. Creating a world that is detailed, introduce characters that are detailed and to explain things in detail. To build upon things, further and further, until the end.
If you can deal with the slow pace of the battle system in the beginning, you will really enjoy it later on. Opening more orbment slots, inserting Quartz (Materia in this game), getting new Arts (spells in this game) and that kinda stuff makes it fun to experiment with in battle later on.
It has cliches like any other game/anime, but that's not a bad thing. It's how writers handle these cliches. And I think, Trails in the Sky handles it better than anything I've ever seen and played.
I'm not really good at writing detailed reviews, but I hope this made you somewhat more interested in the game.

Revloution is less a video game and more of an interactive movie.  And a masterful one at that.  Clocking in at two hours, there really isn't much to go into detail about.  As long as you understand that you're not
so much as experiencing I think you'll come away feeling very positively about Revolution.
Visually the game is nothing to write home about.  Character models are iffy at best, background characters have little detail and overall the game isn't exceptional to look at it.  The animations are stiff and the portions where you're physically controlling Reza are horrendously bad.  But that's ok.  It doesn't take away from the experience because it doesn't impede the narrative.
The story here is amazing and well written.  Based on real events, it's basically an interactive time capsule and having zero knowledge of the Revolution I felt educated and informed.  The voice acting in this was PHENOMENAL.  The actors/actresses really pulled the narrative together with strong, convincing performances and in the brief time I knew this world and its characters I was able to attach to them and get intertwined in the story.
Revolution needs to be experienced to really understand what it has to offer.  Again, it's not a game and more of a visual novel of sorts.  If you enjoy Telltale games even a little, you'll enjoy Revolution as it has a strong story and very little interactive elements.  If you want something to enjoy that's a nice change of pace from typical gaming fare, and you enjoy stories and incredible performances, Revolution will find a sweet spot with you.

I played through a major ending and tried one or two branches, in 6 hours. I didn't get to additional major endings, but have read that there are different endings. I found this game's story immersive and gripping, and the art quite good, though there were small gripes I had with the walking speed and handling.
My favourite part about this game is the story. It plays like a Telltale game, with choice selection by your character in intense situations as the story progresses. What you do affects the people around you and potential results of major events.
The story is based on true events, and I found this way of learning about historical events very immersive. Walking around in the streets you can check out the local foods, listen to local radio... it was a virtual cultural tour for me.
I recall finding a magazine or cassette (I forgot exactly what) featuring the legendary singer Googoosh, which one of my close friends who is Persian, has often fondly talked about. This small detail in the game really had an emotional impact on me, because when I heard about this old singer in my real life I was kind of interested but didn't understand the context in which she was famous. Seeing a mention of her in the game however, as people yelled and screamed, and gunshots were ringing throughout the marketplace, really put into context how influential these cultural artifacts are and it was something I could relate to after playing the game. I really enjoyed learning about the history and culture from a game perspective, and look forward to more games like this.
One other thing that stuck out to me were the characters, I found all the main characters quite interesting and could sympathize/ empathize with them. We get to learn about the main character's family and how differing political opinions, especially in a revolution with heavy political consequences, can tear apart a family though they still love each other. This historical event really has torn apart many people's relations yet you can empathize with how strong human emotions can be, under these intense circumstances.
A small gripe was the walking handling by which I mean that sometimes the camera would move in strange ways and the walking speed wouldn't match up. Just a small thing which irritated me a couple times but wouldn't really affect the whole story in a major way.
Overall I recommend this game for the superb characters and cultural immersion. Do keep in mind that it will probably last around 5~8 hours, which depending on you could be short or the perfect length.

What's good about this is that it gives a concrete sense of what it may have been like to be in the middle of the revolution, including just the scale of the street protests. Several of the concrete artifacts that one finds are also interesting.
Unfortunately, the game frequently forces one to make arbitrary choices because one lacks the relevant background information. (This is partly my historical ignorance, but it's equally a lack of context about, e.g., who is whom.) The action sequence "mini-games" also proved contrived and moderately annoying. The result is a story that's only sometimes compelling.

Cons

Given the difficulties in creating this kind of a game that can be expected to a degree, but it would have been nice to see your decisions having a bit more influence on the course of the flashbacks you experience.

Overall I'd recommend it because it shines a light on an interesting part of history. Its a decent indie game for a topic that frankly larger studios have ignored.

A horror comedy that challenges you to outsmart several demons while fixing a broken program aimed at a chance of escaping whatever hell you're trapped in. From the opening moments of the game you're confronted with a start menu that refuses to work. You have to investigate other options to figure out why. This involves fixing the “code” of the software. Nothing too complex, the puzzle segments of the game presents a key that lowers line by line, from beginning to end, over and over again in a loop.
Your tasked with replacing certain lines with different Uno-style blocks and arranging them in a way that forces the key to the correct end point, thus fixing the option to play. These involve arrows that make the key jump lines, while eventually becoming more complex with added teleportation and duplication mechanics later on.

Soon enough you make your way into Pony Island after fixing the start option and you're presented with a pretty lame game. You play as a pony controlled with the mouse. The left button jumps and you can rotate your head by moving the mouse around. Jump over the gates. Do it again. YAY! YOU WIN!!! Now, insert your soul to continue.

If you're looking for a great, unique horror game, you've found it. I couldn't recommend this game enough. Outsmarting the evil at work feels so satisfying. Every click, drag, fix, and play with Pony Island feels like progress. That dull hum of the machine, the slow uncovering of secrets and various encounters with characters via text messaging all work very well to create a genuinely unsettling atmosphere. Everything great about the Horror genera is here with an interesting narrative that's heavy with laughs and fun to play.

I held off on writing my review until I got to Savage Coast, still haven't done a dungeon yet though, and I'm glad I held off because I don't have to rewrite my kneejerk reaction which was influenced by other negative reviews, the biggest influence being a review saying you were walked through investigations and they were dumbed down. This has not been the case with any of the investigation missions from the Kingsmouth area, they are the same as they were in The Secret World. The only walking through I have seen is on track/chase missions, the addition of the visual 'enhancement' mode for folloving tracks or fleeing monsters, which honestly I have mixed feelings regarding. I made it through them in TSW without the tracking assistance but was annoyed at the number of times I had to backtrack because I couldn't see the blood on the ground in the dark. That annoyance is gone, plus or minus, I really haven't decided yet.
I am still figuring out weapons and good combos for builds. That said, most weapons can be DPS or Support and Survival, haven't figured out best for tank and heal yet but I was never good at either in TSW. Overall every weapon is more powerful and more flexible outside of groups. There are improvements for every weapon and things missing from TSW that I miss but it's a complete overhaul and the one thing missing I won't miss is Aegis.
As a grandmaster purchaser I'm glad to see it carry over but disappointed with the lack of an auram replacement for the Funcom points bonus, especially with how much itemization has gone from in-game purchases to cash shop purchases. I think they went overboard in making things auram (cash shop, same thing) purchases which were origunally available from in-game vendors, example: the rotating clothing available in the Hatian market, I think overall the removal of in-game merchants is a big flavour detraction, as is the ability to buy skill and ability points from the cash shop just by hitting unlock in something you don't have the points for. It is unclear what vanity items which used to come as a package come with the purchase of one of the items as there is no cash shop window showing what is available yet and the old problem of unusable cash shop emotes not having a place to be purchased.
Still, with the things I don't like, I look at it and am glad Funcom shunted it to Steam without entirely removing themselves from the picture rather than shut the game down. I have seen too many online games I like shut down. Some were bought back from the dead but at the expense of only holding the developers' in name only and will never see new content. I have my issues with the change to Steam, the main one being constant disconnects, but overall I would recommend Secret World Legends and plan to continue to play myself.
I have gotten a lot further since the above part of my review and the disconnects have gone from constant to seldom. The way weappons are powered up is a grind for people like me who have no budget to spend on games right now, but for those who can afford it you can pretty much buy your weapons to max, even buy skills and abilities beyond your level, so in this regard it is a pay to win game but there are things you can't buy, experience, mission completions, brains... there are things that won't be a cakewalk no matter how much you buy in gear and abilities. There have been a lot of people who quit pretty quickly because of difficulty.
Something that will take getting used to for many people is Investigation Missions, as Funcom wrote, slightly paraphrased because I don't remember it exactly word for word, 'you won't always find everything you need for an investigation in the game, you will have to look at things external from the game sometimes'
I get frustrated at times because of the player driven economy, which is broken in my opinion, but probably not in the opinions of those with the monay to be on the seller side of the cash shop 'exchange' system. Many things don't go the way I would like them to but the game was my favourite game before migrating to Steam and it remains my favourire game.

Pros
- Its free to start
- The story requires no cash investment to experience
- Story is the best of any mmo I have played
- Atmosphere is amazing
- The currency exchange does mitigate some headaches of the f2p model
- Decent inventory system that doesn't hamper f2p players as much as it appears
- Combat is easy to grasp
- Gear system almost never makes time investment wasted
- Pretty good events that give good items
Cons
- Login rewards are about as exciting as bingo at a nursing home
- The Museum is just a tacked on haphazard currency sink
- The key system for dungeons,scenarios and raids are painful to both F2P players and patron subscribers
- Dungeons get very boring after doing them a few times.
- Funcom tries too hard at endgame to get you to open your wallet
- Combat is wonky in some areas like ground abilities not hitting mobs on certain terrain.
- Some achievements are rage inducing due to bugs and shoddy game design.
- Events are boring after you do them once
- Unlocking all weapons is a chore unless you open your wallet
Why do I not recommend this game after 190 hours? If I could go back and get my 190 hours back knowing how stonewalled progression is by dailies I would. The key system is depressing at best; abhorent at worst and upgrading to Patron to try to mitigate how bad the daily system is is a placebo. The worst part about this game is once your done with using your keys on dungeons, scenarios and lairs then there is literally nothing to do besides grind the same quests or go get rekt in shambala by people who play 24/7 and have legendary gear. That is basically endgame in a nutshell.
Another problem with this game is how badly they balanced it between Patrons and F2P players and it really shows that this game needed more work before being released as a F2P game.
Unless their F2P, subscription and endgame system is reworked I would just steer clear because this game isn't worth the time investment if endgame is just an elaborate net to catch whales.

I'm only a little over an hour into this game and let me tell you my first impressions.
First, as many have eloquently put, if you're a fan of JRPGs, this is for you. It's very much a JRPG and everything good that comes with it. The gameplay is great, battles promise a lot of diversity and the story offers just enough flexibility that you'll wonder, "What if I didn't get Dad that paper?" or "What if I rushed in without Joshua?" while still maintaining enough structure that you are experiencing a well thought out and developed experience. Such fluidity in the story and setting combined with excellent presentation allow you to feel that the world exists around you, which granted, may be preemptive of me to say, appears to be an accurate assessment of how the game is going to play out from here onward.
But I do have some complaints in that it is a JRPG, and with that comes some grievances in dialogue and storytelling. It's great, don't get me wrong, the localization is of the highest grade and a clear amount of polish and love was put into not only translating the game from Japanese, but also adapting it so that nothing comes across as lost in translation. Of course, that being said, I couldn't help but twist my lips at how "on point" the characters appear at first glance. The retorts are sharp and witty, consistently, which to some may come across as scripted. Because they are. This may not bother you, as the dialogue is funny and witty and sophisticated, but it bothered me. This is a common trait of JRPGs and especially in the beginning of stories, and to this game's credit, it has a lot of story to establish in a short amount of time, so better to get it out of the way now. Hopefully the characters will humanize a little better later on.
Also, keep in mind that this game is a port of a port of a game that was originally released on Japanese PC's way back in 2004, and while it has aged considerably well, if you're expecting the same kind of flashy graphics as in Agarest which embodies a similar art style, you'll get some of that, but just remember this game is over a decade old at this point. That isn't to say that, with that in consideration, the game isn't good looking and charming, because it is, but just keep that in mind.
All in all, with just an hour into what is being toted as a 40-50 hour game, I'm looking forward to the remaining 39 hours. And at $16.99 at the time of writing, the price ain't half bad either.

"JRPG fans, will probably enjoy this title."
To be brutally honest. The screenshots don't do the graphics justice. They are apart of the game and all, but when you actually play it, it looks fairly terrible. That being said, I feel that the focus of this game was anything but the graphics. I've played up to the prologue, which to that point, I think I can justify any pros and cons I have with it.
Firstly, I felt that at the very start, the information was being crammed down your throat. I know it's because they want you to start understanding what these characters are about, but still, it really bugged me. But about 10 minutes in, it lightens up to a much more comfortable feel. The main characters banter back and forth, ALMOST everyone has there own name and a minor amount of character backstory, and the world seems to interlock with everything very well. The setting is steampunk and magic is just this focus of these sources of power, which power anything mechanical. It's all fairly clever.
Secondly, the controls and combat. The controls, bug me alittle. They are rebindable, so this is barely a complaint, but if you leave default on, its either aim with the mouse, or arrow keys, which was alittle jarring. Outside of combat though, the movement was fine and I didn't really have trouble moving at all. The combat, which is grid and turn based, is fairly nice. Everyone in the battle has a portait on the left in order of who's attacking next. Using arts, (magic) will take a turn to summon, using Crafts (Abilities) will take points out of another bar which will increase within taking and dealing damage, and it carries over battles. There's also a surprise attack system, where sneaking up to a monster and charging at them from behind gives you a massive advantage, and vice versa. Theres also npc's that get involved aswell, which won't fight and may or may not be targets to the monsters.
So far, I've enjoyed the time I've been playing, which the prologue, I'd say is about 6-7 hours long, but this was me walking around, attacking alot of monsters and talking to alot of people. I've run into several crashes, which I think were related to having the aspect ratio uneven. The game seemingly needs to run in a square window, otherwise it may have problems. Aswell as I've managed to get stuck in a npc before, so I couldn't move but I got out of that without too much hassle. Really, In the end, this is not a shiny game. Theres 2D sprites, polygons, you name it. But so far, the characters are mildly interesting, the plot is typical, but still enjoyable, and the combat can get challenging depending on how much you grind, but theres so difficulty options. Otherwise, I personally am enjoying this game, mostly to see more things that are based around this universe and I've enjoyed a good portion of the game, when there not shoving too much information in one conversation. JRPG fans, will probably enjoy this title.

Unbelievable world building and detail, well-developed characters, careful deliberate pacing (although slow due to having to set up a huge saga as its first entry) and a well-written script all contribute to creating a world that pulls you in and is populated by characters you care about. Despite the huge amount of text in this game (yeah by the way, stay away if you don't like reading) I found myself savoring each and every line in the game, even those by random NPCs.
It's like reading a good fantasy novel, it really is the best world building and such work that I've seen in a JRPG, most likely ever.
That would be reason enough to jump in, but the RPG underneath that world is also fun, balanced, and somewhat nostalgic.
Battles have that "everything matters" feeling, a sort of mix between a strategy game and a traditional RPG system. Character progression is tied to the story, but gets really good after about the midpoint in the game, and battles ramp up in strategic scope as you go along.
Overall, this should not be missed by fans of JRPGs, or anyone that enjoys good narrative and world building in video games, especially the more literary types who are accostumed to diving into fantasy novels and taking in all the details and workings of a fictional world to heart as it slowly unravels in your head.
By the way, the random NPCs who roam around the village and such? The soldiers? The innkeepers? They have character arcs.
Character. Arcs.
That's all. There's no overstating the narrative and world detail that goes into this series.
Get it.

Great JRPG with some serious story/character development. Gonna start right out and say if you dislike dialoge heavy RPGs you'd best skip it, lol
Anways, this is a turn-based JRPG with combat that involves a grid with players and enemies having a certain movement range and attack range - its not FF style where everyone lines up in a row and whacks each other. Spells are rather unique and vaguely similar to FF7's Materia in that each characater has an "Orbment" that they can slot "Quartz" into and depending on the color and amount of Quartz you'll aquire new spells for use - sorta confusing at first but it works out to allow you more character customization than most JRPGs.
The game's story seems to be driven by the "Bracer" guild in which the main characters belong to. These Bracers take jobs at the guild job board and complete them. There are main Story jobs and then Minor jobs and quite a few at that! Its nice to have side quests more directed and meaningful, imo. The more jobs you complete the higher your guild rank increases and the better your rewards.
All-in-all its a VERY solid JRPG with a great deal of humor but also isn't afraid to be serious. Most importantly, though, is its fun and addicting! This is most definitely one of the most in-depth and long JRPG stories you'll find, every NPC has many, many things to say as the story develops and you'll find yourself going back to them to see how they are responding to events and what changes they've undergone!

This game is neither a rpg or a beat 'n' up. You have to complete quests and every quest is a complete level. There's no open world, there is only one possible way to go on. In every level you can find hidden gold which you need to buy armor, weapons and healing potions before you start a level/quest and you unlock new characters. And that's it. No level ups, no experience and no inventory. Before a quest starts you just choose a character like a warrior, mage or archer and buy him equippment. There's no a big difference between the weapons and armor, it's just like: pay more gold and it do more damage. Once a quest started you run with your character through a scripted tube-level and kill everything you meet. Sounds like fun, but the fighting-system is bad. I just played as warrior and he could only attack. If you equip a shield you can block, but there aren't special abilities or something similar. Certainly interesting and worth playing, but doesn't quite have the spark that makes the Katamari series so fun.
Story
The end of the world is coming, at the hands of a giant demon with the head of a fish. You might not be able to stop it, but with a magic puppet you have for some reason, you intend to pick up as much as you can before you run out of time. Just a little weird, and something I had forgotten after leaving the Steam store page.
Presentation
Graphically, some okay graphics. You know what you are looking st and picking up, and the ways those items are integrated into the puppet are pretty nice. Locations look nice, and it is difficult to fault the game here.
As for music and sound effects, there isn't much to say. The menu music is something I enjoyed listen to, but the rest is rather boring, and the sound effects are sparse, with some clicks for menu items along with sucking sounds and a bounce effect while wandering the levels.
Controls
Does the job. No Katamari style dual stick movement here. You use the mouse to navigate the menus, while within levels, WASD or arrow keys move the puppet while the mouse is used to control the camera. This game also has partial controller support, which allows you to use a gamepad for movement, but doesn't enable anything else on the pad. I much preferred using this as moving with the 360 analog stick felt more accurate for me, even without camera control.
Gameplay
Provided you have played a Katamari game in the past, you should already know what to expect. Move around the levels, picking up items smaller than yourself, with the goal of picking up as many items as you can before the time run out. The only change is that you are no longer rolling a ball, but moving a weird puppet around the level. This puppet will absorb smaller items while bouncing off larger ones, so you want to get as many smaller items as you can to help increase your size. At the start of the level, you might be rolling up toy cars and donuts, and finishing up with fire trucks and sky scrapers. Each level has a time limit where you have to pick up as much as you can to get a higher rank, requiring at least an A to unlock each level. This score isn't based on your size, but on items you have picked up, so picking up a couple of bottle will help that more than a bus. Took me a while to realize this when I was going for higher ranks to beat the game.
Lifespan
This game has a total of 12 levels to play in, each supporting three gameplay modes, though you need to beat 11 of the levels in order to unlock the extra modes. The standard mode is Timed, where you play as described above. The first extra mod is Timeless, which you attempting to pick up a certain number of items as fast as you can, despite the name. The other is Exploration, allowing you to do as you want in any of the 12 levels. There are also a number of achievements, ranging from reaching a certain number of items during your play time, finding a certain item in several of the levels, and resetting your save and then beating all 12 levels in one go. I don't see myself going for that last one any time soon.
So, not a bad game, but despite the similarities, it is no Katamari either. I say give it a purchase when it hits a sale.
It's pretty much Katamari with legs, but it's a fun and solidly done indie game.

If you enjoyed WD1, you're going to enjoy this one. The game is really fun, it never feels old, every single mission is different (something like the witcher 3 did). There are multiple ways to complete a mission (enter guns blazing, send drones or stealth).
The shooting isn't as strong as it was on WD1, the game actually encourages you to be stealthy but it doesn't forgive, even if you're seen for 0.1s, everyone starts looking for you and shooting. (that should be fixed). Although, you get some really nice toys like the drones to do all the job for you (my favorite way to play the game xD)
The city is really cool, it feels alive, there are multiple NPCs doing different activities and just "living their life" (NPCs kill other NPCs, bully, dance, take selfies, photobomb your selfies, etc.
The AI isn't good enough sadly... for example, if there is a small accident or just a car in their way that doesn't move, the whole traffic gets stuck or try to avoid the car just to fail and crash into another car... creating a deadlock. another example is that you can stay out of the "red area" and send a drone into this restricted zone, if the drone is spotted they'll search for you, but even if they actually find you and you're outside of the red area they won't shoot you... they just walk around you shouting stuff like "SHOW YOURSELF" or "I LOST HIM".
The driving is okay, it's arcade and gets the job done... and the physics, meh... they could have worked more on that.
Multiplayer... I haven't played much CO-OP but hacking other people and being bounty hunter is really fun, the huge improvement is that there are no loading screens (unless the other player is really far away), you get notifications when another player is nearby or they just pop up into your game, it is really organic.
The game runs well on my gtx 970 (ultra+high settings) but there is an annoying stuttering while driving (it seems like more people are having this issue as well), no issues while on foot though.
In any case, this game is a huuuuge improvement from the first game for people that didn't like it (personally, I enjoyed it), I'm really happy, people are enjoying it and giving good reviews, I had high hopes on this game and it delivered.

Light and highly abstracted simulation of mercenary operations in the Congo during the rebellion of 1964-5. Recommend only for the casual gamer or a gamer new to wargames.

CONGO MERC:  SOLO MINI-GAME WITH TOO MANY BUGS
The Congo in Africa has long been a focus of conflict due to its natural resources, which continue to attract the attention of foreign powers and businesses to this very day.  CONGO MERC is a single-player event-based historical game loosely covering the Simba rebellion (the word 'simba' in Kiswahili means 'lion' in English) of 1961-64, at the height of the Cold War.  You control foreign mercenaries plus Belgian (and Congolese? what about them?) and exiled Cuban units, fighting Congolese Simba separatist rebels and their Soviet-Cuban allies.
The Simbas were supporters of Patrice Lumumba, the Congolese independence leader and first democratically elected leader of Congo.  After peaceful independence from former colonial power Belgium in 1960, and being elected Prime Minister of Congo, Lumumba was captured and executed by pro-U.S. separatists in Congo's resource-rich Katanga state in 1961.  Crisis and civil war ensued, and in 1964 Simba rebels declared an independent Congo People's Republic covering much of the east of the country with capital in Stanleyville (now the city of Kisangani).  The Simbas took several hundred non-African settlers, businessmen and missionaries hostage, eventually killing about 200 of them.  Military assistance for the breakaway People's Republic came from the Soviet Union and Fidel Castro's Cuba, who sent revolutionary Ché Guevara and others to help.  This in turn led the U.S. to intervene by supplying mercenaries, such as anti-Castro Cubans trained by the C.I.A., plus U.S. Air Force assets in support of Belgian paratroopers and commandos.  Within a few months the Simbas were militarily defeated, bringing an end to the breakaway People's Republic with the occupation of Stanleyville by foreign fighters and Congolese troops.  Finally, in 1965 a coup d'état handed control over all of Congo to pro-U.S. military leader Joseph Mobutu, probably the bloodiest dictator of sub-Saharan Africa.  It is noteworthy that these important historical details are mostly absent from CONGO MERC, with a disclaimer that the designers do not intend to imply "approval or support" regarding the events, actors, politics or ideas depicted by their game.  Hot topic!
CONGO MERC was originally published by Decision Games as a table-top mini-game in their COMMANDO SERIES.  Every game in this series was designed for solo play only, using Event Cards and Mission Cards to randomize your goals and your opponent's behavior.  So there is no game AI, with most decisions of your computer opponent being the result of randomly choosing an Event Card, not multiple rule-based strategies as with real AI.  So the low price makes sense.
However, CONGO MERC has bugs which prevent me from using important features, like air reinforcement prior to battle, because it freezes the game requiring a forced quit without the chance to save your game.  It could take several updates before CONGO MERC runs smoothly enough to use all its features and options.
CONGO MERC uses a map of the Congo, divided into regions connected by roads, as well as by air transport and lake transport on Lake Tanganyika.  Regions are of two kind, countryside or town, with some towns having airstrips.  You recruit units, organize them into groups, and fight the Simbas and their Cuban allies as you move from region to region searching for hostages to rescue.  Your units have different specializations with different capabilities, like sappers who can blow safes and bypass roadblocks, paratroopers who can do air insertion and air reinforcement before battles, psy-ops who can provide new card draws on randomized events, supply columns who can carry hostages and affect battles, and more.  Randomized events occur as units move into new regions, like ambushing or being ambushed, finding intel, receiving military aid and having your operation reviewed by the United Nations.  Gameplay uses a fungible point system to recruit units, move them, engage in recon, etc.
Combat in CONGO MERC is simple, with each attacking unit receiving a certain number of throws with a die, similar to HexWar's 1775: REBELLION game about the American Revolutionary War.  You must order your units for attack/defense, with the first unit of one player attacking the first unit of the other player, and so on alternating one-by-one until every unit has attacked.  This repeats until every unit on one side or the other has been panicked or killed -- there is no retreat.  A lot is determined by who attacks first and by the number of die throws available.  There is no variable odds combat, only die throws registering the same damages against any kind of defender whatsoever, regardless of unit type.  This seems to ignore the different defensive capabilities of e.g. armored units.  But it does force you to think about how to order your units for combat, and whether and how to increase attack die throws, for example due to terrain (extra die throw for Simba units attacking in towns) or air support (four extra die throws for your attacking unit).
At the price of a few bucks, CONGO MERC provides a few hours' worth of simple solo gameplay through an interesting historical scenario.  But really that's it.  So much historical detail has been left out of the game that you don't know much about the units you command and fight against or the goals you pursue. (For example, presumably the leader Mike represents famed mercenary leader Mike Hoare, but in the game he is just Mike with no last name, so maybe it's not Mike Hoare.)  Randomization means you are playing against a die- and card-driven computer opponent, not real AI.  Bugs mean you will have to force-quit several times without saving, and will only be able to play to the end of the campaign if you remember what not to do so the game won't freeze.
I wish the publisher HexWar had better quality control because some of their games are historically interesting but have annoying bugs that significantly interfere with play. CONGO MERC is one of them.  Too bad because the historical novelty plus the low price should appeal to turn-based historical gamers.  Please, just fix the bugs so the game can be played using all of its features!  Then it can be evaluated on its true strengths and weaknesses.  Until that happens I must regrettably hold off recommending CONGO MERC.

Steam reports I only have 1 hour in the game... that's because I could not get the game to work at all via Steam. That hour is accumulated 'black screen' time over three hours of trying to get it working. I ended up going to the TSWL site and used their client... worked 100% fine the first time.... I've subsequently logged about 10-15 hours so far.
Pros:
* Free to play, and up to level 16 have not found the NEED to spend real money yet. I doubt I'll be playing long enough to verify this at or near max level, (see 'cons).
* Decent graphics. Honestly was expecting a bit better, as this was released this year, (2017).
* Unique theme of rpg & zombie killer. Even has some stealth elements, (although no way to 'sneak' or even crouch).
* The quests are enjoyable, but not TOO easy. Story quests sometimes make you think a bit, and some side quests lack any kind of direction. These you really have to 'figure out', that's cool... not enough of that element these days in games.
* Technically sound. Plays smooth with only one or two timy stutters in my short play time. Decent load times, voice acting is ALMOST perfect, and IS perfect most of the time. NPC models look good.
Cons:
* Only one free character slot, and each additional is $10, (ten bucks worth of 'aurum'.. the game-store currency). Personally, I thyink that's pretty steep. If it were half that, I'd have bought an additional slot, even though I probably won't stick around long-term. I had to delete a character each time I wanted to try a different class. Fortunately, the 'delete character' is instant with no CD on re-creation...
* The game is quite average. It's not the exciting, 'play-into-the-wee-hours-of-the-morning' game that I was looking for. I can tell how much I like a game by how long my first play session is. This one was about an hour and a half, which is really short for the first-time session.
* Leveling additional weapons besides the ones your class starts with seems to take forever and a day. Even to just get them up to where they are somewhat useful, at least in the levels I have played.
* Could not find in any menu how to be able to zoom the camera in and out while playing. Only able to do so with the 'esc' menu up. This was really annoying. I scoured the menus at length and could not locate any setting to adjust/change this.
* The upgrade system for weapons seems great at first, but quickly loses it's appeal and contributes to the games overall averageness.
I'll probably play the game a bit longer, maybe it'll get better as you level up. Fortunately for TSWL, there's nothing else around right now that I don't completely hate... so I'll play for a while more. Gonna recommend this game because some will love it, and those who hate it will hate it for what it does right.

Lastfight is a 3d arena brawler/fighter. The game is very much inspired from Capcom’s Power Stone. It's a pretty fun game. The color schemes, graphics, dialog etc. will remind you of a 70’s flick. The story mode revolves around the good ol’ “rescue your girlfriend from the evil people” plot.
The game’s graphics look superb with a sort of cartoony look yet it’s a bit different. The characters and the environment have a clean look art-style to them. Like there is not much details on anything but everything looks so sharp and neat, almost like cel-shaded.  I liked these graphics a lot. The game is a bit demanding, I had quite a few FPS drops during my gameplay but setting the graphics quality to high from Fantastic fixed those issues. So if you want to play the game at the best settings you better have a good PC, though there shouldn’t be any problem for lower end pc’s to play the game at low or even normal graphics presets.
There’s plenty of sound tracks in the game and they’re very nice to hear as well. The music sounds like 70’s fast paced almost pop-like music. The character voices, and other sounds are pretty solid too.
You can play local co-op or play the story mode. The story mode starts off with 2 characters. You get to play with either Duke or Richard. In between each fight there are cut scenes and some of the story unfolds. Both the characters’ story is same but some dialog/cut scene will vary depending on who you play with.
Other than story mode you can co-op with friends and play 2 vs. 2 matches which can be extremely fun. You can also play the versus mode with AI if you don’t have any friends hanging around and you feel like playing. The game is basically a very fun party game in versus mode. The controls are fully rebindable so you should have no problem setting up with friends.
The fighting mechanics are pretty simple. You can pick up and throw objects and they respawn so you can do it all over again. There are also power pickups and weapon pickups, e.g. you can pick up the Spartan (I think) helmet and it’ll transform you into Zeus and give you lightning attack for a short while. Pick up weapons like a rocket launcher which you can use to blast your opponent, boxing gloves etc. Picking up different power ups at the same time can also transform you into a much powerful character and you can wreak havoc.
You have a dash ability which you can use to dodge objects thrown at you. You also have a grab ability which you can either use on objects to pick up and throw at enemies or grab the enemy themselves and throw them. You can also block. When blocking, a bubble surrounds your character and the damage enemy does is blocked, timing it correctly can save you from a brutal punishment. Your character can also jump which is used on stages with multiple steps etc. There’s a total of 10 characters and 8 stages. Every character and stage have their own unique weapon/object pickups and abilities, though most characters feel very similar to each other in playstyle.
A short gameplay of the first story mission can be found below:
A very fun party game, the story mode is also nice but sort of short but the game’s real strong suit is the versus mode which can be endless amount of fun with friends or even AI. If you like Power stone and like fighting games in general, you will love this game.

Enclave is clearly a ported console game from a different generation.  While it permits key mapping, it fails to allow the player to save where they want; instead, it comes in episodes that must be finished before one's place is saved.
The game fails to make much use of the mouse, relying largely on the mouse buttons to hit stuff and do things, while movement is keyboard based.  The game has "gold" scattered around each section, and keeps track of how much is available vs. how much the player has collected in some action game-esque scorekeeping.
The real annoyance remains the "on-the-rails" style of play that Enclave delivers.  It's pretty, it seems to have its heart in the right place, but it gives the player no freedom.  One quest at a time, with marks for how much gold you collect, and then on to the next.  You cannot even open a door until the necessary trigger event(s) have been completed.
To be honest, this is really not a game that I would call an RPG.  Action, yes.  Adventure, sure.  But it lacks most of what makes a good RPG - including multiple active quests and ability to stray from the path.  I didn't even see character building in the short time I spent in the Enclave world.
I had such high hopes for this game, but it is time to resume the search for a good RPG.

When I first beat this game, I hated it like everyone else seems to. But after playing all of the campaigns and the Mercenaries mode, I realized that this game is a hell of a lot of fun if you go into it not expecting horror whatsoever. I actually kind of feel sad now that future Resident Evil titles won't be like this, because this game has systems in it that other games don't that make you feel like an action hero in a leather jacket. Things like the excellent dodge system that gives you unprecedented mobilty, the ability to Quick-Shot and do insane moves, the really good and responsive melee combat system, and all of the different unique animations for each and every character. I really enjoy playing it now as long as I skip all the cutscenes and play with a co-op partner.
Of course, the story mode is nothing special and it's filled with constant interruptions, bad pacing, and the writing isn't spectacular either. But I did enjoy seeing Leon and Chris again, off on another adventure. Jake isn't bad either, I guess, but maybe I just have a Troy Baker bias. And maybe it has to do with the fact that Jake can use kung fu while nobody else can.
I think that the gameplay is good enough that if the campaign were better, this game would have been huge. It's a shame that the campaign doesn't give you the opportunity or necessity to really use all of your special moves, and I confess I beat the game just as a standard third person shooter without bothering to learn any of it the first time, which is why I hated it in the beginning. This is why you should at least buy the game on sale to play Mercenaries, which is so good here that it could be a game on its own.
Still, I'd give this game a chance. Don't expect anything great out of the campaign, and expect it to suck every once in a while, but when it's good, it's REALLY good.

Unbelievable world building and detail, well-developed characters, careful deliberate pacing (although slow due to having to set up a huge saga as its first entry) and a well-written script all contribute to creating a world that pulls you in and is populated by characters you care about. Despite the huge amount of text in this game (yeah by the way, stay away if you don't like reading) I found myself savoring each and every line in the game, even those by random NPCs.
It's like reading a good fantasy novel, it really is the best world building and such work that I've seen in a JRPG, most likely ever.
That would be reason enough to jump in, but the RPG underneath that world is also fun, balanced, and somewhat nostalgic.
Battles have that "everything matters" feeling, a sort of mix between a strategy game and a traditional RPG system. Character progression is tied to the story, but gets really good after about the midpoint in the game, and battles ramp up in strategic scope as you go along.
Overall, this should not be missed by fans of JRPGs, or anyone that enjoys good narrative and world building in video games, especially the more literary types who are accostumed to diving into fantasy novels and taking in all the details and workings of a fictional world to heart as it slowly unravels in your head.
By the way, the random NPCs who roam around the village and such? The soldiers? The innkeepers? They have character arcs.
Character. Arcs.
That's all. There's no overstating the narrative and world detail that goes into this series.
Get it.

Great JRPG with some serious story/character development. Gonna start right out and say if you dislike dialoge heavy RPGs you'd best skip it, lol
Anways, this is a turn-based JRPG with combat that involves a grid with players and enemies having a certain movement range and attack range - its not FF style where everyone lines up in a row and whacks each other. Spells are rather unique and vaguely similar to FF7's Materia in that each characater has an "Orbment" that they can slot "Quartz" into and depending on the color and amount of Quartz you'll aquire new spells for use - sorta confusing at first but it works out to allow you more character customization than most JRPGs.
The game's story seems to be driven by the "Bracer" guild in which the main characters belong to. These Bracers take jobs at the guild job board and complete them. There are main Story jobs and then Minor jobs and quite a few at that! Its nice to have side quests more directed and meaningful, imo. The more jobs you complete the higher your guild rank increases and the better your rewards.
All-in-all its a VERY solid JRPG with a great deal of humor but also isn't afraid to be serious. Most importantly, though, is its fun and addicting! This is most definitely one of the most in-depth and long JRPG stories you'll find, every NPC has many, many things to say as the story develops and you'll find yourself going back to them to see how they are responding to events and what changes they've undergone!

The gameplay itself is simply the most traditional old school japanese RPG style gameplay. Fixed characters, unskippable scene transitions (you can skip dialogues by keep clicking), conservative romance, challenging boss fights, interesting combat paper scissors rock mechanism (which is quite old by today standards). This game afterall, is already a decade old.
Music was beautifully composed, and stood among the monumental video game musics in Japan at that time. Character design is old school, just like the old Chrono Triggers FF series and inherited the same writing style of its peers (Ys series). However if you are looking for something like BG 2 or DA:O kind of epic stories and characters, this is not your game. Not that it's bad, it's just nothing like that. It's traditional Japanese only fit with a twist of western fantasy drawings. The romance has no sex involved and the western style of bluntness to express yourself is considered reckless or vulgar in many cases. So you might have to put on another pair of shoes if you're new to Asian culture.
It pleases me that Falcom remains one of the few Japanese devs that still stick to their guns to keep the fun element as it is in a JRPG, instead of trying to please the modern crowd turning RPGs into action games. Even though they are only publishing console versions for their latest titles, I do hope the sale figures in Steam could let them consider a come back in PC market.

Getting positively surprised by video games is getting more rare each passing day since video games are evolving and there aren't really that many new tricks you can show.
on the other hand showed that not all games have to be cut out copies of other games. While not everything was original in Fields XY it certainly did surprise me by how fun the gameplay was. Puzzles and platforming? Sign me up!
While the idea of making a "two player game for one" isn't that new it's still a rather rare to see executed well. Fields XY combines a classic puzzle elements with platforming and some strategy. You control two different colored squares, red and blue, and navigate through the levels dealing with different kind of hazards and puzzles that will make you scratch your head a time or two. The red square will control like a platformer. You move and jump while avoiding hazards and collecting orbs to open doors while the blue square can move freely through the space and will not be harmed by hazards but it will leave a physical trail behind it that will fill space and thus create platforms or walls to either access new places or block something, like grey spaces which are required for you to open different kinds of doors to reach the end of the level, with each of the squares having their own level exit. You pretty much have two different kinds of games inside one.
You may have already guessed where the tough, and fun, part of the game comes. While you need to control both of the squares to complete the level and co-operatively navigate through the level with each of the squares you can mess up the level with a single bad move from the blue square. While you can help the red square reach higher places or get over a hazard you can block its way too. And no, there really is no way to complete the later levels of the game without the help of each other. So while you have the simplier platformer gameplay with the red square you need to calculate your path with the blue square. Remember, one bad move and your level progress will be gone. Fortunately, the levels are rather short so you don't really have to fear of failing a time or two. And what would a puzzle game be without some difficulties.
While the gameplay is fun there are a couple of things I need to address. The soundtrack, while being okay, only consists two tracks: menu music and the in-game music. After a couple of levels you will get sick of the soundtrack so you're better off muting the game and play your own music in the background. Also, there are quite some crashes with the level editor as of now. I didn't get the level editor to work at all. When I was trying to save a level the game just simply crashes. So if you are eager on creating levels for the game I'd suggest for you to wait a while until the crashing is fixed.
Overall Fields XY is a fine game. It's fun, has pretty nice graphical style which suits the gameplay well and level editor so you can play more levels as soon as people create more of them. It's well worth playing for any puzzle fan.

Please note I received this game for free, for participating as a tester. Fields XY is a fun puzzle platformer game, currently with 50 levels. You have to control 2 characters in order to reach the end, as you progress this becomes increasingly difficult with some levels taking multiple tries and a lot of concentration to successfully complete. There is also a best score for each level, if you are up for the challenge. Overall I would recommend this as a small and fun game to play every so often.

TL;DR: A buggy interactive graphic novel with a generic but engaging story, fantastic music and art, but not really tense, suspenseful, or bringing much new to the table.
I was a Kickstarter backer, and I backed this game because I was excited over the idea of a thriller interactive graphic novel. Unfortunately, it did not quite live up to my expectations, and I believe there are better Japanese thrillers to be played.
Pros:
- The music! The music is fantastic. Like, truly fantastic. If the soundtrack becomes available, I might pick it up. It really does help build the atmosphere (because most of the rest of the game provides very little) in a way that really carries the narrative. The fast upbeat music is hypnotic, the slow intense music really provides a lot of tension.
- The art is very good. I wish it was a bit more animated, but in general the character models are really solid. Reina in particular is a lot of fun to look at.
Cons:
- The narrative branching and decision making is mainly saved for the last half hour of the game. There is very little in terms of decision making or puzzle solving in the hours before the end.
- The entire story is told through dialogue, which is at times not particularly interesting.
- There are lots of bugs. Things look clickable that aren't, other things are clickable but you can't see them.
- It's a thriller, but there are very few thrills and very little tension. A few jump scares here or there, but overall very little in terms of suspense. In fact, it's almost too lighthearted at times. There are mechanics for your sanity and some other statistics, but they never once came into play for me, and it was like they never mattered at any point.
Neutral:
- The story is fairly generic for an interactive novel, but it is interesting enough to carry the game. I was at least interested in moving to the next section to figure out what was going on, and even though the resolution is somewhat bleh, the characters are engaging enough to carry the player along.
Overall, unless you *really* like interactive novels where you have very little agency as the player, there are better games available.
5/10

LastFight is an excellent arena fighting game.  It is fun and casual-like, anyone can enjoy this game even if you're not a pro at fighting games.  I highly recommend this game.
Gameplay is fairly straightforward and with simple controls, you have:  attack, special attack, grab dodge, jump, block and dash.  There are no special inputs that you need to do to pull off combos they are all preset, so you just keep tapping the attack button and the character will pull off their unique moveset.
What makes this game unique is there are items in the game that spawn and you can throw them at players.  There are also powerups that you can grab and transform into a super being for a limited time and wreak havoc.
Each character in this game are all unique, you will definitely find a favorite.  The stages are well designed and are fun to fight in.
The replay value lies in the versus mode, you can team up with bots and fight against bots.  Just start a game and start brawlin to the death.  The story mode is VERY short, I completed it in 20-30 minutes, and there are only two characters with story missions.  They are pretty much the same fight-wise
I have no gripes with this game.  All I want is more characters, modes, and stages.  From a hours to money standpoint I would say you will get your money's worth if you have friends over.  Playing solo can get tiring and not really worth it at full price.

Some are simple stages and some up the ante with hazzards that make you think of Power Stone 2 but you're still relagated to one arena.
The story was both good and bad. It's good in the sense that it doesn't take itself too seriously and is actually pretty funny. There's story transitions that last under a 40 seconds per fight so it's really quick but there are only two character campaigns in a roster of 10 characters. That's kinda sad man... Also the story has a very spotty anti drug message that seems to get lost in the fact that you win fights by taking the very same drugs you're mad at everyone else for taking.
Also, I kinda wish there was a tutorial. The game is simple enough to jump in and go ham but the AI starts doing some high level business that you kinda wish you could pull off.
All and all, this is a solid effort but it does need a tad more in the area of content for my liking. It's essentially a party game but I'd like to see the developers make more with it. I'm not sure it's done enough with the license to make me start going after LASTMAN as a series to follow and I do wish there was more content on display.
I will say that getting it for it's $13 price is decent if you can part with that much for a bare bones brawler, especally if you're itching for a Power Stone fix. Otherwise, wait for a sale that takes a tad more off the top. If you can get it for $12 or less I can definitely recommend. The game is good but it shows potential to be better.

Developed by French based developers Piranaking and based on also French comic book Lastman Last Fight is essentially the Power Stone game we have been waiting for Capcom to make for the last 16 years.
Back in the days of the Dreamcast the original Powerstone was one of my favourite games. It was different to pretty much all other fighting games at the time and was an absolute blast to play. The sequel inventively names Power Stone 2 added an extra 2 players and actually in my mind was not quite as good but overall I have been aching for a threequel for a good decade and a half.
Well Capcom aren't going to give me what I wanted but alas Last Fight seems like it is going to give it a damn good go. The game sees you in an arena with full movement and the ability to pick up and use weapons as well as fight. As Powerstone power-ups appear that when all connected transform you into a stronger special character that generally leads to you destroying you opponent.
The story mode follows Duke Diamonds or Richard Aldana in a mission to save Richard’s girlfriend who have been kidnapped by a secret organisation amongst an epidemic of drug crazed rioting. Its pretty silly but fits the theme of the game well.
The cast of 10 characters features a nice wide range of characters from aliens, to hobos, to goat faced businessmen but generally playing as them is pretty similar and there is not a massive diverse range of abilities. There are 4 different transformations to experience and these radically alter the style of play and are all pretty different. Some are better than others but all were fun to be and were always a key part of winning a fight.
There are a number of different weapons to also pickup most of which are simply used to throw at your opponent but there are a few things such as rocket launchers that add depth to the gameplay. One of the biggest gripes I have with the game however is that there is just not enough in the way of difference amongst the stages with most being square arenas not filled with an awful lot. Powerstone had a lot more things to interactive (or at least I remember it having) and the game could definitely do with a few more things to play with in the stages.
The game however is great fun especially when played with friends. Currently there is only local multiplayer available which is a shame and as is the case with most indie games there probably never will be online multiplayer but if there ever was a case for using Nvidia’s screen share feature this is definitely a good one.
I have generally enjoyed playing LASTFIGHT and it evokes a lot of fond memories of Powerstone. Sure it’s not perfect but it’s a fun game that is worth playing for all fight fans and fans of Capcom’s aforementioned Dreamcast Brawler as its probably the best you are going to get and at £10 you really can't go wrong.

This game left enough of an impression on me to write my very first Steam review, so here goes.
I'll preface this by saying, if you're looking at the store description, and screenshots, and videos, and it's even the slightest bit interesting to you, there's a good chance you'll like it. It took me a few months to finally pick this up and I really regret not buying this sooner.
I'm not going to beat around the bush. I love this game. The story is intense and interesting, the music is great, the animation fluid. Everything about this game just ticks all the right boxes for me. If you're into aesthetics and atmosphere, this game oozes with it.
As for the gameplay: It's your basic point-and-click adventure at heart. However this is mostly just a vehicle to carry the story itself. There's no pixel hunting, everything you can interact with is highlighted as soon as you near it. The "puzzles" really just amount to simple busy work or running back and forth talking to NPCs. Nothing special there.
One unique mechanic however is the introduction of the SPIN system. Depending on how you act to NPCs or treat the world around you, various stats of Ito's psyche can change postively or negatively and affect how NPCs react back to you. Paired along with this are the introduction of many choices throughout the game of how to interact with the plot. Choosing to drink at a bar, using your gun to skip some backtracking instead of looking for another solution to a puzzle, resorting to violence, all of these affect your stats in some way.
On your first playthough, the game autosaves constantly and only allows one save file, which can lead to some really intense situations. Coupled with the intense music, there were plenty of moments that really had me on edge.
Which leads me to my next point: Multiple Endings. There are quite a few different endings to get, and after your first clear of the game you unlock a New Game + mode which lets you save multiple files and skip some dialogue. (Still not all of the dialogue, and unfortunately there's still a lot to click through.)
(Addendum after second playthrough: There are actually quite a few bonus scenes and even an extra ending in NG+ so the play time isn't *quite* this short but I'll leave my first paragraph here regardless.)
Now for the one big negative I have against this: The length. At the time of writing this I have just gotten my first ending at 4.6 hours. If you care about ending hunting that's obviously not a big deal and can even be a positive but it needs to be said. Do I regret spending this much for so little? Not. At. All. I still feel this game was worth every penny, and there's still enough meat here to leave a satisfying experience.
There is so much attention to detail here and a lot of small things really add up to an awesome experience. From the animated cutscenes to the backgrounds to the story itself to the music (have I mentioned the music is great yet?), I'm going to remember this game for a long time and I REALLY hope Cherrymochi follow through with a sequel. I'll definitely be watching for it.
If you buy this, do yourself a favor. Set Discord to busy, turn off the Steam overlay, turn your lights off, put on earphones, and enjoy the ride.

Tokyo Dark is a great game that I enjoyed quite a lot, and I would recommend giving it a chance even if you aren't the type to enjoy VNs.
The story is perhaps the most important part of these types of games, and I was intrigued and on the edge of my seat from the beginning to the very end. Some scripted scenes were particularly enthralling and gave me goosebumps that few story-driven games can claim. The pacing of the story is good, and there's hardly any downtime before the next character-defining scene. The SPIN system is a cool addition and allows players to observe how their actions affect the narrative. The soundtrack is amazing and fits hauntingly well. There are plenty of endings, and some that require a New Game+, which is nice. The New Game+ also progresses the story, and isn't just another playthrough.
However, as much as I would like to gush about the game there were some shortcomings. The game isn't particularly long, and there aren't many choices that really matter. For example, I thought that being in the favor of certain characters would play a role later on in the story, but you never interact with that character again. Also, the SPIN system feels underutilized, and your parameters don't alter the course of the story all too much. Whether you play as a morally good or corrupt cop, crazy or sane, the majority of the story plays the same. All that changes is dialogue. That's a shame, because the SPIN system was what sold me on the game. Thankfully, the rest of the game is enjoyable to overcome what shortcomings it has.

The Wonderful End of the World is a pretty simple casual game. The concept seemed very alien to me at first despite it's simplicity but I am told this a fairly populated genre although most of the good incarnations are apparently exclusively Asian in origin. Despite glowing recommendations from my friends of these games I am having trouble imagining any game in this genre ever being anything more than a shallow time sink. The kind of game that would probably be at home on a mobile.
The game is very simple. You run around a map consuming objects by running into them. You can only consume stuff smaller than yourself and as you consume more and more objects you become bigger and eventually starts consuming the very map itself. The game is timed and as such it is simply a question of choosing the most optimal route through the map to reach those required high scores.
There is not very much else to say about it. The graphics are not very impressive and the sounds are pretty mediocre. The music is decent however although that is mostly because it is unlikely that you will ever play this game for long enough sessions for it to become stale.
Not really a game that can be recommended as anything more than a simple time waster for when you're bored and only have 5-10 minutes to play.

This game is pretty much everything Watch_Dogs promised, and failed to be. Fantasitc graphics, runs without a hitch, and a likable cast of characters. Where the first game took itself too seriously, this game is full of self-aware humor. It also features a much expanded music library that is magnitudes better; it even has classical music! Even the driving has seen a massive improvement. When I first hit that right trigger and began to accelerate, it was like stepping down on the accelerator of a Tesla Model S. I was floored at the acceleration, and it took a bit for me to get used to the speed in game (although that could be the result of the motion blur, which is pretty intense but worth keeping on). Now, for all that this game does right there are a few issues that I've found with it.
The inclusion of the drones, while being an awesome mechanic, make the game less of a challenge. There are missions where you are able to drone your way through until you reach a point where the message pops up "Only Marcus can complete this part of the Mission." While it can be fun to roll or fly about with the drones, I find I am able to rely on them too much (as if a drone gets destroyed, I just have to wait for the cooldown to get a new one.)
I also found that some of the new characters that are introduced as part of the missions are just dropped in with no real explanation of who they are, even though they seem to know of Marcus and his friends long before the game has begun. It would've been nice to get to know who these people are, so that they aren't just flashing in and out of the story.
Finally I find that there is a conflict between the character of Marcus, and the ability to simply roll through the game shooting everything up with your printed arsenal. It's strange to me that a guy that was wrongfully accused of a crime would then go out and shoot up a bunch of random people. (But hey, it's a game, and you're free to do what you will with it. I tend to go with the entirely nonlethal approach, just 'cause, so it's nice thye left it up to the player to decide on how to play the game.)
In closing, I think this is the first time an Ubisoft PC port has gone so smoothly. For the stability that this game has right out of the box, it was worth the added wait. Would recomend to anyone looking for something with quirky characters, just the right amount of self-awareness, great vehicle handling, and a beautifully rendered San Fransico to explore (I know I'll be driving around this game for a long time to come)

In saying that, you can just call the police on a crime like this, which is probably a better way to deal with. But for ME it just seemed a little strange watching everyone freak out as if you're in the wrong for stepping in on a crime they were almost oblivious to beforehand.

1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a choice-driven historical narrative game developed and published by iNK Stories. You play as Reza Shirazi, a photographer journalist who recently returned to Iran after studying in Germany. He returns amidst a political and populist uprising against the King, the Shah. The uprising is due to the growing income inequality between the rich and poor. This review will cover the story and characters, gameplay, and the soundtrack.
1979 features an excellent and highly-researched story recounting the history of the 1979 Revolution in Iran. Your character observes the widespread protests and takes photos of these events, assumingly for press in global newspapers. The story feels episodic because as television shows do, the story provides background on the revolution, jumps into it brewing up, and then ends. I completed 1979 in 2.5 hours, so it was not overly long, but I did not feel like it was a waste of money. Rather, it provides an excellent insight and perspective into the entire conflict. Briefly, I think 1979 should have been episodic because some portions of the story felt rushed and I think being episodic would have allowed the developers to expand on the story.
The characters are interesting because they are similar in their overall aims but contrast in their approaches. The main characters include Reza, who wanted to be neutral in the conflict, Babak, Ali, and Bibi. Note, there are various other characters, but I do not want to spoil it. As accurately depicted with history, the main protagonists want to spark a revolution because they hate the Shah's Government of pro-Western policies such as free trade, foreign investment, and so forth. This allows a percentage of the population to cooperate and spur anti-Western sentiment. I love the dialogue because it allows all characters to clearly emphasise what side they are on, may it be opposing the Government or supporting the Government.
I really enjoyed the overall story and characters and their different traits. I did not know much about the Iranian Revolution but the game provided excellent explanations on what it was about, why did it happen, and who really were the bad faction(s). The characters made it interesting particularly due to their internal conflict about how they wanted to achieve the revolution.
The game incorporates simple gameplay. You play from a third-person perspective when manoeuvring. When the game goes into a cut scene, it is cinematic. And, the overall gameplay relates to Reza capturing photos with his camera, therefore taking photos is in first-person. The photos really add a nice wrinkle because they allow you to feel like an outsider capturing information of within a conflict. I noticed some bugs with movement. Specifically, when clicking on something while moving, the game would freeze on you. Also, I found it difficult to walk in tight areas because people blocked you if you walked into them.
1979 features a 'stories' feature, which means whenever you take a photo, there will be an in-depth explanation of what that photo really meant in history and why. I really like this feature because I want to learn more about the conflict and culture and it provided me that. It is optional, so for individuals wanting to play the game and be done with it can have it their way as well. However, the stories feature was clunky because it was difficult to smoothly transition between it and back into the game. Furthermore, I noticed a bug with the wrong information playing on the wrong story.
1979 has a small, but strong soundtrack to accompany the story. I believe the soundtrack ultimately fits the vibe and atmosphere of the revolution because the music represents bloodshed and conflict. But, it also has sounds to enhance the cut scenes and  the stories told within those cut scenes. Therefore, I really like the overall soundtrack.
1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a very good game. I really liked understanding the premise of the conflict and I commend the developers for developing a strongly-researched and non-partisan story. My highlight was the characters and their dialogue because it allowed them to easily showcase their personality, there reasoning, and heighten the intensity within the game. I encountered various small bugs that did not hamper the game. At $11.99, I recommend this game. It is only 2.5 hours long, but  I was thoroughly invested into this as the story continued and made me eager for a potential sequel.
8.75/10
- Story and its historical counterpart.
- The game captured through a photographer that could choose to be non-violent or violent.
- Brilliant dialogue that showcased the diverse personalities.
- Decision-making aspect and how that determines outcomes into the game.
- The story felt rushed, I feel some sections could have been expanded on.
- Stories functionality is clunky.
- Some sparse gameplay bugs.

When Enclave came out in 2003 I was engaged in other pursuits and games, so it came and passed fairly under my radar. I managed to snatch it in a promo campaign so with fresh eyes I gave it a go. Having played first few missions, my first impressions are positive.
Yes, even after all this time, after more than 10 years, two more generations of consoles and after unimaginable enhancment in overall quality of graphic, production, but playability also, I can say I can still feel the solid (for its time, of course) design and interesting gameplay mechanics. What's different than current standards is that the game is devided in small separate areas with missions in them, rather than one seemingly conected open world. But the missions are short, have a coherency in the level design and can be replayed ad infinitum, if you left some secret with gold hidden. The combat is fun and diverse, 'cause you can pick one of many characters (classes) which all have several different spots for different equipment, so your options of killing baddies are fairly broad.
The story is fairly standard fantasy fare with lots of strange names and metric tones of exposition in the begining. If you like the genre, it seems standard entertainment, but if you find all the apostrophes annoying, you won't like it.
So overal verdict: much more things are positive, than negative, so a solid "yes" recomendation. If you manage to snatch it in some sale and like the 3d action RPG-light genre, you can find enjoyment in the game. If not, then there's no place for such an old game in todays saturated market.

If you don't mind a lot of reading and clicking after every sentence, and you're a fan of JRPGs, or even anime/manga, Trails in the Sky is definitely something that should be on your radar.  Whether or not you should purchase it now, just after release on Steam, is another matter entirely.  There was obviously no distributed alpha/beta stage to this development/conversion judging from the myriad fatal crash reporting.  Essentially, this means you are, currently, paying for a game that (in the current trend) is really an "Early Access", although feature complete, game.  With that said, IF you can get it to run stable, it's definitely worth the investment.
As of the 2 hour mark, I had to run the game, which then minimized itself, and stayed minimized no matter how I tried to access it, for over half an hour on the 20th run try or so.  After that half hour it did let me switch to it and resolved to a black screen that then began playing the intro a few minutes later.  The game played normally after that, but on two other machines I still can't get it to run.  One of these exceeds system specs by only a bit (i3,4GB,256MB) and the game loads normally but crashes after a few minutes of play.  The other minimizes as the first machine described.  Both of those machines are WELL beyond system spec.  I'll update this review once I've gotten more play time in for myself and gotten it running on these other machines.  But my advice, unless you're able to stomach potential fatal bugs, is to wait until the forums stop reporting crash bugs.
