Great premise but poor execution.
Among other things, I teach game design to middle school students, and I'd love to have a substantive RPG I could share with my female students. I thought this might be it - but it isn't. The problem isn't the premise, or the occasionally mature content. Rather, the problem is the execution. Far too often, the game contradicts itself. Far too often, the narrative breaks the fundamental rule of storytelling, telling you stuff instead of showing you stuff. And the RPG mechanics, while they bring back fond memories of FFII and FFIII, are pretty standard, and quickly get old.
An example. Vices as demons is a common but useful metaphor, and it could have been a solid foundation for a game that was both fun and thoughtful. Unfortunately, the very first demon battle (about 3 hours into the game) is just like every other battle. Before the battle began, the game told me in words that that this fantasy demon was a metaphor for the real problems of a real-world human. However, with the bland RPG battle mechanics, the game told me that this fantasy demon was just a bunch of stats - no different from a snake, bird, goblin, or manticore. Further, after defeating the demon, my princess was exactly the same person that she was before the battle began. There was no nifty mechanic, pithy punchline, no change-of-heart epiphany. At the end of the battle, all I got was a Scroll of Return - allowing me to teleport out of the dungeon. This was a huge missed opportunity.
On the bright side - the designers put lots of nice touches into the visuals and the UI. It's clear they cared about the game, and that care shines through the cracks in the narrative and the design. I just wish they'd been more consistently faithful to the premise, and had crafted mechanics that supported and enriched the narrative.
The completionist in me may someday sit down to finish this game so that I can lay claim all the achievements. Right now, I feel done. I'm a little curious about the story, but not so curious that I'm willing to slog through more cookie-cutter dungeons or consequence-less battles.

This is an open-world RPGMaker-based game where the protagonist Aerin Goldheart signed a contract with the demon of desire Izdul Kalag to make her husband Tommy Wocrome love her with all his heart. Things didn't turn out well as planned and Aerin has to travel through the world with her companions and defeat 5 different demons, each representing a different dark part of the princess to be able to break out of her curse and clear her husband's possession.
For an open-world RPG, the game is relatively easy to finish, with an estimated playtime of around 15 hours and doesn't require much grinding for experience levels or loot drops. The combat is simple and very consistent, with every character using the same weapon from start to end of game and only one optional jewellery slot to protect against a special negative effect or to enhance a certain combat ability. There are very few instances of failed or missed combat abilities or magic not working on allies or enemies that have no special resistance to that form of attack. The only con is the scaling up of prices for potions and elixirs with character level, which reduces the motivation to grind for loot and hoard 99 units of potions or elixirs. Among the side-quests available in the game, they are short and all can be completed without too much travelling or grinding for specific high-quality mob loot.
The graphics and soundtracks are great, it would have been nice if the game allows the take screenshot button on Steam to work. The deluxe edition is recommended when at discount as it includes the OST and the strategy guide which is needed to finish certain side-quests that require travelling to a specific area.

If you're looking for an exciting story that respectfully and accurately reflects the Iranian revolution of the late 70's, look no further.
The voice acting and dialog work well to immerse the player in the story, which itself is a careful balance between historically complex and emotional material. The characters' motives make sense in context of their experiences, and many decisions in the game that only lend themselves to bad consequences show how dire the situation really was.
It's clear that the game was made by an indie developer. Animations of extras are crude and 3d models are recycled, but this doesn't take away much from the experience and the game accomplishes everything it sets out to do very well. If you're interested in history or other cultures, you must pick this up. Hopefully, we'll see more games like this in the future.

Off-Peak is a great game for someone looking to kill some time with something unique. It's even more amazing for someone who enjoys the abstract art, music and dialogue that comes with this game. Like me.

This game is not perfect.
This game has issues.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Inviting world. The more you play, the more you want to explore and find out the secrets this location holds.
2. Interesting art. The fun and vibrate art contrasts insanely well with the more dark and depressing art placed around your given area. Not only that, but the art itself is just so dang pretty!

4. The incredible music. Archie Pelago. That's a name I soon won't forget. Their relaxing tones go hand in hand with the atmosphere this game brings. Their music is so good. The feelings every one of their songs give you. Superb.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The cons for this game:
1. Clipping issues. Invisible walls are NOT placed correctly. I've found myself reloading the game multiple times because of the walls trapping me.
2. No saving. You CANNOT save your progress. This wouldn't be such an issue if the game didn't trap you in walls. Making you reload to the beginning and making your progress null and void.
3. Art is not touching the walls. Some art is floating from the walls of the train station. Placement issues.
4. Poor optimization. I found myself struggling to even get 30 frames. Playing on all low settings and windowed mode. Some areas are not effected by this for some reason. After entering a random building, the frames decide to shoot up to 60 or so. After leaving that random building, the frames drop again.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Off-Peak is a fun, quick and free game to play for anyone with some free time to spare.

This is one of the best JRPGs you can play on PC.
Simply put, Trails in the Sky gets just about everything right. The characters are well-written and likeable, the battle system is fast but has a decent amount of tactical depth, and the graphics get the job done. It is never a chore to play. There's never some element of it that feels unnecessary or excessive, unlike many JRPGs of the past several years. I must also commend the excellent mouse control - while you can play it with a gamepad, movement and menu navigation via the mouse is so simple and easy that there's just no reason to do so.
What truly elevates Trails, though, is the attention to detail. The characters may seem like archetypes at first (the tomboy, the angsty young man with the hidden past, the wannabe-Casanova, etc), the dialogue (and there is a LOT of dialogue) makes them all feel very human and more difficult to categorize so simply. NPCs have new dialogue after every cutscene, letting you follow their little stories if you choose to do so. There's a lot of worldbuilding, too: the setting doesn't feel like it exists solely to show off impressive vistas and impossible places, but feels grounded in a very internally consistent way. While not a lot of it is forced upon you, there's a wealth of detail makes it feel far less like a playground for adventure and more like a living, breathing world.
It isn't all roses, though. While the worst of the issues that plagued the launch appear to have been solved and I haven't seen any crashes recently, there are still reports of crashing on area transitions, videos not playing correctly, and black boxes around objects. Be sure you know what you're getting into and prepare for the possibility of having to work to get a stable and playable game. It's worth it, though.

Obviously won't be everybody's cup of tea. But if you have fond memories of playing games like Grandia, or Suikoden, or most any other Playstation-generation JRPG for hours on end, devoting entire weekends to them, and if you've been dying to play a game like those again, then I can pretty safely say that this is probably your kind of game to play. It might not stack up by itself so far (as I write this review, I'm only ten hours in and only just beat the prologue), but it's definitely doing its job and bringing back those fuzzy warm memories.

TLDR:I FOR ONE I RECOMMEND THIS GAME WITH ALL MY HEART. This game was terrible on release filled with bugs, glitches, lag, and ping abusers. With recent patches the game has been fixed immensely and the playerbase has tripled since the announcement of the next release of operators. Ubisoft has come a long way here and they havent shown any signs of slowing down with the constant progress that barrages this game as of late. Sure there are still a few glitches with hit reg and peekers advantage but ubisoft has been picking away at it aggressively these last couple of months. Just a reminder to buy the standard edition if you dont wish to grind your life away getting all the operators. So goodluck and have the best of fun in this game!
First things first; starter edition WARNING because they do not allow you to transfer to the normal game. In the normal game 1st year operators  cost 500/1000/1500/2000 in game points in order to unlock, and 2nd year+ operators cost 25,000 each. HOWEVER, in the starter edition it starts you off with 2 free first year operators, BUT every 1st year operator afterwards cost you 12,500 in game points. Keep in mind with the operators in the normal game being significantly cheaper you could literally get an operator every 2-3 games if the games are long enough which could take just a bit under an hour. With the starter edition you are stuck with them costing 12,500 which would take about 10 hours if you won every game you played, or 20 because your points are literally halved when you lose. Let's say on average itll take you about 15 hours for each 1st year operator. Ongoing, you still have to worry about getting the 2nd year operators which cost 25,000 in game points with both copies. Not knowing all of this I bought the starter edition but I've been playing grinding games forever and I work so I was able to throw a couple extra bucks for the year two season pass.
With the sales going on right now the regular edition is much more cost efficient than the starters edition is because of the fact that there is much less of a grind and you get the refreshing feel of a new operator much more consistently. The operators all have their own unique playstyles, considering this; some are aggressive, passive, and a bit in the middle. There are utility characters, shoving characters, carry-ish characters, and peeking characters. Their playstyles are very unique, because each operators abilities and guns mold the type of playstyle that the normal player will use them for.  Also, Year 2 is almost coming to an end and the community continues to grow immensely which is amazing for someone that loves to consistently play this game.
The community is a game of russion roulette because at times you'll run into some super fun and chill people that you will more than likely befriend, but other times you'll run into super toxic people that'll tk and abuse you in chat, sadly you can only mute voice chat. Communication is a HUGE key in ranked because you'll need to call out roamers and where people are camping. Queueing with friends is the best choice since you know eachothers playstyles and might've come up with your own callouts while learning to play the game. There are games with communities that are much worse such as dota and overwatch, to where there aren't many games that have a better community unless you play ranked.
There are 5 major ranked categories in order of copper, bronze, silver, gold, platinum, and diamond.  The ranked system is pretty fair in terms of pairing you up with people of the same rank up until you hit mid plat then theres a chance  you'll be playing against high golds or low diamonds. Connecting this to my last paragraph; groups wont be paired against other groups in this game. If you play solo Q theres no way of saying you'll face up against other solo Qers, or a stack of 5 to where your team is stuck with a duo and 3 solos. Returning to what I said; you should play with friends or even Q up with randoms if they were super chill and a similar rank. The better the communication you have the better you'll be at ranking up.
There are different speeds in the game that drastically change the playstyle of those operators. There are 3 speed and 1 armor who are very fast and harder to shoot, but can pretty much be 2 tapped. There are 2 speed and 2 armor that are a bit slower but are also a bit tankier in return who are about 3-4 taps away from death. I didn't know much about the Iranian Revolution before I read the comic Persepolis by Marjane Satrapi. I highly appreciate those personal works of art that tell a perspective you won't find in articles or Wikipedia, but that are crucial to understand the complexity of the society at this time and get you much more invested in history than facts.
That's why I recommend this game. Though kind of short (roughly up to three hours) and importing the problems I have with Telltale games, I really enjoyed the mixture of historical events presented with original material and some details about Persian culture and what Iranian life was in the 70s.
What I didn't like was the timer and the pseudo decisions you could make. Most of the times it felt stupid, gamey and unnecessary to tell the story.  Same goes for the action passages and quick time events. Instead of copying that from Telltale, the creators should have added more depth to the characters, which is completely missing - or solely relying on unexplained stereotypes.
Another problem I have with the game is the lack of interactivity. Many scenes are more movie than game where you can only react with a text box you couldn't completely read because of the timer.
The usage of the camera as gameplay element and way to tell the role of the media in times like these, was something I really enjoyed. Though it's more a searching for the right spot to shoot  instead of a real free form tool, I like how it helped you exploring a scene more followed by a comparison of original pictures from that event. These photos, background informations and also the use of Farsi in combination with English is what left a strong impression on me.

Very good, but rather short JRPG. The music in this little gem is really great. One of the best soundtracks I've listened to in a while. The graphics are rather standard for an RPG Maker game, but some effects and a distinct set of tiles for each location creates a pleasant to look at game. The story isn't very deep, but it's well written and gives enough background.
The gameplay isn't without flaws though. There's the odd auto leveling of prices for inns and items. I guess it's meant to balance out the higher rewards you get from stronger enemies, but it just feels wrong. The other thing that is worth mentioning is the 'streamlined' equipment. There's only one accessory slot to equip something and the selection of equipable items only covers protection against the various status effects, more HP or MP and a small boost to attack. There's only one special accessory that you can get for completing a side quest. At least two slots and a bit more variation could have helped here.
The enemy variety and the boss fights are again very good. You won't find any 'recolored' enemies in this game. Each area/dungeon has its unique set of enemies and you will need a bit of strategy to get past them. The overall difficulty isn't very high, but it's not a casual game either. Make sure you save up enough potions before you enter any boss fights.
The game is only 15 hours long (including all side quests) and there's not that much to discover outside of the main path. A good amount of that time is grinding for levels as the lack of equipment forces you to make up for it by leveling your characters. It doesn't get too boring though even if the dungeons don't hold any surprises. You hunt for a switch or two and figure out which paths are dead ends. That's pretty much it. Still the game doesn't feel boring because the dungeons don't drag on too much and as mentioned above each location feels unique.
Overall it's a very solid JRPG with a bit wonky gameplay mechanics, but a beautiful soundtrack, a good variety of locations and enemies and an entertaining story. Well worth the 5 bucks.

Tokyo Dark is a psychological thriller visual novel with supernatural themes and light point-and-click gameplay. The story follows detective Ito as she slowly discovers her connections to a mysterious young girl, a cursed mask and a door leading to the dark.
As the game's title suggests, Tokyo Dark is full of mature themes, including murder, corruption, suicide and abuse. This may intrugue some while putting others off.
The major highlight of Tokyo Dark is its unique "SPIN" system (Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, Neurosis), in which gameplay choices and actions affect Ito's mental state and how characters around her perceive her. Depending on your score for each SPIN attribute, certain choices are available to you, which can lead to one of many story endings. Through this SPIN system, Tokyo Dark claims having a true "every choice matters" gameplay experience (though feel free to read my thoughts on this system in the "My Personal Opinion" section).

Tokyo Dark is my second experience with the Square Enix Collective Project. I'm not very big on visual novels, though I really enjoyed the Danganronpa series and was looking for a similar thriller/mystery type game. And before I dive too deep, I'd like to say that I enjoyed Tokyo Dark as a whole, but it has it's flaws.
For having so many endings, Tokyo Dark is still extremely linear. Throughout the game, you'll come across numerous obstacles, like a locked door for example. There are almost always exactly two ways to deal with the obstacle: use brute force, or backtrack to find a specific item that avoids force. The end result, however, is really the same no matter which option you pick. The only difference is that using force or violence has a negative impact on your SPIN attributes.
So what happens if your SPIN attributes decrease? let's say you choose to shoot the lock off the door to progress, rather than find a key. This action gives Ito a sanity score of -10, which means that she becomes slightly more insane. Other than this leading to one of the potential endings, my exact sanity score seemed irrelevant to the game (and this felt true for every attribute).
Getting to the point, the SPIN system didn't seem as impactful as I thought it would be, as it was specific individual actions that determined which choices (and subsequently, which endings) I could make later on. This invalidated the importance of many micro-decisions that revolved around influencing SPIN, decentivizing me to care about these decisions.
Despite the weakness of the SPIN system, I still thoroughly enjoyed the game's linear main story and multiple branching endings. My first full playthrough took ~6 hours, with subsequent ending unlocking tacking on several more. I highly encourage players to spend time unlocking endings, as each builds upon the overall psychological theme of Tokyo Dark.
For a relatively short visual novel, I personally don't think this game is worth $18. However, if it's ever on sale, it's worth a playthrough for those interested in a short, mature, psychological visual novel.

An excellent game that combines the Japanese visual novel genre with a more western adventure game feel. The result is a noir detective story that frequently strays into psychological horror territory.
It will have you questioning reality – flashbacks, dream sequences, floating masks, and multiple endings - including an obligatory “Insanity” ending that is reminiscent of movies like Inception. At one point, while playing in a dark room, I looked away from the screen for a moment and thought I saw one of those creepy floating masks the game likes to use to mess with you. Probably more a case of bright screen + dark room = seeing weird stuff, but it fit in with the game’s creepiness factor, so I mention it here.
The game uses a points-like system to track your decision making progress, with Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, and Neurosis meters. These can change the gameplay, from making your character respond negatively in stressful situations, to opening up new routes of investigation. Of course, the stats will also affect the game’s ending, of which there are 11.
When you finish the game for the first time, you gain access to save points and a New Game + mode that breaks the fourth wall more than a little. You also gain the option to skip large portions of dialogue, however, I’ve found it interesting how certain conversations change when comparing them to the first playthrough. My only complaint is how tedious the game becomes when you’re simply trying to click through to get to a new section or ending you hadn’t yet seen. More skipping options would have been nice – but I also think more save slots (in ng+) could eliminate some of this frustration.
All summarized, the atmosphere of this game is fantastic – drawing you in and leaving you wondering what the hell just happened. The music and sound effects are perfect to create that sense of dread and tension. 9/10

Based on running the WAD in GZDoom.
While a sequel to Heretic, Hexen also manages to do its own thing. There are now three characters to choose from: Fighter, Cleric, and Mage. There's a focus on melee combat with the Fighter and Cleric classes. The puzzles are noticably trickier to solve than in Heretic. Some of the enemies in the later stages are tougher than in Heretic. Both the visual style and overall tone is darker than in Heretic. Hexen could have easily been a game outside of Heretic's universe.
While I prefer Heretic, Hexen is worth owning and very fun for its own reasons.
While Steam's version is perfectly playable via DOSBox emulation, I highly suggest copying the HERETIC.WAD file to ZDoom or GZDoom (which looks better thanks to OpenGL) and running it that way. ZDoom and GZDoom provide mouse-aiming and modern FPS controls. The Steam releases of Heretic and Hexen contain the same WAD files as the original CD ROM releases. The GZDoom source port is how I've enjoyed Heretic and Hexen for years now.

Imagine DOOM.  Now imagine DOOM with everything changed.  From the simpler AI, to larger things such as the way weapons function.  Hexen completely undoes the "Doom clone" formula by NOT cloning it, and instead may have been one of the earliest attempts, if not the creator, of the "First Person Slasher".
There are 3 classes in Hexen, each with different weapons and abilities, but who also use certain items differently.  This immediately creates a desire to replay as a different class, seeing what you missed out on (and oh, what you will be missing out on).  Play as the fighter and gain access to weapons such as electrified battle axes, empowered longswords, and explosive warhammers.  Play as the cleric and use his mace,  a powerful magical serpent staff, fire gauntlets that burn enemies, or a weapon that literally SHOOTS GHOSTS.  Or lastly, play as the Mage, and use his wand, freeze enemies with blasts of ice, electrify enemies at a distance, or use the boss-killer Bloodscourge, which homes in on targets and tears them to shreds.
There's a plethora of enemies to combat in Hexen, all with lovely sprite art to represent them.  From two-headed Ogre's to Swamp Lurking reptilians, the enemies are varied in both appearance and tactics.  The centaur will use its shield to reflect attacks, the swampish Stalker will hide underneath the groggy swamp water before rising to attack, and the Dark Bishop, which can fly and and disorient the player by creating illusions of itself as it moves.
The worlds are as varied as the enemies are, rich in atmosphere and attention to detail, and all with their own environmental hazards.
There is one criticism though, which can be a death-blow to the game for some, but the need for players to actively hunt for switches in order to continue, and solve environmental puzzles are core parts of the game in order to complete it.  While the environments aren't too bad, one must pay very close attention to the text after pressing a switch, which can tell you varying amounts of information about what it has opened or activated.
I would highly recommend a walk-through for these parts for newcomers or more casual-oriented players, solely for the fact that it offers so much else in terms of gameplay, immersion, and originality.  There are also a number of highly respected wads available which have won Cacowards.

This review is mainly based on the PSP port of the game and will be updated with a more comprehensive comparison after I get farther into the Steam version.
Trails in the Sky is about a 30-35 hour JRPG that involves action, comedy, mystery, minor puzzle solving and quizzes, tactical combat, and a well-developed cast of characters. The deep story is fairly linear and a player has to be well-prepared for characters to move in and out of their party (don't get too attached to any one character as your main healer, for example, because after that chapter's over they may be gone). This movement can make for interesting gameplay as the player has to make tactical decisions about how to spread out and use their "orbments," which are the game's mechanic that give magic and special abilities to characters, especially as certain characters are better suited to certain types of orbments (e.g., Joshua's first orbment slot requires something time-based).
The characters themselves are all really charming in their own ways and will swiftly grow on you, even the ones that you don't recruit within your party. I'm especially fond of the four main female characters you encounter (Estelle, Kloe, Scherazard, and Tita), whom are all different and fun. Even better, the game frequently passes the Bechdel test and we get to see the four women interacting. None of them becomes the "token girl" you see in so many RPGs.
While I haven't played the other two games in the trilogy (as they haven't been brought over yet!), I'm eager to see what happens next. I haven't found anything on XSEED's website that says either way (though Wikipedia tells me "by the end of 2014") but I'm hoping the PC release will mean we'll get the next two games somewhere down the line either in this format or for the PS Vita.
UPDATE: Now that I've finished the game on PC, a few quick notes. After about the fourth day after release, I didn't notice any real bugs that affect gameplay, so the quick patching XSEED did seems to have worked. Further, it was really nice to turn the HD text back on as the other version gave me a headache to read. I definitely like the enhanced control systems -- you can choose to play with just a keyboard, just a mouse, mouse + keyboard, or even use a gamepad (such as an Xbox controller, which is what I generally use for PC gaming). The range of control systems meant that I could switch back and forth fairly easily if I needed to (e.g., I'd switch from a controller to the keyboard to give my hands a rest from clutching). There didn't seem to be anything major that changed in terms of the story line at all but I definitely appreciated the graphics more playing on PC vs. the PSP/Vita. I'm fairly nearsighted (if I don't have my glasses on I can't see more than about 10 inches away from my face) so playing on a tiny screen like the Vita can be a little frustrating. So it was nice to see the graphics blown up, especially since I didn't really notice any lost quality.

The best game on the PSP and the best JRPG of the last decade finally makes it's way officially to PC in English, instantly making it one of the best games on Steam.
Trails in the Sky is a throwback to the PS1 era of JRPG's that cuts out the clutter, pacing problems, imbalance, inconsistent writing/localization, shallow mechanics, and general
bs that age them so poorly. It is the first of a trilogy of JRPG's that have exceptional level of detail in its world building, yet tells a gripping, perfectly paced story. The massive undertaking of localizing this game into English was only accomplished through the blood, sweat, and tears shed by the XSEED staff. The localization is not just competent, it is one of the finest this medium has seen.
But a perfect localization of a fantastic story in an RPG would ring hallow if the game was not worth the 50 hour investment. Thankfully, Trails has a brilliant battle system that both accomplishes simplicity and accessibility in its design and has a satisfying depth of customization and strategy. It features a swath of compelling and rewarding side quests, a fantastic soundtrack that lives up to the expectations of a Nihon Falcom title, a diverse and memorable cast of characters, and a fantastic story that follows Estelle and Joshua's journey across the kingdom of Liberl.
Trails in the Sky is not just a great Japanese RPG, it's everything you could ever want out of a Japanese RPG.

Need for Speed Hot Pursuit is the first game of the franchise to be developed by developer studio Criterion Games who before had a long history of quality games, mainly known for the popular Burnout franchise with all times classic such as Burnout 3 Takedown and Burnout Paradise which revolutionized the arcade racing genre.
And immidiately you notice many similarities to the Burnout games, the game offers no tuning or any visual customization outside a few paint schemes, the cars endure much more visual damage than any previous NFS title and most importantly the physics and game modes are very Burnout inspired.
However you also immidiately see the NFS inspired mechanics such as the cop-racer rivalry and actual licensed cars and of course the hot pursuit brand lastly used 1999.
It does not offer an ambitious story, cut scenes or characters but it does have a very defined identity and it executes its idea extremely well.
By that i mean the physics as always are very well done and the spectacular map design helps the physics very much, there is basically no narrow city, just like the old Hot Pursuit the game happens on Highways to allow you plenty of freedom for beautiful high speed drifts.
Unlike previous Burnout games this time the cars have a Health bar and require multiple damage hits in order to be taken down which fits the game really well because Criterion has tried something completely new with the 4 power-ups they have introduced. All power ups are very well thought out and seem quite balanced.
The game also includes many game modes that thankfully are all fun so the game never gets repetitive and boring.
The car list is solid, obviously the cars do not drive like their real versions but they are different and it does not feel like one car is too fast or too slow.
It is a really well polished game.
Of course it is not a flawless game, the physics sometimes feel clumsy, if you fail a drift in a short cut, you might hit the wall to the right...and then to the left...and then to the right again because normal steering is not extremely effective which makes sense because the game encourages you to drift but it does lead to these weird situations.
The AI sadly uses the infamous rubber band mechanics which leads to weird situations where the AI accelerates or drives different to your capabilities, sometimes you see yourself using the very impressive Turbo power up which makes you very quickf or a short time and somehow you see the cops keeping the same distance like theyre also using the Turbo power up at the same time which they do not have.
For the Single player you will take about 10-12 hours, the multiplayer was fun at release when people played it, the servers are still alive in 2018 but you wont find random players in there so you gotta have friends to use that feature.
And even 8 years after release, the graphics are still very impressive, it runs on 60 FPS (sadly locked), the sounds are incredible, the presentation is superb, it is Criterion at their best.
This game feels like it could have had an even better sequel with a more interesting and bigger map, with more cars, perhaps even tuning but Criterion was used to develop Most Wanted 2012 and after that died as a developer unfortunately.
Overall this is an 8/10 for me, clear recommendation, this game has the mechanics and physics nailed down which basically makes it the only NFS title worth playing in 2018 since those aspects dont age.
What prevents this game from a higher score is the scale of the game, it is a game very heavily focused on its mechanics without much else which makes it a bit dry and soulless and once youre done with the Single player events, there is not much else to do, it does not offer much replayability outside wanting to beat a friend with the Autolog feature.
If you are interested in the racing game genre, you can check out my curator page which gives you an overview for all kinds of great racing games on Steam

We all know the Story of Watch_Dogs 1, the failed game, the "
" of what was supposed to be a really good and new game. And so many, including me, thought Watch_Dogs 2 was gonna be the same.
We were wrong.
I am surprised myself that I get to say that Watch_Dogs 2 is actually a really good, fun game.
Of course, it has it's problems, it's not perfect, but for a Ubisoft game, especially in the Watch_Dogs franchise, it is incredible.
The story
is really great. And yes, it is repedetive, but because of how differently you can approach every missions, it's actually fun to do something a couple of times. Or all the time.
In the beginning I was hooked, excited and actually calm. The driving has improved a lot, the physics though, well,
Yes, you can still wheely at 100km/h with Choppers and do backflips when you hit cars. No big deal, am I right.
But it feels better. Not chunky like in Watch_Dogs 1. I actually like driving in this game. Yep, I just said that.
The world doesn't feel empty or repetitive, I barely come across a person with the same name or text. The audio conversations you can listen to actually
like real conversations. Texts do too, just not as much. Someone tried hard.
You can also find dogs ingame, which you can pet and you will get reactions from civilians from this.
Something important:
Yes.
Unlike Watch_Dogs 1 you can kill civlians without a consequence. I like this feature, not because I am a heartless person, but because it's realistic. They sometimes call you out if you are in a restricted area or try to fight you if you almost ran them over. You can then either pull out your gun and just aim at them or actually
them.
Also; the cops are lousy. For real.
Lately I just ragequit. If my PC doesn't.
Yes, I get bluescreens from this game, but I may have fixed the problem for this. We'll see.
But you wanna know why I quit? Let me tell you.
if I play a story mission for 50 minutes after dying 4 times, I get creative and I eventually make it through.
And I did.
And as usual, everyone gets alerted and search the area for me which (since the city is open at all times and most buildings have
cover possibilities) I run for my life.
invisible walls make that impossible.
So I died. Again.
At this point I am really frustrated, but I completed the objective and think I can just start from there, right?
You can't. The game doesn't have checkpoints and you will have to start the mission from the
beginning. And it has been getting worse with the introduction of better and stronger enemies, which need around 100 rounds in the head to die. No joke.
Pros:
- Open City at all times
- Fast Travel to stores, caffe's and bars
- You can interact in those open interior places
- Much more texts, calls & Personalities on the street
- A lot of interesting places to see and visit
- You can take selfies and get followers for certain locations
- Driving improved a lot
- Hacking is not just a press of a button, multiple options
- Nice graphics this time
- Good combat
- Create your own weapons in the 3D printer
- Interesting characters, even though sometimes the audio is out of sync
- Good cut scenes, no overlap
- Costumizable clothes on character, paintjobs for guns and cars
- Be a Uber driver 'cause why not
- A lot to do beside side and main quests
- You can infiltrate the Ubisoft Office in a side mission
- Aiden Pearce apparance & quest
- (So far) a good story
Con's:
- No checkpoints in missions
- Physics
- Fast alerting enemies
- 360° vision on some enemies
- Marcus refuses to climb sometimes
- Can't walk over fences if they are below you
- Invisible walls
- Can't squeeze between objects you obviously  fit through
- Enemies get stuck in those spaces
- Controls (especially on the controller) are  a bit overwhelming at first
- (For me) Bluescreens with the High Texture Pack
As of now:
I recommend this game, even though it's driving me insane.
It is still a very, very good game. It's enjoyable and beautiful and you can just roam around and explore. You don't have to do missions if you don't want to.
It has issues, but the positive stuff is better than the negative.
I suggest you go and play it yourself.
But.
Checkpoints. Please, fix it.

Once upon a time I loved this game. Then they didn't update the story for 1.5 years. They also trivialized my character's progress and made it impossible to recreate her unique look.
Play it for free if you love mysteries, Halloween, ookie spookies, and things that go bump in the night. In 2017 there are better story games out there, but few of them provide a Lovecraftian global conspiracy theory that asks more questions than it answers.
The enigmatic throughline becomes tiresome, eventually, as does the inane gear upgrade system, being locked into starter weapons (short of rolling up a new character), level requirements on main story missions, and the need to pay non-trivial amounts of currency for basic quality of life features that other free-to-play and microtransaction-based games offer as part of the base package.
There's no point to paying for anything - you get so little for your investment. Spend time here if you wish, but nothing more.

I've played my fair share of The Secret World outside of Steam.  I think the game has great atmosphere, quests, writing, voice acting (for a MMO), and relatively decent graphics.  In particular, I love that a number of the quests make you REALLY think; I even had to solve morse code for one of them, which was no easy task.
However, the game lacks one very, all-important element that makes me drift away from it every single time I try to sink my teeth into it:  FUN FACTOR.  The Secret World is just not FUN.  The combat is absolutely boring.  The traversal is absolutely boring.  Social interaction is absolutely boring (let's just call this an online single player game, shall we?).  Your leveling and skill progression is absolutely boring.  Not even a well-voiced shotgun-wielding granny can make this game more enjoyable.
Sure, TSW has some of the best dialog in MMOs, but that doesn't really matter when your character just stands there like a stump, with nothing to say the entire time.  You make zero choices during dialog.  You get the exact same spiel every other player gets.  It's a good spiel, even GREAT by MMO standards, but it's still uninvolving.
And then, there's the whole thing where Funcom actually DELETED everyone's character they'd worked so hard on, whiping the slate clean for the new free-to-play Secret World Legends.  My character I'd spent over 60 hours on is just gone.  Poof.  Goodbye.  Nice knowing ya.  Does this sound like a company you want to give your precious time to?  I think you know the answer to that one.

Hexen is Heretic's sequel, but quite different - It doesn't follow the "beat X level, then go to the next" formula. The gameplay relies on puzzle solving in different "hub" maps, where you can access 4-6 other via portals in any order. This game is a small little gem...with a few flaws.
The story: Nothing special. A cursed princess on a journey to save herself and find true love.
Could be interesting, only that there is much interaction between the characters...and the NPC's.
Sound: OK.
Gameplay:  Well, of course there is grinding. Much grinding. Thats because your characters can only equip one item.
ONE.  And in the game there is only ONE item worth to be equipped...you get it after a sidequest.
Sidequests...only a very few. Most of them are bring me x-items...and the rewards are not worth the trouble.
Of course your characters can learn skills. After you level up and solving one of the quests you get points you can spend
for new skills. But again there are only a very few skills. Halve way through the story you have learned all skills.

For winning fights you get exp. and some items you can sell. No money gained. Not a big problem, because the only
time you need it is for resting in an inn...oh, you could spend it for potions, but you'll find enough in chests.

At first, when I saw the promotional screenshots for the game, I was appalled. Not only by what I saw as below average mapping (at least by RosePortal's usual high standards, compared to many other RPGs out there it doesn't stand out that much) but also horribly small characters that had barely anything redeemable to them. And the battle system - goodbye side-view custom battles, here we go, pre-made "first person" combat with sprites not really animated at all.
And yet, I gave this game a chance and played it through. In full.
And I don't regret one single minute.
Why? Like I said, graphics-wise the game is very much below RosePortal's usual average. It's not all that about the RTP tileset: the resource can be used to create beautiful environments that would be very much on par with Whisper of a Rose's (it just didn't happen here, instead we have a bunch of square-looking mazes), it's more about the characters, both the playable and NPC ones as well as the monsters. RosePortal made it a habit to have each monster fully animated in combat, here we have a simulation of movement by close-up effects or stretching and un-stretching the enemy pictures. The character sprites are RPG Maker VX Ace's defaults, meaning they occupy one tile (that provides little room for them to look good) instead of RosePortal's regular, whooping three. While the environments are varied, some of them just don't look authentic. Instead of posting a series of trees or a large unpenetrable layer of bushes/trees as the level "wall", RosePortal applied the one tile that I think shouldn't be used: a tree trunk on a black background... that looks grotesque when seen on the corners as the blackness between the trees would have been understandable in the middle but not at the corner. A few of the maps seem empty and barely decorated/filled with content, I'm mainly looking at the Old Dayaz desert area and Maplefield. The only actual custom graphics I've noticed are: the title screen and the intro movie, which both are really well done.
However, I'm bringing up what I said before: I don't regret one single minute spent on playing this game, not one bit. And that is because, quite frankly, The Princess' Heart delivers much more in terms of other departments than in terms of just visuals.
Let's start with the music. It's, again, downright beautiful. RosePortal have once again delivered an alluring, orchestral-sounding set of musical pieces which all fit quite well into the game's environments and narrative. I can't say it more clearly: buy the Deluxe version, just for the soundtrack alone, the music being already in the game files be damned. They deserve support just for the quality of that soundtrack alone. My absolute favorites are Dark Heavens (the demon boss combat theme) and The Beyond, named after one of the game's areas. Epicness absolutely ensues. Not a single RTP track was used in the making of this game, a stark contrast with the visual layer.
As far as the gameplay goes, this is your standard jRPG fare with a wee little twist. Just a little. There is no crafting option nor there are any weapons to be picked up (so that option is useless), instead like in Sweet Lily Dreams, the only thing we can equip our characters with are accessories. The combat system is simplistic but works - albeit it does have two new options. First, some spells have an area of effect - so a single-target spell may actually hit some neighbouring targets if you choose the right victim. That can actually save you a lot of MP which would normally be used for all-enemy-targeting spells. Second, you can swap characters in the active party not only outside of battles but also in-between turns! This can get you out of sticky situations - if some characters get knocked out and you have no means to bring them back, simply replace them with others, fully healed and just waiting to kick the monsters' butts. I happened to use this feature just once, on the final boss, but it sure counts: when it was almost dead and I knew my current party doesn't have what it takes to kill it in one volley nor will they survive its next attack, I just replaced them and in three further turns, the battle was over. I was the one left standing.
About the battles: they aren't a chore but they can be a challenge. Areas can technically be completed outside the beaten track as besides the final three dungeons, you can reach pretty much every location quite early on in the game. Enemies do NOT respawn in-between level sections most of the time, so you have to leave to the World Map - this may be a lifesaver if you're particularly wasted after just narrowly beating That One Boss. They do however have quite a level of difficulty, also due to the scarcity of items. There isn't an abundance: there's just what you get from the chests plus what you'll buy in the shops but with one catch: the prices rise alongside your overall character level so you won't be able to afford 999 of those Elixirs or Magic Waters. Most of the time, you need to make do with what you have found from chests. Money isn't earned by just winning the battle either, nor is it rewarded by the completion of a quest - you need to sell what you've acquired from battles in order to make some money.
About quests... well, there's just eleven of them, so not that all much, but then again a game advertised as 15-hour is less than a half of what you'd spend on Whisper of a Rose, so that number would kind of fit. What irks me is their overall lack of variety. Half of the sidequests involve you bringing the questgiver a bunch of high-quality drops from the monsters. The others do make much more sense but there's more than one occasion of the trope "Guide Dang It" being invoked. And it's a bad trope to invoke. I mean particularly the Cambolton Fortress quest involving the king's soul. Honestly, given what the Counselor was saying, one would think that the first place one should visit is the desert city Daragit. Uh... suffice it to say that it's a waste of time. The solution is right there in Cambolton, it's just so non-intuitive and so hard to spot that I literally needed a guide to complete it and I wasn't the only one, judging from the forums. A couple quests end in a really anti-climatic way, such as the Arsonist one (why didn't I get the option to deal with the guilty party?!) or the Emily exorcism one (props for the "Exorcism of Emily Rose" reference by the way) - why wasn't I able to actually WHACK the possessing demon instead of just having it expelled like someone snapped a finger and said "begone"? Yep, the sidequests definitely lack polish. The only reward you'll ever get for them is Journey Points which are used to learn skills. And again, there's a glaring issue: at some point (as a little grinding
recommended to progress smoothly and you also get JPs after gaining character levels) there's simply TOO MUCH of these points to spend'em.

This story is not true. Those were the first words to greet me into this game after some rather awkward form of configuration. Just like how you don't hang out at alcoholics anonymous meetings for a laugh, don't come to this game expecting a documentary style affair. Don't come into this game expecting a lot, it saves a lot of disappointment in the long run.
Well, as if that little statement didn't give away my opinion on this. I should elaborate. The Princess' Heart is a story written from the perspective of an adolscent girl and like everyone's early work, this is just awful.
The princess herself is a brat. Totally irredeemable. The captain has no backbone. These two are introduced to us and are just flat out unlikable, how does one get invested in the story when the characters themselves actively fight your interest if you decide to give it a chance? You are punished for starting a new game.
It doesn't get any better from there. Bland plot points, one dimensional characters and just poor mapping. The game uses RTP which is included in RPG Maker and the built in character generator for the character sprites and faces. I maintain there is nothing wrong with that, however when you have a place called a Ridge, why is it suddenly floating in the sky?
The world itself feels empty. Characters sprouting the some few lines as nauseum. In a dungeon, there may only be a few things to interact with, some treasure chests and a switch or two if you're lucky. No flavour text, just events important to the plot and that's it. Here's another map you have to walk through until you get to the next non-interactive moment. A > B > C. Perhaps it opens up afterwards, I don't know. I doubt I'm going to find out.

Didn't know what to expect in terms of audio. It was a pleasant surprise to hear the intro music and the music for each locale. Each of tracks to the locations represented each location's "feel" and theme very well. The music is very well made that it somehow stuck itself in head like bumping 90's track.
Minor gripe: A certain enemy type that has a high pitched battle intro sound, that's all.
As it is a game with a party system, you can expect variation in each character's strength and weakness.
As for me I can't seem to work out the importance/strength of this one character that you will encounter in one of the first few locales. So I will usually alternate between every other character to play to their strengths when encountering different enemies except for this one character.
Banter/Interactions between characters is what makes them memorable. However I felt that it toned down a tad bit as the game progresses.
Battles have a turn-based combat system reminiscent of other RPG-Maker games (which isn't a bad thing necessarily)
Where you have the general "attack", "special/magic", "guard" moves etc and also to which you can try to escape from combat when things turn sour.
After each combat it will yield you with experience points and items that the enemy drops. These items then can be sold to acquire potions, rings etc.
A minor gripe: The item system, you will find yourself selling a lot of those item drops from battles because it doesn't have any use to them. If you play too much RPG games you might find yourself feeling that more could be done with those items, such as a crafting system where you can make special potions, enchant a ring or something along those lines. But if you can overlook that aspect then there won't be an issue at all.
Since the game does not have any difficulty settings, I was surprised to see certain locations that has really challenging enemies if you happen to enter those locations a little to early. So do expect a small portion of the game to level up your characters before you progress into a new area or you would find your party decimated over and over.
Getting into this game to beta test it, I was expecting (not hoping) to encounter certain bugs or maybe even a typo here and there in the dialogue. However much to my surprise, there wasn't any bugs encountered which was breath of fresh air, wish the same thing can be said about my house.
As with other RPG-Maker games you get what you see in terms of the graphics of the game.
The art style is up at the standard of other good RPG-Maker & Visual Novels you can think of.
Don't let the initial cliché start of the story stop you from playing as it gains momentum as the minutes tick by. The initial cliché start will be a distant memory as story pans out.
A good note to take is that I expected the game to on the range of 6-8 hours but that doesn't seem to be the case as it is rather longer than I had expected but that could also vary from each player's play style.
For a person who is easily put off from an RPG-Maker game like how some people are put off with pixel graphics games, I would say to give this game a shot if you're open to trying and giving a game of this nature a chance and who knows you might be finding yourself having some fun relaxing time in this game.
The minor gripes stated above is based on personal preference that can be overlooked and vary from person to person.
But with a game that is fundamentally & mechanically well made as this, its hard to not recommend it.

Note: I was one of the original betatesters for the original release, as well as one of testers for the Steam release.
The Princess’ Heart is another RPG developed by Roseportal Games. It was their third commercial game, after successes like Whisper of a Rose and Sweet Lily Dreams (both available through Steam). It does not share the same universe as those games and looks and feels more like a traditional JRPG.
The Princess’ Heart has a nice plot, if a bit short, however its characters make up for it quite well. I found them very unexpected and they often surprised me. There’s 9 party members in total, one of which is optional. I would have liked to see some more party interaction.
Graphics are pretty standard, but used wisely and correctly in my opinion. It also feels more traditional, because of the standard graphics.
As for gameplay, there’s no difficulty modes, but as the battles are well balanced and the monsters don’t respawn until you’ve left the dungeon completely, it doesn’t feel necessarily. I liked that I could change the party formation easily, which is quite necessary as most battles require you to do so.  Some of the dungeons are mazes and loop, which I quite enjoyed as a challenge.
All in all I recommend this game to every strategic RPG lover.

Alright, kiddo, here's the deal with the deal. You want more JRPGs on Steam, right? Of course you do. You have your Final Fantasy, you have your Agarest, you have a few others, but you want more. I want more. We all want more. Guess what Trails in the Sky is. That's right; a JRPG. You buy it, you tell publishers "hey dudes look there's a market for this genre."
And are you the type of person who sees a bunch of games starring rugged white guys with guns and gets sad that there aren't more female game protagonists? Well, you see that person with the staff and the ponytails up there? Guess what that person is. Female? You bet your sweet buttery biscuits she's female. Her name is Estelle. She's pretty interesting. And there are three other playable ladies in the game. They're all interesting also. And there's four dudes as well, and all of them are interesting. Everyone is really frigging interesting.
"But I don't want to give money to some jerky big-name game publisher. Who is getting my hard-earned regional currency?" Wise up, you dingus; your hard-earned regional currency is going to XSEED. You know how awesome XSEED is, mofos? Really really awesome. More awesome than you and I put together.
As for the game itself? Alright, fine, let me serious up for a minute. *ahem*
Call me odd, but when it comes to JRPGs, I'm the type of person that prefers strong gameplay over a strong story. Don't get me wrong, I have no problem with video games as a storytelling medium (hell, the entire genre of visual novels exists for this exact purpose), but if I really want a good story, then I have both a library card and a Netflix subscription to take advantage of. I play video games because I want to, you know, *play a game*. Because of this, I'm much more likely to enjoy - as well as replay - JRPGs that favor complex gameplay over a compelling story (Pokemon, Golden Sun, Final Fantasy V) than JRPGs that favor a compelling story over complex gameplay (Lunar, Earthbound, Final Fantasy IV).
The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is one of the only exceptions.
That's not to say that the gameplay is bad; think of the battle system as a cross between Final Fantasy VII and Final Fantasy Tactics. It's fun, it moves at a good pace, and it features the *classiest* damn battle music I have ever heard. The thing to be aware of before diving in, though, is that the game is broken up into five chapters, with each chapter having its own locations, dungeons, sidequests, enemies, and so on. Once you complete a chapter and move on to the next one, you can't go back, meaning that anything you missed is now completely inaccessible. Even within the individual chapters, the sidequests (of which there are a TON, a plus in my book) have relatively small timeframes; there are also a bunch that aren't even listed until you happen to bump into them, including a couple that make me seriously wonder how anyone at Falcom could think that players could complete them all without a guide. While the sidequests are, of course, optional, they do offer some nifty rewards, challenging battles, and humorous cutscenes, and if nothing else, it's frustrating to be at the endgame and be missing only one or two entries in the bestiary or recipe book.
But Trails in the Sky features quite literally the most vibrant, detailed world of any JRPG I have ever played.
This game has an immense amount of text, and XSEED did an absolutely wonderful job translating it for English-speaking audiences. Be aware that the story is not fast-paced in the slightest - it's a slow burn with an emphasis on character interactions and world-building. Because of this, the cutscenes in Trails tend to take a long time, like many other entries in the genre, but the writing is so strong and the characters so likable that you won't mind at all. Even beyond the main characters and story, you rarely have to go far to find an NPC with something interesting to say - not a whole lot of "Welcome to Corneria" or "Press Start to open the menu" here. (Protip: reexamine each treasure chest after opening.)
Interesting characters. Vibrant world. Stellar soundtrack. JRPGs. XSEED. Come on.
All I can say is that if you have a fondness for JRPGs from the SNES/PS1 era, BUY THIS GAME! You owe it to yourself to do so.

Resident Evil 6 is a good game in all the wrong ways. You love it for what it is and hate it for what it isn't. What it is, is a high-octane rollercoaster ride of loud noises, explosions and a lot of gore. What it isn't is a survival horror game with quiet, subtle moments and interesting puzzles. If your intention with a sequel is to change the genre of its series then going the complete opposite direction of the original with no regard to the source material is seldom the way to go. You need to pay homage in a delicate and deliberate way to the original while creating something fresh that both old and new players will enjoy. While the sales numbers for Resident Evil 6 could certainly claim that they were successful in the latter, the same can not be said of the former.

The gore is pretty great and the guns feel like they have a lot of weight behind them when you shoot. The best part about the game is that there is no environmental exposition. This allows the player to fully focus on the gameplay instead of exploration. I don't see that very often and I believe it's noteworthy. There are some truly amazing set pieces in the game as well, such as the section in the streets in the beginning of the Leon chapter. Unfortunately these experiences are too few and far in between.

Expectations can hamper anyone's experience of anything, be it a movie or a video game. Since I'd heard so many negative things about Resident Evil 6 I decided I was going to go into it without any expectations and judge it on face value. After launching the game my immediate reaction was frustration towards restrictive controls and movement such as the inability to run in certain sections as well as the inability to skip cutscenes I'd already seen. There's a part where you're supposed to protect someone and I didn't touch the controller through the entire encounter and it just automatically sent me to the next section. It all felt like the game wanted to only show me certain things at certain times and never give me the freedom to actually play the game by myself. I find it extraordinary that a game this action-packed can manage to be as boring as it is when it comes down to it. You can just run past the enemies most of the time and since they can't grab you they aren't any kind of a real threat. That wouldn't have been such a big problem had the story or the characters been more interesting.

If the gunplay had been a little smoother and not as sluggish as it is I would have enjoyed the game a lot more. But it's impossible to move around and aim gracefully and accurately because of varying sensitivity. It's a true shame because shooting is fun and the gore looks great. Had they changed the controls and movement to be more responsive it would have been an excellent shooter. Instead it tries to be survival horror as well and falls short on both as a result.

I was surprised at Leon's actions in the beginning of the game when he tries to reason with a zombie. Here's Leon, arguably the most experienced of all the Resident Evil characters and he's making a classic rookie zombie mistake in the opening scene. I just don't buy it. It wasn't until I got to the Jake campaign 15 hours in that I started to enjoy myself a little. It had more than just senseless shooting and loud noises all the time with some actual pacing and character development. This was actually the most shocking part of the whole game. Because at this point you've been sitting through so much mind-numbing action shlock that you've forgotten you were a human being. "Oh, that's right, I'm still alive, and I'm playing a game I guess... Wait, did something happen!?"

This is something of a Telltale-style edutainment game. Just be warned that the game is exceptionally short (less than three hours), so you might want to wait for a sale. It's also rather sad this is not in episodic format, as a lot of interesting characters are introduced and choices are being made, so you'd like to follow up on their future outcome.

A clear labor of love, and a historically rich experience. Didn't realize until the very end that it was co-written by Brian Wood, but it makes sense in retrospect.
On a gameplay level, this is kind of the King's Quest to Telltale's Monkey Island (wait, didn't Telltale actually make some not-great Monkey Island games? Forget that. This metaphor takes place in the 90s). It's less forgiving. It's more frustrating. It's less robust and less entertaining. The whole thing is about as long as a single Telltale episode. But if you're interested in the history, or you generally like the (modern) Telltale approach to games, it's worth checking out, especially if you can get it on sale.

1979 Revolution: Black Friday is an adventure point and click game developed and published by iNKstories, releasing on PC, PS3, 360 and iOS in April 2016.  The game focuses on the Iranian Revolution, from 1979 that led to the overthrow of the dictatorial regime of Shah Mohammed Reza Pahlavi in Iran.
The game play is your run of the mill point and click adventure game, but resembles more of a Telltale style environment, where timed dialog choices are prominent throughout the story, as well as quick time events. Thankfully the QTEs are few and far between, allowing you chance to sit back and relax the main element of this game, the gripping story.
The most important feature of a point and click game is obviously going to be the plot, 1979 Revolution ticks all of the right boxes there. Following a historical timeline of events with slight blurred lines between reality and what you see in the game, we follow Reza and his good friend Babek as they look to exploit the terrorist regime in Iran to start a revolution. You meet important characters along the way and you will develop relationships with them depending on actions and dialog choices throughout. The story takes you through dips, turns and dramatic outcomes, and potentially leaves the plot open for a sequel. I thoroughly enjoyed the story of this game, not only is it an interesting plot, but it teaches you something, which is always an added bonus when it comes to video games.
Graphically this game looks decent, nothing spectacular, but there are hundreds of worse looking titles out there. It looks like an early GTA title in terms of textures, animations and work environments. Still pleasant to look at, but don’t expect state of the art graphics and clean cut visuals here. The voice acting on the other hand is brilliant, all characters are well voiced and fit their character’s perfectly. This game would not be what it is today without this top notch voice acting. I can’t imagine I would of enjoyed it nearly as much if it was text based.
There isn’t any difficulty to 1979, The only time you will fail at any point is if you miss a QTE, and then you can simply replay it and pay more attention! While the game does have different choices to take throughout the plot, the ultimate ending will near enough be the same regardless, which is a bit of a shame as I always like it when games clearly make your choices matter.
It is also worth noting that this game is very short.  The story is spread out across 18 chapters, but this still only took me under an hour to complete. You will find a bit of replayability though due to the different paths you may follow, as well as tons of collectibles and achievements to hunt for as well. For me though, I’m only going to want to play through it once.
Overall, 1979 is a really good adventure game, but the only thing that lets it down is the lack of content that gives this game any longevity. If the story could be expanded or lead onto maybe an Episode 2, then it would be well worth the £8.99 but purely because it is so short, I can only recommend 1979 Revolution: Black Friday when it is on sale.

An interesting twist on a platform game. The single player game is not particularly difficult, as you can pretty much take all the time you need within reason. The real challenge lies in achieving a stronger performance. Become faster, and faster, find the gems, snatch the yarn, battle cats, find the hats, avoid being eaten by... whatever those hairy beasts are supposed to be... Sound strange? That's because it is just plain bizarre. In a good way.
Battleblock is not the average platformer. It is a mix of many concepts into a single fluid game held together by Behemoth's quirky art style and off brand humor. The single player campaign offers a decent experience, but if you have a friend to play with it rises to a whole new level. The mutiplayer campaign is 'cooperative" in that the goal is to navigate levels that cannot be completed alone. The reality is, more often than not, friends sabotaging each other and finding more and more hilarious ways to betray the trust of their partner until a truce is reached, the level finishes, and it all starts again...
As for BattleBlock Theater, I am definitely a fan.

As a huge fan of visual novels with attributes and choices, this tickled me to no end. I loved it a lot, to be honest.
The story was nice and easy to digest. A fantastic mystery/point and click/visual novel game which takes it's title quite seriously.
Tokyo Dark has many twists and turns with an occasional jump scare all wrapped in a blanket of creepy.  You play as the protagonist, Detective Ayami ito, who is struggling to stay sane and figure out what the heck is going on with the case her partner was working.   It starts off with a bang and doesn't let go as you dive headfirst into creepy cults and ancient artifacts dealing with the supernatural.
The visual novel portion of the game is pretty well written with themes of lost loves, morality and how much control we may or may not have over our lives.  The player must often make choices which lead down varying paths depending on how Ito reacted which also ties into the game's very creative stats system called SPIN (Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, Neurosis).

- Sanity goes down as you experience horrible events and incidents but can be restored through making sure to enjoy the smaller things in life like playing with your cat.
- Professionalism depends on your demeanor on the job and how you approach people and situations.  Shoot the lock off a door or find another way in, etc.
- Investigation changes how focused Ito is during situations such as if she isn't focused enough she may not be able to notice a clue or ask a certain line of questioning.
- Neurosis deals with how often you repeat things such as walking back and forth, talking to people repeatedly etc.  Higher neurosis stat may make Ito more paranoid...
The music is fitting for every area/situation.  Heavy somber tones as you explore the darker alleyways but lighter tunes while during the day and exploring the occasional happier places.
Without giving away too much, I would say that the multiple endings are worth finding and that loose ends are almost all tied up.  Overall it was a great game that I can recommend with an 8.5/10.

Katamari, but with better level design and controls, need I say more? Yes. Yes, I do need to say more.
See, The Wonderful End of the World has some advantages over katamari, such as the vastly more sane control scheme, and the generically more interesting and fun level design. However... it doesn't have the humour of Katamari, nor does it have nearly the same budget or "feel" to it in the same way. In Katamari, you knew when you picked up a new item easily, due to the big extra bump on your ball, in TWEOTW (yeah it doesn't even acronym well), you just kinda inflate a little bit bigger on occasion.
Is TWEOTW better than Katamari? No. But it is your only real option if you don't own a console to play a katamari style game on the computer without resorting to an emulator (I'm not including the steambox in this =P ).
One thing people have to keep in mind, however, is that it doesn't matter if TWEOTW is a "rip off" of katamari... it's simply in the same genre, nothing more. Yes, Katamari pretty much created the genre, and there haven't been many since due to a small niche audience, but you may as well berate Starcraft 2 for sucking because it's just copying Dune 2, a game of which most people haven't even heard of any longer. The entire RTS genre was literally created by Dune 2, however, so... it's the exact same argument, and it doesn't make any more sense there than it does in saying The Wonderful End of the World is a katamari clone. As such, I won't be using that as part of my marking for score, because it's completely irrelevant.
What I can say, is that TWEOTW does get kinda dull semi-fast. I can play it for about 10-30 minutes at a time, then just shut it off. The thing is, though, I have quite a few hours played... why? Because it's honestly enjoyable and relaxing. It's FUN. I can come back, ease into the game and just veg out for a few minutes after getting home from work, if I'm half asleep late at night and need just a bit longer before I'm truly ready for bed, or if I'm feeling ill, or bored and have nothing else to do, or am waiting on someone.
TWEOTW is good. It's not great, but it's certainly good. You probably won't sit down and stomach playing it for sixteen hours straight, but half an hour here, fifteen minutes there, just as a nice relaxing "I don't have to think about anything, and can just have fun" it's perfect for.
To that end, it's good at what it does, and it's distinctively different enough from Katamari to deserve to be it's own game, even if it's clearly within the same genre.
Final Verdict:
Not the best game in the world, but it serves a very useful purpose in the average gamer's library. It's the closest thing you can get to Katamari on the computer without an emulator, and to be honest, it's really kinda fun.
Overall Score: About 70%. It's worth the price to be paid, but those who have played katamari before may have slightly raised expectations and may want to wait until it's on sale.

HeXen takes everything that made Heretic great, and multiplies it by about 10. The graphics, weapons, enviornment, and enemies feel so much more real, and I fing myself getting more invested into HeXen than I did in Heretic (not to say that Heretic is a bad game).

While I appreciate some of the efforts this game made, and definitely liked it more than the original Heretic (which I threw in the bin after being Gygax'd to death for no reason for the 27th time in the same level), ultimately HeXen has to rate a "meh" at best.
One of the few efforts I've seen to make a straight-up fantasy FPS, like Heretic, HeXen is basically Doom with D&D trappings and a greater emphasis on puzzles and pickups. As typical of Doom-clones, the plot is bare-bones at best, limited to melodramatic text narration between levels before tossing you back into things. Your weapon selection is fairly limited by the standards of FPSes of the era, getting four based on which of three (largely interchangeable) classes you picked at the start. A basic weapon that doesn't burn ammo, a blue mana weapon, a green mana weapon, and a super-weapon assembled from three parts that uses both.
While largely passable as it's hard to mess Doom's basic formula up, HeXen isn't without its problems. Despite being a pretty standard mechanic, it is INCREDIBLY easy to sequence break and strand yourself using crouch, as basically any hole that can be entered with it was only intended as a viewport by the devs. Also, some of the levels don't do a very good job at directing you, leading to several moments where I was left basically headbutting every wall on the level looking for the way forward. Finally, while it kept levels from getting boring after they were emptied out, the game's habit of spawning an infinite number of ettins into the level over time was rather obnoxious, and wouldn't have been necessary at all if they had simply included a few more hints as to what you were supposed to be doing.
One positive remark, on the other hand, is that while extremely easy due to the sheer number of unused powerups I had sitting in my inventory at that point, the final boss is a rare treat in Doom-clones in that it actually has some basic mechanics and phases, rather than being a simple overpowered enemy with a billion health to empty the last of your ammunition into. Didn't do much to make it a challenge, but it's encouraging to see the effort made at least.
In the end though, I can't recommend simply because there are both better Doom-clones and better dungeon crawlers on the market. Mediocre with a pinch of shoddy level design isn't enough to earn a thumbs up even if it's largely inoffensive.

I had alot of fun beta testing this game for steam release, would be speedrunners have me to thank for adding 4 hours to their runs, no sequence breaks for you hehe XD
To start off my review, my opionion of the game was pretty low starting out. The intro gave me the impression that the plot was going to be quite dark. Having a few innocent guards executed near the begining reinforced my suspicions. The gamplay which ill cover later, also bothered me at first and i was almost ready to send the game back and not play anymore. That said, I am glad i pushed past that, as overall i realy enjoyed the game. It just took some warming up to. The plot was not nearly as dark as the intro made it feel for me.
Gameplay Mechanics(7/10): There were a few mechanics that irked me while playing, Such as entirely disabling dash in any combat area, making navigating already comquered areas much slower. or that Shop items never change, the price just goes up with your level, making it harder and harder to purchase everything. I ended up just not bothering to use consumable items and found it easier to grind till the area couldnt hurt me.
There were also some mechanics i loved in the game, such as the ability to swap out your entire party once per combat, even boss battles, this has saved me many times. As you progress and unlock more skills the initially dull encounters start becoming very fun and engaging, there are so many ways to play your party strategically. The skills make the battles, as other than an accessory that allows double turns, most equipment in the game is rather dull and pointless. there are only accessories, armor and weapon do not change. also strange how many characters fight with some variation of fisticuffs.
Graphics: The engine used to create a game is not an excuse for the quality of the game. As with most RPGM games I feel i cant really even grade this catagory, other than the "retro feel" it does not stand up to current industry standards, though its what you will see in most RPGM games.
Characters(9/10): I very much enjoyed the banter between characters and the personality of each one, and no character felt worthless in my party so the battle balance was well done. the only flaw i find is there isnt enough screen time to showcae these characters, and few of them grow past what they start as.
Story(8/10): I feel this could have been much more than it was. while i did end up enjoying it quite a bit, there are alot of gaps between story moments, and the story moments were short and sweet. I do feel the needless deaths of countless guards was a bit much compared to the light heartedness of the story that follows. I started off with a negetive bias but enjoyed the game enough to get back into the story, and i feel that while too short, it was a good story.
Overall: not without its flaws and frustration, but far better than a great many other games out there, and overall quite enjoyable even with the issues. Dont expect the next bioshock 2 out of it, but dont pass it up either.
EDIT:
In light of the recently released deluxe version, im afraid my overall opinion of this game has dropped conciderably. making 3 in game skills only available by spending extra money is kinda messed up. x.x
