"Greetings mortal. Are you ready to die."
-Korax
Story
Korax(the second Serpent Rider) has taken over the world of Cronos and has corrupted it's leaders. Now one of three heroes must go kill Korax and save the land. Once again I have nothing to say except that Korax actually insults you in every hub. I like that.
Gameplay
The game has three characters you can play as: the Cleric, the Mage and the Warrior.
The Cleric starts out pretty bad with a weak weapon but soon gets some of the best weapons and the flask can really destroy groups if used right.
The Mage is my favorite as he has good range with weapons and while I didn't like he's ultimate weapon, his other weapons can carry you.
I didn't finish the Warrior as while he does have a good starter weapon, I knew I wasn't gotta have fun with cause I like range in my FPS.
One of the unique gameplay features is that the game use a hub system. Every hub is divided into several levels and you have to go back and forth to pull switches and find keys. While I don't mind this as it encourages exploration, there's no way of no knowing what the switch did and you might have to be lucky in finding the level that has the next key or switch that you have to get and you might get lost.
You have twelve weapons in the game, but each class has four. a starter that use no ammo, a blue and green weapon, I called that they use blue and green ammo and the ultimate weapon which can only be used when you find the three parts to it. The enemies, while simple, are varied and can be difficult if you don't know what you doing. Ex. you first fight with two headed goons that just wack you with club, but in the same level, you meet flying imps that rapidly fire fireballs, and these things tend to appear in groups. and these are the foes you start with.
The inventory is still here with some old toys like the health potion and the one that turns enemies into animals(this time pigs.) and new ones like the flask which is a different bomb for each class and one toy that can summon a MAULOTAUR!!
Also, there's jumping and some minor jumping parts.
Presentation
Don't care much about the music, it's just there. The art design and presentation however is great despite being dark and brown and grey. Each level has a different theme to it and you can tell where you are by knowing what design it is. In the first hub, each level portal is surrounded by the textures you see in the level, but when you see fire themes and textures in the ice level means there's a portal to the fire level nearby.
This is both a minor and major point both there's a lot a little details added like destroying glass leaves some shards on the ground or when you overkill a grunt, his club will be laying somewhere away from the corpse. Heck, even the way some doors open is pretty cool for a DOOM engine game.
Verdict
I like this game and while I would personally give it an nine, the lack of direction holds it back so instead it's:
7/10

Like most other Iranians, I get very excited about anything that has to do with us and our history, so when I heard about this game's existence I bought it right away. Now that I finished my first time playing it, as much as I hate to ruin the 69 reviews I thought I could share my thoughts:
I can't recall any other game that really focused on a historical event like this and not only told the story but also let the player become a part of it. You can make some choices that really help your character or the ones around him, or be their doom. That's already something that quite a few big game titles don't manage.
But the story telling is flawed. Some characters have no personality or are so rarely there that there is really no reason to care for them, and there aren't many characters to begin with. I ended up only caring for two characters, and the second mostly just because his role just hit home for me.
And just when things are really heating up, the game ends. And it's not even a big ending that really feels like one, it's more like listening to music and during the chorus your speakers just suddenly die. A lot of questions should have been answered, but aren't even mentioned again, and you simply don't get much deeper into what was happening which is a pity.
The gameplay was not that interesting for me aside from choosing what to say and occasionally how to act. What you can do most of all is looking for things and collecting them, which then give you a little insight on both what was happening during the revolution and also Iranian culture as it was back then and still is now, which is neat for those who don't know much about Iran but still perhaps too little for those who really know nothing.
More important information can be collected by taking photos, and you do that in a very basic "click at the right moment" minigame. Depending on how well the photo turns out, the more information you get.
There's also everybody's favourite thing in gaming history: Quick time events! *sarcasm*
Also, on two occasions I had to patch up people who were hurt and I have to say that that were just silly. Especially having to put bandages around the wounds, it looked really bad and out of place compared to the style in the rest of the game.
The game looks alright. It's rather obvious to tell which character models were worked on longer and which ones were rushed, and in just one scene, standing on one spot, I could count up to almost 10 copy-pasted NPCs. But I really did like the style they went with and enjoyed looking at the character I play. The environments were also done nicely, it really reminded me of walking down a street in Tehran.
I have the luck of rarely ever getting glitches and such in games, but there was this one point where I walked into a half circle of people in the hope that I could collect something in the middle, but then Babak closed the circle and I couldn't get out because he just wouldn't move. I had to restart the whole sequence and stay away from groups from then on which probably made me miss out on some things.
So, tl;dr: while this game is very flawed, it does go down an interesting path and I did enjoy my time playing it. It doesn't cost much, so I do recommend it as both a small "collect stuff and achievements" game if you enjoy those and an alternative to a short and probably biased documentary.

In most of these narrative-heavy, decision-based games, when I need to make a decision - especially early on - regarding which character I'm going to side with, I have trouble because the choice is presented in the form "Side With X / Side With Y", where I have no idea which of the characters is X and which is Y. That wasn't a problem in this game: the characterization is so good that I could recognize each of the characters almost from the moment I was introduced to them. That attention to detail and quality storytelling continues throughout the entire game.
While there are issues - character models are re-used a bit too much, controls are janky, decisions aren't nearly as important as they seem to be - the game really does an amazing job of putting you into the setting, to a degree I've not seen before in any of the other narrative-based games I've played. I've read a lot about Iran's history, especially about the 1979 revolution, but the things the game showed about the revolution, culture and society of that era - both in-game and the real-life videos and photos integrated into the game - do so much to help you see how things really were at the time. I highly recommend this game.

A groundbreaking way to immerse the player in history.
The game pummels you with a series of heart wrenching twists and turns on an emotional rollercoaster, but, to an extent, you have a feeling of agency, choice, that you would not get with a movie. I would love to see this applied to the Iran-Iraq war, the fall of the Berlin wall, Vichy France, Mao's China, Tienanmen Square, the Viet Nam and Iraq wars, the French Revolution, the Bolshevik Revolution, the Great Depression, the US CIvil war, Roman occupied Judea, and so much more!
The game puts you in the role of a photographer, that seemingly neutral arbiter of truth, and yet it shows not only the events outside the frame, but just how imbued with personal feelings photography is. The game has a passable 3D world that you can navigate in line with the story, and voice actors speaking a mix of Farsi and English. The sound effects and ambient sounds are immersive. There are "Dragon's Lair" style action sequences that I loved, other mini games that I liked - such as bandaging a wound, and button mashing minigames that I felt could have been done better. The white diamonds that help you hone in on the action quickly are perfectly done. The home movies and photographs are a splendid touch.
There is some replayability in trying to explore other paths the player can take, finding all the historical points of interest, as well as acheivements and cards. 1979 is true to the medium of PC games, and not just a documentary masquerading as a game; it is a game, and a good one.
This is a must play for anyone with a connection to Iran, or an interest in geopolitics and modern history. The game was even handed with the various political factions involved in the Revolution, leaving the player with an understanding of the motivations, without trying to favor any particular creed.
The game is priced at the price of a movie ticket, and about as long for the first playthorugh: fair.

Fantastic gaming experience.  Negative reviews are almost universally from original Secret World players that are scared of change or angry at having to start over.  What they dont mention is that the player population on the original client was dying and that this transition to Free to Play injected new life into the formula while keeping the fundamentals the same.  It basically saved their game.  It has opened up the experience for new players, casual and elitist alike, and allowed them to experience what is one of, if not the best, storylines in any MMO.  Its now a game that is easier to get into, but still allows for the min/max high end gameplay at endgame for those that care to pursue.  It is understandable that the vets are upset with some of the changes but it is unfortunate that they are voicing this over Steam reviews and potentially disuading new players from enjoying a great game.  For a new player, the changes mean nothing.
Population seems very healthy, with almost 0 wait time for Dungeons/instances.  Cash shop is unobtrusive and provides mostly vanity items - buying actual gameplay upgrades is possible but hardly necessary or practical and anything that can be purchased in this regard can be earned in game. Combat feels fluid and fast paced - mixing gunplay, magic, and melee.  Investigation missions are absolute genius and totally unique in the genre.  Developers are active on the forums and Discord.  NPCs are voice acted and extremely well done - it is obvious that the game had high production values.  Music is top notch.  The story is dark and refrences more horror tropes than could be listed - Demons, Lovecraftian horrors, ghosts, zombies, cults, cannibals, secret societies, (insert any other horror concept you can think of).  The game is also very adult and was obviously made for a mature audience, which is refreshing in todays age where developers are scared to allienate a younger demographic.
And once again, the game is FREE.

Looking back to when I was first introduced to computer gaming, I distincly remember the classic Point-n-Click adventure game 'Return to Zork'. I guess that began my interest in Video Games, especially as a story telling media.
So when an email hit my inbox from SquareEnix Collective about a Western point-n-click adventure twist to the Japanese visual novel genre my interest was immediatly caught.
Then, after fully reading the email, I was to learn it was going to be a narrative driven psycological thriller.
Well that had me throwing my wallet at the screen yelling "Take my MONEY!", and once the opportunity to become a 'Backer' in the development of Tokyo Dark via Kickstarter, I jumped in with both feet.
Follwing the development of the game has been quite a trip. Monthly updates from the development team. Coupled with Beta build downloads for backers (Along with demo's available at SquareEnix's booth at San Diego Comic Con 2016) the ability to get 'hands on' during some of the early stages was only whetting my appetite for what was shaping up to a be a Point-n-Click Psycological Thriller Game I'd longed for.
With other games media quoting games like 'Life Is Strange' for gameplay and story telling from psychological thriller movies like 'Se7en', who am I to argue, I totally agree.
Players manage Detective Ito's Sanity, Professionalisim, Investigation, and Neurosis (SPIN) through your decisions, and interactions with the other characters and the environment.
However, be forewarned, there is an Auto Save function meaning you have to 'Live' with the consequence of your actions. No going back to 'fix' a mistake, you're taking ownership of that choice. You either keep going, or start again from the beginning... and why would you go back to the beginning? You should keep going, see how deep that rabbit hole is, Alice.. Sorry Ito, and reach the conclusion.
There's 11 different endings in Tokyo Dark, and a lot of choices to be made getting there. So you're going to get plenty of re-playability in this title. I like that very much. There's a few too many AAA Titles out there that are far too singular with their story severly limiting the ability to 'go back' and try something different.
Do I think I'm going to get my moneys worth from my pledge 2 years ago? Yes, no hesitation. Hell I'll buy it again if I need to (Also some people I know may get given copies by me because I want them to play it)
Is it worth what they're asking (Price wise) here on Steam? Absolutly 100%
Tl/Dr:
Want a Point-n-Click Psycological Thriller set in Tokyo? If yes. Then buy Tokyo Dark by Cherrymochi

Different level designs, different monsters, and new music tracks (including an actual game over sound that fits a horror style arcade game), would really go a long way with this one. A good horror game to start you 6 year old with, maybe, but being not scary enough to fit the horror theme and not interesting enough to play without it doesn't give this game much replayability.

“It's not Resident Evil!” That's probably the main criticism of Resident Evil 6, and to be fair, it's probably accurate. RE6 is an action packed cover shooter, and you know what? I thought it was super entertaining. RE6 boasts the same great cast of characters you'd come to know if you are fan of Resident Evil, but it introduces some new ones along the way. My favorite campaign is actually that of Jake and Sherry, and one of them is a newcomer.
The action, while slightly repetitive, is kept mostly distinct over the course of the three main campaigns. Leon has the slightly grittier zombie apocalypse, Chris fights uber bioweapons, while Jake plays homage to Nemesis. It's all larger-than-life, action packed, energy-charged, and I can't bring myself to hate it. I also like some of the changes to the mainline mechanics, like the stamina system changes, and melee combat.
Resident Evil 6 is like that popcorn flick that's trite and predictable, but you're still watching it due to the charismatic lead and the flashy action sequences. It may not have a whole lot of substance, but it has heart in spades.

1979 Revolution is harrowing, but very good. When i first saw it appear on Greenlight i voted it up immediately - Telltale-style interactive movies are not normally my cup of tea, but the idea of a game placing you as a photojournalist into a significant moment in history is genius. It does not disappoint. You don't even play anyone of consequence - you're just a kid with a camera - but that means you are really playing everyone of consequence. Walking amongst the youth, the radicals, the oppressed, the protestors... It's a unique opportunity to be able to document everyday people's lives, their struggle in a complicated time.
The sound design is exceptional, and the acting is perfect - it really feels like you are being caught up in a movement you can't control, something bigger than you - something exciting, frightening, confusing. My main complaint is that the camera is clumsy and keeps you trapped in small, barely-interactive areas, but that's fairly standard for this genre. This ain't no Life is Strange. But the setting is extremely refreshing - historical settings outside of the West are rare in gaming, and this is a particularly interesting one. The story builds well, the atmosphere is electric, and i had to blink away a few tears at the end. Excellent.

One of the most important games I've ever played.1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a historical game about the 1979 Iranian revolution. It is very close to that of the Telltale game series.
the mix of choices, QTE, and Photography, Exploration all blend well together. The strength coming from having the real life pictures next to the one’s you took. I found myself meticulously trying to recreate all the photographs to the originals. Photos also provide a means to learn about the actual events, culture, and people that influenced the Revolution. By the way, there is a tremendous amount of content in this game in regards to learning about the revolution, history, and culture of Iran. This is where the games stands apart from pretty much anything. the voice acting in the game, are as good as any AAA title. With an extremely talented cast of Iranian actors the really bring it on the performance front. All the sounds from the environments are great as well, and really bring you to Tehran.
The developer claims the plot is based on a real story. The protagonist, Reza, is from a wealthy family. He studied abroad in Germany. When he came back to Iran, he almost came across the ongoing revolution by accident. Iran was not it once was anymore. After seeing what he saw, he decided to participate in it. Whereas, his involvement troubled him with countless dilemmas, compelling him to pick sides. On one hand there is his brother, on the other are his friends and cousin. You choices affect how the game progresses. Walking on the street, you feel as if you are living through the revolution yourself. Seeing people protesting and suffering, you are compelled to feel sympathetic towards them. The political figures in this game are entirely real. When I was the graffiti of Khomeini on the street, I was like "Oh my God!" and my heart was beating so fast. This game does not pick a political side nor try to preach you liberal democracy. Instead, it tells you the paradox and contradiction existed in the revolution, making the choices hard to make. Ideal is idealistic because it is not reality. The moment when you threw the stone, it changed you forever. Is violence necessary? Is family more important than ideal? Is life more important than freedom? There's no good guy or bad guy in this game, it's all perspective.
If you're a fan of TellTale games, you'll enjoy this...
A unique Iranian perspective on an interesting historical period, and a solid game with good storytelling on par with Telltale games.
There needs to be more games like this.

Enclave is a fast paced and unforgiving game. Imho it is quite underrated and misrepresented. First of all it´s not an RPG game...
Basically you have a campaign with a mission after another. Instead of locking you into on character you can swap between them at beginning of any missions. You are not locked into any gear decisions either. So you dont buy and sell stuff. You simply can start with any item combo that correlates with the accumulated wealth so far. After completing certain missions, you unlock new tier of items. This freedom of choice made the game quite enjoyable.
In Enclave as most enemies are capable of wiping you pretty fast on hard difficulty. An assasin can simply hit you once in the head with an arrow or a melee charracter can bash you off a cliff. Therefore, you must always be on your toes. Most maps are filled with traps that can kill you instantly. While many whine about these, practically every one of these can be spotted. You just have to be alert.
There are many type of maps from simple towns, into caves and hounted houses. Level design is boosted by top notch music. Voice acting is also decent to say the least. Perhaps the most memorable map was Arc Moor fortress in light campaign. It is located in the middle of a volcano with only a narrow bridge leading to it. Naturally you have to get in while dodging arrows while trying to kite those heavy armored melees.
There found only 2 major flaws in this game. 1. Swimming with mlook. When you turn, your movement momentarely stops. This makes swimming dreadfull on PC. 2. AI cant find paths in certain areas. Many also complained about no saves. On hard difficulty you dont even have checkpoints. So you have to able to go in, kill your target, pick that expensive loot and get away alive. Makes it way more thrilling.
Naturally Enclave Graphics are outdated but for 2,5€ sale this game was a pretty neat bargain. It's actually best buy for me since Psychonauts. While it aint your basic 90 metascore game, it sure shouldn´t be as low as 71.

While it's been awhile since I've played the first game, I feel like the story in the first was MUCH better.  The story in this game felt extremely weak, and really felt like a matter of "just becase".  While the motivations of the character in the first game were purly revenge, I feel like it worked better overall.
Especially the part with T-Bone; in this he sorta just stumbles on in and instantly trusts this group, whereas in the original (if I remember correctly) it took Aiden a lot more work to get T-Bone's trust.
Futhermore, this game was very short and just didn't feel right.
I did enjoy the game, as the gameplay was fun, but it wasn't worth whatever price I paid.  Honestly after playing this, I'd much rather have just replayed the original.
What I found with the first, was all the side characters were great but Aiden himself was boring.  With this game, I found all the characters to be fairly bland.
As for if I'd recommend the game or not, really I'm neutral on it.  It's a fun game and you'll probably enjoy it, but only if you're not playing it for the story.  I like how weighty the cars feel, although they're very awkward whenever they get into the air.
There's also quite a few bugs in the game, but I've not run into anything game breaking.
And one final thing, I feel like the RC quadcopter and jumper really took away from the game.  At least, the jumper anyway.  The quadcopter was nice for scouting, but the jumper could be used to complete pretty much every mission without ever putting yourself in danger (with a few exceptions).  If the jumper was detected it was no big deal, whereas if you were detected it was a much bigger deal.
Essentially the jumper made stealth irrelevant.  I'm sure if I had just avoided using it I'd have had more fun, as I never really ended up using the environment to my advantage.  In fact, really all I ever did was use the quadcopter to view the enemies and call the police and gangs on them (which was fun to watch the meyhem, but still).
Also, Dedsec are extremely hypocritical I find.  They complain about how the system is manipulating people and then essentially manipulate people themselves, etc.
Really I found the first a lot more fun.
The final thing I'll say is I don't regret buying this or playing it.  I did enjoy it, but I don't think it holds up to the first in terms of story (which is the main thing I play a game for).

Well, keep in mind I don't like horror and paranormal-related stuff and I've always been reluctant about point'n'click games. Tokyo Dark just appealed me out of nowhere, resulting me to give it a try even if I don't like the genre. But, it was so much more surprising that I would ever imagine.
Pros.
► Graphism, artworks are pretty clean while some levels are really welldone. The promoted cutscence made by that one studio looks fine but no need to bet on in neither. UI is pretty clean too.
► Audio, pretty great OST for an indie game and overall sound effects work great in installing the game's ambiance.
► Storyline, I've really hooked the storyline. Despite all the psycological horror theme, I've really enjoyed every bit of it. From detective business, to police HQ moment, to help people out and everything after that. Well built stroy with a good amout of definitive choices and momentum changing choices.
► Characters design, the main grills characters (Itō -you- and Reina), especially Itō-waifu, own a pretty unique and well-created design. However Tanaka (your partner) falls a bit into a perfect, caring and altruistic hasbundo cliché
► Deep ambiance, Tokyo Dark has no trouble to quickly create its own ambiance leading to insanity moments, crutial decision-making momentum and sometimes a more relaxed pace.
► Optimisation, runs smoothly without any trouble.
► SPIN system, nice touch to the game leading advanced character design.
► Visual novel and point'n'click hybird, well it is an interesting hybrid to be honest, having the freedom of point'n'click and the story-telling of a visual novel.
► Endings, this game own 11 different endings resulting of your choices plus 6 secondary endings linked to background characters which is pretty impressive tbh. About the ending I've chose (spoilers mah bois),
.
Neutrals.
► User Interface hitboxes, even if I have said the UI looks good, it unfortunately, sometimes, has bugged hitboxes, leading to pick the wrong button. Also, on some startup, the location info seems bugged leading to everyplace is called "<LOCATION>" or something like that.
► Game design new trends, like placing a puzzle with lights in the middle of a chase or put longass but interesting stories when approching the end. It's not a bad point because it keeps us on track with the game, it's just a little underwhelming, which, I think, was the point.
Cons.
► Unnecessary "jumpscares", it's not proper jumpscares hopefully but I got startled every single time from the beginning to the moment you have to pack things in your office (because I don't found any of them later) leading me to be really tense up to the end. Shoutout to the flashing mask in a deep dialogue in the sewer tho.
► Resolutions settings, there is N O N E.
► Dialogue interface that rarely mixes the person that speaks or rarely forget to add your interlocutor sprite.
► Dialogue interface hiding UI and other gamebreaking bugs, while the previous cons doesn't really affect the game, those will make you restart a new game  because they lead to corrupted savegame files, as far from what I heard. For exemple,

TL;DR.
If you're startled at almost anything I still will recommend you Tokyo Dark with all my heart due to his great storyline, possibilities, great detective aspect, uniqueness and non horror cliché game design. And because of Itō, of course. Over all a fun time. Looks stunning and plays very smooth. Wasnt really sure what to expect having never played the first installment, someone sold it to me as GTA but you can hack stuff and I have to say that isnt far off the mark. It's defintely its own brand and feel but has the same open city world, vehicle and combat controls you'd expect from a GTA game, however the simularities end there. What I enjoyed the most was the multiple ways you can attack every mission; want to sneak around popping bad guys like Sam Fisher? No problem. Or would you like to ghost your way in and back out, enemies none the wiser? Got you covered. If you really want you can just go in the front door guns blazing. That being said there isnt any effect on the game based on what play style you adapt; the rewards, plot advacement, and reaction from other characters is the same whether or not you go though as super smooth and stealthy super hacker, or a ruthless gun toating psychopath.
This causes a bit of a disconect as the entire game the main characters are stylizing themselves as heroes fighting agaist the Orwellian "Man" and trying to fight big data through a grass roots movement, while the protaganist is running around with a grenade launcher pancaking cop cars. Would have been great if they introduced some type of morality mechanic, or at least a couple differnt endings based on your actions and relationships with the main characters; this seems like a no brainer for this type of long form open world game.
That being said the characters are pretty unique and well fleshed out, and the main missions are well planned and a good challenge level. Just when it would start to feel a little repetative with the "break in here and hack this sever" routine over and over again you'd get a really unique and fun mission. That being said the side missions are pretty shallow content wise. Again I'll compare it back to GTA where every side missions felt like a main mission all in itself, with unique characters and a stand alone mini plot of sorts. In Watch Dogs you dont get that feel at all, and it felt like I was just doing busy body work to unlock more skills. One or two side missions are fun and I particularly enjoyed the ATM exploit mission chain, however many of them are pretty bland.

Tokyo Dark is categorized as an Aventure/Visual Novel hybrid but in actuality it's mostly point & click and text without much adventure. There's one very simple puzzle in the entire game and the rest of the gameplay consists of going back and forth talking to people, along with interacting with or picking up a few objects along the way. This doesn't necessarily make the game bad, but it doesn't require much thought to progress in the game, so if you buy the game don't put your thinking cap on cuz you likely won't need it.
With as much text this game has, you think it would appeal more to fans of visual novels, but I can't recommend it for that. The story and character interactions are ultimately dull and the quality is on par with just about any generic horror movie. I think it could've been more enjoyable if it had full voice acting, which I was surprised to find that it didn't have. There was a voice acting stretch goal for the Kickstarter which was met, plus $225k canadian dollars were pledged for the project in total, so they definitely should have had the funding for full voice acting. $225k for this game alone is overkill considering the lack of quality put into it, which leaves me wondering what most of that money went into. As the game is now, it barely has any voice overs, and they're all for Detective Ito. The lack of voice acting was a major disappointment for me, being a Kickstarter backer.
The "Beautifully animated sequences produced by Graphinica" are quite short and forgettable. I appreciate that there are animated scenes in the game, but it doesn't add much substance to it. It's kind of like a "special feature" added to lure people in, but when you try the product you hardly even notice it. The soundtrack is well made fitting the horror vibe well enough, and the art quality is decent. I would have preferred a better UI design. The settings menu is lazily designed, not letting you adjust voice/sound effects/music volumes individually is slightly annoying.
The S.P.I.N (Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, Neurosis) system seems like it would have more consequences in concept, but it ends up being more of a gimmick. It's required to manipulate your SPIN stats to get a few endings so there is some use to it, though I've gotten 6 endings (including the true ending) without paying much attention to the choices I've made. Despite what the store page says, I don't remember encountering any different character dialogue/reactions based on what my stats were. I can't speak for all of the endings, but the endings that I played through were uninteresting and predictable. Nothing shocked me, no twists or anything, just boring. The ending branches aren't sophisticated so you can probably get all of them in 2 or 3 complete playthroughs (a lot of them branch at 2 choices near the end of the game) using a guide without too much hassle. New Game+ is unlocked after your first playthrough which enables you to skip some previously read text (but not all) and unlocks save slots making endings more accessible.
Each ending route will take about 6 hours to finish initially, with each additional route being much shorter once you skip text in NG+. At a total of 11 endings, there is a fair amount of replayability, but not much content. IMO the endings don't warrant multiple playthroughs, they weren't interesting enough to me and they artificially inflate the small amount of content available. I'd expect more quality at $18 than this, especially after the amount of funding they got from Kickstarter. If you're dead set on buying it I suggest waiting for it to go on sale for $5 or an eventual Humble bundle (which will likely happen since it's published by Square Enix).

It seems like some of what was hinted at in the Kickstarter fell by the wayside (it seemed like they had aimed for more interactivity, but maybe they couldn't quite figure out how to work it out well enough), but the game still holds up well because of the solid story, decent storyline choices, and the great atmosphere (which is why I backed it in the first place).  Replayability is rather high if  you want to experience different events and endings. I'm not a big fan of point-and-click or visual novel games, but there was always something intriguing about this game regardless. And it's the story. If you want a good story, well... here you go.

There is so much wrong with this game.  It's probably the reason why they decided to change the style of the franchise back to a survival/horror approach in RE7 and the original games (RE0, 1, 2, 3, and CV) instead of an action/horror approach (RE4, REV1, 5, REV2, and 6).  I liked all of the action based games but NOT RE6.  Story aside...
-The action is way over the top and is mindless action
-Due to that it's only worth one playthrough and I don't think my brain can take another.
-Camera angles are unacceptable.
-Some genius thought it would be a great idea to switch from 3rd person to a fixed camera/moving camera angles (like the original games) during life and death situations where you're running away from something that can insta-kill you.  There were moments where I died 10-15 times in a row because I couldn't get pass an unplayable part.
-There are also many camera angles when the camera is trying to show you "all of the action" but not show you where your going...so you can't see where your going.  It's like running blind.  This can kill you over and over as well.
-The controls are terrible.  RE0-CV and RE4-REV2 had similar controls respectively.  RE6 doesn't follow the modern games and takes a different approach.   It utilizes the whole keyboard do to different things and there a lot of key bindings to add to the confusion.
-There are to many cutscene events.  The ones that involve button tapping are fine but the keybinding ones can get confusing especially if they're really fast.  That can cause deaths as well.
-The menus and inventory screens take a different approach.  They're confusing for navigation and require you to also utilize the whole keyboard.  Some reason going through the menu doesn't pause the game.  You're still live with the character crouching and looking down at his phone to simulate going through the menu.  That's a no no with the amount of enemies.
-Having four different campaigns is way to repetitive and gets confusing.  It's repetitive because the characters are going through most of the same areas.  If they wanted this many star characters, they should have taken a Revelations approach in one single campaign where different characters have different chapters.  Have one character take the lead role, like Leon.
-The story is fine.  It's the classic bioterrorist attack with some new virus and it's all of the heros jobs to stop it.
-But they're some really frusterating scenes.  No Spoilers: Like when characters aren't observant or when they some reason don't say something to defuse a situation.
With that being said, RE6 reminds me of a really bad RE4.  RE6 has the same lead producer/supervisor that created RE4 (one of the best games in the franchise, if not the best).  I think he thought it'd be a great idea to take the same elements of RE4 and just turn the volume to maximum for RE6, which clearly had terrible results.
Although the Leon campaign is just about bearable this game truly is the♥♥♥♥♥cancer of the francise.

Hexen is the successor to Heretic, and Raven Software worked really hard attempting to make it a superior experience in numerous ways.
The biggest are the addition of character classes. In Hexen you can pick between playing as a Warrior, a Cleric, and a Mage. Each of these classes has different weapons, playstyles and powerups affect them differently. This greatly adds to the game's replayability and the multiplayer.
Alongside that Hexen has hub levels. However part of my gripes with the game revolve around the level design. Hexen requires a great deal of backtracking in it's level design, and you can expect to have to return to prior levels regularly inorder to solve puzzles. This can get very confusing as the game goes on since you can get stuck very easily and have to constantly search old levels for the solution to a puzzle.
However the game does redeem itself by how great it's combat is. Once you get beyond the sometimes annoying level design you have a very enjoyable hack and slash, not one of Raven's best games mind you but still worth playing.

Remember when games were made by people who loved them and put extreme effort into making them to the absolute best of their ability? Probably not. Hexen: Beyond Heretic is easily up there with the greatest of all time. Easily. Everytime I play this I cannot fathom how once such a great industry, overflowing with talent turned into the bland, dumbed-down, soulless mess it is today. We've come down from seeing hundreds of great games and a handful of masterpieces yearly to seeing maybe 1 or 2 semi decent games every 4 years if we're lucky!
Hexen, while essentially a first person action fantasy game, takes a lot of influence from RPG games of that era, offering expansive exploration that see's you backtrack through earlier stages of the game to access areas previously unavailable until aquiring a key from a later part in the game. The level design is jaw droppingly amazing, some of the best ever, consisting of sprawling non-linear layouts which are almost psychotically well thought out. There are traps, puzzles scattered through-out the levels as well as hordes of blood thirsty minions to hack into pieces.
The setting is very similar to that of Heretic and the gameplay to an extent. There are different classes to choose from,  each with their own strengths and weaknesses and each with their own diverse weapons and spells, the classes consist of;
The Fighter - Melee focused character with weapons more suited for striking range.
The Cleric - Which is an all rounder class, mixing the ability to fight with the ability to cast spells.
The Mage - Which is self explanatory, the mage starts off weak, with weak spells that are suited for ranged attacks until he becomes a badass later in the game with spells that allow him to fly.
Hexen is truly a masterpiece, a work of art, a crowning achievement in gaming, if you haven't played it already I suggest you do so immediately and if you have played it I suggest you play it again. Put down your bland whack-a-mole/military shooters and play a real game!

Let's take a moment to travel back in time. Far, far back in time when a door opening horizontally in a Doom game was considered impressive. Seriously, in 1995 that was an excellent demonstration of the improved Doom engine. So was the fact that levels spanned multiple maps,
. Hole. Lee. ****.
Ok, so, not so impressive these days. However, it is still a fun game. You choose from three different classes - your generic brawler, your clichéd wizard, and an in-between cleric. Each character has four different weapons and two different types of mana to power the weapons. Gameplay is very much like Doom, in that you are searching for the exit to a level, which you get by finding secrets and keys. While the plot (yes there is a plot, just not much of one) doesn't change at all based on your characters, the gameplay does. The brawler uses mostly melee weapons, while the wizard uses projectiles. The game is broken into five episodes, each of which contains several maps. You'll need to get through a bunch of locked gates by finding keys and magical items. There's a wide range of difficulty, both from your character class as well as a difficulty settings.
While the game obviously isn't going to be offering anything new, it isn't just for people who played it 20 years ago. It's still a fun game with great atmosphere and some interesting puzzles. After downloading it, just make sure you get the ZDoom engine for it. It wasn't updated at all for the Steam release, so it looks really ugly out of the box. ZDoom increases the resolution to modern standards and adds a bunch of new features as well.

It seems that the character the player plays (Reza) can be a reasonable guy a second, then a maniac another. It just seems forced into the game that once I make a violent option, I'm pretty much crapped out of the game atmosphere. However, it doesn't seem to change anything. The story still goes on.
So let me put down the pros & cons...
Pros:
- Great visuals (I'd rate this game a bit better than Telltale's game visual quality)
- Great story
- Emotional choices
Cons:
- Biased story (I know there's more to the actual story than what the game presents)
- Meaningless ending (Once it ends, I couldn't help but say, "That's it?")
- Short game (~2 hours)
Good bang for the buck. I recommend the game, but I'm disappointed with the ending. Hope they make a continuation to this story.

If you've seen the 2012 movie Argo, you're probably somewhat familiar with the Iranian Revolution. But Argo only really touches on, one piece of the timeline of the revolution; the Iranian hostage crisis and the six Americans that escaped out of Iran. Black Friday seeks to tell the whole story of the Revolution, as a point-and-click adventure game.
You play as Reza Shirazi, a journalist, photographing the events of his home city, in Tehran, Iran. But there are multiple people in his life calling for him to join their side. Babak, his cousin, is involved with the protests of the revolution, but only wants to get their message across through nonviolence. Ali, his other cousin, is much more heavily involved with the revolution, and is willing to do anything to help the revolution, even if it means resorting to violence. While Reza's brother Hossein is a member of the SAVAK, Iran's police force, and persuades Reza to avoid going to the protests, out of fear that it will get their family in trouble. It's up to Reza to make a choice to merely take the role of a photographer, or revolutionary.
The gameplay should feel familiar to anyone who've played any Telltale's recent games, as it's clearly taking influence from their style. Can move around freely, in the parts of the game that aren't interactive cutscenes, and have a cursor you can use to examine anything in the environment. Many times you will be given up to four dialogue options at the bottom of the screen, which can affect how the game progresses. One gameplay mechanic that isn't taken from Telltale is the ability to take photos. As I said, you play as a photographer, and will be prompted to take photos of important events related to the Revolution. When in photo-mode you will see the photo-op as if looking through a camera, and must time the shot right in order to get a clear picture. Many of the pictures you take are inspired by real-life historical photographs, and the game will show you a comparisson page between the photo you took, and the real photo, along with historical facts relating to the photos.
This is actually a concept I'd wanted to see done in a game at some point. I love the idea of being a photographer, documenting history, and sometimes having to make a choice of exposing a moment of injustice, or intervening and stopping the injustice yourself.
The game does a good job at depicting the state of Iran in 1978-1980. You can feel the frustration and outrage the people of Iran feel. Everyone's attire looks appropriate for the period, and you get to see a lot of Iranian culture. It never ceases to give you interesting, and at times intense photo opportunities. Including one where you have to make a choice of whether to capture a photo of a policeman beating a protester, or running in and stopping the brutality.
The game also did a good job in humanizing the characters, even the ones that you might not like. For example, they make Hossein a very understandable character. He might be hard on Reza and angry at the revolution, but the game depicts him more as a man trying to continue to support his family and not lose his job, than just some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who abuses his power.
Also, like the game Never Alone, this is an excellent educational game. It clearly did its research on the historical events it presents to the player. I could ligitimately see this game being recommeneded to students by history professors in the future.
One complaint I do have is that this was a lot shorter than I'd thought it would be. I managed to complete it in about 90 minutes. And the game ends on a big cliff-hanger, which makes me hope that there's going to be more, like with Telltale's games. But as of writing this I haven't heard when or if any more episodes will be released, so I'm cautiously optimistic. I really hope we'll hear more about future episodes, as this game has me hooked.
If you're a fan of Telltale's games or you're a history junkie I would definitely recommened this game. The only thing I might advise is wait and see if a second episode will be released if you want a more longer experience.

This game was put in the Point & Click adventure game category, but it's not really Point & Click. The majority of this game is using W, S, A, D keys to move around, it’s allot more of an adventure game than anything else.
The whole story revolves around the toppling of the Shah and the Islamic institution of Ayatollah Khomeini who is a stark Muslim leader. In modern days you will hear Iranian people comparing pre 1979 when people look normal (by western standards) and free because of their ability to express art, music, voting, media and clothing. Past 1979 is when this Muslim dictator began to enforce Sharia law and made women veil up, they were refused to vote, voting was totally rigged, music and art were suppressed, people’s liberties were crushed and the police was used as a form of gang to squash any opposition views by kidnapping them and killing them. Many people consider the Islamic state today to be oppressive and many Iranians want to fight for the true freedom of their country that the Shah tried to instill. Sadly many Iranians today still refuse to acknowledge that Islam is the main culprit to their demise and that it was their own doing which caused them to collapse.
The game itself is a bias representation of a view point during this 1979 revolution. You are put in the spot of a young photographer who has trivial choices by which he can play out the story arc. The game itself isn’t bad, but there are a few things that took away from my experience. For one I found the combat sequences unappealing and very outdated. Granted this is a low end adventure game primarily designed to deliver a story element, but I found repetitive character models everywhere and I felt like the low detail of the engine didn’t really capture the struggle or aesthetic of Iranian life. I also didn’t like the educational pictures that you would get upon taking a snap shot yourself, they tie in with my first point in that the games aesthetic is more esoteric than representational.
Without spoiling too much, if you’re the type of person who wants to indulge into what most Iranians see as a representation of their struggle and their political turning point, then it’s not a bad play.
If you're the type of person that wants factual and political truth, with situations and events that resemble what really happened, then this game is probably not for you.
Keep in mind these type of games are heavily bias and for people like myself who like to make up their own mind, it doesn’t overly appeal.

From my perspective, I viewed this rendition of history as heavily pro-Tudeh (the Communist Party of Iran) and though it touches on the application of fiqh to Communists from the religious characters within in the game, "1979 Revolution: Black Friday" communicates its narrative as the Arab Spring in another lacquer. And that's a shame really. There is no equivalency to be drawn between the current Sunni revolutionary movements and the Iranian Revolution proper.
The developers did their homework for sure, but I couldn't get my character to become a Shia fundamentalist or lead him to become a basiji so what's the point of player driven actions or agency? Though Reza (the protagonist) is clearly Westernized, it didn't permit me the option of having a developing narrative drive a connection towards increasing his faith.
As an honest assessment, this game's presentation falls into this terrible milquetoast middle ground that simultaneously would♥♥♥♥♥♥off Shah loyalist expats and a contemporary Shia as the Tudeh are portrayed as harmless, albeit naive, saints. They're only critiqued as hypocritical, or worst of all, taken for the fools that they were. Aside from those notes, the game is a "rah rah go student revolutionary movements" within a general context and retelling that Pahlavi was a pretty bad leader (I agree only in part to this sentiment) and that the SAVAK weren't a friendly bunch.
The game does highlight what Iranian life was like from 1953 on as it modernized and, though there are some shoutouts to Mohammad Mosaddegh's overthrow courtesy of MI6 and the CIA through Operation Ajax, this only serves to reaffirm the developer's bias to the effect of -- "Wow, isn't it such a shame that Iran became an Islamic Republic."
To illustrate better, I'll draw my thoughts from another angle: imagine if the insufferable coming of age movie "Garden State" (2004) were combined with a youth political drama. Yeah, I can feel your excitement building already.
Another, different, and probably more substantive critique I could provide for those unaware of the political, social, or historical components within the game is that it could've been more expansive with a branching plot. You, Reza, the player, are permanently stuck as a dumb collaborator with naive revolutionaries. In this way, "1979 Revolution" truly sticks to history as it occurred.
Welp, those are my thoughts about this adventure game from a self-anointed, self-styled, and perhaps in this case, immodest scholar of the Middle East.

There's a lot to talk about with this game, so buckle up! I'll be addressing the game in different portions, so if you want to see a certain topic or game mode, prepare to scroll a little bit.
CAMPAIGN:
I really have no strong opinion on the campaign, other than that it is of fun. It's really cool that Treyarch decided to prepare multiplayer campaign levels for this game, and that makes it infinitely more interesting and replayable than any other CoD campaign in the series. The progression system is kind of neat, but ultimately kind of worthless since there are certain builds that will just let you steamroll the game on any difficulty. Additionally, I don't really feel compelled to play it outside of maybe grinding for achievements since the unlocks for the other modes don't really add much. The camos you unlock in the campaign are fairly ugly in comparison to the ones found in Zombies and Multiplayer and don't really warrant an unlock at all. Overall, the campaign is just OK. If you have some friends to play it with, it can be a great time, but other than that I wouldn't really bother.
FREERUN:
Freerun is a neat little mode added in Black Ops 3 that lets you race on a few different parkour courses, testing your skills with the game mechanics and speed of input and reaction. I have not played very much of this mode since it does not interest me personally, but it is very well done and I can appreciate the effort that has gone into making it work. I love when CoD has little bonus modes or fun side distractions to break up the monotony of grinding Multiplayer games, so stuff like this is really the way to go. I think this can be absolutley great for the right person, making them want to grind out new times and beat their friends scores, and that if you own the game you owe it to yourself to give it a try.
MULTIPLAYER:
If you've played a CoD game before, you know kind of what to expect. Kind of. The Pick 10 system is back and as good as ever, making choosing that attachment or extra perk feel interesting and game changing as opposed to older games in the series that just let you stack up your class with too many strengths and not enough weaknesses. In addition, the new Specialist system makes the game much more interesting to play and makes you feel like you can have an impact on the game even if you're not doing too well. I am of mixed opinion on this right now, as the Specialist weapons and abilities are fun to use, but feel completely obnoxious and OP to play against. That, in my humble opinion, is a huge game design flaw. Nothing should ever feel like that in a game, especially after I've already put in so much time and effort trying to learn it. That being said, this brings me to my next point: DLC weapons and the over abudance of certain weapons. DLC weapons unabashedly feel like the best weapons in the entire game. One of the newer ones, the PPsh, feels unstoppable. I asked a few Prestige Masters, who shall remain unamed at their request, what they thought. One told me he was tired of playing the game and losing when people of lower skill could just buy their way to the gun and beat him without being good, one told me she thought Treyarch had made a huge mistake, and finally the third I reviewed said it was one of the most overpowered guns he'd ever seen. Taken with a grain of salt, the DLC weapons and the loot crate system are the worst in any game I've ever played. They directly alter gameplay and make you better at it. The melee weapons are fine since they have been patched to play the same as the Combat Knife, which everyone has, but the actual guns are just stupidly powerful in some cases and really make the experience suck. In addition, its almost impossible to get them without paying money or playing an extreme amount. Hats off to Treyarch for trying to add a Contract system in order to get more players the guns and skins, but Activision and their stupid pay to win systems for CoD really need to stop. That's all I'll say on the issue since this is sort of absorbing my addressing of the Multiplayer mode as a whole. In addition to DLC weapons, some weapons are just overused. This is not really the developers fault persay, but some of them are just too easy to use. Shotguns are the flavor of the month, and you will not find a game without someone who just either camps in one easy to abuse area with a shotgun or someone who is very good at sliding/manuevring who can outgun you with a shotgun. The second one is forgiveable since its up to player skill, but the fact that most of the maps can easily encourage camping and silly tactics like waiting for people to spawn so you can kill them is very disappointing. Even this far into the series life, it cannot simpy fix these issues with having set spawns or some similar fix that many indie games and even competitors have impelemented. That being said, many of the new maps are well designed and make good use of the new mechanics. I like that the developers haven't forgotten how much fun it was to witness things happening in the map outside of your fight with the other team, like the train on a map I forgot the name of the runs through the middle and can kill you if you get hit, or change the pace of the firefight by blocking off certain routes to run. CoD has always had very expressive design in its maps, and Black Ops 3 is no different. The DLC maps especially are very cool, and I really enjoy the remasters they made to fan-favorites like Raid from Black Ops 2. Unfortunately, this leads me to my next point: Map availability. There is an event going on at the time of writing that lets everyone try the DLC maps for free, but other than that, you will never play on a DLC map in public matchmaking. It sounds hyperbolic, but if even one person doesn't have the DLC, the automatic map algorithim will knock every DLC map out of the pool of choices for the players. It really is silly and makes the DLC feel a lot less meaningul and a lot more like fluff and crap to suck your wallet dry. To be clear, I only pick on the game so much because I love it and feel like it can be much more than it is right now. Overall, CoD's fantastic multiplayer action returns in full force with new mechanics and fun maps, only hindered by silly, decade old problems for the series and Activision's desperate attempts to remain relevant in the DLC scene in the current year.
ZOMBIES:
Saved the best for last! I truly think that this iteration of Zombies is one of the best for the entire series. I'm spending such little time on it because its just good. I don't need a paragraphs long diatribe for this one, just hear this: The leveling system is great, the DLC maps feel meaningful and different while providing and interesting story and challenge, the Gobblegum system is much more fair and interesting than the loot crates in multiplayer, and Theater mode is dope. The only issue is finding players, but many dedicated players (like me!) will play with you on any map. The one tiny issue I have is that Gobblegums can kind of be bought with money, making high round runs easier in theory. However, I will be the first to say that this game is hard as nails and even getting powerups and free perks from the Gobblegums will not save you if you're bad at the game. This balances out the only really glaring issue with the mode outright, and makes the experience feel a more genuine and intense.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Black Ops 3 and hope to have even more enjoyable games with the new DLC. This game is in essence a port, and with that comes a suprisingly robust and feature full settings menu for a CoD game. Very well done and well optimized. The games price tag is a little hefty, coming at $100 USD if you want the full experience. I would recommend waiting for a sale or getting the game on a site like HumbleBundle when the price goes down, but overall the game is of superior quality and Treyarch did a fantastic job with it.

I'm redoing this review to fit my 100 hours into Secret World Legends. I'll probably update it if anything comes up when I'll hit end-game but as of now this will do. You can read the old review here
if you're really interested in how I changed my opinion and, as always
. We have no other way to let the developers know our unhappiness with the newest state of the game if not by reviewing the game in the manner we think it's most fitting. Of course, if someone gives a negative review just because they like being a d*ick, then it's on them. But this is my own view of what the game has become. You cna say "yeah" or yell "no", but this is still my own review.
Ayy. I judged the game harshly? No, I didn't. I still retain
of what I had previously written on this review and my negative thumb-down won't change it.
Let me start with the real issues:
- a.k.a. please, don't do that.
The Gear Progression is one of the most tiring and non-sensical pieces of art I've ever seen in an MMORPG: you have to fuse stuff together, to get your own stuff to a high level, but it's not worth it if your own equipment doesn't have at least two pips at the bottom and by the time you notice that you've just sunk all of your time into upgrading a 1pip weapon, you'll want to physically remove yourself from the room.
It's tiring and grating how you have to go panning for gold to either get a higher pip piece of equipment (even when you do all missions in a region, the best rate you can get for a
piece of green 3pip equipment is approx. 1 on 50 satchels (which means 50 missions and side missions by the way) and how you have to keep grinding missions to upgrade all of your stuff. All in all, it's just... downright boring and not rewarding in the least, mind me. I do have all my equipment at 3pip and it's only because my best friend found it and traded it with me. On my own? I managed to only drop
wrist talisman that had 3pips. It's... very grating and insulting, to be honest.
- where am I going with this?
If I told you that I feel like the non-sensical "level" of the TSW days made me feel more accomplished than seeing my character max out her level just shy out of Scorched Desert, would that make you laugh? The new level system feels stale and improvised at best: if you're doing everything (and I mean EVERYTHING - from rare mobs to exploration to all missions) with a Patron membership, chances are you will reach CotSG at level 50, with little to nothing to show for it as the rate you get AP and SP has been somewhat nerfed and now it can't keep up with the rate I go forward with the game. It's... unaccomplishing, really. It feels you're going up but at the same time just staying in one place. Still. Unmoving.
- why do you even play without this on?
I sunk 100 hours on SWL to understand that Patron privileges
get you far. It's not a P2W strategy but it is most definitely a good strategy to get you sinking money into a subscription. In poor words: me and my friend started playing without membership, then we stopped at Savage Coast. We got back, he was still free and I have a 30 days sub, result? I am level 50 in City of The Sun God, I have filled out one Passive Ability page and filling out the second (shotgun/blade), filled out four Active Abilty Pages (I will get into this issue later, hold onto it), I have steadily 60k MoFs to sink into my equipment upgrades and Aurum exchange. Him? It's a miracle he caps 10k sometimes. being Patron just makes everything smoother, I suppose. A lot whole smoother. Which isn't really fair when it comes to people wanting to play the game for free and finding out that most mission will ask them to wait for 3 days.
- NNGHHH.
The ability Wheel is done for, no more interesting weapon combinations, no more swapping builds and weapons without feeling like you've been punished by the Outer Gods and a fair balance between SP and AP gains.
Active Ability pages have little active ability to themselves and are easy to fill immediately (I filled my Shotgun/Blade one in almost two days and then I went on to fill the others, capping Elemental and Blood) while Passive Skills are... treacherously long to fill. Most of them are connected to some abilities you might have already pakced in your build and will prove essential in some ways, but you can't get to them due to the fact that they added "perma stat booster" in between. It's just... very unfairly unbalanced? You cap at 50, which will roughly mean you will be able to get from 5 to 3 different Skills at any given time you're capping (before it was 90 or so) and that doesn't bode well when you have a long
of abilities to get. While this works for APs because they're less than passives, this doesn't work with the latter because it just becomes a game of "who can cap and get one ability before having to grind again".
A lot of stuff is still broken, a lot of missions still bug out (now more than ever), GMs are seldom present (I opened a ticket THREE days ago about a mission that bugged out on me and I couldn't finish it at all and they never replied while on TSW they seemed to be promptly present for anything wrong that might have occurred) but the story, the plotline the
thing this game has to offer is there, in all of its pristine glory.
So play it for the story, don't stay for the horrendous changes they've made.

TL;DR If you are a returning player... you are probably not going to like SWL, but if you are a new player I would still recommend giving it a try; just do not spend any money on it - enjoy the ambiance and story, then quit.
Disclaimer: I was a "grand master" aka "lifetime patron" of TSW and loved it dearly, here in I will try to review SWL objectively and without lingering biases either for or against SWL.
TSW was the original game; it had its flaws, but still had a decent player base.  Funcom wanted to try and revitalize that player base by "re-releasing" what they would consider an enhanced edition; but in-so-doing they alienated many of their long-time players, because while the original game is still able to be downloaded and played, it has become a ghost town and the new game... well we'll cover that in the next section.
SWL is essentially the same game except for a few differences; the graphics engine is supposed to be updated... tho from my experience I've notice little difference. The combat system has been completely over-hauled - the new system is... well it is noob friendly, the old system had a high learning curve to understand but once understood allowed for many more interesting and unique builds than the new dumbed down version does.  Some examples; ALL builds now have almost exactly the same optimal dps regardless of what weapons or dps abilities you use.  Passive abilities used to be mix & match to your heart's content, now each only applies to one active ability - so while you can still mix & match doing so would be stupid if you do not have the linked active ability equipped.  Additionally, they have revamped gear progression; gone are the runes/essences, instead you merge similar items together to "level" one of them up - it is an insanely long grind to get gear to maximum level... and throughout the process you will be tempted to spend real life money to accelerate your progression.  Since SWL is F2P there are countless "micro-transactions" and this time they are not just on cosmetics, they have essentially made the game pay-to-win; if you wanted to, you could take a lvl 1 and instantly level his skill trees to maximum, convert your bought currency to AH currency and fully gear out your level one as far as your real world money would last.
That said, this review is marked as "Yes, I would recommend this game," why?  Because SWL has the same story and ambiance as TSW had, and despite its flaws those parts are still fantastic.  I LOVE the world setting they created here, I've never found anything else quite like it and was the reason I paid for lifetime subscription in the first place.  Returning players will have already experienced that, and so there is no need for them to go through it a 2nd time unless they want to, but for new players I would still recommend giving it a playthrough just to experience this world and its stories.
If you ARE a returning player please read MizoreYukii's excellent guide on how to transfer your TSW vanity items into SWL, just keep in mind that if you make any mistakes or anything goes wrong during the transfer, customer service will not do anything for you.

This game is not for people who have only played DOOM-cubed. This game is for people who played ClassicDOOM on DOS. Released during the same era of gaming, Hexen is, as the title suggests, the sequel to Heretic.  I actually never played this in its heyday, so this is actually a new experience for me.  I didn't understand the hub system when I was younger, so never actually touched Hexen until just recently.
In this game, instead of being just one "DOOMguy" or "Corvus/Hereticguy/FantasyDOOMguy," you can choose one of three classes: a Fighter, a Cleric, or Mage.  Each have their strengths and weaknesses, and will actually use certain items/powerups in the game differently, most notably the Flechette.  The demos that play if you don't create a new game are a bit misleading, as they suggest that each class has a different set of levels to playthrough.  Or, they did for me anyway.  I quickly figured out that is not the case, and was a little disappointed at first, but quickly got over it.  Now that I'm older, I understand the Hub system better and am able to navigate through the levels easier.  One thing I would stress: explore everywhere.  Don't leave any portion of your maps blank if you can help it.  Some important switches are hidden in easily-disregarded places, and you will find yourself stuck if you don't throw/flip them.
People looking for "new and exciting ame mechanics" will likely be very disappointed.  As far as I know, this particular iteration of a hub system has not been recreated for any other (popular) FPS-type game outside the Heretic franchise.  But, if you played these games and similar during their heyday, I would highly recommend getting them for a trip down Memory Lane.
(Also, the price of these games in the bundle can't be beat.  Ten bucks for four games?  That's $2.50 USD per game!)

This game is a PC version of Katamari Damacy, almost exactly.
Basically, you start off small, and absorb things around you to grow, which allows you to aborb bigger things and explore more of the level. It's a fun concept that's fun to play, both in Katamari Damacy and in this game.
The main downsides are the length and the map sizes. The game is way too short, and it can easily be beaten 100% in a few hours, max. The maps are also a bit too small, and most of them can be fully explored in 2-3 minutes.
If you're not familiar with this type of game, it is absolutely worth trying. Get a Katamari title if you have the right platform for one of them, and if not, try this game. I got it for half price at $5, and it was worth it, barely. I had a lot of fun, but you don't get much playtime for your money.

Fun adventure game with a Japanese twist. I really liked the story and the main character Detective Itou. The only downside is for a game with 11 endings the NG+ skipping needs some work. I don't want to have to click 40 times to get through dialogue I've definitely already seen. If this was rectified seeing the alternative endings would be less of a slog.

Tokyo Dark looks interesting, but it doesn't go much further than that. The storyline is essentially just a mash-up of various Japanese horror tropes like they were trying to check as many boxes as they could, and it all comes together to form a plot that basically never manages to surprise you. It's advertised as a mix of point-and-click adventure and visual novel, but in reality it's basically just a visual novel that also lets you walk around. There's a grand total of a single puzzle that amounts to clicking on flickering lights in order, and occasionally you get the choice of either skipping a 'puzzle' by shooting something or taking a few steps to the left to click on something else to solve it a different way.
The game presents itself as being similar to Telltale's choice-based adventure games, and you have a 4-way stat system for Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, and Neurosis, but neither of these matter much in practice. Most of the time the game is too scared to punish you for any of the minor choices, and in my two playthroughs so far the stats haven't made any visible difference at all. The game has 11 endings, but the replay feature barely works so it's hard to justify trying to get all of them - you only get the ability to manually save after your first playthrough, but you're limited to 6 save slots and can only save at predetermined points in the story, and some of these spots are poorly placed so that you have to scroll through several minutes of text to get back to them. There is a skip function, but it's just as broken, and half the time it won't let you skip text you've already read while other times it
let you skip text you
read before. I only got what seems to be the two "main" endings, but I really don't care enough to go back and look for the other 9.
It isn't an awful game, but I think it's at least overpriced at $18. It's fairly buggy and the features that do work seem half-finished at best, and chances are the story is nothing you haven't seen before. If it'd been priced at $10 I could maybe recommend it, but it's not worth almost 20.

I completed this (haven't bothered with New Game + yet), so it's obviously not terrible or anything like that, but on balance I'm struggling to outright recommend it. If there were a "Neutral" option, I'd probably choose it, as I can see it appealing to some people, but be aware that it's not really a Point and Click Adventure in the sense that most people would understand.
Yes, you do point and click to walk around the scenes and interact with people, but in 4.5 hours of gameplay, it only has one actual puzzle (where you have to push a series of buttons in the correct order), and one mini-game (an arcade machine). Mostly, the game leads you by the nose to the next bit of the story with very little freedom.
There is a karma type system, where the choices you make affect later conversation options and the ending, which seems quite well developed with lots of branching paths. The game also makes a big deal about your "SPIN" stats (Sanity, Professionalism, Investigation, Neurosis), but in practice they don't seem to have much impact on gameplay and can largely be ignored.
So, as a Point and Click Adventure, it fails spectacularly due to the near-complete lack of puzzles, which is why I'm choosing to not recommend it. If however you can accept it as a supernatural thriller "visual novel", then I guess you would probably enjoy it and moving around the gameworld does in fairness add a lot to feeling immersed in the story.
(Parently advisory: The story and themes are dark and mature, this is not a game for kids).

From my perspective, I viewed this rendition of history as heavily pro-Tudeh (the Communist Party of Iran) and though it touches on the application of fiqh to Communists from the religious characters within in the game, "1979 Revolution: Black Friday" communicates its narrative as the Arab Spring in another lacquer. And that's a shame really. There is no equivalency to be drawn between the current Sunni revolutionary movements and the Iranian Revolution proper.
The developers did their homework for sure, but I couldn't get my character to become a Shia fundamentalist or lead him to become a basiji so what's the point of player driven actions or agency? Though Reza (the protagonist) is clearly Westernized, it didn't permit me the option of having a developing narrative drive a connection towards increasing his faith.
As an honest assessment, this game's presentation falls into this terrible milquetoast middle ground that simultaneously would♥♥♥♥♥♥off Shah loyalist expats and a contemporary Shia as the Tudeh are portrayed as harmless, albeit naive, saints. They're only critiqued as hypocritical, or worst of all, taken for the fools that they were. Aside from those notes, the game is a "rah rah go student revolutionary movements" within a general context and retelling that Pahlavi was a pretty bad leader (I agree only in part to this sentiment) and that the SAVAK weren't a friendly bunch.
The game does highlight what Iranian life was like from 1953 on as it modernized and, though there are some shoutouts to Mohammad Mosaddegh's overthrow courtesy of MI6 and the CIA through Operation Ajax, this only serves to reaffirm the developer's bias to the effect of -- "Wow, isn't it such a shame that Iran became an Islamic Republic."
To illustrate better, I'll draw my thoughts from another angle: imagine if the insufferable coming of age movie "Garden State" (2004) were combined with a youth political drama. Yeah, I can feel your excitement building already.
Another, different, and probably more substantive critique I could provide for those unaware of the political, social, or historical components within the game is that it could've been more expansive with a branching plot. You, Reza, the player, are permanently stuck as a dumb collaborator with naive revolutionaries. In this way, "1979 Revolution" truly sticks to history as it occurred.
Welp, those are my thoughts about this adventure game from a self-anointed, self-styled, and perhaps in this case, immodest scholar of the Middle East.

As someone who study history professionally, I sometimes do not like some mainstream historical games that are eurocentric and politicized. Out of curiosity, I purchased this game the moment it came out because the topic always fascinates me. Before playing it, I thought this game is more or less going to be another game preaching you how bad Khomeini was and how he "stole" the revolution. However and fortunately, I was completely wrong.
The developer claims the plot is based on a real story. The protagonist, Reza, is from a wealthy family. He studied abroad in Germany. When he came back to Iran, he almost came across the ongoing revolution by accident. Iran was not it once was anymore. After seeing what he saw, he decided to participate in it. Whereas, his involvement troubled him with countless dilemmas, compelling him to pick sides. On one hand there is his brother, on the other are his friends and cousin. You choices affect how the game progresses.
This game excites the hell out of me. Walking on the street, you feel as if you are living through the revolution yourself. Seeing people protesting and suffering, you are compelled to feel sympathetic towards them. The political figures in this game are entirely real. When I was the graffiti of Khomeini on the street, I was like "Oh my God!" and my heart was beating so fast.
Yes, historical figures matter. But history is, in fact, made possible by the little people. This game does not pick a political side nor try to preach you liberal democracy. Instead, it tells you the paradox and contradiction existed in the revolution, making the choices hard to make. Ideal is idealistic because it is not reality. The moment when you threw the stone, it changed you forever. Is violence necessary? Is family more important than ideal? Is life more important than freedom? Would you sacrifice the 1/3 for the other 2/3? You are the one to answer these questions that we are still unable to answer today.
I feel I can relate to this game so much. I also come from a wealthy family. My parents also lived through a different revolution. I am also idealistic yet realistic. My ideal betrays my spectrum but I feel it is right. My reality does not allow me to follow my ideal if I were to keep my status. I believe in democracy yet I see authoritarianism as a highly efficient system. I love my family yet I want to pursue my ideal.
I think we all are Reza. We are all as contradictory as the choices we make in this game.
