Overall rating:
7.5/10
Description:
an historical choice based narative set during the Iranian islamic revolution, it's like someone hired TellTale to make a history lesson
Expected completion time:
between 1.5 - 3 hours depending on how much exploring you do
For those who like:
Telltale, Valient hearts: the great war, Life is Strange
What I liked?
unlike most choice based naratives, this game was heavily inspired by real people and makes you feel like you're actually in the middle of a country on the brink of revolution. it is also set during a very important part of modern history that doesn't get alot of attention, so i'm glad that these kinds of games are being made.
what i also liked was how orgainc the dialog was, the voice acting is great (with a few familiar voices from some well know voice actors) and the interactions felt really natural (take note dev's, real people talk over each other)
What I didn’t like?
the game mechanics were sub-par, the time to make choices were often too short to make a proper decision, the "stories" were organised terribly (which is important for completionests like me). the game also had a few technical issues, at one point i was reading some background info in the menue and the story continued without me, which caused me to miss some important plot details so i had to go back and reply some of the game. plus i didn't like the ending (which i'll get to shortly)
basically the whole game was riddles with rookie mistakes, which may or may not be important for this kind of narritive, but the devil is in the details.
Value for money?:
personally i would say that for a 3-hour game the price is a little high (11.99)
Collectables/Extras?:
there is ALOT of extra info, mainly on historical events, and details about the culture and politics of Iran at the time of the revolution. which is great for someone who loves the extra history lesson (i.e. me).
Ending?
i was dissapointed that the game concluded with a binary ending. it was also clear that the devs put more effort into one
ending over the other, and both endings felt.....unfinished. like it should have cut to "to be continued" but never did. which lost the game a few points in my book (ending are important).
Things of note:
this is really recent history, the islamic revolution was big turning point in the politics of the middle east, and we're still dealing with the aftermath today. this is the kind of game that not everyone will enjoy, but everyone SHOULD play.
Improvements?
at the time of this review (9/April/2016) the game could do with a patch or two, and the promis of a sequal may make the ending feel a bit more satisfying.

OK, the dust has settled, SWL has had time to get the kinks worked out and here is my current opinion.
The biggest turnoff for me, is how some of the games basic elements are now artificially locked behind daily limits.  Not a paywall... A Daily limit on how many quests and things you can do that will actually yeild spendable cash.
I get it, it means inflation due to grinding and farming will be minimized.  Hoorah  *tiny bit of pathetic confetti* But it also means if you really want something that someone is charging 30K credits for, you will need to either:
A:  have 3 characters and run each through the Daily mission allotment, each netting around 10K credits.
OR...
B:  wait 3 days, doing daily missions on one character.
OR
C:  You spend real money on Aurum, and convert that to in game cash... *It's almost like the Devs are trying to give us shady incentives to feel FORCED to buy in game currency!
PLEASE NOTE that subscribing, no longer appears to give you Aurum (WTF?) nor does it unshackle you from the Daily limits.   So lets say you are like me, and decide to support the game with VIP status.  Now I STILL need to spend MORE money for things that USED to be included with a membership...
ALSO Note, that the way the Daily's work, is most of the daily tasks are to complete 3 missions (side, or Regular), some of those can take a good long time, so if you log in for half an hour and only finish 1 or 2 missions, you won't get anything unless you stick around another 15-20 minutes to beat a 3rd.  Furthermore, you would need to complete ALL the dailys to get close to 10K... So playing casually will mean you won't get much at all.
IMHO these are ABSOLUTELY Terrible design decisions, because it partially nerfs any reason to play for long beyond the initial daily payout.  Oh sure, you still get XP, you still get shards, you still get whatever else.
But It's so transparently greedy IMHO.
Worse than that, there is almost no reason to subscribe, indeed, Playing for free Vs VIP has so few real benefits now (Oh sure, double XP and shards I guess... So now you can get to max level and epic gear long before you hit Transylvania), that subbing doesn't seem to be worth it.
Now you probably notice I'm not talking much about the game, and that should tell you something.
YES, they dramatically improved combat gameplay.  But in the process they managed to dumb down a lot of elements of the game.  From deck building, to some quests which now have WAY too obvious glowing clue markers that they didn't have before.
In the past, if you had to follow a Blood Trail, you had to look for the blood on the ground and make educated decisions on which way to go to find the next splotch.  Now, this enhancer thing activates and the blood is highlighted in blue light... that flashes and blinks for you.
They didn't go quite so far in other quests, but they do have more nav markers than before.  At least investigation missions are largely unchanged or improved.
Bottom line - As a FREE to play game, this is still one of the first ones I reccomend to anyone who hasn't played one before.
For a free game you get dozens of hours of really unique and original content.  Unless you hate the quirky style of the characters and personalities, or the subject matter, you will be sucked into an intricate world setting that DESERVES not just respect, but IMHO is the most well fleshed out and immersive IP to come out for an MMO EVER.
I love the games setting so much that I wish they would make source books for PNP RPGS or something.  If they have already, let me know in the comments.
So, I give this game a hesitant THUMBS UP.
The gameplay is great, the puzzles and story telling are Worthy of a single player game. The plot and setting are GREAT, and the ammount of content you get for free is astonishing.
But that greedy daily limit on cash rewards thing, kills it for me, and really means I got no reason to log in sometimes... Heck even the lack of a proper cash store is annoying, Ironic I know.
So yeah TRY before you buy anything, But unless you hate the genre, I'd say you got nothing to lose but bandwidth and install time.
Good luck!

While it hasn't aged that well, it hasn't aged terribly either. All the core things that made this game interesting and fun to play are still there today. Interesting usable items, strange puzzles that can often lead you to an early grave, and vicious enemies waiting to club you to death, or burn your corpse to a crisp.
There are three classes you can play in this game, and all have weaponry and stats unique to them. All of them offer a slightly different take on playing through the game, and after trying them all out for the first area or so, you'll quickly choose one as a favorite.
Interesting level design, cool weapons and items, surpise enemy attacks, and fast game play keep this game going strong until the end. If you're looking for an alternative to Doom, or maybe even Quake this would be it. Especially since it has the whole fantasy genre twist to go with it, and a bit better level design and interactivity.
If you can figure out how to get multiplayer going in this game, it is definitly worth it. There's nothing quite as nice as slaughtering tons of demons with a buddy, and having help figuring out puzzles and finding keys strewn through out the well designed levels.
However don't expect to have an easy way to do it. All the methods I could find seemed some what difficult to attempt to set up a game, even with third party programs such as Hamachi, it's a bit difficult to figure it out, and get a game running with a friend. There's probably a guide somewhere out there that will assist you in this, if only playing with friends is a deal breaker for you.
Pick this game up if you enjoy playing old school FPS shooters. This one might suprise you, and keep you playing to the end. If you've played it before, it's definitly worth having on here just to blast through a few levels every once in awhile. If you've never played the game before, give it a try, it's worth a spin if you never got to experience it before.

Puddle is a platform-ish game. You have to move your puddle of liquid around the different levels. You don't have full control over the liquid though. The liquid moves depending on gravity and momentum (or other factors, depending on which level you're at). All you can do is angle the screen left or right, making the liquid move that way. The angling also helps you slow down or speed up your liquid. You only need 2 buttons, left and right. The liquids you control differ from level to level. Sometimes, it's a thick goo that sticks well together, othertimes it's an explosive goo that explodes when it crashes against a surface.
Looking at the levels, they really look nice. Graphically, this game is beautiful. Gameplaywise though, some can feel really unfair. You can't see what's ahead, so finishing a level on the first try is very difficult. There are a couple levels where it's not very well explained what you need to do or how the physics have changed from the previous level. There are no checkpoints in any level, meaning you need to complete the entire level in one go. Most of the levels are however quite short.
The game doesn't store its info on the steam servers, so if you uninstall the game, you lose all your progress.
Looking back, I like the idea, but too many levels feel unfair and become unfun. I don't recommand this game. If you want to try this, buy it when on sale.

The game is obviously beautifully designed and the gameplay is refreshingly different, but my first time playing, I didnt give it enough time and thought it was boring. When I finally dragged myself back to it, I found one of the best indie games I have played.
The controls seem simple at first  but you will soon learn there is more to it than just leaning the screen to make water fall down a hole. The hazards start requiring a bit more thinking and you will not always have the luxury of stopping to figure it out. The variety of liquids differ in more ways than just colour and viscosity. You may have trouble keeping some pooled together, others may dissolve or even explode in certain situations. Then there is the occasional change of physics to deal with and keep you on your toes.
This is definately not a game you should try to play through quickly as you will miss its full potential. Just finishing it is one thing but to get all achievements will require some patience and skill and a lot of planning. While difficult in spots, the game does not give the feeling of being impossible. You may pull some hair out but there is always the impression that you can do it if you just move slightly different over a section.
This is definately one of the more memorable and enjoyable indie games I have played. The achievements are well designed and give a sense of being rewarding, not just collecting. The game is challenging, but not near-impossible, so even if you doubt you gaming skills, I would still recommend looking at this game.

You may have noticed that the publisher does not want to put a genre tag on this game, although the description does mention the word 'puzzles'. Well, I understand that but I will name the genre:
is a platformer game. Granted, it's a platformer game that uses unique mechanics in the sense that the 'avatar' is not a classic little man, animal, robot or a ball. But in the end all you do is guide something through a linear, straightforward parcours towards the finish line, while jumping (to avoid falling to your 'death') and while dodging stuff (to avoid getting 'killed' if you touch it). If that's not the very definition of a platformer game, I don't know what is. Assuming the word 'puzzle' implies at least a bit of thinking on how to solve a problem, there is no puzzling whatsoever in
. You always know exactly what needs to be done: there is only one way throug the parcours before you and you'll get through it by trial and error, not by puzzling your way out.
In
, you don't control an avatar directly. You can only press a button to tilt the screen to the right or a button to tilt the screen to the left. As you tilt the screen, gravity will cause the 'avatar' to move. Most of the time, the 'avatar' has something to do with liquids. That means you need to guide either a liquid or a container containing a liquid through a parcours.
The level design is quite impressive. There is a lot of variety in the levels and they are all clearly designed with an eye for detail. But be warned, this is a very difficult game to master. Getting through the later levels will take a lot of practice until you know the parcours pretty much by heart, especially if you want to achieve the best score for each level to get the 'gold medal' the game awards, or for the Steam Achievement.
The graphics are quite nice and vibrant, and they managed to bring a lot of variety to the settings and their backgrounds, which is an impressive feat for a game with a pretty basic concept like this.
The music is all over the place. Sometimes I hardly noticed the music because it was soft and unintrusive, almost 'zen-like'. Other times, you get to hear techno music with a thumping bass beat. I have nothing against either of those music styles, but for a game I think they should pick one because alternating between two completely opposite genres is just weird.

has a lot of strong sides, especially its graphics and its level design. But in the end, for platformer games I weigh the fun factor against the frustration factor. Great platformers are games that manage to provide more fun than frustration. To be a positive experience, it should at least be 50-50. And
fails to balance that equation. It's more like 60% frustration and 40% fun, maybe even 70-30, so I can't recommend this game in general. Only if you're a die-hard platformer gamer or a gamer looking for a nerve-wrecking challenge that

is right up your alley.

I already played Castle Crashers from Behemoth and I liked that game so I went into this one hoping for the same. And I can happily say this game is heaps of fun! However, it is also heaps of rage. You will try to beat those levels over and over and over again. Some because they are timed, others for the best level grade. My advice is to get a gamepad for that because, while keyboard gameplay is okay, it hurts your fingers a lot more. There are 8 areas and each has 9 standard levels, 2 timed boss levels and 3 timed encore levels. You can even find some secrets levels. You can unlock some new weapons (for yarn) and character faces (for gems) along the way to finish each area. The story is funny and will entertain you with narration and videos. Playing alone is nice but where the game really shines is co-op play. The levels are somewhat changed in co-op to emphasize on teamwork of both players. The game is NOT easy, it will make you angry/frustrated a lot, escpecially in co-op play. I played this mostly with my sister and our stress levels were through the roof. After you are done with the base game there are TONS of user-created levels to play. They are of various quality but most are fun. I did not like arena matches that much but it is up to your preference. Overall a great quirky game for anyone who likes platformers!

What I really like is that you're allowed to build your city, and are faced with the issues that comes with growth of it, as of course garbage land fills, power shortages, plumbing needed, traffic jams etc. In that sense, this game is very much like the original Sim City released by Maxis (1989), since there's no disasters, no Godzilla trampling your city, or anything like that. Now, this is what I like with this game, so for others that enjoy these kind of intrusions, that might be a drawback.
All that stuff can be had though, but that is as DLCs. Nothing as far as I'm concerned is needed in the form of DLCs to be able to play this game though, or to experience it as a full game. Instead, if you'd like disasters, you can pick up a disaster DLC, if you want snow, pick up that DLC. Of course Paradox makes money this way, but the only DLC I see that should've been in the game from the start might be After Dark. The bigger content DLCs are somewhat pricey though, but for when you want a new challenge, I suppose one of those might provide that.
All in all, the base game is very good on its own, and contains all you need for hours and hours of citybuilding, and considering that, the ordinary price (€28) is more than fair for this game. If it's on sale I'd consider it close to a steal.

With Never Alone and a few others, it's pretty cool to have videogames about different cultures and histories that you don't ever get in this medium. In this case it's Iran around the time of the Islamic Revolution when anti-establishment sentiment was soaring against the Shah totalitarian regime. It's fascinating to learn about that through the game while having a cohesive and compelling story so it doesn't feel like just a narrated walk through a museum exhibit. All the historical and cultural tidbits you learn and uncover makes for an enlightening experience like the political climate of the time such as about SAVAT or the Mujahideen, Iran's version of backgammon, the food, and why there was such an anti-American fervour.
The game plays like a historical Telltale game where you have player control and moral decisions to make but it's not quite an adventure game and more a cinematic experience. It's well-written drama with moving music and great voice acting. There are large crowd setpieces which are quite impressive for how much detail is packed in for a crowdfunded game (that missed its initial Kickstarter goal of $395K). There are sometimes QTEs which just reminded me of Indigo Prophecy and they can be silly but the most effective one is when you're moving between a hail of bullets and can die pretty easily, so patience and attention to audio cues is key. There's a framed narrative so you're reminiscing about this time of the 1979 Revolution while being interrogated and tortured. You play as Reza, who's a photographer struggling to remain neutral as it becomes increasingly harder to do at the cusp of a revolution. You've been away from the country so it's also a homecoming story. All the photograph taking reminded me of Beyond Good And Evil, so that was great. Often when you take a photo, you can read more info about the real event which reminded me of Never Alone's tapes.
There's a cast of characters that are all interesting (especially Bibi the woman leader of the protests, Babak the close friend, Ali the hothead, and Hossein your brother who's Shah security). Moral decisions relating to them can be trying with your own politics like whether violence such as throwing rocks during a protest is justifiable under such oppression. There's a particular one in the last quarter of the game that will feel like you're given nothing to make such a potentially devastating accusation or who to save which plays into the endings. There are 19 chapters, some of them can zip by in a few minutes while the ones where you're controlling Reza and navigating environments while interacting with hotspots can be longer, so overall it's a 2 hour experience. The story is eventful enough that it doesn't feel short but despite both endings, the abrupt ending(s) is a major cliffhanger. Abrupt not in an artistic sense where there's meaning to it but just as if there will be a continuation to do with other characters.
Despite the intense drama around the revolution, it was the smaller specific moments that stuck with me more. At one point that's not related to the plot, you can decide to pray or not. I've never seen muslim prayer in a videogame ever and have to say it was very faithful with even a step-by-step photo guide. From that prayer, you get a line of dialogue about Prophet Muhammad PBUH that can be used later on. My favourite sequence was spending time in your home with your family, viewing live-action photos, arguing with family members about this political situation, rummaging through items, and coming across this giant stack of home video tapes. The photos and home videos are all live-action which made me wonder if this was autobiographical in a way, and that kind of intimacy was exciting. I wanted to spend more time with these characters and this world, which is why I felt unsatisfied with the ending as I just wanted more. That is probably a good thing.

There's good and bad here. Mostly good, but a little bad.

I've always been wary of games that try to tackle historical events, because they rarely seem to get their subject matter right. There's something disrespectful about historical games like the early Call of Duty titles, which placed players into real wars that real people fought and died in, exploiting those experiences by transforming them into mindless entertainment for the masses. Tackling this kind of heavy subject matter requires a degree of nuance that bleak loadscreen quotations or pressing F to pay respects don't even begin to provide.
1979 Revolution: Black Friday doesn't share those problems. Created by Rockstar Games veteran and Iranian national Navid Khonsari, whose family escaped the turmoil the title aims to portray, the game tells the story of the Iranian Revolution of 1979, which lead to the deposition of the Shah of Iran and the end of the Pahlavi dynasty. The influence of this period in Iranian history cannot be understated, yet knowledge of this point in history remains woefully elusive to the American public consciousness.
It's fitting, then, that the game starts out with so much exposition. This isn't a Call of Duty title looking to capitalize on history as a mere backdrop to action-heavy gameplay. The Telltale-esque title places players into a series of unfolding events as an Iranian photojournalist recently returned home from Germany. Early in the story, players will take a walk through a protest-crowded street, snapping pictures and listening to their companion expound on the issues facing Iran leading up to the 1979 revolution. Westernization, income inequality, government censorship - the developers are clearly aware of their audience's unfamiliarity with the setting and do a fantastic job of the setting the stage for the players.
It all comes naturally; your character, after all, has been out of the country for awhile, so it stands to reason that he might need to be caught up on current events. After snapping a photo, players are presented with a quick blurb of information and given the option to learn more, leading them to small snippets of Iran's history in the game's journal.
Fortunately, unlike many titles tackling heavy subject matter, 1979 Revolution is at least somewhat able to stand on its own as an entertaining game. It's informative without being preachy, and engages players with choice and consequence and quick-time event systems Telltale Games or Life is Strange veterans will find immediately familiar.
1979 Revolution is best described as a political thriller, and it isn't long until your jaunt down exposition lane is interrupted by the proverbial♥♥♥♥♥♥hitting the fan. It's a character driven story, showing Iranian nationals with a variety of different political and religious views reacting as their country is turned upside down. The voice acting is crucially well executed, thanks to a cadre of veteran film actors. Almost everyone involved with the project has a prior work that I've seen or am at least familiar with; I recognized the voice of Mozhan Marnò from The Blacklist, House of Cards, and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night immediately.
The game is an indie title though, and you can tell that the funds for its actors may have been diverted from other areas of its limited budget. The art assets in particular leave a bit to be desired; it will quickly become apparent that character models and animations are being reused for the game's extras. In a game like this though, pursuing flawless writing and voice acting for its characters ultimately should trump almost everything else.
1979 Revolution does end a bit abruptly. It's not as bad as say, The Banner Saga, but I was expecting the narrative to go on for an additional chapter, or maybe for it to show a bit more of the revolution's aftermath. It's not a bad ending per se, but it does sort of build and build and then just end in the middle of its own climax.
Overall, the game succeeds in bringing a historically accurate, better understanding of the titular revolution to those who play it. It's not a deep look and it doesn't get too bogged down in historical details, instead focusing broadly on the people of Iran as they lived through this formative moment in their nation's history. 1979 Revolution is worth checking out on that basis alone if you're interested in experiencing a sample of pre-revolution Iran and how it evolved to become the nation we have today.
If you're not interested in that, I'd find the the title harder to recommend. This is a game of ideas, and it follows that the title is inextricably linked to the message it wants its players to receive. Standing on its own, its narrative isn't as satisfying as a Telltale Game and its gameplay doesn't touch Life is Strange, but if you're generally interested in experiencing a bit of history, that can make the title shine.
1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a short game at just over two hours of total playtime, and is available on Steam for a full price of $12. I'll leave the value judgment up to you.

It's definitely not like the original Secret World. The game has a lot of potential but kind of went the way of Star Wars Galaxies to have a "Third Person, Action/FPS" type of MMO. The result is very jarring as you expect combat to be as dynamic and fluid as similar MMOs like Black Desert Online and Tera, but it falls incredibly short. Each skill is on a timer which varies from quick to long depending on the skill. Tied into this is usually a stat you have to follow and manage (such as overheating for the Magus) which leads you to paying more attention to the quick bars than the actual action. This is very unimmersive and detracts from the whole experience. They way I see it, it's kind of like Final Fantasy XI and XII where battles are real time but it takes time to activate many skills. The result is a dull battle system that feels slow and unnecessarily labored.
The quick bar itself is also terrible. Commands are initiated with both mouse clicks for some, number keys and a few letter keys. The end result is usually a jumbled mess of "shoot, which skill is ready to use and what key is it assigned to?" Sometimes character skills that take longer to activate are assigned to the left mouse click while quick attacks are assigned to "Q" while other characters are reversed. I've played through each class trying to find one that felt right and the premade chracter classes are not that great. I definitely miss the originals ability to mix and match classes to suit your play style (mine was a mix of a mage and an assassin).
The devs should definitely think about reworking some game mechanics again. I got bored after 2.5 hours of playing and trying to force myself to like a class. Some of the missions are still entertaining, but the gameplay itself made me go back to other MMOs. It would also be great if selecting a faction did something more than just a minor cosmetic purpose and had more depth to how missions play out, resolve as well as faction vs faction missions such as Illuminati vs Templars or Illuminati vs Templars vs Dragon.

Quick Summary: Deadlight Director’s Cut is practically identical to the original Deadlight game on Steam, so I’m not sure why it’s a separate entry and not just a DLC (for the new Survival mode). The game is 2D side-scrolling “run to the other end of the level” kind of like Trine, but in a post-apocalyptic world infested with “shadows “(zombies). Your character is human, so there’s no magic or double jumping, just good old fashioned axe chopping and sparse gun slinging.
You play a grizzled survivor named Randall, on a mission to track down your group of survivors, as well as your wife and daughter in the ruined city of Seattle. Along the way you’ll fight or avoid (mostly avoid) the shadows prowling around the city. There aren’t a lot of living humans to be found anymore, and the ones that you do find are even worse than the shadows. Yes, it’s like The Walking Dead television show.
The game is played in 2 dimensional side scrolling perspective, and there are a lot of platforming elements throughout the short game (5 hours?). The fact that your character is a plain old human limits what you can do and where you can go. For example you can only climb on ropes or ladders for a short time before your stamina depletes and you fall off. Since you can’t double jump or wall climb, you’re mostly limited to running across the landscape and climbing over short obstacles.  I played with an Xbox 360 controller and found it much better than mouse and keyboard.
You’ll be traveling with very limited ammunition for your guns, and while you do have a hefty fireman’s axe, the shadows have a ton of health and your stamina bar is limited. Fighting more than 1 shadow at a time leaves you perilously low on stamina. Fortunately a single headshot from your pistol will instantly kill any enemy, but it’s almost always better to run than to fight.  After all this isn’t an RPG and you don’t get money or experience from killing enemies.
You should play Deadlight if:
+You like 2D side scrolling adventure games or post-apocalyptic survival. The graphics are bleak and the story is compelling.
+You want an easy game with easy Steam achievements. You can get 80% or so with minimal effort since most of them are unmissable. Only a few parts of the game are actually hard. You have unlimited lives so you can just try over and over from the numerous checkpoints.
You should NOT play Deadlight if:
-You don’t like tense atmospheric games. That’s about it actually, the game is pretty good, though short.
Overall if you’re looking for a game to knock out in a day and want something easy, Deadlight may be for you. The added Survival mode is quite hard, and I couldn’t last more than a few minutes, though I’m not a hardcore player to begin with.

It's pretty dang short and it has a whole ton of unresolved plot threads. I'd like to see where they go, but we'll have to see if a sequel is made.
Since the game shows a point of view so often not seen in the West, I feel like it's definitely a good idea to try it for its pretty low price point.
Here is why you should get this game:
1. This is the only game I know of about this period of time that doesn't have a political agenda aside from telling this story from a layman's perspective. Reza starts as a sort of outsider having traveled abroad recently, so through his understanding we are able to see how the revolution looked to an everyman (at least in the first flashback sequence).
2. I like how all the pictures taken by the player throughout the game to progress the story are then linked up to the real life pictures that they're based on. It'd be nice if the focus didn't swing wildly back and forth, though.
3. In the scenes where the player is asked to explore the area there is a LOT of detail. I think my favorite scene in the game was going through Reza's house reading all of his parents' letters and watching their films.
4. The price point is a pretty fair one especially when it's on sale like it is now.
5. It lifts pretty heavily from the Telltale style of gameplay (QTE's, exploration sections, timed choices) so if you enjoy that style of storytelling this one fits the bill.
My major hang ups are:
1. The game assumes we know too much. It starts towards the end of things with Reza already a revolutionary working against the Islamic Republic government but his motivations for doing so and his disagreements with the new regime aren't explicitly laid out. All we know is that he doesn't like it.
2. The game leaves a lot of threads just hanging open. One of the major figures in the revolution the player joins seems to want a free Iran, "free from the Soviets, the West, even God," but what exactly that would look like is never really made clear. In addition none of the different parties involved in the revolution have their motivations made clear. The clerics want a cleric backed Iran, the Communists want a Marxist republic, the Mujahadeen want something unclear, but nobody says exactly what their version of Iran would be like. At one point the player has an opportunity to meet all these characters to try and understand them but it seems like it's mostly small talk. Then you never see any of them ever again.
3. The game gives you a bad choice. This is a bit of a spoiler, but the framed narrative for this game is Reza (the player character) is being interrogated by a member of the new government. During this interrogation, a family member joins in for leverage against Reza. Then later on the game gives you a Telltale style "save this person or the other in a limited time" decision for that family member and another one. If you are paying attention you already know that one family member survives this (because he's with you during interrogation) so why on earth would you save him? He makes it!
4. Reza's cousin, Ali, is inexplicably violent. Through the story we learn that he's worked against the government before and he's a wanted man, but he still shows up at every event specifically to encourage violence. He works counter to the goals of the party of which he takes part and everyone seems to still be OK with him being there instead of kicking him out. Not sure why, but it didn't make that much sense to me.
5. Some of the voice acting, especially Reza's during more dramatic moments of the game, is really hammy and kinda hard to believe. Most of it is pretty believable, but Reza is sometimes just hilariously underreacting or hilariously overreacting.
6. Reza seems to catch on to this whole "revolution" thing really quickly. Like at the beginning of the first flash back he's all "Oh geez I don't know guys," but then towards the end of that flashback scene he's pretty much completely convinced that the monarchy should be abolished. Also, what was with the first scene with the communists? Why would Reza, who's literally just heard of Khomeini, start a fight on his behalf?
Overall these hang ups are not major enough to detract from an interesting 2 hours experience for $15. Definitely worth it, but it has its faults.

1979 Revolution: Black Friday is, so far, possibly the most significant game I’ve ever encountered. True, I’ve played games like Beeswing, that were profound on a personal level, but this game is profound on global, historical and personal levels. For this reason, and others, it has already drawn hostility purely for political and social reasons, so I feel justified in attempting to redirect attention toward back toward this important and interesting game while attempting to maintain context. (This is a very early review on a game that is impressive from the very start, and that I expect to elaborate on soon.)
1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a game about the overthrow of the Shah of Iran in 1979, to be replaced by religious fundamentalists. That event is very important to those of us that are Americans (regrettably, the only context I have) because this nation was fully responsible for placing the Shah’s oppressive regime in place, with all the repression and CIA-trained torture of dissenting voices involved. The history of the region, the nation and the time are an extremely critical part of the game, but more so are the people of Iran, both those guilty (to many) of instilling yet another oppressive government, and those innocent of anything beyond wanting happiness and a better life for their families. People just like those all over the world.
One of those innocent characters in 1979 Revolution: Black Friday is a young, male photojournalist named Reza Shirazi, who finds himself caught between his Shah-supporting family and his Ayatollah-supporting friends as he attempts to record the street revolt for posterity. And that’s basically the beginning of the game: Reza in a prison cell being tortured by an historical figure for information and connections, as the game proceeds in flashback form.
Much of 1979 Revolution: Black Friday is caught up in the minutia of the actual proceedings. The events, the people, the places are all (apparently) real, based on personal accounts and news reporting. The story may occasionally seem to bog down in the detailed use of Reza’s camera to record shots matching actual photos of the time, but goes far toward setting a precise, real mood for the player. Each photo taken presents the option to learn the reality behind that person or event, but may be (?) easily avoided on any subsequent playthroughs. When this game is presented as being “based on choices”, it’s an understatement, since choices have repercussions from small to large, and can come fast and furious. Outside the story itself are 39 Steam achievements based on those choices, included many multi-stage achievements. All indications based on the large number of choices are that this game warrants multiple playthroughs.
I was an young adult preparing to graduate college at the time of the 1979 Revolution, and I have distinct memories of the kidnapping and release of the American embassy hostages, as well as the resulting Iran-Contra scandal. Few things have shaken faith in government as universally in my lifetime as knowing that a soon-to-be president traded weapons for trusting American lives (as if baseball cards) with the nation considered by many to be our worst enemy (at that time calling us "the great satan".) And possibly worst of all was that our president (Reagan) left the nation, the hostages, and their families tortured in the ignorance of the illegal deal he had previously (and secretly) made to free them for little reason more than to embarrass the outgoing president, Jimmy Carter. All that is important context to this game being played in the 21st century, but not essential to enjoyment. Perhaps a quick read-through of the following would be helpful before starting 1979 Revolution: Black Friday to have a more complete understanding of the complicated relationship between the people and nations of Iran and the USA from that time until today:

1979 Revolution: Black Friday isn’t for everyone. But it should be considered by everyone.

Resident Evil 6 is the ninth installment of the series, and the sixth from the main games. Following the main story, the U.S President comes clean for the first time regarding the events from Raccoon City in 1998. This is a major breakthrough, but not everyone is happy about such revelations. Meanwhile, other bio-terrorists attacks across the world are spreading, and it's Raccoon City reunion all over again.
The campaign is split into 4 main paths, each with two characters (except for the Ada Wong's campaign), they all share the same events, but with different perspectives, with interwoven storylines. Each pair shares a different version of what happens and their efforts to help save the world.
In theory, Resident Evil 6 had everything to be a massive success, in paper that is. Capcom went all in, and focused everything in the storyline and direction wise. The final result is very different, and not a good one either.
Design wise, this game a top tier when comes to visuals; zombies looks fantastic for a 2012 game, they are detailed, and very impressive. Monsters are interesting and bizarre, and each area is pretty detailed and appealing. Visuals do look fantastic, but design is not always about visual realization.
Mechanically this game is a mess, and there's no other way to put it. The franchise was never open world, but the player always had a sense of exploration, and that's completely revoked from this sixth game. The levels are more linear than ever, going straight from point A to point B. It's still possible to snoop around for extra gear, but the game contradicts that idea by respawning zombies endless in 85% of the game's areas. This contradicts exploration and teaches the player not to, even though some nice extras being available despising the small levels.
Levels are now filled with cut scenes which doesn't stop the game flow, and allows enemies to keep moving and positioning themselves in spots not comfortable for the player. This also creates some weird camera angles, or forcing the player to focus on a certain area, despising enemies nearby!
Enemies only react to the presence of the player, despising the fact that other teammates may be nearby. This miserable concept is more noticeable during the Chris campaign, where both creatures and agents are mixed, and only start engaging if the player is in the area. This is ridiculous, and offers no gameplay balance or team play.
Character position is still problematic, even though Capcom updated the player's visibility over the protagonists, they could still improve it further. The cover system is another joke, it's over complicated and doesn't sit well with the gameplay, making avoidable at all times!
As gameplay goes, Resident Evil 6 adds nothing new to the franchise, other then an embaressement for the hardcore fans of the series, and anyone who actually played good games in the past!
At best, Resident Evil reflects Capcom's wish not to create a game, but to develop another movie, an interactive movie that follows the player, giving them a hand, or even more, playing the game for them. The concept behind this game is based purely to appeal to an audience outside of Japan. Supporting this, we have wrestling moves, frenetic action to a point where it's just ridiculous to watch, and the extensive try outs for an epic moment!
In game menus are also indicative of Capcom's losing its own credibility, by using a system very identical do Dead Space, which was clearly the inspiration source. These menus work terrible in Resident Evil, as they pop-in while in-game, and changing weapons, or managing inventory space is now frustrating and terrible due to respawnable zombies mentioned above. The ironic thing is that the Pause menu is still present, but works as a pause, nothing else.
Cutscenes are extremely well directed, with great angles, cool camera shots, and interesting storytelling, and that's a great thing. Not many things are good, but some indeed are. AI partners improved a lot since previous game. Team mates can no longer die, and thus making this title a much less frustrating one.
The campaigns are consistent in length and varying in design, each character has a very strong plot, worthy of a novel for the fans. Bosses are not the best, but they are interesting to fight and watch their mutations.
The game's core is definitely in the Mercenaries mode, where competing for a better score is where the best players are at. The online mode is interesting with cool maps such as The Catacombs and Chaos City. DLC extras are worth the fun if you have friends to play with!
Overall Resident Evil 6 is a disaster, and makes Resident Evil 5 being a significantly much better game! An overpriced quick-time event action game, with no horror at all, and delivering an insipid gameplay.

Have you ever played a game that left such strong impressions that you came up with alternate titles for it?
My list:
"Resident Evil: QTE"
"Resident Evil: Michael Bay"
"Instant Failure States"
"Least Likely Things to Happen in an Action Game"
And my personal favorite:
"Immersion Dumpster Fire"
My point of reference is that I go way back to the first game in the series, but I'm not a fanboy.  I don't particularly mind SOME of the changes the series has gone through.  I tried hard to like this game, but its good qualities are heavily overshadowed by an enormous amount of bull**** in it.  I almost expected an extensive survey to pop up at the end simply because in a lot of ways the game couldn't make up its mind.  It's like they were field-testing lots of different features and couldn't decide on any cohesive themes, not even the same UI for different characters, so they just piled everything into it they could think of into an orgy of WTF.
I'm going to assume you've read other reviews on this game.  Most of what people say is true, for or against, so I'm going to keep this as short as I can.  All four character campaigns are gonna last you about 20 hours, unless you're a perfectionist about scores / collectibles.
This might actually be a good game to inflict on a buddy to share your suffering, as 3/4 campaigns all have one companion they can fill in for in addition to the DLC.  The AI in this role is occasionally dopey, but at least they're immortal with infinite ammunition and are able to revive you.
All the DLC is basically useless though if you're going for single-player.  Two horde modes, two multiplayer-only modes.  This part I don't understand, because the game makes extensive use of a bot AI for single player campaigns, including 3 bots (or 2 players and 2 bots)  at some junctures --- why no bot mode for the multiplayer modes?
I think it was the game's penchant for constantly ripping me out of its own context that got to me, though.  Cheap deaths, enemy mutational mechanics that punish good aim (on occasion, 3 shots centermass = death, 1 headshot = mutation + bullet sponge), an absolutely ungodly amount of QTE trial and error, action heroes with neckbeard stamina, being knocked down multiple times in a row because enemies can still move around while you're being revived, a bad skybox, INCREDIBLY unlikely environmental design/events, the list goes on.
It's sad because the game has some decent production value, some cool monsters, a basic but serviceable story, and starts off with good atmopshere.  I only recommend it if you pay less than 10 dollars for it, preferably if you're going to play with a buddy, and maybe a few year's worth of breaks inbetween runs so you can forget what the game is like.

I’m just breezing through games recently. Well, that happens when none of them are longer than maybe 3 hours. Before playing it, I’ve heard a few things about
that intrigued me and I absolutely chose to not get spoiled about what might await me when I played it, so if you haven’t heard of this game and haven’t played it and are interested in a game that subverts your expectations and offers damn good writing and lasts for an afternoon without outstaying its welcome, just buy it. Don’t watch trailers about it, don’t read reviews or even the game’s description, just go ahead and buy this one. It’s 5 dollars on Steam and I feel like it completely earns that price. Consider everything ahead and all of the marketing for this game a spoiler.
I love metafiction in all its forms. So when I heard that
wasn’t what the name would suggest and that it holds a few secrets that mess with the player, that certainly piqued my interest. But as so often is the case with metafiction, this isn’t about driving a point home, this is just a game that wants to ♥♥♥♥ with the players and get into their heads. And I feel like it does that quite nicely. It constantly changes what types of content it throws at you and it’s really interesting how it mostly keeps its very basic control scheme of pointing and clicking. Only a few times are you required to actually use the keyboard and I find there’s an elegance to presenting the player with so much to do while retaining very basic and simple controls.
As is usual with games that try to subvert the player’s expectations, there are secrets to be found in
as well, in the form of tickets. See, you’re not actually just playing
. You’re playing as a dude standing in an arcade playing the arcade cabinet of
, and you can get tickets for what I assume are more lives for the game. That doesn’t mean that there’s a lives system in the game, just that these tickets are a way to track the amount of secrets you’ve found. And there are quite a few in there, hidden very cleverly. During my initial playthrough I managed to find only half of the tickets, so there is some definite replay value to be found.
But I think the best thing about the game is its length. Metanarratives loose something after the feeling of unease and unfamiliarity wears off and the fantastical becomes mundane. See also Stephen King’s
book series for something that was good enough to sustain a trilogy but drew itself out to 7 novels for some inexplicable reason. So saying that beating
takes less than 3 hours is a good thing, since it never outstays its welcome and manages to keep up a very good pace throughout its runtime.
There are however a few faults that I’d like to address. I liked the presentation, I loved the music and I felt the story it told made great use of the unfamiliar as well as the constant 4th wall breaks. Having your nemesis be Satan himself and you being on a quest to save the thousands of souls he took who played his game was a brilliant way of using blasphemous imagery and using it in a subversive way that doesn’t end up making it tacky. You know, unlike almost everything else that uses satanic imagery. Because just the idea of having Satan sitting at his infernal desk, coding an arcade game is hilarious. But this is just one half of the game.
The actual
arcade game inside the game is a side-scrolling endless runner with shot ‘em up elements and it’s just boring and after the initial introduction to the game it gets frustrating, having to play so many stages of this game that doesn’t actually have anything to do with the
meta-game. Which is a shame since I would’ve loved more densely layered meta-game content to figure out.
Outside of the overused
endless runner game, there isn’t much wrong here. Except the marketing. I get that when you’re creating a subversive meta-game, you desperately want people to notice it and not mistake it for something different. I mean you could go the
route and just play the whole thing straight, but as that game proved, this can also hurt sales, since you’re not properly advertising yourself. But if you do properly advertise yourself, as this game does, it takes away the mystery and that’s already a minor spoiler to the game itself. The fact that there’s a mystery. Even my introduction to this review somewhat spoils what expectations you should have when going into this game, but I honestly don’t know what else to say? I mean I could just put a TL;DR at the start and tell you to just blindly buy it, but that goes against every fiber of my being, because I’d never tell someone to blindly buy anything.
However, this also highlights a problem I see arising in the near future of these subversive meta-games: There have been so many in recent times that I fear oversaturation is going to kick in eventually. I’ve already seen people complain about this particular game coming out and being another one of those games that are cute on the surface but hide more sinister stuff behind the veil. And I guess I can see where people are coming from with this, but I enjoyed myself with this game, since I managed to not get too spoiled by either the marketing or people who’ve played it. But I understand that this is a difficult position to get into and remain. Games with secrets attract followings and word-of-mouth attracts further players who are already spoiled somewhat since they know that what they’re presented with isn’t to be taken at face value.
Not to mention that YouTubers and Twitch streamers are to blame for an influx of games like these that set up a particular expectation and only thinly disguise the real content of the game to hook influencers and thus get more eyes onto their games. It’s a weird discussion that would be worth having, about game developers exploiting gamers to gain free marketing and how an entire industry has sprung up around it.
And yet in the face of all of that, I still can’t say I haven’t enjoyed
for what it is, but I only did because I refused to know anything about it. And that’s a dangerous position to be in.

It looks impressive but that's where it ends. Puddle is yet another water physics puzzle/platformer where the goal is to get your liquid to the end of the level while losing as little as possible. A physics game where you control the tilt of the screen to make a small amount of liquid move through an obstacle course. You get a better score for both being quick and not losing too much liquid.
I thought it was creative and the levels were mostly well designed. Some players dislike the physics of the liquids, but I feel that it is pretty consistent for a simulation game. The camera can be downright awful sometimes as it attempts to keep as much fluid on the screen as possible, which is not a good idea when fast-paced areas cause your liquid to spread out as some parts trail behind. This makes some obstacles frustrating when you are less able to see them coming.
Overall, it's a difficult game and suffers from physics bugs from time to time. I enjoyed it however, and even managed to complete all the acheivments, so it's not impossible.

Where each level is a hub that has smaller levels or dungeons that have secrets, and you wander back and forth to open up new areas here and there. It all unfolds the hub area progressively til you have "solved the puzzle" and can move to next level.
You choose between three characters. One strong in magic, one less o' that but resilient and punchy, and then the middleground.
At times this can be very difficult, and one late boss fight always had a tendency to bug out, to much frustration.
Strong aesthetic, and I owe this game thanks for many hours of mystery and great gameplay.
It's truly been very inspiring to me, and while it's old it still deserves appreciation among newer games.
Til next time.

There’s a lot of tools and a lot to learn. Across the bottom of the screen is a toolbar that contains all the stuff you need to create your city. Initially there is only a limited selection for you to play with. As your population grows more tools become available and the pacing is just perfect.
Features like global policies that can reduce power consumption or increase fire safety are introduced at a rate that never feels like a bombardment. The same goes for buildings and services. Rather than a sit down and read endless pop-ups style tutorial features are gradually introduced so that only small explanations are needed at each stage. It really lets you get hooked even during those often tedious early learning stages. Another reason Skylines is so fun straight from the start is that each and every tool you use is so effortless.
There’s a zone system used that is very similar to everyone’s favourite Sim City game. But again the tools are there for you to make your life easy. Streets come ready equipped with grids attached that you can either paint one square at a time, use a paint brush tool or even a fill tool to create entire blocks easily. Then waiting just a little time everything comes to life as buildings are erected and citizens go about their daily lives.
All this simplicity isn’t to imply that Skylines isn’t complex. Underneath the user friendly interface there are a set of menus and tables that reveal some of the numbers that lie beneath. Finances, happiness, healthcare, education, crime and transport are all detailed enough to make Skylines worthy of any city building fan.
The only thing that some may not like is the slightly sandbox style, especially later in the game. Once the learning curve and introduction of tools is done with there are very little objectives to give you direction.
- Cities offer room for expansion
- Beautifully detailed miniature village style looks
- introduction and learning curve
- Great tool designed
- Lack of objectives

Secret World Legends has story, puzzles, and lore that outshine any AAA title to date. The premise is simple: every myth, legend, and rumor in our world is true. Conspiracies, monsters, magic, it's all part of a secret world hidden beneath our own. The first chapter of the game has you fighting zombies, but this isn't a Walkind Dead MMO. You'll face demons, mummies, cultists, and so much more. This is a horror game but it doesn't rely on cheap jump-scares like so many other games. The horror here is more subtle, disturbing, and story-rich. You won't ger nightmares, but you will be gripped by a compelling story that will keep you enthralled.
SWL is fully voice acted (except for the player) with an amazingly written storyline and immersive environment, It's a great game to play solo and even better with a few friends. A few quests are solo-only but most are groupable and the experience thrives when you can share it with others.
You can't talk about SWL without mentioning the investigation missions, which (if you don't cheat) will have you translating morse code, reading egyptian heiryglyphs, performing occult rituals, and stretching your problem-solving skills to the limit. I've never played a game with so many challenging and outside-the-box puzzles. You should really try to figure everything out without a guide.
Finally, we have to cover the relaunch. SWL is a reset of the game "The Secret World" with a few minor tewaks and a rebase to an F2P model. There is basically no new content and no core game improvements from the old game, but new content is slated to come around the end of 2017. The F2P changes are very controversial (as you can tell from reviews) and enables a cash-based acceleration of gear progression.  Don't make the mistake so many people do - this is not a game where you race through to the endgame. SWL (and TSW before it) is about the story, the experience, and you the player. Let me be clear - you can play through the entire game without grinding for gear and without paying a cent. The endgame is basically nonexistant - harder versions of dungeons and eventually a few token one-boss raids. Do them if you like the game, but it's not the core content and not something to stress over.
My suggestion to you is this: play the game for the immersion and atmosphere, and only stick around for the endgame progression if it appeals to you. The story is not to be missed, so don't cheat yourself by getting caught up in needless gearing and paywalls.

TL;DR: I recommend this game for fans of TellTale/Life is Strange or those interested in learning about history.
I picked up this game after reading about it on RPS and being a fan of TellTale Games and Life is Strange, as well as enjoying 'The Cat and the Coup', a short game about the overthrow of the democratically elected Iranian Prime Minister Mossadegh in 1953. I also like games where you learn things - I always faithfully read the historical notes in Assassin's Creed games and am pleased to see that this game crams in around 100 historical notes.
The game places you as Reza, a young photographer who becomes caught up with revolutionaries during the 1979 Iranian revolution. Similar to a TellTale game, you choose dialogue options based on a time limit and perform key-presses and QTEs for a couple of action sequences. The game also has a photography mechanic, linking the pictures you take to real photos from the time. There are 19 'chapters', which are better called 'scenes' due to their length.
The story is short, but gripping. It throws you straight into a situation and story you know nothing about (unless you're familiar with the 1979 revolution in Iran). This has its pros and cons. It means that you begin by making decisions without really knowing Reza, or why he might want to choose certain options. As you go on, you learn more about the political situation and Reza's life. Rather than creating a character from scratch, you often find things out in later chapters that make you wonder whether you made the right decision. This along with its length and the chance of finding all the historical notes certainly gives it more replay value than a TellTale adventure. However, it may have been nice to learn a bit more about Reza and Iran before being thrown into the story. The historical notes add depth to an otherwise limite story - there simply isn't enough time to build up a strong emotional connection to the characters. I'd say that the story is less character driven than politically driven. You find out more about the revolution, the factions and Iranian culture/history during the game and this informs your choices more than the relationships of the characters.
The game recommends headphones - I used them, but they aren't necessary. The audio is fantastic and helps put you right in the setting. Voice acting is also of a top, profesional standard and occasionally blends farsi phrases into the speech, so keep subtitles on because these are fully English.
However, the gameplay left some things to be desired. The time to choose dialogue option is too short. It makes conversations more realistically paced, but barely gives you the chance to read all the options before you choose. I also experienced some major, frequent framerate drops, and I'm running on a mid-to-high range gaming laptop.
Overall, I'd say this was a very good attempt at making a game that tells the sort of story rarely touched upon in video gaming. Games are often afraid to deal maturely with politics, either having an indistinguishable red/blue faction or a clearly evil enemy organisation. Real world politics is even less commonly used in games. 1979 Revolution deals with this well, teaching us that there is not necessarily a right or wrong side. Instead, politics is messy with many different groups pursuing goals for many different reasons. It has its flaws, so I wouldn't recommend it to everyone, but fans of adventure games or those interested in story-led games should definitely check it out; it's the same price as a movie ticket and the same length for a single playthrough.

I feel this game could have been so much more. It's a great concept, but it just doesn't deliver.
Here you are, playing a game of a certain quality that was, fifteen years ago, free on random websites like miniclip and the likes. Now, here we are, expected to pay $4 for it. This feels like the individual's first take on game design. With that said, it's a good first commercial game for a new developer. However, as a consumer, I don't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about their milestone or not, I wanna discuss whether or not this would have been worth the $4 I could have paid for it and if it is worth the amount of time I invested in it already.
The answer is no, it's not. The idea is good, but the implementation is not. The levels are small, the gameplay is lacking, the destruction is for some reason unsatisfying, and it sorta feels the same no matter the animal choice. The game is just for short amusement, then it gets forgotten. No lie, playing Zoo Tycoon and releasing animals is more interesting and satisfying than this game, and that's suppose to be the premise of this title!
First thing I would change is the park size. You don't leave the screen you see. You don't scroll anywhere as you move to the edge of the screen, it's just it. I feel it would be more interesting if the park was larger with both more to explore and destroy.
Second, I would give the game a better goal rather than ranking up a high score of damage within a set time. How about, maybe, the goal of escaping a park? Then they could have animal captures you gotta avoid and the likes, all trying to prevent you from leaving. It would be interesting.
Finally, I'll say something is wrong with the destruction and people targetting. It's all unsatisfying. You are challenged to get a good score, but I cannot help but feel I don't really care if I get a good score or not in this game, it's all just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to proceed to the next level. Maybe make it so destruction isn't view as necessary for the incentives and focus on making destruction the incentive of actually playing the game?
Overall, I will have to say pass. I'm glad I got a free key, but I won't let that bias my opinion. I don't think this game will deliver the satisfaction you're looking for. It's a shame, it really is. Normally, I try to make a pros and cons list, but I cannot really make one for this game because there isn't enough meat to nitpick or praise for.
4/10

I really loved this game, it was fun and challenging (And insanely rage enducing if you play on Extreme, and go for all the gold medals!), I was really surprised with how many REALLY different levels there are, and how many different liquids you get to be. It stays fresh and new throughout the entire game. Love these kind of indie games, and I'm currently looking for more like this, but this game is unique as hell, so its very hard.

In its concept, Puddle proposes us, quite simply, to lead liquids of varying types from point A to point B, with, of course, a certain number of difficulties along the way and a limit for the minimum of liquid you have to bring to the finish line. Nothing particular here, but, as often, it is the way in which this concept is given form that makes the game really enjoyable.
In the case of Puddle, the art design does a big part of the job. It is smooth, detailed, out of time, and even, on some rare occasions, a bit poetic.
The game is divided into several environments corresponding to a theme, with in each 6 levels. It ranges from the sewers to flora to laboratories, even taking you inside the human body.
While on the environment, there is an electroacoustic music accompanying us in the perillous journey of the liquids, sometimes calm, sometimes dynamic, and I've found the soundtrack quite enjoyable overall (and I'm glad the devs made it available in a dlc, best to be bought during Steam sales).
In terms of gameplay, it couldn't be simpler: just tilt the screen left and right with the arrow keys for the liquid to move forward or backward. Of course, some parts will require that you measure your speed, or that you adjust yourself so as to make good use of the specifities of some of the environments (such as fans, slopes, sticky parts...).
However, the nature of the liquid also comes into play, and it will force you to adapt to each one (water and organic wastes do not move in the same way, obviously). There are, more or less, as much types of liquids as there are environments, but you will find some variations on certain levels.
The last level of each environment will give you a bit of a change in the gameplay, though. It acts as the equivalent of a "boss battle", without a boss, granted, but with added specificities in the task at hand (getting the right amount of two liquids in a glass bottle while it moves on a device, for example). A welcome change after struggling in the previous challenges.
Regarding the difficulty, two settings are proposed: a relatively easy one (I insist on the "relatively"), in the form of chocolate medals (for the "whiny players"), or a hardcore one with metal medals. The rewards are based both on time and on how much liquid you were able to save.
If I didn't really suggest it so far, the devs don't take themselves too seriously, which is a good point in my book.
To finish with, the negative things. There's only one that comes to my mind: the camera.
At some points you will find yourself with your liquid being a bit scattered, either because that's inevitable (hopefully rarely) or because of a miscalculation. In these situations, the camera seems confused so as to how much of a zoom back it must make so that you keep an eye on what has been temporaly lost along the way. More often than not, it will keep its focus on the most forward part of the liquid, making it very difficult  for the player to gather it back. It is a bit annoying considering that, deadly obstacles apart, the game will consider a patch of liquid lagging too much behind as lost, and will remove it from your reserve.
It doesn't spoil the pleasure of playing, far from it, but it is to be noted.
As a side note, and camera appart, the game is not buggy at all, and I don't find it redundant, at least with the way I play to it. For the length of the game... I've got a bit more than five hours on it at the moment of writing, and I have completed 5 out of 8 of the available environments on "whiny" difficulty.
To sum up, a lovely, humorous little game which is quite enjoyable. Best to be played little by little in my view.

Though I originally played this for the N64 back in the day, the game has kept my attention all these years. Hexen (a continuation of the Herretic: Legend of the Serpent Riders) is an early first-person Action Fantasy. A good comparison is the Fantasy version of titles like Doom and Quake, with a storyline similar to the idea of Diablo. The multiplayer was also wicked fun on the console, though I'd love to see if the PC version supports a multiplayer just as good. There are 3 classes (Fighting, Magic(more ranged), and a ballance between the two), each with their own unique weapons and play types. If you're looking for a nostalgic pixilated First Person Fantasy, I highly recomend Hexen!

If you don't like old pixel FPS then you might want to skip this.
"HeXen: Beyond Heretic" stays in the universe from "Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders" where 3 brave heroes goes into the world to find the second Serpent Rider Korax and banish the creature.
HeXen was my first FPS RPG, yes FPS RPG it don't have so much RPG as Fallout 3 but it have the basics like items/inventory, breakable armor and for-the-love-of-god-why-do-we-have puzzles, and if you don't like puzzles and backtracking oooooh then you might just buy Doom instead or Heretic.
I personally like the 3 choices of the characters, the fighter, cleric and mage.
Fighter a beefy one-man-army yet his weakness is the lack of range weapons thou if he got enough mana then he is the beast on the battlefield.
Cleric an all-around guy starts with a meele weapon then the rest are ranged thou his second weapon also grant him a small amount of lifesteal.
Mage the weakest of them all in melee combat, thou he start with a range weapon that doesn't cost mana, his second weapon is an ice spell that freezes his foes, the third spell is lightning that can lockdown foes and the final weapon you get in this game with the mage is his staff that shoots powerful fireballs that will nearly kill all emenies in front of him or seeks his foes.
My rating for this classic game would be 7/10 because:
+1 for the idea of FPS RPG
+1 one of the first DOOM engine games that have jump in it
+1 backtracking with memory of switchs and keys
+9000 INSTANT CLASSIC GAME !!! MUST OWN IT!!!

I remember when the first Deadlight came out in 2012, riding on the back of the popularity of Limbo, a game that exhibited a similar style. I still consider Deadlight as a game that triumphed this style by painting a thoughtful story narrated by a brooding and pensive protagonist. However, the Director’s Cut despite its promises falls flat. While it’s still the same game, but the vow taken by Tequila Works to provide updated graphics still remains unfulfilled in this new edition.
Whatever improvements have been done to the graphics to make the game more visually stunning is simply hard to notice. Perhaps one of the most crucial things missing from the game is that the game developer has made no efforts to improve the weaker parts of the game. One might pause in the beginning of the game to take a look at their surroundings and admire it for a bit. But, after a while, the mundane and repetitive structures somehow start resembling the terrible bleakness of this world.
For a side-scrolling platform that relies heavily on a graphic novelesque narration, the story lacks depth and is predictable at best. In fact, one of the weakest elements of the game has to be Randall Wayne, the protagonist who struggles to express himself throughout the game and character growth is conveniently thrown out of the window by the time you start thinking about taking the game seriously. Finding journal entries of the protagonist in parts of the world where he has never been is downright silly. With all the realism that is part of the game, the inclusion of this strange feature in order to boost character growth does not sit well with me.
It took me a solid 4 hours to finish this game, and needless to say, if you are looking for games similar to this one, there are far better ones out there now. The gameplay felt fun in 2012, but not anymore. The control scheme is still pretty indifferent and sometimes you are just dependent on pure luck to survive. It would be unfair to say that the game is completely devoid of tense moments, though. During the very best moments, it will still make you anxious, as you clutch onto your dear life for survival. But, in the end, this does not justify a new Director’s Cut release. A desperate cash-grabbing move of a game that is only meant to be picked up during a sale for the lovers of this genre and the original.

Deadlight is a game that I saw popping in out of steam sales for a while. I always thought about getting it, but always saw mixed opinions on the game. I never got it and promptly forgot about it. Years later it ended up in a humble bundle I recently got, and I thought that I already had it at this point I might as well give it ago. The basic premise is there are zombies and you gotta try and track down your wife and daughter. Despite the simplistic premise the game's story manages to be really engaging. The cutscenes are also great looking with a very well done comic book style with some very nice art. On top of all that the game has surprisingly good voice acting. the visuals are also very appealing. The game it self looks good, but there is so much detail going on in the backgrounds that it really just takes the visual style up a notch. However this game isn’t perfect. There isn’t one clear cause for the problems with the game, I find it's mostly just a bunch of little annoyances. Say for example maybe the game didn’t give you enough time to react to something, or maybe one platforming section is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, or the game doesn’t make it clear what you're supposed to do. Little things like this plague the game. However I don’t think these annoyances are consistent enough to say it makes the game a chore, but on the other hand it does take it down a peg. Overall I think this game is rather good, and worth buying. It’s only  around 4 hours long but I think that works to its advantage. It doesn’t drag on and tells a story that feels complete without any padding thrown in.

Greetings from a fellow game-director
VIDEO VERSION:
------------------------------------------------------------
First off, let's start with saying that this game is unique. It's unique to get a 2D side-scroller that features large HQ modern anime-sprites instead of small retro garbage visuals. This is extra rare on Steam, there are even less of them here. If you think this is not a rare combo, and that it is mundane......well, then you know jack about the game industry. So, kudos to the dev for that.
BUT! The game has a gimmick wich also is the biggest flaw in the game in my opinion.
A side-scroller where you move the player by clicking and dragging the mouse is horrible and a disgusting feeling that gets tiresome and eventually causes pain in the hand, especially when the rest of the game must be progressed through by the mouse. This mouse-walking also makes movements inaccurate. It is extremely easy to run past your intended destination. It seems that the director was so desperate in making a point-and-click game that he forgot
ergonomics and......well, common sense. It would have been better to move with the WASD and then do the interactions with the mouse. It can thus still qualify as a point-and-click, so calm down. No need to panic. As it is now, this is a flaw wich is not just a flaw, but it is bad game-design.
The other flaw is a flaw wich is so typical to Asian games that it almost becomes cultural. Chronic if you will. An overload of (uninteresting) dialogue. Tons of text. Text that is not really important for the story. That's not good. And that too, makes the hand hurt from all the clicking.
Stop it, get some help.
The good parts are the visuals as said. As well as the atmosphere combined with the soundtrack.
The soundtrack is ambient, but it is more sound-design than actual music. Grand textures, drones and SFXs forms "music" that sounds like something coming from the mastermind Diego Stocco.
Top that with choices & consequence system and fully animated cutscenes, and this game is truly
a rare gem of a kind we don't have many of

The neutral:

The bad:

I expected more from this game to be honest. The story isn't bad but it is too predictable. I've unlocked each ending listed in the achievements and experimented with majority (if not all) of the dialogue, hoping to find something that would have more of that "wow that's an unexpected plot twist"/"-shocked-" factor but it lacked in that department. It does do nicely on the feels though.
Overall, I did enjoy playing the game so I would recommend this to those who like horror/psychological thriller point and click sidescrollers or visual novels. Just do not have high expectations on plot twists and enjoy the game for what it is.
