A truly unique and extraordinary gaming experience,
at first glance seems weird and keeps you wondering what is this game about. However after spending a few minutes with the game you get a clue about what's really happening with the game.
Spoiling the plot and puzzles of the game would certainly drain the magic which lies withing every level of Pony Island. Without revealing too much information, there's plenty of puzzles and secrets to be found, nothing that will hinder progress or force you to open guide, yet at the same time challenging enough to give you a (sometimes false) sense of satisfaction when you finally finish a level of find a secret.
The game is riddled with meta references, to the point of absolute ridiculousness and at the same time it fits with the overall narrative (?) of the game. Truth be told, there's little replay I value once you find all the secrets and the game itself is quite short, yet at the same time Pony Island is superb at being overally bizarre and extremely fascinating to play through.
You could argue that the game might have a few similarities with Undertale, on the overall pixely style,
references, story-telling devices, but truth be told Pony Island a very unique experience and dare I say a breath of fresh air for gaming.
I'd like to thank the developers for the innovative ideas and it is without a doubt I have to say this game is a must buy for everyone, it is definitely worth it to get this gem and I'm hopeful we will see more in the future, via a spinoff or an outright sequel.

I'd say it's worth what I paid for it ($3 on sale), but I'm not sure it's worth the time spent. The game has some good ideas but the gameplay and the narrative weren't compelling enough to keep me engaged. It's reminiscent of Undertale in a few ways, but Undertale succeeded in hooking my emotions into the characters and backstory in a way Pony Island did not. When the game ended I did not feel any compulsion to dig into the rest of the story that I missed, to try to find secret endings, etc.
I'd say the first 15 minutes of the game are its strongest, when you first break through the facade and interact with the "desktop" of the system and the narrative picks up. I don't feel the game delivered on that opening ambition.
I think the game would have benefited from a slower burn and actually trying to play up a psychological horror angle (not sure why it has that tag, I wouldn't classify it as such) with a bit less tongue in cheek. The antagonist(s) weren't actually all that menacing.
From a gameplay perspective, the core Pony game (and its variations) was adequate but not super fun in and of itself. The "hacking" puzzles were okay but a bit clunky to move pieces around with the mouse. I appreciated how some puzzles had hints in garbled code. Hunting down tickets was moderately engaging.
I just wish the game had gotten me to care a bit more.

Resident Evil around the world!
Leon, Chris, Ada and newcomer Jake travel around the world fighting off all sorts of zombies and other nasties. Each of the four campaigns center on one of the four main characters and their respective partners, each telling the same story from a different point of view. As usual someone has gotten hold of some bioweapons that can turn everyone into zombies or worse, and it's up to our heroes to save the day.
The game plays pretty well. Just like Resident Evil 5, Resident Evil 6 also has little to do with the older games in the series. However, the controls in this game feel very smooth, and if you're able to master how the fighting and shooting works, it can be a lot of fun. Yes, there are quick-time events scattered throughout the game, but the main part of the game where you shoot, stab, hit, throw, run, dodge and so on, is very well done.
Personally, playing as Ada Wong was something that I had been wanting to do for a while, and getting to know more about her was a plus. The rest of the story, while maybe a bit over the top, was also pretty interesting. The only minus would probably have to be that the villains felt kind of meh, but that's a minor detail.
All in all I enjoyed Resident Evil 6, and do not think that it deserves all the hate it got on release. Luckily, going by the more recent reviews, more and more people seem to give the game the credit it deserves.
If you're a fan of the Resident Evil games (especially Resident Evil 5) or third person shooters in general, then you will probably enjoy this game as well.

Notrium.
I don't have words for this game. Probably one of my most favoured games of all time, I can't believe it's on Steam! I dropped the $1.99 in about a second!
Notrium is a survival game. You play as one of 4 characters from a crew that crashlands on an alien planet. Your goal is to survive, be it that you find a way offworld, or take presedence over the locals and become ze' ubermanche. There is the Human, Alien, Android and Psionic. I personally prefer the Human and Alien to the other two races, because of the amount of gameplay each presents. Notrium hits the "Survival" Part right on the money. You constantly have to moniter your temperature and hunger, as well as focusing on the whole NOT DYING part. I sincerely hope Ville releases workshop for this game, due to the huge amount of moddability. Someone modded this into a side scroller guys! How crazy is that? Insanity aside, $1.99 is a small price to pay for a game with this kind of content. Definitely worth the time you'll spend dying over and over again.

A hidden gem of the early indie game scene, Notrium has finally come to Steam. This game was doing survival in a hostile world long before Minecraft popularized the genre. Crafting, alien landscapes, multiple playable races, solid modding community, the works. An incredible game, more so for the time it was released, it still holds up today. For the incredibly low asking price, this game is highly recommended.

This classic game is definitely worth playing to any survival game enthusiast. In fact, when it comes to futuristic survival games, this one is a pioneer. It covers multiple races with distinct gameplay strategies, crafting, a nicely written back-story and loads of aliens to kill... or be killed by. It's also moddable to the point enabling the creation of expansions to the original game, or just something completely different.
Although its introduction to Steam and the improvements available in the Special Surprise Edition (™?) are a fresh breeze to the game, this version brings the same spirit of the freeware versions from 2003 and onwards. In fact, one of these earlier versions of Notrium is open-source. Hence, my greatest inclination of buying it here is to support the (very) nice developers behind it. It's still worth every cent.

Should've been more expensive compared to other games on Steamy (but a fine cost considering it began as a freeware), but sadly not many users do not know of it or find it eerie perhaps. Much more easier to play that Robinson's Requiem & Deus, concerning early survival games.

The game reminds me a lot of The Banner Saga.  Visually it's excellent, with great character art and animation.  It has a consistent well-drawn, apocalyptic punk comic book look that creates a fun interesting world.  Just like The Banner Saga, though, it's all looks.  The tactical gameplay is just too simple and too unbalanced to be much fun beyond the first couple hours when you're learning the game.
The game is simply broken in its current state.  The normal difficulty level is impossible (and not in a fun way like FTL, Binding of Isaac, Dark Souls kind of way.   Enemy characters quickly outpace your team.  You'll soon find yourself up against enemies that can one-hit-perma-death-kill your characters that you've struggled unsuccessfully to level up to a semi competitive state, since only kills count for experience.  The battles are very straightforward and don't offer enough options to employ much in the way of any strategy beyond hiding behind cover, waiting for enemies to come to you, and then hitting them with everything you've got when they're in range.  You have the option to use weapon strikes from your vehicle, which are highly effective, but you soon realize that if you use them at all you'll soon run out of the resources.
After getting slaughtered again and again, I decided to try easy, but in that mode the flaws in the game just become more apparent.  You have enough resources to use the battle equalizers, but they start to feel overpowered.  Dropping bombs on your enemies to win every difficult battle just doesn't feel very strategic or fun.  The developers were clearly going for a rogue-like kind of design, where you should expect to die many times, but where it fails in this is that each game feels the same.  There aren't enough unique things to find and the way you improve your characters feels too simple and restrictive to be any fun.  You can't find new armor or weapons for your characters, you only get to modify one stat when they level up (it barely seems to make any difference what you choose) and finally the real kicker is that the characters cap out at LEVEL 4!!! WTF?  I thought I was experiencing a glitch when I managed to kill 21 enemies with a character and was unable to level up after the 12th kill.  This just killed my interest in the game.  I was hoping to level my Rookie into a Veteran and then on to Elite and then perhaps discover new skills and abilities leveling beyond that.  As it is a Rookie can only reach Veteran and never become Elite.
I really wanted to get into this game the way I did FTL but unfortunately it's closer to The Banner Saga.

I picked this up at launch, and thought it looked so perfect for my tastes.  Turns out, it felt extremely half-baked, and just plain not fun.  I have since tried it again since the redux, and it started so much better!  And then, within a half hour in, it became complete crap again.  They cannot get difficulty balanced to save their lives.  You cannot take 6+ enemies on at once with the 4 units you get.  It's just barely possible.  You lose recruits far faster than you could ever recruit/level them.  It's absurdly punishing, and I've restarted 6 campaigns so far this morning.  I'm writing this now because I just cannot bother continueing.  They want to have a really punishing game where you have to deal with loss, not unlike your Darkest Dungeons, XCOM, Dark souls even - but they don't pull it off.  It literally feels impossible to succeed.  You go from fighting 2 enemies, which is way easy, to 4 - often tough bigger enemies among them - to fighting 6+ dudes with far more health and damage than you could even hope to achieve.  They swarm and obliterate your team.  Don't bother unless you are the top 1% of game players.  Even then, not sure it'd be "fun" - just stressful.

Summary:  This is not a very strict no, but still, 'No'.
This game isn't so bad, but it's just not something worth investing much time in.  There are plenty of things you'll have to ignore about it to really enjoy it, and other options are out there.
The gameplay, relative to other similar strategy games, is fairly elementary.  As a mixture of Oregon Trail and any given tactics game, the Oregon trail piece is merely 'take every opportunity, sometimes don't, and if you run low on a thing, get more thing in the tactics piece, while the tactics portion is "Hide behind cover, and let them come to you."  You have to ignore the monotony of either portion.  It's one of those games where you very easily could ignore all the text, see a couple pictures, and just let things happen around you.
The story is pretty lackluster, as well.  Dialogue is shoddy and has a weird, offputting attitude.  It's Mad max without the credibility.  If you ignore the text here, too, it also makes the game significantly better and almost easier to get through.
The interface is workable and reasonable, but average.  The graphics clearly took some time to make, but are average.  All in all, it's ok if you're easy;  And that's ok by me, but anyone who'd ask me about this game?  It's a steady, but polite no.

Great concept and all, but terrible execution.  Levels require an annoying amount of precision that just can't be achieved with liquids... at least not liquids as non-cohesive as these.  What's more, some levels seem almost designed to force you to lose large amounts of liquid, such as levers that you have to "pull" dropping down and bottlenecking the liquid behind it while the rest of it races forwards for no clear reason.  Some of the levels seem like they were tested for use with a solid ball, and the liquids were put in there as an afterthought.  What's worse is that most levels require you to know what's ahead and plan for it even though you've never seen it; and many of those require you to be at some particular speed between letting the liquid just do its thing and full tilt.
And the kicker is that the game has the nerve to call you a "whiner" (read:  about as close to "little b*tch" as it can while keeping a kid-friendly rating)  when you want to play
mode or can't get past the clunky controls and poor level design.
All in all, 5/10.  Absolutely great concept, but the poor controls and poorer level design just make it an infuriating game.

Behemoths studios are well known by their goofy style of games as seeing on the animals with diarrhea in Castel Crashers.  Fortunately for everyone this style remains on all their games and we see this on the last one, Battleblock Theater. Since the very begging with the narrator’s maniac monologue to the funny scenes with cats terrorizing the little beings we see that one of the main purposes of the game is to make you laugh. But that is not the only purpose of the game, every single level is a challenge against time to complete the puzzle. These puzzles can be as easy as just run and jump through the blocks and cat enemies, to be as difficult as having blocks that disappear, one side entrance blocks, chronometer stages, hidden paths, enemies with weapons, and a full co-op experience. All these while listening to the most useful tips from the narrator as “You are doing it wrong, do it right.”
The whole story begins when a ship full of friends, and also Hatty Hattington “King friend of friendship kingdom” and your nameless protagonist crashes on an abandon island full of cat guards that only want you to entertain the audience. When they capture your 300 friends and Hatty Hattington, your only option is to go through more than 80 levels to amuse the cats and gain jewels used on the store to free your prisoner friends. It is this way that you will unlock new heads for your character to customize.
The set of movements to your disposal will be very reduce to only jumping, punching, throwing objects, and helping friends to jump higher. It is a very reduced and disappointing variety however, this will be enough to bring lots of fun to the player. In the multiplayer you will be able to play with your friends in different competitions like, horse races, and fighting. Besides all this you will have the option to create levels of your own so that you and your friends can play on them. This game is more than just a bunch of blocks, cats, and funny characters. It is a whole gaming experience with challenging puzzles and some really pessimistic encouragement.

The gameplay for Last Soldier is quite straight forward.
You are a soldier stationed in the jungle, who is facing attacks by giant mutant spiders.
However, the soldier only stands in one spot during all of the attacks, so the game is not very entertaining.
You just need to click fast on the spiders to shoot them.
The only really hard part about the game is lasting long enough to get the "kill 2500 spiders" (in one life) achievement - although, the developer has said that he will make the spider achievements cummulative.
*** Update, Sept. 2017 *** The developer has now made the kills cummulative, which makes getting all of the game's achievements much easier.
In some ways Last Soldier is more like a clicker game, as you just spend hours spamming fast clicking all over the screen - there's not a lot of skill involved in doing that, it's more a case of doing it until your hand hurts, and it puts you in the running to get a repetitive strain injury (RSI).
*** With the cummulative kills update, going for all of the achievements in the game is a more reasonable affair (previously, it would take too long, and - as I found out after spending too much time trying - it just wasn't worth it).
The update has therefore improved the game.
However, the entertainment value of the game is very low.
Basically, once you've shot a few spiders, you've played the entire game; all the rest is just spamming your left-click button, which is not entertaining, not fun, and not skillful - in fact, after a short while, it just gets more painful rather than anything else (even more painful if you end up with RSI because of this game).
If you get a coupon which enables you to buy the game for 20 cents, or similar, then maybe get it for about 15-30 minutes of gameplay.
Apart from that, I would suggest that you don't bother getting the game.
(Whilst this is a largely negative review of the game, it should be acknowledged that the developer has listened to the suggestions of players and has updated the game accordingly. Well done.)

It's priced like an iOS game, which is good because that's what it plays like. It feels like this was made for a school project, in which case I'd give it a B.
Graphics: The graphics are very rudimentary polygons, which makes me think it would look a lot nicer if it was just 2D. If 3D was one of the parameters for your school project, then disregard that.
Story: Do you expect a story? You are man with gun. You must kill spiders.
Gameplay: Surprisingly good if I'm being honest. There are a multitude of upgrades that you can buy with the coins you get from dead spiders. When you kill a certain amount of spiders, bigger ones will start to come. It appears that all 3 types of spiders give the same amount of coins (5) despite the fact that the first type takes 2 bullets to kill and the third takes about 10.
Difficulty: There is none. I played for like 20 minutes straight and never died. Perhaps you'd die if you didn't buy the damage upgrades, though.
There isn't much here, but it's 99 goddamn cents. I'm still gonna say don't buy it unless you've got a couple bucks lying around because, I mean, you could find functionally identical but better games for free on Newgrounds and such.
P.S. Note to the Dev: 4 of the achievements are improperly capitalized and 1 says the singular spider, not the plural spiders.
P.P.S. Suggestions: Perhaps multiple weapons, since you already have the shop figured out.

Puddle is a puzzle-platform game that makes clever use of advanced physics to let you move all kinds of liquids through different obstacle courses. While the idea itself sounds rather straightforward, the execution is certainly not. The first levels, using water as a liquid, are not too difficult and I thought "tihs game is going to be a piece of cake". But how wrong I was (am actually). Difficulty goes up steeply and the developers have really thought of all kinds of possible liquid and obstacles to make life ever more difficult. Water, oil, goo, fertilizer, nitroglycerine, all pass the review and all ask for a different approach. This keeps the game interesting, since the visual context changes accordingly to the liquid being processed. And since the visuals are really outstanding for an in essence static background, the developers have done a good job.
But after a couple of hours, my interest in the game diminished since I got tired of the trial-and-error which seemed to be necessary in some of the later levels. So I let the game rest for a couple of weeks, and picked it up again recently. Now I pick up some levels ad random and try to get more of the Steam achievements, which are a clever addition to the game. All in all, this game is a nice sideway away from any larger-scale gaming projects, but don't expect anything more really. If Steam reviews would have a "neutral" option, this one would get one. But in the end I give it a "thumbs up", if only for an original idea being well executed, with a lot of love for the project being involved.

TL;DR
Here's Puddle, a game I found during the Paris's sales. At first, maybe it's hard to decide whether or not to buy it. I mean, you only tilt the screen to the left and right, moving liquids, but this game is incredibly... incredible! So yes, this is a "I go from this point to another" game, but you don't directly control what you lead to the end.
Let me explain myself. Basically, you control a liquid by tilting the screen to the left and right (I think this game was first designed for mobile). Sounds boring, uh? Well destroy this thought right now. Not only are the graphics awesome to my eyes, but the every liquids are different and this creates unique and diversified gameplay. You have coffee, ink, lava, even a liquid that doesn't fall from the top to the bottom but... from the bottom to the top! Some are heavy and falls quickly, some are compact and stick to stuff, some explode... I couldn't even name all the particularities off the top of my head, there are so much! And I haven't even finished the game while I'm writing this!
However, people that are easily disgusted shouldn't play this. The body chapter made me slightly wince and I myself am someone that is not easily disgusted by this kind of stuff. The following chapter is the sewers and ain't really better. Also, if you're not patient, unless you want to start to be patient, this is not really a game you should be looking for. However, if you're ready to spend a chunk of your time on difficult levels, go on. The game offers to use "Whines" to skip levels but you know, I want to keep my honor and not use them to be proud to say "I completed all the Puddle levels"...
About being patient, some levels are special sometimes, and also harder. They usually are at the beginning and end of every chapters. There, you don't always control liquids but most of the time, there always are liquids involved. One time you control a souvenir ball where the liquid is inside the ball, another time you control lasers and need not to burn the liquid in addition of doing something else at the same time to finish the level... Consider those levels as introductions and bosses. I really like the idea.
If I revise everything, Puddle has reaaaally simple controls but the particularities of the liquids make the gameplay unique every time. Also, you don't always control liquids, so it diversifies the way to play. But of you're not patient and easily disgusted it's not the game for you. If you're a fanatic of physics, however, you should like it.

A game that everyone seems to hate but I think I'm the only one in the world that sees this for its merits.
Pretty damn good as an action shooter, horrifying bad for a horror game as it takes a very huge departure from the rest of the series and instead sacrifices survival horror for a pretty in-depth shooter that has a very Capcom feel to its design and aesthetic.
Hopping into this game thinking that it would be like the classic RE games would really disappoint you, and honestly I do think that the story mode is pretty damn bad and is only worth stomaching just to unlock more characters for the excellent Mercenaries mode.
Don't really need to say much about the story other than its just a messy continuation of the series that tries to get the entire RE cast together for this huge Michael Bay-esque bonanza because UMBRELLA IS BACK, NOW WITH A NEO PREFIX. Starring incomprehensible monster designs, beautiful fashion model protagonists and MT Frameworks proving how well-oiled of an engine it is. Resident Evil has never been about the story, let's be honest here.
Now that's out of the way, please for the love of god just play Mercenaries. As more of an expansion to RE5/Mercenaries 3D's ruleset (150 enemies max, rankings are D to S instead of stars, melee kills add time, etc) it shines much more due to the new moves that characters have such as sliding, counter melee hits, Coup de Grace kills, and many more beautifully animated Wrestling-inspired attacks which each character has their own specific modes.
This game also includes all of the DLC for free such as the extra Versus modes (personal favorite being Predator- which allows you to play as Tyrant/Mr X/Nemesis 2.0 and hunt down survivors to see who of 8 people can cause the most damage) and the glorious Mercenaries No Mercy mode, which cranks up the enemy spawns to a stupid amount and raises the max enemy count to 300 while also adding a Left 4 Dead 2 crossover character/monster pack.
This game goes on sale quite often, so you're bound to get this for a very VERY cheap price. Very fun game that I wish people would be less brutal with and see that its one of the finest action shooters out there. If you want a survival horror game, stay far FAR away from this and get the RE1 Remake. If you want to play a very fun arcade/action shooter: get this and Resident Evil 4 and 5

Overall I'd give this game an 8/10, and I can strongly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of puzzles, platforming, and physics.

Bite Size Review - DeathSpank
The Good:
- Colourful and pleasant art style
- Funny writing and voice acting
- Combat is fun
- Music is good
- Eating food regains health and makes funny sounds
The Bad:
- Can only carry a few healing potions, when did this become a thing in RPGs to limit healing???!
- Map does not show quest objectives
- You'll pick up a quest and the objective will be somewhere on the other side of the world
- Puzzle solving feels like a third wheel on what I would consider a very light an enjoyable RPG otherwise
The Verdict:
The best way to describe this game would be as a light RPG with hack and slash combat with the occasional puzzle solving. It sounds all good until I tell you that the quest system kind of sucks, and I was constantly wondering where to go for the next objective. As well there are a few puzzles in the game that really throw me for a loop and are the type of puzzles seen in 90s adventure games.
An example of one such puzzle is at some point you get a wheel in the game, and need to use it as a gear inside a dam, to lower the water outside of the damn. In any other game you would just put the wheel in and it would work. However in this game it gives you a hint to remove the wood from the wheel. I then spent a good 10 minutes trying to combine the wheel with fire items in my inventory hoping to burn the wood off since some of the puzzles require combining items. This did not work - also at this point I had run out of fortune cookies, which are used in the game to get hints on how to complete puzzles in this game. So when I finally quit the game and typed it into google, the answer turned out to be "take the wheel to the termite hill east of the damn, drop it, and the termites will eat the wood off of it." For those who have not played the game, it is incredibly easy to miss this hill when going to the damn.
So it's moments like these (and there were a few in the game) that really frustrated me, because rather than playing the game I had to jump out and google the answer. I would have rather the game give you all of the hints for each puzzle if you wanted them, and maybe reward players who didn't use hints, because any game that requires you to alt-tab to find the answer is not doing a good job of guiding the player in my opinion. That all being said though I still recommend this game for its art style, music, fun combat, and cleaver writing and dialogue - just keep in mind the puzzles and quest system that really should have had some kind of map to help it - will cause a few moments of frustration along the way.

Deathspank is a comedy adventure based on a weird hero in a purple spedo (no I’m not kidding you) who goes on a medieval/steampunk quest to save the land from a tyrannical overlord named Lord Von Prong. Along the way he meet a slew of people who will help him defeat Von Prong, with some draw backs. You gradually venture through the world righting wrongs and helping other random people with simple tasks, like settling a married couples problems. Eventually you figure out what he’s doing and the destruction he’s done.
The gameplay is incredibly boring, despite the controls are easy to master. Most of the quests are nothing but fetch quests. You go to a certain location and either kill a certain creature a dozen or so times or find a certain item. Also it locks you out of certain areas before you’re anywhere near that level so it strips some exploration from you due to the fact that you can’t discover things early like in the Elder Scrolls series. All fighting is just clicking and popping potions. This doesn’t require any skill and only makes it more irritating when many areas can easily overwhelm you with enemies. The terrain is limited and lacks interactivity, despite it being well pixelated.
The graphics are lavishly cartoony and are well shaded. The 2d houses are a nice touch to the game because it leaves room so you can click behind the building and go around it. Other times it allows you to pick up items from enemies you’ve killed behind buildings. There are even areas that the depths in the terrain curves and makes it whole experience feel like you are truly trapped in a small world. To a certain extent it feels like a throw back to top down third person games even though a lot of the world seems like it trys to just round out everything and not over tax whatever system you’re playing it on.
I just completely hate the jokes. Out of all the dialogue and story, which is just bland, the jokes stand out for being the most terrible part of the game. To a certain extent I will admit that comedy is difficult to do in video games. However, after years of experiencing the gaming culture, and how many people take time to go out of their way to mock themselves, the jokes would fall short due to how generic they feel and simplicity of the jokes. Like they have a few pieces of armor that are given names to play off of other RPG cliches, like the Gauntlets of Awesomeness. Then they’ll have quests to get chicken lips and the reason the witch wants you to get them basically amounts to “Why not?” It’s just lame. Its like they’re late to the party and everyone has already talked about the♥♥♥♥♥♥they wanted to and are drunk or asleep. I’m not saying they need to change their humor but a lot of it is too intentional and forced.
I was disappointed by this game. People keep saying its hilarious or a good ‘comedy game.’ It was rarely funny and the few jokes that did make me chuckle was almost reminiscent of kid humor or some decent play on words. The gameplay was completely boring. There isn’t any real skill to it all. There’s even a option to let the system chose the best armor for you. At most you just need to stock up on potions and grind grind grind your way to level 20 and after that everything else is cake. Even older games like the original Diablo took more skill then this. Also the story, as said before is super generic.

The turn-based tactical combat and the comic book art style had me looking forward to this title for a while and I was happy to jump into Skyshine's post-apocalyptic world.  I've never played any rogue-likes before by I'm no stranger to permadeath and I don't tend to shy away from difficult games so I thought this would immediately be a good fit for me.  I was wrong.
The tactical combat has a great design.  It was fun to play around with the four unique units and learn their abilities and how they synergize to best plan ways to take out my foes.  While the combat isn't necessarily deep, the units and battle map allow for good flexibility in how to approach different skirmishes earning the combat design a fair comparison to chess.  The characters are animated very fluidly and the death animations in particular are satisfying without being excessively gory.
The initial battles are simple enough to help the player learn how combat works, but the difficulty soon scales up with the player frequently being outnumbered by units that are more powerful than the player's units.  This will cost the lives of precious combatants making future battles that much harder however, this difficulty can be offset by the area-of-effect Dozer Weapons and the Equalizer buffs that can be found as the world map is explored.  Even so, I found myself rage quitting and restarting more than once due to a particularly bad run of luck on the battlefield.
I've encountered a few bugs but none of them game breaking.  I lost more than a few good men in combat when my turn was ended prematurely, but this bug seems to be related to the use of specific Equalizers so it's easy enough to work around.  On a few other occasions, the game froze during battle but the menu was responsive so I was able to quit the game and restart the combat.  On a couple other occasions I had quit the game after a particularly difficult encounter only to return to the game hours later in a saved state that was prior to me engaging the encounter.  Even after completing the encounter again and advancing to the next encounter in an attempt to force the game to update and save my progress, I had to replay the encounter again because my progress wasn't recorded correctly.  I understand the spirit of rogue-likes is to accept consequences and not save scum, but in the absence of a manual save option bugs like these should be ironed out.  These bugs are frustrating, but the patient player can overcome them.
Outside of combat and bugs, Skysine's BEDLAM is a demanding resource management game.  The world map requires crude (fuel) to traverse and meat (food) to feed the inhabitants of your Dozer.  Additionally, Power Cells can be collected and spent to upgrade your Dozer's efficiency as well as aid you in combat with area-of-effect attacks.  The Equalizer buffs that are also used in combat and consume either crude or meat.  In this way more fuel, food, and power can be sacrificed to spare your combatants, the other vital resource of the game.  Figuring out how to strike this balance will help you traverse the world of BEDLAM, which includes many points of interest.  In order to gain entry to the location of the final boss, you'll need to collect relics that are highlighted on the map.  Other points of interest include resource pick-ups as well as Elite Units to fight and have join your dozer.  The numerous unmarked locations on the map that you'll visit can result in a skirmish, gaining resources, finding rogue combatants to join your Dozer, power-ups for your Dozer, or nothing at all.  There is a good variety of different events and outcomes such that the player never knows what to expect and also has to balance the possibility of gaining much needed resources versus getting into a fight while his experienced units are recovering from the last battle.
It took me about 8 hours to figure out how to succeed at the game and another 8 hours to actually complete one run through of the campaign.  Those first 8 hours were frustrating and at times even discouraging, but having made it to the end, I'm satisfied with the experience and look forward to starting another campaign to see if the early game is any easier after the experience of my first game or if it is just as punishing as I remember.  If you're patient, I recommend Skyshine's BEDLAM.  If not and you have high expectations in general, you may not enjoy this one.

Just like its predecessor samurai_jazz, this game may come up as a tough sell. But I'd REALLY love to see a speedrun of this game!
Samurai Jazz is, in a way, a hymn to traditional games that goes beyond what we may be used to: not only it looks retro, it also feels retro in terms of timing-related difficulty spikes.
Following the foosteps of samurai_jazz, you control a beret-wielding samurai that must slice through its enemies. Unlike the original samurai_jazz, however, this game plays like a typical platformer with jumping at its core. Expect the precise timings of 'jumping' and 'dashing' to be your main cause of trouble from this game, but also the most exciting part to look at.
Ironically enough, this switch in gameplay mechanics actually works for the better, when compared to its predecessor: you won't accidentally access some areas by mistake and there aren't that many issues caused by perspective, for you only go right, let and jump.
My main issue with this game, though, is not the fact that it's too difficult or that it seems cheap: it is, indeed, challenging and it should have autosaves for each time you change a room, but that sets the game apart, in my opinion. Rather, it's the fact that, sometimes, it feels like there are either bugs regarding jumping mechanics or something that wasn't explained to begin with. Right at the end of the game, for example, after sliding through a wall, I could jump, dash and then jump again. But some other times, I could only dash and jump. I can assume this is a bug, and it's a big game-breaking in my opinion, but not that serious. There seems, however, to be a way to jump higher which I never managed to  completely understand, and that was REALLY important at the end of the game: I believe it was caused by jumping while pressing the trigger for dashing, but I never managed to fully grasp it. It might've been just dumb luck!
I had another major issue concerning the interface. Like the first game, one might have difficulty setting all objects you can interact with apart. I felt this to be the most troublesome in a stage containing many gates that seemed well shut and, at the end, only one of them could be accessed to at a time. I had to watch a walkthrough to pass this part of the game, and since timing skill is the main focus of the game, this type of situation doesn't benefit the game itself. It just seems cheap!
I do still recommend this game, though, and it seems more polished than the original samurai_jazz. And for the price of a buck, I can still see Shin Samurai Jazz getting a cult following around speedrunners.

Shin Samurai Jazz Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Shin Samurai Jazz is a platform-adventure game. It combines the likes of film noir and samurai cinema, presenting them with 8-bit graphics, an electro-jazz soundtrack, and a comic/manga-like style creating a unique atmosphere. Unlike its predecessor, samurai_jazz, Shin Samurai Jazz features jumping mechanics inspired by chuunori, an old technique used in kabuki theatre to give the illusion of flying. It's combat mechanics consist of hacking and slashing with the ability to juggle enemies and perform mid-air combinations, also inspired by chuunori. While the adventure elements remain intact, the puzzles are more complex with varied level designs and enemy placements/attack patterns that make use of the game's mechanics.
You think the combat would give it a Ninja Gaiden feel, but it doesn't. Combat only serves to occasionally offer you a cheap death after a period of tough (but repetitive and built around the awful controls) platforming. Half the time you want to jump away from a wall you turn right back into it. The other half your character just falls straight down off the wall because the controls appear to have never been actually considered. I wouldn't be surprised if the developer had never even actually played this game and kept rehashing particularly bad super meat boy levels that he never actually tested. Either way, this is unrepentant trash that is only difficult because 90% of the platforming is wall jumping off spiked walls with ever decreasing non-spiked surface area. This would be less offensive if the controls for wall jumping were good. They aren't.
I wanted to like this game, but even for a retro title, the combat is unacceptable. The soundtrack is nice yes, but it doesnt make up for lack of depth in the gameplay. The menu is hellish, and the graphics leave lots to be wanted. There are many retro games that just look "nice", this isn't one of them.

Better than Samurai Jazz, for sure, but still not worth the time. It's easier, in some ways, and certainly less frustrating (with the exception of the end, which had no saves, so I decided I didn't want to play this anymore...).
The level design is 90% filler, and there is one obstacle that, while cool, the game uses over and over and over again (which is to use dash to pass under and obstacle, followed by a double jump into a higher wall). Aside from this, which is a good use of the game's mechanics (though overused to death), the rest is just a way of prolonging the game long enough to be worth money (?)... I mean, the whole game consists of going into several buildings to key a key to the next, to get a key to the next, to get a key to the next, to finally get into the building you wanted to in the first place.
There a part in a mall where there are like 10 different door that you need to try out whenever you get a new key. It's absolutely pointless. Especially, as I mentioned, when the game has one good trick that it simply uses everywhere.
The enemies are varied enough, but quickly get redundant when you find the strategy. The combat isn't bad, but it's too outdated to keep up. It's mostly about keeping your distance, and timing attacks to keep enemies stunned.
I also don't really understand why the music gets so much praise. It certainly has a very definity style, but it's mostly elevator music. And it doesn't really play along with the game. It's just background elevator music...
Not much else to say. The platforming isn't bad, in places, but it could use far more variety. And you start with every ability from the start, so the game can't really build different sections for when you have only x or y ability, and them build up from there.
I realize that my impressions are very negative, but I just don't see the point in playing this game. The story is simply an excuse to get you from place to place, doing the same things over and over again.
But at least it's an improvement over the last one. Maybe his later games are good.

I was one of the first people to get mega hyped over W_D1's E3 trailer. Years of hyped waiting and when it finally came out... Well, you know the deal. Truth be told, i don't hate W_D. I do think it was very poorly made, written and voice acted but it isnt a bad game by any means. Still, just like with NMS, my hype had collapsed pretty fast, but as the credits went by Ubisoft hinted at a future for the series. Ubisoft is the company everyone loves to hate and for good reason, but this year, they've been trying to right by us. Everyone told me W_D2 would be trash,♥♥♥♥♥♥ broken, etc. but I stayed stubborn that Ubisoft would learn from their mistakes this year. Boy, did they ever.
You play as Marcus Holloway, a 20 something hacker with a bone to pick with Blume and ctOS. This fact (and the hat) are the only resemblances to the first game you can find. Marcus is an upbeat, strong, positive and brilliant person and makes for a fantastic protagonist thats enjoyable to play as and he keeps his character together very well through the whole game. Joining DedSec itself, the characters the game introduces to you are full of life and really come alive through the amazing mo-cap and superb voice acting. The game doesnt just leave them out to dry either (rip jordi); through the whole game you spend time with the members of DedSec, learning more about them and seeing just how vast and varied their personalities are and the ambitions and haunts that drive them, bringing together a very well written cast of characters thats shocking for Ubisoft standards.
Unfortunately, the gun-gameplay somewhat betrays Marcus' identity. W_D2 cuts the giant one-man-army weapon wheel from the first game in half but giving you plenty of freedom to go non-lethal, complete ghost, hack-master, war machine or any other playstyle you can think of. However, the whole guns-blazing schtick doesnt slide with Marcus' personality, and the game just functions assuming you did everything non-lethal, even if you didnt. That being said, the gameplay is better than ever before; taking notes from the recent AC's, W_D2 allows you to approach a mission in dozens of different ways to suit any kind of need and playstyle. Marcus doesnt even have to go in; if you want, you can make your drones do everything. The drones are a fantastic addition to the game that expand player freedom in ways most games recently could not, giving the player tons of fun new things to do and ways to do them. The entire world has been designed with the core concept of player freedom in mind. Almost shockingly, the Parkour is the best in any video game so far, and in fact even puts AC parkour to shame (pretty ironic). Marcus' flips, spins and dives are very smoothly animated and flow perfectly without a moment of disruption, making for some very cool moves.
The story is very standard for Ubisoft; its no longer a super edgy story about revenge, instead the game adopts a much more prankster and light hearted feel for the story that makes players feel a lot more inclined to explore and have fun with the very well made and extremely detailed Bay Area. That being said, however, the further into the game you go, the story begins to weigh a little bit as the importance of what DedSec and Marcus are doing begins to take importance. It still doesnt take the player away from the fun, but know that there is some solid story under all those pop culture references and l33t sp3@k. The world feels extremely alive; NPCs arent just random polygons walking down the street for no reason, you can find them doing all kinds of crazy things, even stealing cars and getting arrested, raving at parties, proposing to their partners, the level of detail that has gone into this game is insane, and its all these little things that come together to bring the Bay Area into a level of life that's so hard to find in modern video games.
The hacking has been revamped completely. While the whole "Press X to hack" concept hasnt changed in theory, it has been remapped to allow for fast, on-the-go and quick reaction timing. This was necessary because each and every hackable device now has various functions you can set, such as a proximity trap, noise attractor, timed power-down, distraction, and many more that change across each and every device you hack. The player is a lot more involved in the hacking now and has far more options and choices to make, which solves the first game's problem of fire-and-forget when it came to hacking. The car hacking is one of the best new features that change how driving (and PVP as well) works completely. It was so intricate that I was able to perfectly drive a car via remote control commands for over 200 miles. Relatedly, this is for those of us who hated W_D1's driving with a passion (so basically, all of us): the driving feature was outsourced to the studio behind Driver and the change is MASSIVE; super slick and smooth driving with tight controls and the capability to do all the 2fast4u tricks you can imagine, driving in W_D2 is finally no longer a trip to satan's carnival.
The Online element is a big game changer. Bad Blood's coop was very lackluster and dissapointing, mainly because the game didnt give you much to work with. With all the options in W_D2 however, each coop mission feels like an action movie for you and your buddy to pull off some sick infiltrations and look really cool while doing it. The missions are short but very well structured and balanced for coop play, theres never a moment where one of you will feel useless. The Bounty Hunter feature is great, nothing feels better than to waste some punk who thought they were gonna take you out, and even the vice versa applies. It's a great, chaotic, explosion-filled mode thats great to play... If you can find someone. This seems to be the hardest matchmaking to sign up for, sadly. The Invasion Hacking from the first game is largely the same, but the way you play it has changed completely due to the presence of the drones. The quadcopter is slightly unbalanced in this mode though, and I hope a nerf for it comes soon. Even then, if you're good with hiding and not placed in the middle of nowhere, you can still win easily. They're not kidding when they emphasize Seamless; all these online elements happen naturally in your world as you play as if they were scripted. The only times you'll ever have to load into an online feature is if it fast-travels you to a target thats too far away. If you're not happy with how often they appear passively in your game, you can always set up matchmaking to get into one. The PVP element of W_D1 was always the best part of the game and while thats not the case in W_D2, you'll still have a great time no matter what your skill level is.
This is the game we were waiting for, W_D1 dissapointed a lot of us but Ubisoft has completely turned things around with this entry. Not only is it one of the best open world games on the market, being able to contend with the likes of GTA V (if not better!), but it is buckets of fun to play for countless hours long after you've finished the game. 420/10 would hack a car to crush me against a wall again. ... And again.

Over the past year, I’ve played through well over a hundred platformers ranging from the Atari 2600 to the modern gen.  I honestly needed a proverbial shot in the arm to regain my passion for gaming, so I decided to focus on my favorite genre for awhile.  Even so, among the countless platformers that I’ve played, Rayman Origins is near the top.  As far as modern, non-indie games go, it absolutely tears through the admittedly small (volume-wise) competition.  The “New” Super Mario Bros. series is the Mega Bloks to Rayman’s metaphorical Legos.  As in, one of them doesn’t fit / feel quite right while the other is practically infallible.
Rayman Origins is a master class for what I like to call the "floaty" platformer genre.  The controls are fluid to the point of absurdity.  The developers clearly spent time garnering their own unique feel, rather than simply copying the mechanics of platformers of the past, and it paid off beautifully.  What’s more, the sound design complements the gameplay in a way that can only be truly understood by actually experiencing it first-hand.  Even if the game’s aesthetics weren’t as wonderful as they are, I would still wholeheartedly encourage anyone to pick this up.  It doesn't matter if they're not a fan of the genre.  In fact, this would be a great place to start.

One caveat though.  Rayman Legends, the sequel to this, includes about two thirds of the levels featured in this game as “remastered” versions.  That makes Legends the better deal monetarily.  However, I find that Origins’ level progression flows better than Legends.  So actually, just buy both and be enjoy yourself.  Because it doesn’t really get much better than this.

The NEXUS! update solved a lot of problems people had, but fails to solve the biggest problem: it's simply not fun.
This game is a mix of <FTL, Fallout, XCOM, you know the drill. Name awesome games to trick people into thinking your game is awesome too>, but simply fails to generate fun.
Do sidequests? Well yes, otherwise you'll run out of stuff even sooner. Which leads to several screens giving you the option of throwing away your previously invested materials or continuing on, with no clue what outcomes continuing could give.
"You see a shack. Investigate (y/n)?" does not suddenly make me want to retreat. I cannot guess the dangers nor the benefits this could give me. There is no choice.
Even when encountering a trader, where the choices of trade or don't trade would be an actual choice, it doesn't say the numbers. Trade food for fuel. How much? Not a clue. Just a wild guess whether you'll be happy with the results.
Combat is apparently a lot better in NEXUS(never played before it) but is still quite stale. The enemies simply have better numbers. Health, damage, and amount of troops. The retaliation of gunmen is fun, but they have to live for that to happen. Pretty hard if every enemy one/two-shots you.
But that's okay, there is a rock-paper-scissors thing going on: shotgun melee dudes so they have to walk back to you(and lose 40% damage), snipe gunmen so they can't retaliate(I thought being inside 2 squares would do it too, but when counterattacking they lose their minimum range for some reason), slice up snipers so they can't attack back, and pewpew the close-rangers with gunmen I guess?
Except you don't know the enemies' composition when choosing your team. You don't enter a sniper gym and use all your melee pokemon, you simply don't know what will happen. Good luck planning!
I did a quickly failed normal run and a halfway-through easy run, but that was enough to see what the game had to offer. That is, without unlocking. But that won't change much. The starting weapons/equalizers mostly.
Which are about the only way to even the odds. But cost prohibitively much to use on a regular basis.
But even in Easy, where I have tons of resources so far, it's not FUN. Sure, I can heal 4+ hit points with every character each turn. And then? They can slice 3 damage off of the 25hp boss for another turn? It's just a battle of numbers.
There is no line of sight, no Overwatch(if you say you're part XCOM, that's a must), no special abilities each character can use only once each battle, no upgrade trees(the "fallout" means "lore-wise only")(damage all the way, one more hp won't let you survive another blow, but one more damage might give the enemy one less turn)... Just clicking through screen after screen like a robot.
If it would be relatively simple to write a bot that plays exactly like I would, so that I think it through once and then stop thinking, the game fails to be fun.

This game is over 13 years old now, and the graphics could almost be called "pixel art" today. But at their time the JA series were some of the first games to include individual voice acting for so many characters, and it's still one of the best turn-based strategy games you can find anywhere.
+ The soldiers are actual individuals, up to the point that some won't join your team if you've already hired certain others (e.g. their ex). Their comments often made my day. :)
+ Open landscape with a lot of things to find. It's up to you where you go first, if you rush or take it slowly, and you can win the game without having been everywhere if you want.
+ The AI is neither super-clever nor super-dumb; you can ambush the enemies quite easily, but they aren't dumb enough to make you feel safe at any time.
+ The story makes sense, and the antagonist Deidranna (who's regularly shown in short cinematics shouting at her assistant) is really the type of person you wanna defeat once and for all.
Definitely recommended (if it works on your system).

One of my favourite hidden gems from the PS3. Deathspank is a short, charming Action RPG parody with a pop-up book aesthetic.
Combat revolves around building combos and executing crits by attacking with three weapons at the same time. The controls are tight and it feels good with either keyboard/mouse or a controller.
Deathspank is a good choice for anyone that enjoys ARPGs, but doesn't want the lengthy time investment that comes with the genre.

Most of the hero acting like superheroes with chessy lines straight from an action movie.
This game has a lot of content, but it's a step down quality wise.
I have played with my brother RE 5 in one go with enjoyment, but in RE 6 we already got bored after the first campaign.
The new characters are very generic, there are a lot of forced sequences where you can't control your char, but enemies can still hit you which is not a good solution. You rarely have the feeling that you are in danger, you just shoot stuff!
Important tips are shoved into the loading screen were I mostly can't read it because it's loading too fast. Only after playing through the game I tried to read some guide and was surprised that I missed so many moves and tactics.
Mercenaries mode is still a lot of fun. I enjoyed it more than the whole campaigns lol.
There is also a similar mode, but in L4D style which is quite fun too!
The other gamemodes are pretty much dead and mostly empty.
All in all I can't really call this a Resident Evil game anymore, but on the other hand if you have zero expectation and like it fast paced then this might be a game for you.

In today's world, underfunded, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥developers can feel free to rleease as many partial games as they like, charging a steep 50% discount on 1/3 of a game, they then re-sell to you 3 times over, making 150% off a title they could have sold to you as a full product. Seasons, disaters, transit, etc. things other games had at release, they decided would be best served as a side of DLC for another $20.
I haven't touched this game for months mainly because this DLC obsession backfires at a point. It's daunting to think of how much some of these changes may affect my little city and what they all do. As far as I'm concerned, my purchase got me 25% of what this game currently is. If you tally all of this up, with the potential DLC included, this can be considered a $100 game. And now we see how math works against the DLC craze.

Where is the fun? I'm playing this game and I can't find anything fun about it. It is sort of like Animal Crossing, but nowhere near as fun. There is no day/night cycle that I'm aware of. You basically wander around an island fixing it up. You do menial tasks over and over again to level up. You can fish, collect bugs, plant fruits, crops, and trees. You can also decorate your house with stuff you buy from the catalogue. Decorating your house isn't nearly rewarding as in animal crossing, where you can sell your stuff to make a big profit. I'm going to continue to play this game and see where the fun will lead. What I would like to see: multiple save files, if they're not already in the game. This would allow multiple people in a family to try out the game. I just can't see doing chores as fun. Also, a day/night feature would be nice. Another thing I didn't like about this game was the fact you were given items to start out with, i.e furniture. You should start with the bare essentials; and everything else is something you have to buy. I started out with some sports items, some Asian furniture, and a few other things. Really takes the fun out of game as you're rewarded for doing nothing. I understand getting rewards for doing quests, but it should only be that. I can't recommend this game as there are too many flaws. Maybe there will be a light at the end of the rainbow, but I'm not holding my breath. I'll continue to play this game, as stated earlier, and see if it gets better.

All the characters are well written, I especially like Francis and Angus.
Farming is somewhat limited, but for HC-farming we have other games, and this game clearly does not aim to be one of them. Sometimes placing objects feels somewhat limited, as the grid is quite big and there is so much unusable space around buildings, so I can't make all my decorating fantasies true. With Stargunner being a mid-1990s game you should expect a level of difficulty that is uncommon in modern games. With that being said I don’t think it’s all that much more difficult than other titles in the bullet-hell genre. The game demands that you have more than just good reflexes as the upgrades you buy and when you choose to use nukes makes a big difference (for example: having a credit drone in the second level during the asteroid field will earn you a lot of credits).
The graphics are dated but look fine 21 years on. The two announcer voices are a little muffled due to the fidelity of audio format but are acceptable. Some useful options are available using the function keys (in true pre-2000s game style) including invincibility (F8) for those of you who want to learn the levels inside out and find 100% of the secrets.
It’s a classic PC game from Apogee and it’s free. Give it a try. Don’t give up. Get good: it builds character.

The end of an era: The last game released by Apogee was a good way to go out. This is a side-scrolling shmup that is still fast and fun. It's definitely influenced by the Gradius series, even including a vocal prompt with each new power up. Enemies have varied attack patterns, and will even speed up and slow down as they approach your ship. And speaking of your ship, power ups are plentiful, and there is a fair amount of upgrades available for purchase within the game. The only possible negative might be for its aesthetics: Stargunner features a bright, primary color palette and oversized enemies, while I prefer smaller targets and a darker, grittier feel. The bottom line is this: Just because it's free, doesn't mean it's not worth playing. I'd pay for this. If you're a shmup fan, get it and enjoy! Recommended.

Skyshine's Bedlam provides an interesting tale of a game.  A free update becomes available that effectively works to rebalance and rework the entirety of the combat system.  For the $2 I was able to buy this game for, it's been fun.  The animations are nice, the character models polished, the art style impeccable, but as I went through these seven hours of gameplay, I felt something that I've not felt before in any game; the overwhelming sense that I nor anyone else would be able to effectively complete it.
You're tasked with dispatching crews of murderous thugs on your way to picking up vital relics on a journey across a wasteland, collecting resources and new crew along the way.  The concept sounds fun, and the early game is fun, but there's this nasty thing called a threat level...  As the threat level increases, thigns get harder.  The more successful you are the more challenge is presented to you.  In concept this makes perfect sense, a slow escalation of difficulty as you prove yourself capable for the denizens of Bedlam.  The unfortunate side effects come across by way of many of the other mechanisms in this game.

1.  Your soldiers have a level cap.  There is only so much improvement to be had by your soldiers and they stop once reaching level 4, this means choosing between either damage, health, or movement 4 times and four times only.  All of the enemies you face get increasing health reserves and ever greater damage capabilities.  In a toe to toe fight, this means your crew loses.  So this is why you'd want to use teamwork, but I'll show you why that doesn't work either.
2.  Your crew size is limited to a size of four when deploying.  Doesn't matter the size of the battle, the stakes at hand (are they inside your vehicle and losing will result in everyone dying?  Better send out only four guys, the others are still on break) you only get four members to deploy.  This makes for a decent squad in early game, where you combine damage output to mitigate harm to your own crew on these small groups of enemies.  However, once you get to a certain threat level, you're facing 6, 7, 8 high health high damage enemies, you just can't keep up effectively.  You end up facing mass numbers of enemies far stronger and tougher than your units can even hope to aspire to be and the game expects you to just roll with the punches.  The game then wants you to use these things called equalizers to balance it out, giving you an advantage over the enemy.  This is also problematic
3.  The tools the game gives you to account for the large number of enemies are insufficient.  A super macdaddy nuke deals twelve damage in a large radius.  Early game this is enough to kill or wipe off most of the opposition.  Mid-game however, the enemies shrug it off and you need to follow it up with attacks by your own soldiers.  Of which you have four, of which maybe only 2 are in range to attack, one of which will certainly die from the remaining 4 enemies nearby if he tries to move in.  This means that even when constantly spending valuable resources that you'll need for every single battle thereafter, you fnd yourself in a situation where it's not your skill against the enemy that matters, it's however many buffs you were lucky enough to find by random chance at this point.  Hopefully you were lucky enough to get the 2x damage boost, if not... oh well...
The game's mechanics work against eachother and don't balance out.  You can't play the game without them but they're not sufficient enough to play the game adequately.  It makes sense why it went on sale for $2, because they knew this.  You can't sell a game for $20 that you can't ever hope to finish and gain meaningful progress.  I say avoid this game, for $2 it's worth the pretty lights, but once you get past that, you'll only find frustration.

One of the most telling signs, in my opinion at least, that a game designer is doing something really right is when I can spot his or her fingerprints immediately on a game. Eric Chahi's fingerprints are all over Another World and Heart of Darkness, for example, but one can feel his presence in Flashback's DNA, too, even if it's clear that the game wasn't his own work. Jordan Mechner's cinematic eye is similarly unmistakable, and elements of it can be felt most powerfully on another game from this author...but Larry Stover (aka Blaze Epic) rightly holds his place as a game visionary of his own, and his titles, though influenced by Mechner, have a distinct flavor of their own, and can be recognized by his fingerprints as readily as Chahi's and Mechner's titles can be recognized by theirs.
If Mechner is Cheb Khaled, then Stover is Rachid Taha, a little wilder, a little earthier, a little more raw and visceral, and a little less constrained by form. The ponderousness of the flesh evident in the inertia of Mechner's unnamed Karateka and Prince is remembered but not heeded. Blaze Epic's games feature protagonists that soar, float, defy gravity, and whose true capabilities grow apparent only when you silence the empirical "traffic cop" chasing after them, demanding they stop making a mockery of physics. These games have flow, have a tight, bespoke timing and range of motion that would remind one of a slightly less punishing Ninja Gaiden (the NES version in particular), and a large part of their reward sets in once you enter their "zone," and flow with the almost-flying protagonist. The controls of the game feel strange and alien until you learn to move with them, and then you're Zatoichi for a glorious moment.
Blaze Epic's games share a few common qualities; they're all finesse-driven platformers with a decidedly retro graphics style. (I taste SMS influence in particular, as the Jump/Boxer cover art suggests.) Significant, small differences tune the physics and flow of each title, but there will be much jumping, and the games' magic comes from learning what one can do with jumps. There will be many frustrating deaths. There will be many "missed it by that much" moments. Seeing the next screen is a palpable reward. For all that the simple combat controls seem, at first glance, to be button-spammingly simple, success in the game is much more about finding rhythms than rapidly hammering triggers. The controls are frustratingly literal in the way anyone fond of third-generation consoles will immediately recognize and love-while-hating.
Having set the stage, let me tell you why Shin Samurai Jazz is my favorite of these titles.
The world of Shin Samurai Jazz is a noir pulp novel steeped in Jazz Age chic, with a rather Moby-esque low-key electrojazz soundtrack that anchors one in tones of rainy streets at night, distant music and laughter, secrets and mysteries. The atmosphere drips, and the mixture of goons and yokai encountered, with their markedly different combat styles, keep the fights interesting and particularly varied. Yes, you can try to power through by hammering the attack button, but learning your deceptively varied move set and employing it wisely has proven to be a far more useful strategy, in my experience. Once you really get the hang of dashing back and forth, dropping in and out of stance, and hurling enemies aloft for airborne slicing and dicing while taking advantage of the chuunori-inspired jump-and-dash physics, you'll appreciate just how much variety there can be in a one-attack-button game, and how much of a difference learning your moves makes.
The jump-puzzle elements work much the same way; learning your moveset, and slipping "into the zone" with the game's physics, is instrumental. You'll practice double-jumps, jump-and-dash, wall rebounding, wall climbing and sliding, and folks who just rush in and spam the jump button will find some of the trickier levels quite daunting. Understanding one's range of moves, and their relative advantages, is key. That's true, to a degree, in every game, but Shin Samurai Jazz elevates this to a real brightly-polished art. For all that you have a limited number of buttons and moves to worry about, knowing them, and knowing when and how to use them effectively, plays a large role in the game. So many "retro" action-jump-and-run titles focus so heavily on timing and pixel-perfect placement that they neglect to reward good mastery of one's range of options, and good planning, aside from pitch-perfect execution. Whether Shin Samurai Jazz is maddening or simply satisfyingly tricky is, in my experience at least, more a question of how well you speak its language.
Jumping, wall-rebounding, and clever timing play a role in many Blaze Epic games. If you find you'd like simpler combat and more of those deathtrap jumping levels, the Ninjahtic series will probably make you quite happy, and if you'd like even more of a nod to Mechner, The Way Of The Pixelated Fist is his most recognizable love letter to Karateka and Prince of Persia. Shin Samurai Jazz, however, remains my favorite of the titles, for its compelling atmosphere and flavor, and for its surprisingly versatile and mood-reinforcing moveset.
I enjoyed the NES Ninja Gaiden back in the day, quite a bit. Shin Samurai Jazz brings back much of what I loved about it, while fixing a few of the things I really didn't, like the very trouble-prone wallgrab and climb.
Finally, I don't normally discuss price as a factor, but the dollar-or-two pricing scheme of Blaze Epic's games really bumps them to must-owns, if the retro action-platformer with third-gen-console-style difficulty appeals to you. This one or Ninjahtic would both make excellent introductions to the Blaze Epic game family, and as fond of I am of Ninjahtic, I'd personally give Shin Samurai Jazz a recommendation over it, as I think it expresses not just the game mechanics, but the thematic and atmospheric je-ne-sais-quoi, that makes Blaze Epic titles so lovely.
You make a name for yourself as a creator by sticking your neck out, owning a "flavor" and saying, "This is what I'm about." Blaze Epic's games have quite a recognizable tone and character, and of course, tastes will differ, and this little storm of third-gen-consoles and remixed-Japan will not appeal to everyone. They'll surely appeal to some, though, myself emphatically counted among their numbers, and if you're even remotely curious as to whether they're for you, this is a splendid straight-into-the-deep-end plunge into the heart of Blaze Epic's catalog.

After just under four hours and countless deaths I completed Shin Samurai Jazz, a mash-up of retro sensibilites and the more modern trend of masochistic platforming. At the low price of a dollar this makes for an easy recommendation but the game is not for everyone. If you are frustrated easily or have no affection for classic game design you should probably avoid this title. On the flip side, if you like a challenge and long for the days of gaming on an NES or SMS than I think this is a true gem of a game and an absolute steal at a dollar. Chances are if you watched the preview video here on Steam and thought "That looks amazing" than you will love this game once you adjust to the controls.
A lot of indie games these days go the "Retro" route because it is the "In thing" or  considered "easy" but I don't find that to be the case here. This game was clearly crafted by someone with a great admiration for classic game design and personally I think it feels right. Authentic, if you will. If you appreciate that than by all means give the game a shot.
At first play the controls will feel a bit stiff but give it some time. Once you get a handle on things you will be flying around the screen deftly avoiding spikes as you make your way through the architectural death traps and easily take out groups of foes. I had no issues at all with the controls once I grasped how everything worked. Learning when to jump and when to air dash is all part of the fun and when it clicks you will be begging for more.
Combat is somewhat simple but offers enough to keep it fresh I think. You have one attack button and pressing that in succession performs a basic combo that can knock some enemies back. I loved that enemy bodies will damage anyone in their path. It was especially fun to knock an enemy into another and send them flying off the platform into spikes. You can also perform a dash attack by simply dashing and attacking and this too will knock some foes back. Finally you can hold up and press attack to send an enemy into the air for a nice juggle combo and yes, his falling body can smack into other enemies. And that is about it for the most part. Like many games of the 8bit era, a lot of the combat comes down to learning a foe's pattern and then putting that knowledge to use. Many times enemies will be placed in ways to make you rethink your typical strategies and keep you on your toes. While we aren't talking about a super in-depth combat system I feel that it never wears out its welcome and is far better than it may seem at first glance.
That being said, the bulk of the gameplay is  definitely the spike-filled platforming. You will be using every trick up your sleave to make it through some of these death traps and later stages can be quite brutal. You will die and a few may frustrate you but I never once felt the game was unfair. When I died it was because I wasn't good enough to complete that section not because of something designed to fool you. These platforming segments are well designed and there are no surprises. It may ask a bit of your skill but you can leave your luck at home. The one complaint I'd levy at the game is found within these platforming sections but since it is consistant I can't really dock the game for it. Still, I felt I should mention it. Should your feet dip below the bottom of the screen you will die, regardless if a well timed double jump or dash could have saved you. This accounted for most of my deaths but again, it is designed this way and is consistant so once I got used to it it wasn't as big of an issue.
A smaller porttion of the gameplay is the adventuring segments. This generally involves entering buildings and recieving cryptic hints on where to head next. Get a hamburger bun so the restaurant can make a burger for you to give a guy who will trade you his key. It is really a minor diversion meant to break up the flow of the game and keep it feeling fresh. I love that nothing is spelled out for you but there is nothing really all that taxing here with few opportunities to actually get lost. It is within these sections that you can save your game. Simply enter the market and talk to the worker. You have three slots.
A quick snippet on the difficulty. As I said, it is tough but fair. I've heard complaints of checkpoints being too far apart but I don't find that to be the case. Each room is designed to be completed in one go and dying at any point in a room puts you at the start of that room. That there are infinite retries and it starts instantly upon death with no waiting period cuts back on any feelings of anger or tedium. Look at it like a run in one of the Trials games.  If you are the type to save state your way through emulated NES games though, the game may seem cruel. If you were used to gaming on the actual hardware back when it was current, well, you might find the infinite retries a bit easy. Either way, I stand by my assessment that the difficutly is high but fair.
The music is great and very relaxing. It suits the game well and compliments the action by offering a nice mellow atmosphere when you are risking death constantly. The look of the game is either amazing or putrid depending on your outlook. I love it. It really captures that 8bit feel  and the design is right up my alley. My only issue is that the spikes can somethimes blend into the background due to color choices.
Just want to touch on the controls for a second. I highly recommend using a 360 pad as I can't imagine some of these areas on a keyboard. The main menu strangely is controlled by the number keys on the keyboard. Once you get in-game you can perform everything else via the controller save for...saving... which is handled via the numbers as well. If you do not have a 360 controller you may want to avoid the game. I can't in good faith recommend it on a keyboard.
Overall, I had a great time with this title and will be buying the dev's other games right away. There is plenty of game here for an absurdly low price. If you have even an inkling that you would like this than I urge you to give it a shot. I've paid far more for far less...
